answer: The evidence provided does not state whether a GED certificate is an acceptable proof of identification. The documents mention that acceptable proofs of identity are listed in the DMV Document Guide and refer to points-based proof of identity, but none of the evidence lists a GED certificate as valid or invalid proof of identification.

Yes. Bills can help as proof of New York State residence: the DMV requires two different proofs of New York State residence, such as a utility bill, bank statement, or mortgage statement (P.O. Box not acceptable). Online bill printouts, such as a phone or electricity bill, can also serve as proof documents.

If you don't have your original U.S. birth certificate handy, the New York State Department of Health Vital Records office can help you obtain vital records in the state. Alternatively, you can order vital records online from New York and many other states through an independent partner, VitalChek Network Inc., at vitalchek.com. You may also already have more proof documents than you think, or be able to get some—for example, a bank debit card with your name preprinted on it (some banks issue one the same day you open an account) or online bill printouts such as a phone or electricity bill.

Paying customers must include a deposit with the application, and the first deposit must be enough to pay for two months of searches. When the application is accepted, the deposit is added to the new account balance, and search fees are subtracted from the account balance as searches are made. Payment by credit card is not available at this time.

You will know your application has been accepted because, after reviewing it, if it is complete the DMV will create an account for you and send you your account number and password. If your application is not complete, they will return it with an explanation and further instructions.

If you personally did not perform the search the DMV inquired about, check with the other users of your DIAL-IN account to see if one of them performed the search. If none of the known users performed the search, contact the DMV immediately.
If you performed the search on behalf of a client, you will need to show permissible use of your client and your client-agent relationship.

Yes. To register a vehicle in New York State, you must have New York State-issued automobile liability insurance coverage. If you do not maintain the coverage, the DMV can suspend your vehicle registration and your driver license. Out-of-state insurance coverage of any type is not accepted for a vehicle registered in New York.

To register a vehicle in New York, you need New York State auto liability insurance coverage. Your insurance company will issue proof of insurance in two ways: it will give you two original NY State Insurance ID Cards (or provide access to a digital electronic NY State Insurance ID Card), and it will send an electronic notice of insurance coverage to the DMV. When you go to the DMV office, bring one copy or form of your Insurance ID Card; the DMV office will keep the paper card, and you should keep the other paper card with the vehicle as your proof of insurance. Anyone operating your vehicle must be able to provide proof of insurance.

Yes. If you reside outside New York City and are exempt from the vehicle use tax in the county where you reside or have a business, you complete form UT-11C. If you reside in New York City and are exempt from the NYC vehicle use tax, you get form UT-11 from a local DMV office or a DMV Call Center. For questions about these taxes, ask the city or county where you reside or have a business.

To determine whether you must pay the vehicle use tax, read the table in the DMV's commercial vehicle registration fees, vehicle use taxes and supplemental fees information. Residents of New York City and several counties in New York must pay a vehicle use tax when they register a commercial vehicle or renew a commercial vehicle registration, and the DMV collects these taxes for the city and the counties. If you have questions about these taxes, ask the city or county where you reside or have a business. If you reside outside New York City and are exempt from the vehicle use tax in the county where you reside or have a business, complete form UT-11C; if you reside in New York City and are exempt from the NYC vehicle use tax, get form UT-11 from a local DMV office or a DMV Call Center.

If you qualify for a refund, the process depends on the type of refund. For a first-year registration fee refund, you must apply within 60 days of the registration issue date by sending a completed and signed Request for Refund (MV-215) form, the original registration document stub, and the unused registration sticker to the address on the MV-215 form; DMV will process the refund if you are eligible. For a full 2-year refund (registration never used, within 60 days), you must surrender the vehicle plates and the unused registration sticker and stub at a DMV office and request a 2-year refund; if eligible, the office issues a receipt showing "two year refund." More generally, when you surrender your vehicle plates you may be eligible for a refund, and if you are eligible and do not request a transfer receipt, DMV will process your refund automatically and you will receive it in the mail in several weeks.

The evidence does not specifically address whether you can get a refund when you already have plates with a longer expiration than the ones you are turning in. Generally, when you surrender vehicle plates to the DMV, you may be eligible to transfer the remaining registration credit to another vehicle you want to register, or get a refund for the registration fee. Whether you receive a refund depends on the circumstances; see the registration refunds information for surrendered plates. Note that transfer credit can only be used for a new original registration, not a registration renewal, and the new registration would expire the same day as your old registration.

Yes. If you changed your name, you can still get a refund. Surrender the vehicle plates at a DMV office and request a transfer receipt, not a refund receipt. Then send to the address on the Request for Refund MV-215 form: a completed and signed Request for Refund MV-215, documents proving the name change (a photocopy of the marriage certificate, divorce documents, or other court papers), and the transfer receipt. The DMV will issue your refund in your new name, if eligible.

Yes, you can renew a non-driver ID by mail in many cases. If you already have an Enhanced or REAL ID, or you want to keep your Standard ID, you can renew by mail, and your document type will stay the same. However, you cannot renew by mail if you have a REAL ID or Enhanced non-driver ID with a photo that is over 16 years old; you must come into an office to take a new picture. Also, if your Temporary Visitor status has been extended, you must go to a DMV office with updated paperwork. If you are overseas, you must renew through the mail. To renew by mail, complete the renewal notice sent to you and return it in the envelope provided with payment by check or money order payable to "Commissioner of Motor Vehicles"; if you did not receive a renewal notice, you can use the Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (MV-44).

To get proof of SSI, you can use one of the following documents: a Notice of Award notifying you that you are eligible for SSI benefits, a Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) letter, a Notice of change in payment, an SSA-L8151 Third Party Query (TPQY) letter, a Report of Confidential Social Security Information SSA-2258, or a Benefit Verification letter. For the Benefit Verification letter, you must call the Social Security Administration in advance at 1-800-772-1213 to obtain it. If you apply by mail, send a photocopy of your proof of SSI; if you come to a DMV office, bring an original copy of the proof.

The evidence does not state that the refund amount is different for everyone. It describes how a refund amount is determined using a specific example: if you paid $137.50 to register your vehicle for two years, including $62.50 for two years of registration ($31.25 per year), $50.00 for the title certificate, and $25.00 for the vehicle plates, and you surrender the plates during the first year, you qualify for a refund of $30.25. That refund is the $31.25 fee for the second year of registration minus a $1 processing fee, and there is no refund of other fees or taxes. The evidence also notes that your Receipt FS-6 T indicates whether you are eligible for a refund when you surrender your plates.

The evidence describes acceptable proofs of ownership by vehicle type but does not provide a complete list of the proofs needed to transfer a title to a New York State title. For cars, trucks, and motorcycles of model year 1973 or newer, the acceptable proof of ownership is either the original New York State Certificate of Title, or, if the state does not provide a title document because of a lien, an electronic title printout from the DMV; the transfer section must be notarized if the proof is a Certificate of Title from certain states. For model year 1972 or older vehicles, the acceptable proof is either an original or certified copy of a NY State Transferable Registration or acceptable proof from another state, and the owner can use the transferable registration and a bill of sale. Without proper proof of ownership, a New York State Certificate of Title will not be issued and registration may not be allowed. If the listed proofs are not available, contact a DMV Call Center or motor vehicle office before purchasing.
Yes. Enhanced driver licenses, permits, or non-driver IDs, and valid U.S. Passports are already REAL ID compliant and can be used to board a flight.

A restricted use license is issued by the DMV to a driver who qualifies and whose license is suspended or revoked because of violations or incidents that are not alcohol or drug-related, or because of some drug-related violations. You must apply for a conditional or restricted use license in person at a DMV office (available at most, but not all, offices). Drivers from other states who meet the other requirements can receive a restricted driving privilege to drive in NY State, with the same restrictions as for a NY State license holder.

To change your address and mailing information, you can update it online through your my Social Security account if you receive Social Security benefits (retirement, survivors, or disability) or are enrolled in Medicare. Log in to or create a free my Social Security account, select the My Profile link on the right side of the screen, select the Update Contact Information button and enter your address information, select when you would like to schedule the update, then select Next, and review and verify your information and select Submit. This online service is not currently available to people who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) or who do not have a U.S. mailing address; however, if you receive SSI, you can check the address on record via the My Profile tab on my Social Security.

You can ask that your replacement document be sent to an address different from the one on your document when you order by mail or at a DMV office. However, you cannot use a temporary address when you order online. The document will be mailed to the mailing address currently on DMV records or an alternate address you provide, and it takes about 10 days to arrive by mail.

The evidence does not directly state whether you must obtain a newer version of your ID when renewing with a name and address change. It indicates that after an address change is processed, links are provided to order replacement duplicate documents showing your new address, and that there are fees to order those replacement documents. It also notes that if you want to replace your documents by mail, you should include payment. Whether a replacement ID is required in your specific situation is not established by the provided evidence.

Yes. Because you need to change your name, you must go to a DMV office; the evidence says there is no need to come to a DMV office unless you need to change your name or want a new photo, and that to change your name or other non-address information you will need to go to a DMV office. You must visit your local DMV office and bring proof of the change, including a completed application for a legal name change. Regarding the temporary address, when you order by mail or at a DMV office you can ask that your replacement document be sent to an address different from the address on your document, but you cannot use a temporary address when ordering online.

The evidence does not describe what happens if an inspection tag cannot be used. The available evidence covers inspection requirements, expired inspections, extensions, and out-of-state inspections, but it does not address an inspection tag that cannot be used.
Mail the completed VS-118 Replacement Inspection Sticker/Label Request form to the address printed on the form.

If your local DMV office does not list the certification test, you must go to a different DMV office that offers the escort driver certification test. Not all DMV offices offer the test; if an office offers it, this is indicated in the "Office Hours" area for that office. You can call the DMV office where you plan to take the test to be sure the test is offered at that location. At the office, complete the Vehicle Escort Driver Application (MV-65) and take the written test; no appointment is needed.

Your DMV document does not expire on the Temporary Visitor expiration date, nor does your privilege to drive in New York. The expiration date from your DHS document is added to your New York State permit, driver license, or non-driver ID card, and the document will have 'TEMPORARY VISITOR' on it. If your temporary visitor status gets extended, you must bring updated DHS paperwork to a DMV office so records can be updated and your license renewed; your new license will have your new temporary visitor expiration date.

To take the escort driver certification test, you must complete the Vehicle Escort Driver Application (MV-65). If you have a NY State driver license, you must bring it with you to the DMV office. If your driver license was issued by another state, you must bring your valid driver license and additional identification; see the DMV Document Guide for acceptable additional identification.

The evidence does not explain how to pay for additional driving classes. It only describes how to pay for additional road tests after failing: you can pay online or by phone, and you must have a valid learner permit or driver license, provide your DMV ID Number from your Learner Permit Client ID Number and your date of birth, have no other road tests currently available, and pay the fee with a credit card.

If your learner permit expires before your next road test, you must get a new learner permit. You can still schedule another road test, but you must pay additional fees if you failed your first two road tests, and you will need to wait at least one day to take the test again.

To cancel your road test, you must cancel your appointment before you can search for a new date, and you cannot have more than one appointment at a time. You can schedule, cancel, or reschedule a road test online or by phone (1-518-402-2100). Note that tests can also be cancelled, rescheduled, or relocated by the DMV because of bad weather or road construction, so check the DMV cancellations, closings, and delays webpage or call before leaving for your test.

The evidence does not describe what happens if you plead guilty to a traffic ticket outside the five boroughs of New York City. It only says that in other parts of New York State, traffic violations are processed in the local criminal or traffic court where the offense occurred, and that you should contact that court directly to answer these types of tickets. For TVB tickets issued in New York City, you can plead guilty and pay, but that process does not apply to tickets outside the five boroughs.

To plead guilty, check the "guilty" box on the back of the ticket, fill in the requested information, and sign it. You can then either mail it with your payment to the Albany address listed on the ticket, or bring your payment to any TVB office. Payment may be made by Visa or Mastercard, or by a check or money order payable to the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles, and you should include the total fines and surcharges listed on the ticket for your violation. You may also plead guilty using the Traffic Ticket Pleas, Hearings and Payments online transaction. Note that you may not plead guilty by mail if the charge will result in license or registration suspension or revocation upon conviction, such as driving without insurance or a third speeding violation within 18 months; in that case you will be notified that you must go to the TVB to answer the charge in person.

To pay a TVB traffic ticket, you can answer most tickets online and pay the fine and surcharge with your credit card. You can also plead guilty by checking the "guilty" box on the back of the ticket, filling in the requested information, signing it, and either mailing it with your payment to the Albany address listed on the ticket or bringing your payment to any TVB office. Payment may be made by Visa or Mastercard, or by a check or money order payable to the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles, and you should include the total fines and surcharges listed on the ticket. Note that you may not plead guilty by mail if the charge would result in license or registration suspension or revocation upon conviction.

You can generally plead guilty by mail: enter your plea on the ticket, include the appropriate fee payable to the Commissioner of Motor Vehicles, and mail it to the Traffic Violations Plea Unit, P.O. Box 2950 - ESP, Albany, NY 12220-0950. However, you may not plead guilty by mail if the charge will result in license or registration suspension or revocation upon conviction, such as driving without insurance or a third speeding violation within 18 months; in that case you will be notified that you must go to the TVB to answer the charge in person.

To get a New York State driver license when you do not have a license from another state or country, you must pass a written test, complete a 5-hour pre-licensing course, and pass a road test. You should apply for a New York State driver license if you become a resident of New York State.

No. An Enhanced license is not required to change from a Class D to a Class E license. The change process uses the MV-44 application, and you only need to complete the document guide for a REAL ID or Enhanced if you want one; if you want a Standard license marked "NOT FOR FEDERAL PURPOSES," you can bring your current NY State license as proof of identity. An Enhanced or REAL ID is only needed to board a domestic flight (starting October 2020) unless you have a passport.

Yes. Under the problem driver restriction, approval for a driver license or permit with the restriction will be withdrawn if you are convicted of certain violations, and a cell phone or texting violation is expressly listed among them. This means a cell phone violation can affect your ability to obtain or retain the restricted license tied to your reinstatement.

If your revocation was not due to an alcohol-related incident, the problem driver restriction remains in effect for two years from the date you receive your driver license or permit, and it cannot be removed earlier.

To remove an ignition interlock restriction from your driver license, your ignition interlock monitor must give you a form stating that you are no longer required to install and maintain the ignition interlock device in motor vehicles you own or operate. You must take this form to a local DMV office and apply for a new document without the restriction. Note that an interlock restriction imposed by a court under Leandra's Law is removed by DMV under the orders of the court and is monitored by the court and designated monitors.

The evidence does not describe what would happen if you receive another ticket or violation before the interlock is removed. It only addresses related topics such as how the interlock restriction is imposed and removed, and consequences tied to accumulating traffic violations in the context of problem driver restrictions, but it does not state the specific outcome for a new ticket or violation while the interlock remains in place.

To remove a lienholder from your title certificate, you do not need to go to your local DMV; you can mail the required items. Send your original current title certificate (photocopies are not accepted), original proof that the lien was satisfied (photocopies are not accepted), and a check or money order for $20.00 payable to "Commissioner of Motor Vehicles" to: Lien Release, NYS DMV Title Services, 6 Empire State Plaza, Albany, NY 12228-0331. The DMV will mail your certificate of title that does not list the lien in 60 to 90 days; a DMV office cannot give you the title certificate. Acceptable proof that a lien is satisfied includes either a Notice of Recorded Lien MV-901 signed by an authorized officer of the lienholder indicating the lien is satisfied, or a letter from the lienholder on the loan company's official letterhead signed by an authorized officer that identifies the vehicle and indicates the lien is satisfied. If the lienholder is a person and not a loan company, the letter must be notarized. If your title certificate is lost, send an Application for a Duplicate Certificate of Title MV-902 and the original proof that the lien is satisfied to the address above or bring them to a DMV office; the fee is $20.00. Also note that if you sell a vehicle, you do not need to remove the lien from the certificate of title—you can give the original title and original lien release to the buyer.
Under the Graduated License Law, the restrictions apply to drivers under 18 years of age who have a junior learner permit or junior driver license Class DJ, MJ, or DJMJ.

To remove a lienholder from a title certificate, you do not need to go to your local DMV; you can mail the following items: original proof that the lien was satisfied (photocopies are not accepted), your current original title certificate (photocopies not accepted), and a check or money order for $20.00 payable to "Commissioner of Motor Vehicles," to Lien Release, NYS DMV Title Services, 6 Empire State Plaza, Albany, NY 12228-0331. The DMV will mail your certificate of title. The proof letter must be signed by an authorized officer, identify the vehicle, and indicate the lien is satisfied; if the lienholder is a person rather than a loan company, the letter must be notarized. If your title certificate is lost, send an Application for a Duplicate Certificate of Title (MV-902) and the original proof that the lien is satisfied to the address above or bring them to a DMV office; the fee is $20.00, and the DMV processes a duplicate title that does not list the lien. If your lienholder has an account with the DMV's Electronic Lien Transfer system (ELT), they can file to remove the lien electronically, but a new title will not be automatically sent to you—you will still need to send in your title, proof of satisfaction, and a fee, or apply for a duplicate title. If you are selling the vehicle, you do not need to remove the lien; you can give the original title and original lien release to the buyer.
If the inspection sticker is expired more than 60 days, the fine is between $50 and $100.
If the inspection sticker on your vehicle expired in the past 60 days, you can receive a fine of $25 to $50.

Yes. Trailer and boat registration fees are calculated differently from other vehicle registration fees, and the online service cannot be used to estimate them; instead, you must see the instructions for registering a trailer or a boat. For passenger and commercial vehicles, fees are determined using the registration fee and county use tax charts.

If you register your vehicle in another state, you must surrender your New York State vehicle plates (and registration) to the New York DMV. You should do this before your New York liability insurance coverage ends; if you do not turn in your plate, the DMV will suspend your registration and can suspend your driver license. Once you register in another state and surrender the New York plates to the New York DMV, you can get insurance in the other state, and that insurance must meet the requirements of the state where your vehicle is registered.

The proof should include a copy of your out-of-state registration in your name, along with a copy of your out-of-state insurance if available, sent to the NYS Department of Motor Vehicles Financial Security Bureau, PO BOX 2725, Albany NY 12220-0725. All proof must include the name and address of the registrant, and the year, make and vehicle identification number (VIN) of the vehicle.

If the sponsor cannot conduct the course or any part of the course, they must give you the option to receive a full refund of all course fees. The sponsor can also offer you the option to reschedule the course, if and when it is available. Note that if you fail the course by not meeting completion requirements or minimum test scores, you cannot receive credit or point and insurance reduction; a sponsor may offer to let you retake the same course at no additional cost, but is not required to do so.

To exchange an out-of-state license for a New York license, you must do so within 30 days of becoming a New York resident. Your out-of-state license must have your photograph, be valid or expired less than 24 months, and have been issued at least 6 months before you apply (unless it is a commercial driver license, which can have been valid for any amount of time). You cannot exchange a license that is suspended or revoked, lost or stolen, a hardship or employment-only license, or marked non-renewable or non-transferable. The transaction can only be processed in person at a DMV office. You will need to pass a vision test at the DMV or bring a completed Eye Test Report (MV-619), surrender your out-of-state license (unless lost or stolen), and bring proof of identity. You will receive a temporary non-photo license document, and your new license should arrive by mail in about 2 weeks. Your New York license will be valid for 5 years. If your out-of-state photo license does not show the issue date, get a certified driver license record or letter from the issuing state indicating the date of issue; if you cannot get one, you must apply for a new, original driver license. If your out-of-state license is suspended or revoked, you cannot apply for a NY license until you remove the suspension or revocation and bring a valid license meeting the requirements.

If the on-site investigation is approved, the automotive facilities inspector (AFI) will arrive to inspect your facility and will check that you have the required items. The evidence does not describe any further steps or outcomes beyond the inspection itself.

The starter kit components are: Book of Registry (Police Book), Bills of sale (Retail Certificate of Sale (MV-50)), Odometer Statements (except ATV and Boat Dealers), and Warranty Forms (except ATV and Boat Dealers). All forms must comply with current Regulations for Motor Vehicle Dealers and Transporters (CR-78).

To resolve a vehicle repair issue with the auto repair shop before filing a complaint, first attempt to resolve the issue with the management of the business. Keep a written record of all contacts with management in addition to details about the repair, and keep copies of work orders and invoices as proof of your attempts to resolve the problem. Many misunderstandings can be resolved through a calm, honest discussion. If a satisfactory resolution is not reached and you wish to file a complaint, you must submit a Vehicle Safety Complaint Report along with any supporting documents to the DMV Consumer & Facilities Services Complaint Unit.

The Repair Shop Act is the law under which the DMV handles auto repair shop complaints and violations. Under it, thousands of dollars are returned to consumers each year through mediation and restitution, and hundreds of vehicles are repaired at no additional cost. It also helps make highways safer by promoting quality auto repairs. It works best when consumers shop wisely for repairs, keep records of their dealings with shops, and discuss repairs with shop management to avoid misunderstandings. If a DMV investigation indicates a shop violated the Repair Shop Act or regulations, DMV will either send a warning letter or schedule a hearing.

Under the Graduated License Law, drivers under 18 with a junior learner permit or junior driver license (Class DJ, MJ, or DJMJ) face restrictions in addition to the learner permit restrictions that apply to everyone. The specific restrictions depend on whether you hold a junior learner permit or junior driver license and on where and when you drive in New York State; driving privileges vary by geographic region, including Upstate New York (defined as any county north of a certain point). If you do not comply with these restrictions, your junior learner permit or junior driver license could be suspended or revoked for 60 days. Separately, regardless of age, a learner permit holder may not drive unless accompanied by a supervising driver age 21 or older who has a valid license for the vehicle being driven, and may not drive on certain streets, bridges, tunnels, parkways, or in a DMV road test area. The evidence does not specify the full details of each regional restriction.

Yes. You can transfer the title certificate and give the new owner the original proof that any lien listed on the title certificate was satisfied, keeping a copy of the proof for your records. When the new owner applies for a registration and title certificate, the DMV receives the title certificate and the proof that the lien is satisfied, and when the DMV processes the new owner's title certificate, the lien is removed. If the new owner does not provide the original proof that the lien is satisfied, the lienholder is listed on the title certificate of the new owner.

If the lienholder has your title certificate, the common practice in many other states is that the lienholder keeps the title certificate until the lien is satisfied, then sends it to the owner. If your vehicle is registered in New York State and you receive the out-of-state title certificate from the lienholder, you should send that title certificate to the Title Services Bureau at the address shown. The DMV will then send you a NYS title certificate, and there is no fee because you already paid the title certificate fee when you registered your vehicle in New York.

If your son cannot maintain continuous auto insurance coverage, he must surrender his vehicle registration and plates to the DMV immediately — this should be done before his New York State coverage ends for any reason. If he does not turn in the plates, the DMV will suspend his registration and can suspend his driver license. A driver license becomes suspended when the lapse is 91 days or more, or if the lapse period has not yet been determined. The evidence does not address what happens if he is unable to get to the DMV during business hours; however, plates can be surrendered by mail, which may be an option given his scheduling constraints.

If your vehicle was registered in another state that issues an inspection sticker, you do not need to have your vehicle inspected immediately after registering in New York. Your out-of-state inspection remains valid until it expires or for one year after the registration date, whichever comes first. When your out-of-state inspection expires, you must get a New York State vehicle inspection. If the previous inspection was performed in a jurisdiction that does not issue an inspection sticker, you must have your vehicle inspected in New York.

If your vehicle was registered in another state that issues an inspection sticker, you do not need to have it inspected immediately. Your out-of-state inspection remains valid until it expires or for one year after the registration date, whichever comes first. When your out-of-state inspection expires, you must get a New York State vehicle inspection. If the previous inspection was performed in a jurisdiction that does not issue an inspection sticker, you must have your vehicle inspected in New York.

No, you do not need to have your vehicle inspected immediately. If your vehicle was registered in another state that issues an inspection sticker, your out-of-state inspection remains valid until it expires or for one year after the registration date, whichever comes first. When your out-of-state inspection expires, you must get a New York State vehicle inspection. (If the previous inspection was performed in a jurisdiction that does not issue an inspection sticker, you must have your vehicle inspected in New York.)

Yes. When the lienholder holds the title certificate, the DMV accepts other proof for registration: a certified photocopy of the out-of-state title certificate in your name, or written verification from the out-of-state motor vehicle title authority that you are the vehicle owner and that the authority sent the original title to the lienholder. If you have neither, the vehicle may still be registered if you present an out-of-state registration document issued in your name. Separately, for proving a lien is satisfied, there are two acceptable proofs: a Notice of Recorded Lien (MV-901) signed by an authorized officer of the lienholder indicating the lien is satisfied, or a letter from the lienholder on the loan company's official letterhead, signed by an authorized officer, identifying the vehicle and indicating the lien is satisfied.

The evidence does not provide a single general mailing address for the New York DMV. It lists several addresses for specific purposes: for an inspection extension, mail your name, current out-of-state mailing address, vehicle year and make, plate number, and inspection sticker number and expiration date to NYS DMV, Bureau of Consumer and Facility Services, Inspection Extension, P.O. Box 2700-ESP, Albany, NY 12220-0700. To change your address by mail, send a completed Address Change (MV-232) form to NYS DMV License Production Bureau, PO Box 2895, Albany, NY 12220-0895. Registration renewals by mail go to New York State Department of Motor Vehicles, Utica Processing Center, P.O. Box 359, Utica, NY 13503.

When you buy or get a vehicle from someone other than a dealer registered with the New York State DMV, you will receive an inspection extension that lasts 10 days from the date of the registration. An inspection issued to the previous registrant is not valid.

You can check your DMV record online using the service called "My License Status, Renewal and Replacement" and look under "License Status" to determine your self-certification driving type, medical certification status, and medical certificate expiration date. If you self-certified to driving types NI and NA, your medical certification status will show as either "Certified" or "Not Certified." Note that DMV enters this data daily, but due to volume it may take a period of time for a driver record to be fully updated.

If you are out of state when your inspection will expire, you can apply for an extension. First, determine whether an expired out-of-state inspection is a violation of law in that state, and ask the authorities whether a New York State inspection extension sticker prevents a ticket for the violation. The extension allows you 10 days from the date the vehicle returns to New York State to get an inspection, and you should allow 14 days for the DMV to process and mail your extension sticker, since you will need it before you return your vehicle to New York. To receive an extension, mail your name and current out-of-state mailing address, the year and make of your vehicle, the vehicle plate number, and the inspection sticker number and expiration date to NYS DMV, Bureau of Consumer and Facility Services, Inspection Extension, P.O. Box 2700-ESP, Albany, NY 12220-0700. When you receive your extension sticker, do not put it on your windshield while your vehicle is out of state; keep the sticker and instructions in your vehicle to show to an out-of-state police officer. The sticker is not a guarantee that a police officer will not issue you a traffic ticket, and there will be no record of an inspection on New York State DMV records. You cannot renew the registration if there is no DMV record of an inspection within the past 12 months; if you must renew before getting a New York State inspection, call 518-486-9786. After you return your vehicle to New York State, write the date the vehicle returned on the extension sticker and attach it to your windshield.
No. When you receive your extension sticker, there will be no record of an inspection on New York State DMV records.

If your inspection sticker came off, you can reattach it to the windshield with clear tape or a small amount of clear adhesive, but an inspection station must still be able to remove it during your next inspection. If the sticker is not usable, you can either have your vehicle re-inspected or order a replacement sticker using the form Request for Replacement Inspection Sticker (VS-118); complete the form and mail it to the address on the form.

If you are out of state (such as in Florida) when your New York inspection will expire, you can apply for an extension. First, determine whether an expired out-of-state inspection is a violation of law in that state, and ask the authorities whether a New York State inspection extension sticker prevents a ticket for the violation. To receive an extension, mail the following information: your name and current out-of-state mailing address, the year and make of your vehicle, the vehicle plate number, and the inspection sticker number and expiration date, to: NYS DMV, Bureau of Consumer and Facility Services, Inspection Extension, P.O. Box 2700-ESP, Albany, NY 12220-0700. Allow 14 days for the DMV to process and mail your extension sticker, since you will need it before returning your vehicle to New York. The extension allows you 10 days from the date the vehicle returns to New York State to get an inspection. When you receive your extension sticker, do not put it on your windshield while your vehicle is out of state; keep the sticker and instructions in your vehicle to show to an out-of-state police officer. Note that the sticker is not a guarantee that a police officer will not issue you a traffic ticket, and there will be no record of an inspection on New York State DMV records. After you return your vehicle to New York State, write the date the vehicle returned to New York on the extension sticker, attach the sticker to your windshield, and get your vehicle inspected within 10 days.

Yes. A GED certificate can be used — if you received one at a community college, you can contact the college for a certified copy. U.S. college transcripts can also be used; you can order them from a college or university you attended, even if you did not graduate there, though you will need a photo ID from the college. Note that the evidence does not specifically confirm these documents as proof of residence for a DMV extension application; it lists them among documents for finding enough proof of ID.

To order personalized plates by mail, use the Application for Custom Plates PDF (form CP-30). Mail the completed form and your payment to: NYS DMV Custom Plates Unit, P.O. Box 2775, Albany, NY 12220. Note that some picture or professional plates can't be purchased by mail. Also, you can't order personalized plates before your vehicle is registered, when renewing your registration, or before transferring a registration; you must have a registration windshield sticker, receipt, and regular series plates issued by DMV before ordering. If your registration expires within the next 60 days, renew it before ordering, and change your address online before ordering if needed.

If you do not have one of the specific identity documents (such as a U.S. driver's license, state-issued non-driver identification card, or U.S. passport), or you cannot get a replacement for one of them within 10 days, Social Security will ask to see other documents. Any documents submitted must be current (not expired) and show your name, identifying information (date of birth or age), and preferably a recent photograph; examples include an employee identification card or school identification card. The evidence addresses proof of identity but does not specifically address documents proving a relationship.

If you no longer have your original U.S. birth certificate or marriage record, the New York State Department of Health Vital Records office can help you obtain vital records in the state. Alternatively, you can order vital records online from New York and many other states through an independent partner, VitalChek Network Inc., at vitalchek.com. You may also already have more proof documents than you think, or be able to get other proof documents—for example, a bank debit card with your name preprinted on it (some banks issue one the same day you open an account) or online bill printouts such as a paperless phone or electricity bill.

An insurance lapse can be caused by any amount of time that your vehicle is registered but not insured. It can occur between the date your insurance is cancelled and the date your new insurance begins, or between the date you register your vehicle and the date your new insurance coverage begins.

The evidence does not say that you should go to a DMV office in response to a suspension letter. It says that if you received a letter stating your license is suspended, the letter means your insurance company notified the DMV that your coverage ended and no other company reported new coverage. If you have insurance, follow the instructions in the letter and contact your company or agent about the problem, asking the company to file a notice of coverage with the DMV electronically. If you do not have insurance, you need to surrender your vehicle registration and plates to the DMV immediately. More generally, you should read the letter or order carefully, answer it quickly, and contact your insurance company immediately, since resolving the problem is your responsibility. The evidence mentions that Form FS-2 is available only at a local DMV Office and that the local DMV Office determines whether an application is accepted or rejected, but it does not state that you should visit a DMV office for a suspension letter.

Yes. When registering your vehicle at the DMV, you should bring one copy or form of your Insurance ID Card. The DMV office will keep the paper card, and you should keep the other paper card with the vehicle as proof of insurance. Your insurance company provides 2 barcoded original NY State Insurance ID cards or access to a digital electronic NY State Insurance ID Card, and the cards plus the electronic notice of insurance coverage together verify your coverage—both are needed.

If your license is suspended for an insurance lapse, you can provide proof that you now have insurance online or by mail; the DMV will then verify your coverage with your insurance company, and you can check your insurance status online. You can also ask your insurance company to file a notice of coverage with the DMV electronically. If your registration has not expired, you must surrender your plates. If you don't have insurance, you need to surrender your vehicle registration and plates to the DMV immediately. The driver license suspension will not end until you have paid the suspension termination fee and have served the suspension.

While the insurance problem is being resolved, keep the plates rather than using the vehicle if your insurance coverage is cancelled, even if you think it is a mistake. If you do not have insurance, you need to surrender your vehicle registration and plates to the DMV immediately. You can get your registration and new plates when the problem is corrected.

The letter means your insurance company notified the DMV that your coverage ended and no other company reported new coverage. If you have insurance, follow the instructions in the letter and contact your company or agent about the problem, and ask your company to file a notice of coverage with the DMV electronically. If you don't have insurance, you need to surrender your vehicle registration and plates to the DMV immediately. More generally, read the letter or order carefully, answer it quickly, and contact your insurance company immediately; resolving the problem is your responsibility, and if you don't, the DMV can suspend your vehicle registration and driver license. Do not use your vehicle if your insurance coverage is cancelled, even if you think it is a mistake, and keep the plates while you resolve the problem with your insurance company. You can also provide proof that you now have insurance online or by mail, after which the DMV will verify your coverage with your insurance company.

An insurance lapse in New York State means there is no liability insurance coverage for a vehicle registered in New York State for a period of time. If there is a lapse of insurance for a vehicle registered to you, the DMV can suspend your registration and driver license. Any amount of time that your vehicle is registered but not insured can cause a lapse in coverage.

If your insurance is cancelled, reinstated, or you get new insurance, your insurance company must notify the DMV electronically. If you receive a DMV letter, you must respond by either proving you have insurance coverage, proving you sold the vehicle, or proving insurance coverage was not required. If you have insurance coverage, also ask your insurance company to file the coverage notice with the DMV.

To avoid a lapse in auto insurance coverage while keeping your DMV registration and driver license current: remember the rule 'no insurance, no plates'; keep the address for your vehicle registration and driver license current with the DMV; have liability coverage from a company licensed by the NYS Department of Financial Services and authorized by the NYS DMV (out-of-state coverage is never acceptable on a vehicle registered in New York); have your insurance company report any changes to the DMV immediately; and turn in your vehicle's license plates at the DMV before you cancel your insurance policy. Also, if you have insurance coverage, do not ask your agent or broker to file an electronic notice of insurance coverage with the DMV.

The evidence does not describe what happens in an accident while you are uninsured. It only addresses the consequences of not maintaining coverage: if you do not maintain auto liability insurance, the DMV can suspend your vehicle registration and your driver license, and if you lack valid coverage you must immediately surrender your registration and vehicle plates. It also notes that it is illegal to operate a motorcycle without proper auto liability insurance. No information is provided about liability, penalties, or other outcomes specifically arising from an accident while uninsured.

The letter means your insurance company notified the DMV that your coverage ended and no other company reported new coverage. If you have insurance, follow the instructions in the letter and contact your insurance company or agent about the problem, and ask your company to file an electronic notice of insurance coverage with the DMV (do not ask your agent or broker to file it). If you do not have liability insurance, you must surrender your vehicle plates and registration to the DMV immediately. You can also provide proof of insurance online or by mail, after which the DMV will verify coverage with your insurance company, and you can check your insurance status online.

If you do not have valid auto liability insurance coverage for your vehicle, you must immediately surrender your registration and vehicle plates to the DMV. The rule is simple: no insurance, no plates. If you do not maintain the required coverage, the DMV can suspend your vehicle registration and your driver license. If you are suspended, you must either surrender your plates to the DMV or, if eligible, pay the optional civil penalty for the entire length of the lapse. Note that motorcycle plates do not have to be surrendered when auto liability insurance lapses, but it is illegal to operate a motorcycle without proper auto liability insurance.

To get a REAL ID from the New York State DMV, you must go to a DMV office in person; you cannot get one online, by phone, or through the mail. You must bring original or certified proof documents to the office, including proof of identity (such as a valid license, birth certificate, or passport) with your full first, middle if applicable, and last name, and proof of your Social Security Number or Social Security Number ineligibility.

To get a New York State REAL ID, you must go to a DMV office in person; it cannot be obtained online, by phone, or by mail. You must bring original or certified proof documents, including proof of identity (such as a valid license, birth certificate, or passport) with your full name, proof of Social Security Number or ineligibility, proof of U.S. citizenship, lawful permanent residency, or temporary lawful status, and two different proofs of New York State residence (such as a utility bill, bank statement, or mortgage statement; P.O. Box not acceptable). The application process also requires the DMV to take a new photo. Regarding school in New York, the evidence states that students from other states or from other nations who attend school in New York State are normally not considered New York State residents, but it does not specify what ID is needed for going to school in New York.

The evidence does not specify a fee for "augmenting" a driver's license. The closest related fees are: $12.50 to change/amend information on a driver license or learner permit, and an additional $30.00 fee for an Enhanced Driver License (EDL) or Enhanced Permit.

Yes. A valid U.S. Passport is already REAL ID compliant and can be used to board a flight. It can also be used for identification, boarding a plane for domestic and international flights, and entry into a federal building or military base. Even if you have a Standard driver's license or ID, you can still board a domestic flight if you have a Passport.

The evidence is internally inconsistent: one passage states that getting a REAL ID is mandatory but is encouraged, while the next passage states that a REAL ID is optional and not needed for activities such as being licensed to drive, voting or registering to vote, entering federal facilities that do not require identification, applying for or receiving federal benefits, accessing health or life-preserving services, or participating in law enforcement proceedings. The evidence also notes that beginning October 1, 2020, a REAL ID-compliant license, permit, or ID card is required to board a domestic flight within the U.S. or enter military bases and certain federal facilities, and that a valid U.S. Passport is already REAL ID compliant and can be used to board a flight.
No. You cannot get a REAL ID online, by phone, or through mail. You need to go to a DMV Office to get a REAL ID.

The evidence identifies three types of ID documents: standard licenses and IDs, REAL IDs, and Enhanced licenses and IDs. Non-citizens are eligible for standard IDs and REAL IDs, but only US Citizens are eligible for Enhanced IDs. Enhanced driver licenses, permits, or non-driver IDs are already REAL ID compliant and can be used to board a flight, as can a valid U.S. Passport. A Standard license will not be allowed to board a domestic flight starting in October 2020 unless you have a Passport. There is no additional cost to get a REAL ID, while applying for an Enhanced Driver License or Enhanced ID Card carries an additional $30 fee. The evidence references a sample of Enhanced, REAL ID, and Standard License but does not describe the visual differences among them.

If the name on your license, permit, or non-driver ID application does not match the name on your identity, lawful status, and Social Security proofs, you must bring court- or government-issued proof documenting the event that caused your name change, such as a marriage license, divorce decree, adoption, or court order document.

No, obtaining a REAL ID is not mandatory. The evidence states that a REAL ID is optional and is not needed for things such as being licensed to drive, voting or registering to vote, entering federal facilities that do not require identification, applying for or receiving federal benefits, accessing health or life-preserving services, or participating in law enforcement proceedings. However, beginning October 1, 2020, the federal government requires a REAL ID-compliant driver's license, permit, or ID card if you wish to use it as identification to board a domestic flight within the U.S. or enter military bases and certain federal facilities. A valid U.S. Passport is already REAL ID compliant and can be used to board a flight.

Yes. The DMV can issue a restricted use license to a driver who qualifies and whose license is suspended or revoked because of violations or incidents that are not alcohol or drug related, or because of some drug-related violations. You must apply for a conditional or restricted use license in person at a DMV office, and this can be done at most, but not all, Motor Vehicles offices.

The evidence covers several points but does not fully answer what additional information is needed. On REAL ID: the New York State DMV began issuing REAL ID licenses, permits, and ID cards on October 30, 2017; you can get a REAL ID at any time but must go to a DMV office (not online, by phone, or by mail); and you must bring original or certified proof documents, including proof of identity such as a valid license, birth certificate, or passport with your full first, middle if applicable, and last name, plus proof of Social Security Number or Social Security Number ineligibility. On conditional and restricted use licenses: you must apply in person at a DMV office, which you can do at most but not all offices, so you should contact your nearest office to find out where you can apply. The DMV can issue a conditional license to a qualified driver whose NY State license was suspended or revoked because of an alcohol or drug-related violation, and the driver must attend an Impaired Driver Program (IDP), previously known as the Drinking Driving Program (DDP), approved by the DMV. The DMV can issue a restricted use license to a driver who qualifies and whose license is suspended or revoked because of violations or incidents that are not alcohol or drug-related, or because of some drug-related violations. Drivers from other states who meet the other requirements can receive a conditional or restricted driving privilege to drive in NY State, with the same conditions or restrictions as for a NY State driver license.

No. A REAL ID is optional and is not needed for being licensed to drive or for voting or registering to vote. It is also not needed for entering federal facilities that do not require a person to present identification, applying for or receiving federal benefits, or accessing health or life-preserving services. A REAL ID (or an Enhanced ID, which is already REAL ID compliant) is what you would need if you want to use your license or ID as identification to board a domestic flight within the U.S. or to enter military bases and certain federal facilities.

The evidence does not establish that it is currently required by law to have a REAL ID. It states that beginning October 1, 2020, the federal government will require a driver license, permit, or ID card to be REAL ID compliant if you wish to use it as identification to board a domestic flight within the U.S., or to enter military bases and certain federal facilities. It also notes that a valid U.S. Passport is already REAL ID compliant and can be used to board a flight, and that if you do not want a REAL ID or Enhanced document, any license, permit, or ID card issued after October 30, 2017 will be marked 'Not for Federal Purposes.'

If you have a Class DJ or MJ learner permit, you must have a minimum of 50 hours of supervised practice driving, including at least 15 hours of driving after sunset, before you take a road test. You must also bring a completed Certification of Supervised Driving (MV-262) signed by your parent or guardian.

Students from other states who attend school in New York State are normally not considered New York State residents, so you do not need to exchange your current out-of-state driver license. Normally you cannot hold a New York State driver license and a driver license from another state at the same time, though there are exceptions (holding more than one commercial driver license is a violation of Federal law). The evidence does not address REAL ID requirements for someone in your situation.

The evidence does not describe REAL ID requirements for someone studying in New York with an out-of-state license. It does state that students from other states who attend school in New York are normally not considered New York State residents, so they do not need to exchange their current driver license, and you can drive in New York with a valid driver license from another state. Normally you cannot hold both a NY State driver license and a driver license from another state at the same time, though there are exceptions. The only REAL ID-related detail provided is that if you have a Standard document and want to change to a REAL ID or Enhanced document, you must come into a DMV office.

No. You cannot get a REAL ID by mail. You can get a REAL ID at any time, but you will need to go to a DMV Office, and you cannot get a REAL ID online, by phone, or through mail. You must bring your original or certified proof documents to the office.

You must carry your Driving School Instructor Certificate (MV-524) whenever you are teaching and whenever you take a customer to a DMV Road Test Site. If a customer or DMV employee asks to see the certificate, you must be able to present it.

After you pass your road test, the examiner will give you an interim license that allows you to drive. You should keep the interim license with your photo learner permit until your new license arrives in the mail in about 2 weeks.

Drivers from other countries can drive in New York State with a valid driver license from their home country and do not need to apply for a New York State driver license unless they become New York State residents. If they choose to get a New York State driver license, they must pass a written test, complete a 5-hour pre-licensing course, and pass a road test. When they pass the road test, they must give their foreign driver license to the DMV road test examiner, and the local DMV office will destroy it after 60 days; those planning to return home and needing their foreign license should ask the road test examiner how to make sure it is not destroyed. An International Driving Permit is not required but is helpful, since it verifies in several languages that the holder has a valid driver license; it can be obtained from authorities in the home country. Students from other countries attending school in New York State are normally not considered residents, so they do not need to exchange their current driver license.

Yes. Only New York State residents need a New York State driver license. You can drive in New York State with a valid driver license from another country, and you do not need to apply for a New York State driver license unless you become a New York State resident.

Drivers from other countries can drive in New York State with a valid driver license from their home country; they do not need a New York State driver license unless they become New York State residents. Only New York State residents need a New York State driver license. If a driver from another country chooses to get a New York State driver license, they must pass a written test, complete a 5-hour pre-licensing course, and pass a road test. When they pass the road test, they must give their foreign driver license to the DMV road test examiner, and the local DMV office will destroy the foreign license after 60 days; if they plan to return home and will need the foreign license, they should ask the road test examiner how to make sure it is not destroyed. An International Driving Permit is not required for driving with a foreign license, but it is helpful because it verifies in several languages that the driver has a valid license, and it can be obtained from authorities in the home country. If the license was issued outside the U.S. or Canada, the driver must apply for a new original New York State driver license at a DMV office. Students from other countries attending school in New York State are normally not considered New York State residents, so they do not need to exchange their current driver license.

Yes. A valid foreign driver's license allows you to drive without a supervising driver, on any street, road, highway, bridge, or tunnel except in a DMV road test area. If your license is printed in a language other than English, you must bring an International Driving Permit or a certified translation of your driver's license to the road test; the translation must be certified by a consulate, the US Department of State, or another official agency and must include your name, date of birth, expiration date of your foreign license, and the types of vehicles it allows you to drive. A supervising driver is only required if you have a NY State learner permit and do not have a valid foreign driver's license.

Drivers from other countries can drive in New York State with a valid driver license from their home country. You do not need to apply for a New York State driver license unless you become a New York State resident. Only New York State residents need New York State driver licenses. If you do choose to get a New York State driver license, you must pass a written test, complete a 5-hour pre-licensing course, and pass a road test. When you pass your road test, you must give your foreign driver license to the DMV road test examiner, and the local DMV office will destroy your foreign driver license after 60 days; if you plan to return to your home country and will need your foreign license, ask the road test examiner how to make sure it is not destroyed. An International Driving Permit is not required but is helpful, as it verifies in several languages that you have a valid driver license; contact the authorities in your home country to get one. Students from other states, countries, or nations who attend school in New York State are normally not considered residents, so they don't need to exchange their current driver license.

If you are not a New York State resident and do not want a New York driver's license, permit, or non-driver ID card, you can drive in New York State with a valid driver license from another country. You do not need to apply for a New York State driver license unless you become a New York State resident. An International Driving Permit is not required, but it is helpful because it verifies in several languages that you have a valid driver license, which helps police officers who cannot read the language on your foreign license; contact the authorities in your home country to get one. Students from other countries who attend school in New York State are normally not considered New York State residents, so they don't need to exchange their current driver license.

No. If you have a valid foreign (Mexican) driver license along with your NY State learner permit, your valid foreign driver license allows you to drive without a supervising driver. You can drive on any street, road, highway, bridge, or tunnel, except in a DMV road test area. A supervising driver is only required if you have a NY State learner permit and do not have a valid foreign driver license; in that case the supervising driver must be age 21 or over and have a valid license to operate the vehicle you drive.

The evidence does not directly address what happens if your foreign driver license is expired. It states that a valid foreign driver license allows you to drive without a supervising driver, and that if you have a NY State learner permit but do not have a valid foreign driver license, NY State law requires a supervising driver age 21 or over with a valid license to ride with you. So an expired license would not qualify as valid, meaning you would need a supervising driver. However, the evidence does not explicitly confirm the effect of an expired license.

Yes. If you have a valid foreign driver license and a NY State learner permit, your valid foreign driver license allows you to drive without a supervising driver (you may drive on any street, road, highway, bridge, or tunnel, except in a DMV road test area). A supervising driver is required only if you have a NY State learner permit and do not have a valid foreign driver license; that supervising driver must be age 21 or over and have a valid driver license to operate the vehicle you drive. As for renewal, as long as the Temporary Visitor status that DMV has on file is not expired, you can renew your license online, through the mail, or in an office.

If your temporary visitor status has been extended, you must bring to a DMV office a completed Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (form MV-44), your updated paperwork from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), and documents that are valid, current and verifiable showing 6 points of identification. You can also go to a DMV office with your updated DHS paperwork so DMV can update its records to show that your Temporary Visitor status has been extended, allowing you to renew your license; your new license will have your new temporary visitor expiration date.

Yes. You do not need to be a US citizen to get a New York driver license, permit, or non-driver ID card. However, if you are not a US citizen, you must have US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) documentation that supports your legal status in this country, and the expiration date from your DHS document is added to your New York State permit, driver license, or non-driver ID card. Non-citizens are eligible for standard IDs and Real IDs, but only US citizens are eligible for Enhanced IDs.

No. If you have a NY State learner permit and do not have a valid foreign driver license, NY State law requires a supervising driver to ride with you. The supervising driver must be age 21 or over and must have a valid driver license to operate the vehicle you drive.

A Temporary Visitor is defined as anyone who is not immigrating to or not residing (living) in the United States. These visitors have US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) documentation that supports their legal status in this country. If you have DHS documents that identify you as a Temporary Visitor, your New York State driver license, permit, or non-driver ID card will have 'TEMPORARY VISITOR' on it, along with the expiration date from your DHS document.

A Snowmobile Club voucher ID is the ID number included on the voucher received by members of a New York State Snowmobile Association (NYSSA) snowmobile club. The ID number is located in the top right corner of the voucher, above the barcode. If you have a current NYSSA voucher, you enter the voucher ID number in the box provided; if you do not have a current voucher, you skip the voucher ID number section. Having a current, valid NYSSA voucher reduces the snowmobile registration fee to $45.00, compared with $100 without one.

If you are not a member of a NYSSA snowmobile club, you do not have a Snowmobile Club voucher ID. A voucher with an ID number is provided to members of a NYSSA snowmobile club, and the ID number is located in the top right corner of the voucher above the barcode. If you do not have a current voucher, you should skip the voucher ID number section. Without a NYSSA voucher, the registration fee is $100 rather than $45.

A NYSSA (New York State Snowmobile Association) Snowmobile Club voucher ID number is an ID number included on a voucher that members of a NYSSA snowmobile club receive. The ID number is located in the top right corner of the voucher, above the barcode. If you have a current NYSSA voucher, you enter the voucher ID number in the box provided; if you do not have a current voucher, you skip the voucher ID number section. Having a current, valid NYSSA voucher also reduces the snowmobile registration fee to $45.00, compared with $100 without a voucher.

A NYSSA (New York State Snowmobile Association) Snowmobile Club voucher ID number is the ID number included on the voucher you receive if you are a member of a NYSSA snowmobile club. The ID number is located in the top right corner of your voucher, above the barcode. If you have a current NYSSA voucher, you enter the voucher ID number in the box provided; if you do not have a current voucher, you skip the voucher ID number section. A current, valid NYSSA voucher also affects the registration fee: with a valid NYSSA voucher the fee is $45.00, while without one the fee is $100.

If your vehicle plates are lost, stolen, or destroyed, you must surrender the vehicle registration to the DMV. If two plates are lost, stolen, or destroyed (or one plate if the vehicle was issued only one plate, such as motorcycles), you need to notify the police and ask them to complete a police report, then bring the police report to a DMV office to surrender the registration. If the plates were lost, stolen, or destroyed in New York State, ask a NY State police agency to complete a 'Certification of Lost License, Permit or Plates' MV-78B, which is only available from law enforcement. If the incident happened outside NY State, get a report printed on the letterhead of a police agency in the state where it happened. If you cannot get a police report, write a statement that includes your plate number and explains why you cannot surrender your NY State plates. If only one plate from a set of two is lost, stolen, or destroyed, you don't need a police report; bring the plate you have to a DMV office to surrender the registration. However, to replace your plates without paying a fee, you must submit a police report or an MV-78B indicating the plate was stolen or destroyed as a result of a crime. You may request a new set of plates at a DMV office.

If you received a Notice of Registration Suspension, you have the right to a hearing before the DMV, and requesting it places the suspension on hold pending the outcome. As the Notice indicates, you may request either an in-person DMV hearing or a hearing by affidavit (a hearing on paper); the Notice provides instructions for submitting the affidavit to DMV, and if you submit it you need not appear. At an in-person hearing you may be represented by an attorney. If you request a hearing and neither appear nor submit your affidavit, your registration will be suspended immediately. Note that at the hearing you may not dispute whether you evaded a toll or failed to pay tolls, fees, or other charges; those issues must be raised with the tolling authority outside the hearing. Alternatively, if you pay all tolls, fees, or other charges owed to the tolling authority, or have them dismissed or transferred, the suspension will not take effect.

If you don't have enough proof of name identification for the DMV, you may already have more proof documents than you think, or you may be able to get some. Suggestions include a bank debit card with your name preprinted on it (some banks issue a card the same day you open an account) and online bill printouts, such as a paperless phone or electricity bill you can print out. If the name on your application doesn't match your identity, lawful status, and social security proofs, you must bring court- or government-issued proof documenting the name change, such as a marriage license, divorce decree, adoption, or court order document.

Yes. A high school diploma or GED can be used as proof of identification, and if you attended a community college you may have received a General Educational Development (GED) certificate, in which case you can contact the college for a certified copy. You can also contact the education department in the state where you graduated for a certified copy.

To exchange your NY State driver license for a non-driver ID card, you can apply by mail or at a DMV office; you cannot apply online. Mail a completed Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (MV-44) with a photocopy of acceptable proof of identity (do not mail your original document) and the required payment to the DMV License Production Bureau, P.O. Box 2688 ESP, Albany, NY 12220-0668, or use an express mail service to DMV License Production Bureau, Room 424A, 6 Empire State Plaza, Albany, NY 12228. To pay a reduced fee or 'No Fee' price based on SSI, you must provide proof of your eligibility for Supplemental Security Income, such as a Notice of Award, Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) letter, Notice of change in payment, SSA-L8151 Third Party Query (TPQY) letter, Report of Confidential Social Security Information SSA-2258, or Benefit Verification letter (call the Social Security Administration in advance at 1-800-772-1213 to obtain this letter). Proof of Supplemental Security Income (SSI) is used to show that you receive SSI benefits. To prove you receive SSI at the DMV, you must bring one of the following original documents (not a photocopy): a Notice of Award notifying you that you are eligible for SSI benefits, a Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) letter, a Notice of change in payment, an SSA-L8151 Third Party Query (TPQY) letter, a Report of Confidential Social Security Information SSA-2258, or a Benefit Verification letter (you must call the SSA in advance at 1-800-772-1213 to obtain this letter). At a DMV office you bring your proof of SSI; by mail you send a copy of your proof of SSI. A Social Security benefit verification letter serves as proof of your SSI benefits and may also be used for loans, housing assistance, mortgage, and other income verification purposes.

To prove you receive SSI, you must bring one of the listed documents to the DMV, and the document must be the original, not a photocopy. Acceptable documents include a Notice of Award notifying you that you are eligible for SSI benefits, a Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) letter, a Notice of change in payment, an SSA-L8151, a Third Party Query (TPQY) letter, a Report of Confidential Social Security Information (SSA-2258), or a Benefit Verification letter (you must call the SSA in advance at 1-800-772-1213 to obtain this letter). At a DMV office, bring proof of SSI; by mail, send a copy of your proof of SSI. Do not mail your original document. The SSI program itself pays benefits to disabled adults and children who have limited income and resources, and benefits are also payable to people 65 and older without disabilities who meet the financial limits.

To prove you receive SSI, you can get a Social Security Benefit Verification Letter, which serves as proof of your Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits. To apply for escort vehicle driver certification, go to a DMV office that offers the escort driver certification test, complete the Vehicle Escort Driver Application (MV-65), and take the written test. A suspension means your driver license or privilege to drive is taken away for a period of time. The suspension can be definite (with a beginning and end date) or indefinite (it does not end until you take a required action). You may need to pay a suspension termination fee, and it is illegal to drive while your license or driving privilege is suspended or revoked. DMV will send a notice called an order to the address on file, and you should follow its instructions. Common reasons for a definite suspension include not having automobile liability insurance, being convicted of an alcohol or drugged driving charge, receiving too many traffic tickets in a certain amount of time, or not following the rules for junior drivers. A suspension for failing to answer a ticket does not indicate you are guilty of the charge; it only indicates you failed to answer the ticket.

If you need to cancel your road test appointment, you can cancel it online or by phone using the DMV Road Test Scheduling System. To reschedule, you must cancel your appointment before you can search for a new date, and you cannot have more than one appointment at a time. Note that tests can also be cancelled, rescheduled, or relocated by the DMV due to bad weather or road construction, so before leaving for your test you should check the DMV cancellations, closings and delays webpage or call 1-518-402-2100. Also, if you are late, the license examiner may need to reschedule your test.
