If your vehicle plates were stolen, you should notify the police and ask them to complete a police report. In New York State, ask a NY State police agency to complete a 'Certification of Lost License, Permit or Plates' form MV-78B (available only from law enforcement). Make a copy of the MV-78B report for your records and bring the original form to a DMV office to surrender your vehicle registration. If the plates were stolen outside of NY State, get a report printed on the letterhead of a police agency in the state where the incident occurred. If the plates are missing, bring your copy of form MV-78B to a DMV office and apply for new plates and reinstatement of your registration.

If your plates are lost, stolen, or destroyed, you must notify the police and ask them to complete a police report. If the plates were lost, stolen, or destroyed in New York State, ask a New York State police agency to complete a 'Certification of Lost License, Permit or Plates' (MV-78B), which is available only from law enforcement. If the incident happened outside New York State, get a report printed on the letterhead of a police agency in the state where the incident occurred. Then bring the police report to a DMV office to surrender the vehicle registration.

You can request a new set of plates at a DMV office. Bring the original plate or the MV-78B/police report/statement, a completed Vehicle Registration/Title Application (MV-82), proof of insurance, and proof of your identity; the DMV will then issue you a new registration and replacement plates. If a plate is lost or destroyed, you must report it and surrender the vehicle registration to the DMV, and the DMV can issue you a new registration and plates. If two plates are lost, stolen, or destroyed (or one plate if the vehicle was issued only one plate, such as a motorcycle), you need to notify the police and ask them to complete a police report, then bring the police report to a DMV office to surrender the registration. If the plates were lost, stolen, or destroyed in New York State, ask a NY State police agency to complete a Certification of Lost License, Permit or Plates (MV-78B); if this happened outside NY State, get a report on the letterhead of a police agency in the state where the incident happened, or if you cannot get a police report, write a statement including your plate number and explaining why you cannot surrender your NY State plates. If one plate from a set of two is lost, stolen, or destroyed, you don't need to complete a police report; bring the plate you have to a DMV office to surrender the registration. If the plate was lost or destroyed, you will need to pay for the new plates and a $3.75 fee to issue a new registration; plates cost $25 for a set of 2 plates or $12.50 for a vehicle issued only one plate (e.g., motorcycles). You don't need to pay a fee to replace stolen plates, but you must provide a police report or an MV-78B indicating the plates were stolen or destroyed as a result of a crime.

Your insurance company will issue proof of insurance in two ways: it will give you two original NY State Insurance ID Cards (or provide access to your digital electronic NY State Insurance ID Card), and it will send an electronic notice of insurance coverage to the DMV (your insurance agent or broker cannot file this notice). Anyone operating your vehicle must be able to provide proof of insurance.

The evidence does not describe a general procedure for obtaining a driver's license if you do not currently have one. To apply for a learner permit, you must be 16 or older and apply in person at a DMV office. Prepare for the written permit test by studying the NY State Driver's Manual and taking practice tests; for the Class D and M permit tests, you must get at least 14 of the 20 multiple-choice questions correct, including correct answers to at least two of the four road-sign questions. Getting a permit is the first step to getting your driver license. Before you can get a license, you must apply for a learner permit at a DMV office and take the written test. After you have a learner permit, you must have supervised driving practice and take a pre-licensing course or driver education course before your road test. Then take and pass your road test before your permit expires; if you pass, the examiner will give you an interim license that allows you to drive, and you should keep the interim license with your photo permit until your new license arrives in the mail in about 2 weeks. If you are under age 18, you must wait at least 6 months from the date you received your learner permit to schedule your road test.

If you have a valid NY license, permit, or ID card, you must bring your original Social Security card or a W-2 with your full SSN. If you have a New York State driver license or identification card, you must bring your Social Security Card or a letter from the Social Security Administration proving your ineligibility to have a Social Security number. If you lost your Social Security Card, you must get a duplicate before coming to the DMV.

If you have a driver license issued in another state (such as Pennsylvania) and you meet the other requirements, you can receive a conditional driving privilege or a restricted driving privilege to drive in New York State. The conditions or restrictions are the same as those for a driver with a New York State driver license. You must apply for a conditional or restricted use license in person at a DMV office; this can be done at most, but not all, Motor Vehicles offices, so contact your nearest office to find out where you can apply.

If you move, you must report a change of residence address on your license, permit, non-driver ID, or vehicle records to the DMV within 10 days. Changing your address with the U.S. Postal Service does not update your DMV records. You can change your address online through MyDMV (using the ID number and document number from your NYS driver license, learner permit, or Non-Driver ID) or by mail by sending a completed Address Change (MV-232) form to the NYS DMV License Production Bureau, PO Box 2895, Albany, NY 12220-0895. You do not need to order new DMV documents with your new address. If you fail to keep your address current, you may miss a suspension order and could be charged with operating an unregistered vehicle and/or aggravated unlicensed operation, both misdemeanors.

If you are overseas (out of the country, abroad), you must replace your license through the mail. Submit a completed Application for Permit, Driver License or Non-Driver ID Card (form MV-44) along with payment of $17.50. It is also recommended that you include a pre-addressed priority mail return envelope with your application to help ensure the license is sent to the correct address.

Drivers from other states: If you have a driver license issued in another state and you meet the other requirements, you can receive a conditional driving privilege or a restricted driving privilege to drive in NY State; the conditions or restrictions are the same as those for a driver with a NY State driver license. Students from other states who attend school in New York State are normally not considered New York State residents, so they don't need to exchange their current driver license. You may drive in New York State with a learner permit issued in another state if you are age 16 or older, your out-of-state learner permit is valid outside the issuing state, you obey all restrictions of the state that issued the learner permit and the general restrictions for learner permit holders in New York State, and, if you are under age 18, the additional restrictions explained in the Graduated Driver License GDL Law. Normally you can't have a NY State driver license and a driver license from another state at the same time, but there are exceptions; however, it is a violation of Federal law to hold more than one commercial driver license (CDL). Regarding tickets: your NY State Driver License will be suspended if you fail to answer a ticket for a moving violation in any state except Alaska, California, Michigan, Montana, Oregon or Wisconsin, and it will remain suspended until you answer the ticket. Drivers from any state except those six will have their driver licenses suspended in their own state for failure to answer a moving violation in New York State. The New York State DMV does not record out-of-state convictions of moving traffic violations of New York State non-commercial licensed drivers, except for traffic offenses committed in Ontario and Quebec, Canada.

The evidence recommends coming to the DMV now to get an Enhanced or REAL ID to avoid a second office visit later, and if you plan to travel and don't have a Passport, upgrading to an Enhanced or REAL ID when you renew. Note that getting an Enhanced or REAL ID is not mandatory; however, a Standard document will not be accepted to board a domestic flight starting in October 2020 unless you have a Passport. A valid U.S. Passport is already REAL ID compliant and can be used to board a flight. Regarding age, TSA does not currently require children under 18 years old to provide identification when traveling with a companion within the United States; the companion will need acceptable identification. This means an 18-year-old is not covered by the under-18 exemption and would need acceptable identification.

The evidence provided does not state how your name will appear on a New York driver license or driving privilege issued to a driver from another state. The evidence only describes eligibility for a conditional or restricted driving privilege for out-of-state drivers and related requirements, without addressing name formatting or display.

Drivers from other states who have a driver license issued in another state may, if they meet the other requirements, receive a conditional driving privilege or a restricted driving privilege to drive in New York State; the conditions or restrictions are the same as those for a driver with a New York State driver license. Students from other states who attend school in New York State are normally not considered residents of New York State, so they don't need to exchange their current driver license. Normally you can't have a NY State driver license and a driver license from another state at the same time, but there are exceptions; however, it is a violation of Federal law to hold more than one commercial driver license (CDL).

Yes. If you have a driver license issued in another state and you meet the other requirements, you can receive a conditional driving privilege or a restricted driving privilege to drive in New York State. The conditions or restrictions are the same as those for a driver with a New York State driver license.

To get a New York State driver license (permit) if you do not have a license from your home country, you must pass a written test, complete a 5-hour pre-licensing course, and pass a road test. Note that visitors generally do not need a New York State license unless they become New York State residents; only New York State residents need New York State driver licenses.

To exchange your out-of-state license at a NY State DMV office, bring a valid out-of-state photo driver license that shows it was valid for at least 6 months (or, instead of a replacement license, an original letter or certified driver abstract from the prior state on agency letterhead, issued within six months, containing your name, address, date of birth, license ID number, license type/class and restrictions, and any convictions, suspensions or revocations). You must also pass a vision test at the DMV or bring a completed Eye Test Report (MV-619), surrender your out-of-state license unless it is lost or stolen, and bring proof of identity (use the DMV guide to find your proofs). For a REAL ID, you must bring original or certified proof documents, including proof of identity such as a valid license, birth certificate or passport with your full first, middle (if applicable) and last name, and proof of Social Security Number or Social Security Number ineligibility.

To get access to a conditional license, you must apply in person at a DMV office. You can do this at most, but not all, Motor Vehicles offices, so contact your nearest office to find out where you can apply. The DMV can issue a conditional license to a qualified driver whose NY State license has been suspended or revoked because of an alcohol or drug-related violation, and the driver must attend an Impaired Driver Program (IDP), previously known as the Drinking Driving Program (DDP), approved by the DMV. You may also be eligible for a conditional license or conditional driving privilege if you participate in New York State's Impaired Driver Program (IDP) or an approved out-of-state program.

A restricted use license can be issued by the DMV to a driver who qualifies and whose license is suspended or revoked because of violations or incidents that are not alcohol or drug-related, or because of some drug-related violations. If you have a driver license issued in another state and meet the other requirements, you can receive a restricted driving privilege to drive in NY State, with the same restrictions as for a driver with a NY State driver license. You must apply for a conditional or restricted use license in person at a DMV office; this is possible at most, but not all, Motor Vehicles offices, so you should contact your nearest office to find out where you can apply.

Yes. If you have a driver license issued in another state and you meet the other requirements, you can receive a conditional driving privilege or a restricted driving privilege to drive in NY State. The conditions or restrictions are the same as those for a driver with a NY State driver license.

You can use proof-of-residence documents that are in your spouse's name if you and your spouse have the same last name, or if you show additional documents that prove your relationship, for example, a marriage certificate. So having the same last name does affect this: it is one of the conditions under which such documents can be used.

If you and your spouse do not have the same last name, you can show additional documents that prove your relationship—for example, a marriage certificate—to use proof-of-residence documents that are in your spouse's name.

The evidence offers suggestions for people who don't have enough proof of name identification to bring to the DMV: you may already have more proof documents than you think, or you may be able to get some. Examples include a bank debit card with your name preprinted on it (some banks issue a card the same day you open an account) and online bill printouts, such as a paperless phone or electricity bill.
Yes. You can print out a copy of a paperless bill, such as a phone bill, electricity/gas bill, water bill, or cable bill.

The evidence does not address whether the suspension you are asking about could have been avoided. It explains that indefinite suspensions can result from reasons such as not answering a traffic ticket, not paying a traffic ticket fine, not filing a motor vehicle accident report, failing to pay child support, unpaid NY State tax debts, or not having automobile liability insurance, and that the suspension notice tells you what you must do to remove the suspension. It also notes that a driver responsibility assessment must be paid by a final date to avoid a suspension. However, none of the evidence states whether, in your specific situation, the suspension could have been avoided.
If you request a DMV hearing but do not appear and do not submit your affidavit, your registration will be suspended immediately.

The evidence does not provide a list of documents a single person can use to prove residence. The closest relevant item is for a New York REAL ID, which requires two different proofs of New York State residence such as a utility bill, bank statement, or mortgage statement (P.O. Box not acceptable). Other evidence mentions records that could show long-term residence outside the United States, but in the context of proving a Social Security number was never assigned, not general proof of residence.
Yes. Divorce papers are listed among the acceptable documents you can use, and you must show the original documents or a certified copy.

The evidence offers suggestions for proof of name identification for the DMV, such as a bank debit card with your name preprinted on it (some banks issue a card the same day you open an account) and online bill printouts (for example, a phone or electricity bill). However, the evidence does not explain why a hearing would be needed for test documents, so that part of the question cannot be answered from the provided evidence.

Yes. You may request a hearing by affidavit, which is a hearing on paper, instead of an in-person DMV hearing. The Notice of Registration Suspension provides instructions about how to submit the affidavit to DMV, and if you submit the affidavit you will not have to appear at a DMV hearing. However, if you request a DMV hearing and do not appear or submit your affidavit, your registration will be suspended immediately.
If you request a DMV hearing but do not appear and do not submit your affidavit, your registration will be suspended immediately.

Yes. You can change your address online with the DMV, and then renew your registration. The online address change applies only to the DMV records you select, and you can later replace your driver license, permit, non-driver ID, and/or registration documents to show the new address. Note that the DMV will not change your address with the USPS or on records outside the DMV records specified, and there is no guarantee the USPS will forward all DMV documents to your new address.

The evidence does not describe what specifically happens if insurance lapses again after you have already provided proof of insurance and updated your address with the DMV. The materials explain that after providing proof of insurance the DMV verifies coverage with your insurance company, and that you can check your insurance status online (E1). They also note that failing to maintain an updated address means you may not learn of an insurance problem, and the DMV will suspend your registration and license (E5), and that suspensions can lead to license and registration consequences including a $750 civil penalty to restore a revoked license (E4). However, no evidence addresses the specific repeat-lapse scenario after proof and address update, so that precise outcome cannot be determined from the provided evidence.

If you don't have your original U.S. birth certificate or marriage record, the New York State Department of Health Vital Records office can help you obtain vital records in the state. Alternatively, you can order vital records online from New York and many other states through an independent partner, VitalChek Network Inc., at vitalchek.com. You may also already have more proof documents than you think, or be able to get some: for example, a bank debit card with your name preprinted on it (some banks issue a card the same day you open an account), or online bill printouts such as a phone or electricity bill.

If your inspection sticker comes off, you can attach it to the windshield again with clear tape or a small amount of clear adhesive. Keep in mind that an inspection station must be able to remove the sticker during your next inspection. If the sticker is not usable, you can have your vehicle re-inspected or order a replacement sticker using the form Request for Replacement Inspection Sticker (VS-118), completing the form and mailing it to the address on the form.

If the inspection sticker is not usable, you can have your vehicle re-inspected or order a replacement sticker using the form Request for Replacement Inspection Sticker (VS-118). Complete the form and mail it to the address on the form. If the sticker simply came off, you can reattach it to the windshield with clear tape or a small amount of clear adhesive, but an inspection station must be able to remove the sticker during your next inspection.

The evidence does not directly address whether divorce papers that include your ex-spouse's information can be used as proof of your own identity. The closest relevant points are: (1) proof-of-residence documents in your spouse's name may be used if you and your spouse share the same last name and you show additional documents proving your relationship, such as a marriage certificate; and (2) a divorce decree is listed as a document that may be accepted to prove a legal name change, not as proof of identity. Because the evidence does not confirm that divorce papers containing your ex's information can serve as identity proof for you, this cannot be answered from the provided evidence.

Yes. For a registration suspension, you may request a hearing by affidavit (a hearing on paper) instead of appearing in person. The Notice of Registration Suspension provides instructions on how to submit the affidavit to the DMV, and if you submit the affidavit you will not have to appear at a DMV hearing. However, if you request a DMV hearing and neither appear nor submit your affidavit, your registration will be suspended immediately.

Yes. If you submit the affidavit, you will not have to appear at a DMV hearing; the affidavit hearing is a hearing on paper, and the Notice of Registration Suspension provides instructions on how to submit it. However, if you request a DMV hearing and neither appear nor submit your affidavit, your registration will be suspended immediately. As for avoiding the suspension, the notice advises that if you pay all of the tolls, fees or other charges owed to the tolling authority, or have them dismissed or transferred, the suspension will not take effect. Note that at the hearing you may not dispute whether you evaded a toll or failed to pay tolls, fees or other charges; those issues must be raised with the tolling authority outside the hearing.
If you request a DMV hearing but do not appear and do not submit your affidavit, your registration will be suspended immediately.

You can submit a complaint, an issue, concern, suspicious activity, or scam through the Feedback Center, either on behalf of yourself or someone else. You can also share positive feedback or review an already submitted case. If you previously submitted a complaint and Federal Student Aid gave you a response you don't agree with or believe is incorrect, follow their procedure for resolving disputes before contacting the Federal Student Aid Ombudsman Group, which is a neutral, informal, and confidential resource to help resolve disputes about your federal student aid. To view, track, or update your case, log in to your account and use Manage Cases. You can also call to speak to an agent for help with submitting your feedback or to ask questions.

If a complaint is filed against you, a Consumer Services Representative (CSR) from the DMV will contact you in an attempt to resolve the complaint. The CSR will explain the nature of the complaint and will inform you of your rights, responsibilities, and your liability. If the complaint is not resolved with the CSR, the case will proceed further. You should also protect your business by keeping a copy of all work orders in an easy-to-access location, and you must follow all consumer protection laws and regulations.

Yes. If a complaint results in a fine, penalty, or suspension, you can be back in business after complete compliance once you pay the fine and/or penalty or serve out your period of suspension. However, if your license, registration, or certification is revoked, you must surrender all supplies and cease to operate. You also have the right to appeal any adverse decision within 60 days of the ALJ's decision by filing the Appeal From DMV Hearing Determination (AA-33A) with the appropriate filing fee.
MyDMV was created by the New York State Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV), in cooperation with the New York State Office of Information Technology Services.

To transfer a registration at a DMV office, bring: the original title or other proof of ownership; your current NY State Insurance ID card (auto liability insurance); your NY State driver license, permit, non-driver ID, or other proof of identity; a completed Application for Registration/Title (MV-82); and payment for fees. Since you live in one of the listed counties (Westchester, Nassau, Suffolk, Rockland, Onondaga, Monroe, or Albany), you can get quicker service by making a reservation online before visiting the office.

You may be eligible for a refund or transfer credit when you surrender your vehicle plates to the DMV. You can transfer the remaining registration credit to another vehicle you want to register, or get a refund for the registration fee, plate fee, title certificate fee, and other fees or taxes paid when you registered. If you are eligible for a refund and do not request a transfer receipt, the DMV will process your refund automatically and you will receive it in the mail in several weeks. If you are not eligible for a refund or you request a transfer receipt, the DMV office issues a Receipt FS-6 T that you can use to transfer the registration to another vehicle. A full 2-year refund of the registration fee is available only if the registration was never used and it is not more than 60 days from the date the registration was issued. The evidence does not address what happens if someone refuses to move their registration.

The evidence does not state whether a copy of the Certificate of Title is acceptable for a vehicle transfer. It only describes requirements for transferring an original title certificate, such as completing the "Transfer by Owner" section on the back of the title and not accepting titles with cross-outs, alterations, or erasures. Because the specific question about carrying a copy is not addressed, there is insufficient evidence to answer it.

For a vehicle that is a 1972 model year or older, the acceptable proof of ownership is either a NY State Transferable Registration (the original or a certified copy, not a photocopy) along with a bill of sale, or acceptable proof of ownership from another state. The transferable registration must be marked "transferable" on the front, and the seller whose name appears on it must sign the back.

The evidence indicates that more information about New York State insurance requirements is available through the NY State Department of Financial Services website (http://www.dfs.gov), which has information about liability insurance and insurance companies licensed in New York. The evidence also refers to learning more about NY State Insurance Requirements, but does not provide a separate contact or source beyond the DFS website.

The evidence provided does not address whether you can print out a copy of the title when doing a transfer. The evidence discusses title transfer procedures, mailing titles, and lien-related transfers, but does not state whether a printed copy of the title is acceptable for a transfer.

Whether you need a refund depends on your situation. If you are eligible for a refund and do not request a transfer receipt, the DMV will process your refund automatically and you will receive it in the mail in several weeks. If you are not eligible for a refund or you request a transfer receipt, the DMV office issues a Receipt FS-6 T that you can use to transfer the registration to another vehicle. To apply for a full 2-year refund of the registration fee, the registration must never have been used and it must be no more than 60 days from the date the registration was issued. To apply for a refund of the first-year registration fee (if you already received a refund for the 2nd year and have the unused registration sticker and stub), you have a maximum of 60 days after the registration was issued and must send a completed and signed Request for Refund MV-215, the original registration document stub, and the unused registration sticker to the address on the MV-215 form. If you changed your name, surrender the vehicle plates at a DMV office and request a transfer receipt (not a refund receipt), then send the MV-215 form, proof of the name change, and the transfer receipt to the address on the form; the DMV will issue the refund in your new name if eligible.

Yes, you need the title (or other acceptable proof of ownership) to transfer a registration to another vehicle; the evidence does not indicate the DMV keeps your title on record for this purpose. For vehicles model year 1973 or newer, you need a NY State Certificate of Title original or certified copy (not a photocopy) with the transfer ownership section completed by the seller, or acceptable proof of ownership from another state. For model year 1972 or older, you need a NY State Transferable Registration original or certified copy (not a photocopy) and a bill of sale, or acceptable proof of ownership.

For a vehicle with a model year of 1972 or older, the proof of ownership required is either a NY State Transferable Registration (original or certified copy, not a photocopy) along with a bill of sale, or acceptable proof of ownership from another state. New York State does not issue a title certificate for any motor vehicle of model year 1972 or older. A transferable registration is issued for a 1972 or older motor vehicle; the transferable portion proves ownership and is used to sell or give ownership to another person, while the registration portion allows the vehicle to be operated on a public road.

The evidence does not say whether the PD-7 form can be sent to you online. It only describes completing the PD-7 Plate Surrender Application PDF and then either mailing it with your plates to the NYS DMV or bringing the plates and PD-7 to a DMV office.

The evidence provided does not address whether more than one vehicle can have the same registration in New York. The cited documents cover topics such as registering out-of-state vehicles, insurance requirements, vehicle types that can be registered, and registration procedures, but none state a rule about duplicate or shared registration numbers across vehicles.

For a car of model year 1972 or older (which includes 1973 or older vehicles), the acceptable proof of ownership is either a NY State Transferable Registration — which must be the original or a certified copy, not a photocopy — or acceptable proof of ownership from another state. To transfer ownership, the owner can use the transferable registration and a bill of sale. The registration document must be marked "transferable" on the front, and the seller whose name appears on the transferable registration must sign the back.
If you don't want to transfer the registration, you must surrender the vehicle plates to the DMV. You may be eligible to receive a refund if you surrender the plates before the registration expires.

Yes. To transfer a registration to another vehicle you own, you must bring the original title or other proof of ownership to a DMV office, along with your current NY State Insurance ID card, proof of identity, a completed Application for Registration/Title (MV-82), and payment for fees.
No. For a vehicle transfer, the proof of ownership must be an original or certified copy of the title, not a photocopy. A printed/photocopy of the title is not acceptable.

Yes. The DMV offers additional resources to help you learn more about transferring a vehicle's title. You can read the DMV brochures "Let the Buyer be Aware" and "Q&A About Your Title Certificate." You can also find the sales tax form Statement of Transaction - Sale or Gift of Motor Vehicle, Trailer, All-Terrain Vehicle (ATV), Vessel (Boat), or Snowmobile (DTF-802) at any motor vehicle office and on the DMV internet site.

If you don't want to transfer the registration, you must surrender the vehicle plates to the DMV. You may be eligible for a refund if you surrender the plates before the registration expires. You should also turn in the plates to a motor vehicle office unless you are transferring them to a replacement vehicle, and always turn in your plates before you cancel liability insurance or before the insurance lapses; otherwise your registration will be suspended and your driver license could be suspended as well.
If you do not have insurance, you need to surrender your vehicle registration and plates to the DMV immediately. The evidence does not specify a different deadline for turning in the registration.
Form FS-2 is available only at a local DMV Office.

If your driver's license or vehicle registration is suspended because of a lapse in automobile liability insurance coverage, you can provide proof that you now have insurance online or by mail. After you provide your proof of insurance, the DMV will verify your coverage with your insurance company. You can check your insurance status online, and you can also check the status of your driver license and vehicle registrations through MyDMV. If you need written confirmation that the DMV cleared a suspension or revocation, you must order your driving record or vehicle abstract. If you don't have insurance, you need to surrender your vehicle registration and plates to the DMV immediately. Also, do not drive any vehicle that is not insured.

If your driver license or vehicle registration is suspended because of a lapse in automobile liability insurance coverage, you can provide proof that you now have insurance online or by mail; the DMV will then verify your coverage with your insurance company, and you can check your insurance status online or check the status of your license and registrations through MyDMV. Ask your insurance company to file a notice of coverage with the DMV electronically (paper proof or email messages are not acceptable, and your agent or broker cannot file it for you). If you don't have insurance, you need to surrender your vehicle registration and plates to the DMV immediately. To determine the lapse period, the plates must be surrendered, reported lost/stolen/confiscated, the registration must expire, the plates must be transferred to another vehicle by DMV, or DMV must receive proof of new or reinstated insurance or other acceptable proof. The driver license suspension will not end until you have paid the suspension termination fee and have served the suspension; you can get your registration and new plates when the problem is corrected. If you need written confirmation that the DMV cleared a suspension or revocation, you must order your driving record or vehicle abstract.

A suspension means your license or driving privilege is taken away for a period of time, and you may need to pay a suspension termination fee. Suspension periods can be definite (with a beginning and end date) or indefinite (which does not end until you take a required action). If you receive an order from DMV, it will tell you what you must do to remove the suspension, so be sure to follow the instructions on the order. Common reasons for indefinite suspensions include not answering a traffic ticket, not paying a traffic ticket fine, not filing a motor vehicle accident report, failing to pay child support, unpaid NY State tax debts, and not having automobile liability insurance. If your license is suspended for a lapse of insurance, you must surrender your plates if your registration has not expired; a driver license becomes suspended when the lapse is 91 days or more or if the lapse period has not yet been determined. The driver license suspension will not end until you have paid the suspension termination fee and served the suspension.
No. Motorcycle plates do not have to be surrendered to the DMV when auto liability insurance lapses. However, it is illegal to operate a motorcycle without proper auto liability insurance.

Read the insurance letter or order carefully, answer it quickly, and contact your insurance company immediately; if there is a problem, it is your responsibility to resolve it, otherwise the DMV can suspend your vehicle registration and driver license. Your response must either prove that you have insurance coverage, prove that you sold the vehicle, or prove that insurance coverage was not required. If you have insurance coverage, ask your insurance company (not your agent or broker) to file an electronic notice of insurance coverage with the DMV. If you do not have liability insurance, or it is about to expire and you do not plan to replace it, you need to surrender your vehicle plates to the DMV immediately. Do not use your vehicle if your insurance coverage is cancelled, even if you think it is a mistake; keep the plates while you resolve a problem with your insurance company, and do surrender your vehicle registration and plates before your insurance coverage ends. Regarding motorcycle plates: you do not need to surrender motorcycle plates if there is a lapse in the liability insurance coverage.

The evidence does not address whether the assistant is aware of a suspension's termination. Regarding revocation: if you receive an order from DMV saying your license or driving privilege is revoked, this means your license has been cancelled and you must get a new one when the revocation period ends. In most cases, before you can get a new license you must first request approval from DMV when the revocation period is over. You may be required to take the written and driving tests again and pay a license reapplication fee. Your application may be denied if you have a high risk driving record or fail to meet DMV requirements, and you may also need to pay a driver civil penalty before your license or driving privilege can be restored. Common reasons for revocations include operating or permitting operation of a vehicle without insurance, being involved in an uninsured motor vehicle accident, or being convicted of an alcohol or drugged driving charge.

If you do not have liability insurance (or it is about to expire and you do not plan to replace it), you must surrender your vehicle plates to the DMV immediately. If you do not have valid auto liability insurance coverage for your vehicle, you must immediately surrender your registration and vehicle plates. Note that motorcycle plates do not have to be surrendered to the DMV when auto liability insurance lapses, though it is illegal to operate a motorcycle without proper auto liability insurance.

If you have a problem with a DMV insurance letter or order, it is your responsibility to resolve it; if you do not, the DMV can suspend your vehicle registration and driver license. Read the letter or order carefully, answer it quickly, and contact your insurance company immediately. If you have insurance, follow the instructions in the letter and contact your company or agent about the problem, and ask your company to file a notice of coverage with the DMV electronically. If you don't have insurance, you need to surrender your vehicle registration and plates to the DMV immediately.

The evidence does not clearly answer whether someone else can turn in the plates for you. It states that you should not give your plates to another person unless that person will surrender them, which suggests another person may be able to surrender the plates on your behalf, but the text is cut off and does not fully confirm this.

Read the letter or order carefully, respond to it quickly, and contact your insurance company immediately. It is your responsibility to resolve any problem; if you do not, the DMV can suspend your vehicle registration and driver license. Your response must either prove that you have insurance coverage, prove that you sold the vehicle, or prove that insurance coverage was not required. If you have insurance, follow the instructions in the letter and contact your company or agent, and ask your company to file a notice of coverage with the DMV electronically. If you do not have insurance, you need to surrender your vehicle registration and plates to the DMV immediately. Do not use your vehicle if your insurance coverage is cancelled, even if you think it is a mistake, and do not keep the plates while you resolve a problem with your insurance company; surrender your registration and plates before your coverage ends.

A suspension means your driver license or privilege to drive is taken away for a period of time before it is returned. There are two types: a definite suspension, which has a clear beginning and end date, and an indefinite suspension, which means you must do something (such as answer a traffic ticket) before the suspension can be cleared. Regarding the termination fee for a pay suspension: the suspension termination fee for a definite suspension is currently $50, unless the suspension was for breaking the NYS Zero Tolerance alcohol law, in which case the fee is $100. If the effective date of your suspension order is before July 6, 2009, the suspension termination fee is $25. For an indefinite suspension, you may also be required to pay a suspension termination fee.

Since you have insurance, follow the instructions in the DMV letter and contact your insurance company or agent about the problem. Ask your company to file a notice of coverage with the DMV electronically. It is your responsibility to resolve the problem; if you do not, the DMV can suspend your vehicle registration and driver license.

If you do not have liability insurance, you must surrender your vehicle plates (and registration) to the DMV immediately. This applies if your insurance is about to expire and you don't plan to replace it. The rule to remember is: no insurance, no plates. If you don't maintain coverage, the DMV can suspend your vehicle registration and driver license.

If you are suspended for an insurance lapse, you can submit proof of insurance online. If the vehicle is not insured and the registration is still valid, you must surrender your registration. Also, if your registration has not expired, you must surrender your plates; a driver license becomes suspended when the lapse is 91 days or more or if the lapse period has not yet been determined. To determine the lapse period, the plates must be surrendered, reported lost/stolen/confiscated, the registration must expire, the plates must be transferred to another vehicle by DMV, or DMV must receive proof of new or reinstated insurance. Additionally, you must pay the DMV a $50 license suspension termination fee.

The evidence does not say whether personalized replacement plates can be received in the parking lot. It only states that new custom plates are mailed and that you should allow at least six weeks for them to arrive, with registration documents mailed separately.

To register to vote in New York State, you must: be a U.S. citizen; be 18 years old by the end of this year; not be in prison or on parole for a felony conviction; and not claim the right to vote elsewhere. Full voter registration requirements are listed on the New York State Board of Elections website.

To plan for future Social Security survivor benefits, consider what your family would need if you died now, since Social Security can help your family if you have earned enough credits through your work. You can earn up to four credits each year; in 2019, for example, you earn one credit for each $1,360 of wages or self-employment income, and at $5,440 you have earned your four credits for the year. The number of credits needed to provide benefits for your survivors depends on your age when you die, and no one needs more than 40 credits (10 years of work) to be eligible for any Social Security benefit, though the younger a person is, the fewer credits they must have for family members to receive survivors benefits. Benefits can be paid to your children and your spouse. Also consider the benefits that may be available if you are the survivor—the spouse, child, or parent of a worker who dies—provided that person worked long enough under Social Security to qualify. If you are a surviving divorced spouse, you could get benefits the same as a widow or widower if your marriage lasted 10 years or more, and remarrying after age 60 (age 50 if disabled) will not affect your eligibility for survivors benefits.

If you don't have enough work credits to be eligible for Social Security Disability benefits, you may possibly qualify for Supplemental Security Income (SSI) if you have limited income and resources. For more information, you can read "Your income and resources" on page 5 of the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) booklet.

Since you have not established U.S. citizenship with the SSA, you need to show proof of U.S. citizenship. Acceptable documents include a U.S. passport, Certificate of Naturalization N-550/N-570, Certificate of Citizenship N-560/N-561, Certificate of Report of Birth DS-1350, or Consular Report of Birth Abroad FS-240/CRBA. Documents must be current and not expired, and receipts showing you applied for a document are not accepted. One document may serve two purposes—for example, a U.S. passport can prove both citizenship and identity.

Yes. You can call Social Security toll-free at 1-800-772-1213. If you are deaf or hard of hearing, you can call the toll-free TTY number at 1-800-325-0778. Representatives can answer questions from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., Monday through Friday, and automated phone service is available 24 hours a day.

The evidence only explains how to get a corrected card when you legally change your name (due to marriage, divorce, court order, or any other reason), and notes that if you are working you should also tell your employer. It does not describe how an adult who is not changing their name and is not working can obtain a corrected Social Security card, so the specific procedure for that situation is not covered by the provided evidence.

Yes. If you don't have a U.S. passport, other documents can serve as proof of U.S. citizenship, such as a U.S. birth certificate, Certificate of Naturalization (N-550/N-570), Certificate of Citizenship (N-560/N-561), Certificate of Report of Birth (DS-1350), or Consular Report of Birth Abroad (FS-240, CRBA). This proof is only required if you have not already established your U.S. citizenship with Social Security. For identity, acceptable documents include a U.S. driver's license or a state-issued non-driver identification card; if you don't have one of these or can't get a replacement within 10 days, Social Security will ask to see other documents.

Yes. Benefits normally stop when a child reaches age 18, but if the child is still a full-time student at a secondary or elementary school at age 18, benefits will continue until the child graduates or until two months after the child becomes age 19, whichever is first. Other evidence similarly states that if the child is a full-time student in an elementary or high school, benefits can continue until age 19.

If the child does not have (or cannot obtain) a State-issued birth certificate recorded before age 5, other documents can be considered to prove the child's age, such as the child's passport. For proof of identity, a U.S. passport is preferred; if unavailable, acceptable alternatives include a State-issued non-driver's identification card, adoption decree, doctor/clinic/hospital record, religious record, school daycare center record, or school identification card. The document must show the child's name and identifying information (age, date of birth, or parents' names), preferably with a recent photograph; a non-photo document may be accepted if it has enough identifying information. The parent's own identity must also be proven with a current, unexpired document showing name and identifying information.

If a state or local law requires you to provide your Social Security number to get general assistance benefits for which you already qualify, and you need a number to meet those state or local requirements, you must bring a letter from the government agency. The letter must be on letterhead stationery (no form letters or photocopies) and must: specifically identify you as the applicant; cite the law requiring you to have a Social Security number; indicate that you meet all the agency's requirements except having the number; and contain an agency contact name and telephone number.

To apply for a replacement Social Security card online, you must be age 18 or older and have a U.S. mailing address (and a my Social Security account). The evidence does not state any separate age or U.S. mailing address requirement for replacing a card by other means.

A foreign-born U.S. citizen adult can replace their Social Security card for free if it is lost or stolen, though a replacement may not be needed since knowing your Social Security number is what's important. Replacement cards are limited to three per year and 10 during your lifetime; legal name changes do not count toward these limits, and you may not be affected by the limits if you can prove you need the card to prevent a significant hardship. You must present original documents or copies certified by the issuing agency—photocopies and notarized copies are not accepted, all documents must be current and not expired, and a receipt showing you applied for the document is not accepted.

The Direct Express card is a debit card you can use to access your benefits, and you don't need a bank account. With the program, your federal benefit payment is deposited directly into your card account, and your monthly benefits are available on your payment day on time, every time. You can use the card to make purchases, pay bills, or get cash at thousands of locations. Signing up is quick and easy: you can call the toll-free Direct Express hotline at 1-800-333-1795, and Social Security can also help you sign up.

To prove your U.S. immigration status when applying for a first Social Security card as a noncitizen adult, you must show your current U.S. immigration document, such as Form I-551 Lawful Permanent Resident Card, Machine Readable Immigrant Visa with your unexpired foreign passport, I-766 Employment Authorization Document (EAD, work permit), or I-94 Arrival/Departure Record or admission stamp in the unexpired foreign passport. If you are an F-1 or M-1 student, you also must show your I-20 Certificate of Eligibility for Nonimmigrant Student Status; if you are a J-1 or J-2 exchange visitor, you must show your DS-2019 Certificate of Eligibility for Exchange Visitor Status. You must present original documents or copies certified by the issuing agency—photocopies and notarized copies are not accepted—and all documents must be current, not expired; a receipt showing you applied for the document is not accepted. In general, only noncitizens who have permission to work from the Department of Homeland Security can apply for a Social Security number.

The evidence provided covers age proof for a U.S.-born adult and for a child, but it does not state what documents a noncitizen adult can use to prove age if a birth certificate cannot be found. The noncitizen adult section in the evidence addresses immigration status, not age proof. Therefore, the specific alternatives for a noncitizen adult without a birth certificate are not established by the evidence.

To get an original Social Security card for a foreign-born U.S. citizen child, you must present original documents or copies certified by the issuing agency; photocopies, notarized copies, expired documents, and receipts showing you applied for a document are not accepted. For proof of U.S. citizenship, only certain documents are accepted, including Certification of Report of Birth DS-1350, Consular Report of Birth Abroad FS-240, U.S. passport, Certificate of Citizenship N-560/N-561, or Certificate of Naturalization N-550/N-570. For proof of age, you must present your child's foreign birth certificate if you have it or can get it within 10 days; if not, other documents such as your child's passport may be considered.

For a foreign-born U.S. citizen child's SSN card, acceptable proof of U.S. citizenship includes: Certification of Report of Birth DS-1350; Consular Report of Birth Abroad FS-240; U.S. passport; Certificate of Citizenship N-560/N-561; and Certificate of Naturalization N-550/N-570. Documents must be originals or copies certified by the issuing agency; photocopies, notarized copies, expired documents, and receipts showing you applied are not accepted. The evidence provided does not address how a parent can appeal a decision about income-related monthly adjustment amounts.

To get an original Social Security card for a foreign-born U.S. citizen child, you must present original documents or copies certified by the issuing agency; photocopies, notarized copies, expired documents, and receipts showing you applied are not accepted. For proof of U.S. citizenship, only certain documents are accepted: Certification of Report of Birth DS-1350; Consular Report of Birth Abroad FS-240; U.S. passport; Certificate of Citizenship N-560/N-561; Certificate of Naturalization N-550/N-570. For age, you must present the child's foreign birth certificate if you have it or can get it within 10 days; if not, other documents such as the child's passport will be considered.

You can learn more about your Social Security benefits by creating a free my Social Security account, which lets you check your earnings history online and get personalized retirement benefit estimates based on your actual earnings through the Retirement Calculator. If you prefer not to create an account or can't set one up, other online and downloadable tools are available to help you estimate your benefit amount. Your benefit amount depends on the earnings shown on your record, so regularly checking your earnings history can help avoid surprises when you start receiving benefits. You may also qualify for benefits as a spouse, divorced spouse, widow/widower, or surviving divorced spouse even if you never worked under Social Security, and certain life changes—such as the death of a spouse or ex-spouse—may make you eligible for a higher benefit. Benefit calculators can help you plan and get estimates of future retirement, disability, and survivors benefits, and you can use your account's Message Center to receive important notices.

Social Security benefits depend on the earnings shown on your record, so regularly checking your earnings history can help avoid surprises when you start receiving benefits. You can find your earnings history on your annual Social Security Statement, and you can create a free my Social Security account to check it online. The Retirement Calculator within my Social Security provides personalized retirement benefit estimates based on your actual earnings, letting you see how changing the date or age you begin receiving benefits affects your future income. If you don't want to create an account or can't set one up, other tools and calculators are available to estimate your benefit amount. Note that retirement benefits cannot be paid until you have 40 credits. You may also qualify for spouse's benefits if you are the spouse or divorced spouse of a retired or disabled worker, or a widow/widower or surviving divorced spouse of a deceased worker, even if you never worked under Social Security.

The evidence only describes the Government Pension Offset (GPO) and how to calculate benefits affected by it; it does not identify what other retirement benefits planner information the user needs instead of the GPO.

The Government Pension Offset (GPO) is a reduction that may apply if you receive a pension for work not covered by Social Security, such as government employment. In that case, any Social Security benefits you may be eligible to receive on your spouse's record may be reduced. Some individuals are exempt from the offset; the factsheet's "When won't my Social Security benefits be reduced?" section explains exemption requirements. To estimate future spouse's, widow's, or widower's benefits under the GPO, you need the estimated gross monthly amount of your pension and your estimated spouse's benefit if you retire at full retirement age.

If your earnings for the prior year are higher than one of the years used to compute your retirement benefit, Social Security will recalculate your benefit amount. The increase is paid retroactive to January of the year after you earned the money. Higher benefits can be important later in life and can increase the future benefit amounts your family and survivors could receive.

There is no single required age; you may start receiving retirement benefits as early as age 62 or as late as age 70. The age you begin collecting affects how much you receive: benefits are reduced if you start before your full retirement age (which is 66 if born 1943–1954, gradually rising to 67 for those born 1960 or later), and delayed retirement credits may be added if benefits start after full retirement age. Other factors to consider include working while receiving benefits and life expectancy. To make an informed choice, review the factors on the SSA's Learn About Retirement Benefits page.

If the deceased was receiving Social Security benefits, you must return the benefit received for the month of death and any later months. For example, if the person died in July, you must return the benefits paid in August. How you return the benefits depends on how the deceased received them: for funds received by direct deposit, contact the bank or other financial institution and request that any funds received for the month of death or later be returned to Social Security; benefits received by check must be returned to Social Security as soon as possible, and you should not cash any checks received for the month in which the person dies or later.

The evidence does not address whether your parents grew up in the 1980s, so that fact does not determine eligibility. What matters is your age: you must be at least 61 years and 9 months old to apply for retirement benefits, and if you are already 62 you may be able to start benefits in the month you apply. You should apply no more than four months before the date you want benefits to start. Family longevity may influence when you choose to start: if your parents and grandparents lived into their 80s or 90s and you expect the same, you may want to delay until full retirement age or later; if they didn't, you may choose to start earlier.

Full retirement age is the age at which a person may first become entitled to full or unreduced retirement benefits (also called "normal retirement age"). It depends on your year of birth: it is 66 if you were born from 1943 to 1954; it increases gradually for those born from 1955 to 1960 (two months added for every birth year); and for anyone born in 1960 or later, full retirement benefits are payable at age 67. Regardless of your full retirement age, you may start receiving benefits as early as age 62 or as late as age 70.

The evidence does not directly address whether replacing a non-citizen child's Social Security card itself causes a tax-filing delay. It does say that if you legally change your child's name and do not tell Social Security, it may delay your tax refund or your child's refund. So a delay is tied to an unreported name change, not to the replacement card request itself.

After you apply for retirement benefits, once the Social Security Administration receives your application, they will review it. After the review, they will contact you if they need more information or if they need to see your documents. They will also let you know if you may be able to receive benefits on another person's record. Note that if you apply more than two months in the future, you will not be able to check the status of your application until one month before you start receiving benefits.

After the review, Social Security will contact you if they need more information or if they need to see your documents. They will also let you know if you may be able to receive benefits on another person's record.
If you were born after 1928 (or in 1929 or later), you need 40 credits to qualify for retirement benefits—usually about 10 years of work.

The evidence does not provide a complete answer to what you must do to be eligible for disability benefits. For VA disability compensation, you may be eligible if you have a current illness or injury (a condition affecting your body or mind) and both of these are true: you served on active duty, active duty for training, or inactive duty training, and you have a disability rating for your service-connected condition, plus at least one additional requirement listed in the criteria. For Social Security disability benefits, the evidence only addresses work credits needed based on your age when disability began: for age 24 to 31, generally credit for working half the time between age 21 and when you become disabled (for example, becoming disabled at age 27 would require 3 years of work, 12 credits, out of the past 6 years between ages 21 and 27); for age 31 or older, generally at least 20 credits in the 10-year period immediately before you become disabled. The evidence also notes that children may qualify on your record if they are unmarried and under age 18, or 18–19 and a full-time student no higher than grade 12, or 18 or older with a disability that started before age 22.

Before you retire, consider how long you expect to receive benefits, your health, and whether anyone else in your family can get benefits on your record. Social Security replaces a percentage of a worker's pre-retirement income based on lifetime earnings, and it should be just one part of your retirement plan. You should understand what you are entitled to, including how your benefit amount is determined and who else in your family might be eligible. If a child also qualifies for benefits, there is a family maximum—generally about 150 to 180 percent of your full retirement benefit—and if qualified family members apply with you, you will be asked for their Social Security numbers and birth certificates. Your spouse may be able to get benefits even if they never worked under Social Security if they are at least 62 and you are receiving retirement benefits.

Medicare Part D is prescription drug coverage that helps pay for medications doctors prescribe for treatment. For more information on the enrollment periods for Part D, you should read Medicare's page. If you receive Medicare and have limited resources and income, you may be eligible for Extra Help with Medicare Prescription Drug Plan Costs. Also, if you have higher income, you'll pay an additional premium amount for Medicare Part B and Medicare prescription drug coverage, called the income-related monthly adjustment amount; this affects less than five percent of people with Medicare, and most people don't pay higher premiums.

If you get stuck on a question while applying online, you can skip to the next question and come back to it later. You can also save your application to finish another time; when you sign in again, go to Return to a Saved Application. If you receive a message that periods, commas, or other special characters aren't allowed for some answers (including addresses), go back and enter the information without those characters. Also, for security reasons the online application warns you if you leave it open without activity for 25 minutes; you can extend your time, but after the third warning you must move to another page or your information will not be saved.

Yes. Your children may qualify for benefits on your record. An eligible child can be your biological child, adopted child, or stepchild, and a dependent grandchild may also qualify. To receive benefits, the child must be unmarried and be under age 18; or 18–19 years old and a full-time student no higher than grade 12; or 18 or older with a disability that started before age 22. Benefits normally stop when children reach age 18 unless they meet one of those exceptions. In survivor situations, your child can get benefits at any age if they were disabled before age 22 and remain disabled, and stepchildren, grandchildren, step grandchildren, or adopted children may receive benefits under certain circumstances.

Yes. The evidence lists several publications you can read for more information on disability benefits, including: Disability Evaluation Under Social Security (also known as The Blue Book, covering medical criteria for evaluating Social Security disability claims), Social Security Disability Benefits, Benefits For Children With Disabilities, What You Need To Know When You Get Disability Benefits, Working While Disabled...How We Can Help, Medicare, Receiving Your Benefits By Direct Deposit, Social Security: When You'll Get Your Benefit, and the Disability Planner. The evidence also references a Benefits Planner: Family Benefits page covering benefits for spouses, divorced spouses, and children.

If you die, Social Security survivors benefits may be available to your surviving family members, provided you worked long enough under Social Security to qualify. Eligible survivors can include a spouse, child, or parent of the deceased worker. Specifically, benefits may be paid to an unmarried child of the deceased who is younger than age 18 (or up to age 19 if a full-time student in an elementary or secondary school), or age 18 or older with a disability that began before age 22. Under certain circumstances, a stepchild, grandchild, step-grandchild, or adopted child may also be eligible, as may parents age 62 or older who were dependent on the deceased for at least half of their support. A widow or widower can receive full benefits at full retirement age for survivors or reduced benefits as early as age 60, and as early as age 50 if disabled and the disability started before the worker's death. Benefits can be paid to your children and a spouse caring for the children even if you don't have the required number of credits, if you have credit for one and one-half years of work (6 credits) in the three years just before your death.

Based on the evidence, you may be able to get spouse's retirement benefits even if you have never worked under Social Security, provided you are at least 62 years of age and your spouse is receiving retirement or disability benefits. You can also qualify for Medicare at age 65. If you are divorced, you may still be able to get benefits on your ex-spouse's record. If you qualify for both your own retirement benefits and spouse's benefits, your own benefits are paid first, and if your spouse's benefit is higher, you would receive the additional amount so the combination equals the higher amount. If you will be eligible for spouse's benefits and have access to your spouse's estimate, the estimated spouse's benefit at your full retirement age is half of your spouse's full retirement age benefit amount, rounded down to the nearest dollar. Note that if you begin receiving benefits between age 62 and full retirement age, the amount will be permanently reduced.

If you do not have a birth certificate, you may request one from the state where you were born. For details on where to write in your state, check the Social Security Administration's information. You may also be asked to provide certain documents to show that you are eligible and to help decide how much your benefits should be. When applying, also bring your bank information so you can sign up for Direct Deposit; if you do not have a bank account, you can sign up for the Direct Express card program.

If your spouse is already receiving benefits when you apply, or if you and your spouse apply at the same time, Social Security will also check your eligibility for benefits as a spouse. If you qualify, your application will automatically serve as a request for spousal benefits. Also, if your spouse qualifies on their own record, their application will include both benefits, and at their full retirement age the spouse's benefit cannot exceed one-half of your full retirement amount.

There is a limit on the total amount family members can receive each month. The limit varies, but it is generally equal to between 150 and 180 percent of the basic benefit rate (for retirement, about 150 to 180 percent of your full retirement benefit; for disability, between 150 and 180 percent of your disability benefit). The total depends on your benefit amount and the number of family members who also qualify on your record. If the sum of the benefits payable to family members is greater than this limit, the benefits will be reduced proportionately. In the disability context, your own benefit will not be affected by the family limit. For survivors, any benefits paid to a surviving divorced spouse based on disability or age won't count toward this maximum amount.

Yes. A child's Social Security card can be replaced for free if it is lost or stolen. Replacement is limited to three cards in a year and 10 during a lifetime, though legal name changes and other exceptions do not count toward these limits, and you may not be affected by the limits if you can prove you need the card to prevent a significant hardship.

Yes. In addition to the publication "Disability Benefits," other disability-related publications include: "What You Need To Know When You Get Social Security Disability Benefits," "Other Disability Publications," "Disability Evaluation Under Social Security" (also known as The Blue Book, covering medical criteria for evaluating Social Security disability claims), "Social Security Disability Benefits," "Benefits For Children With Disabilities," "What You Need To Know When You Get Disability Benefits," "Working While Disabled...How We Can Help," "Medicare," "Receiving Your Benefits By Direct Deposit," "Social Security: When You'll Get Your Benefit," and "Disability Planner."

Based on the evidence, if you delay receiving benefits until the month you reach full retirement age, you may receive your benefits with no limit on your earnings. The earnings limits described in the evidence (such as the 2019 annual limit of $17,640, with $1 deducted for every $2 earned above it) apply only if you are younger than full retirement age for the entire year. Since you are at retirement age, the evidence indicates there is no maximum earnings limit that would reduce your benefits.

If you get stuck on a question while using the online retirement application, you can skip to the next question and come back later. You can also save your application to finish another time; when you sign in again, go to Return to a Saved Application. Additionally, you can start and stop the application without losing any information you entered, and you will have a chance to correct mistakes and go back to make changes until you finish the application.

Yes. To qualify for Social Security disability benefits, you must first have worked in jobs covered by Social Security, and you must have a medical condition that meets Social Security's definition of disability. In addition to meeting the definition of disability, you must have worked long enough and recently enough under Social Security to qualify. Generally, benefits are paid monthly to people who are unable to work for a year or more because of a disability, and benefits usually continue until you are able to work again on a regular basis.

Yes. The Social Security Administration may ask you to provide documents showing that you are eligible, such as: a birth certificate or other proof of birth; proof of U.S. citizenship or lawful alien status if you were not born in the United States; a U.S. military discharge paper if you had military service before 1968; W-2 forms and/or self-employment tax returns for the last year; medical evidence already in your possession (including medical records, doctors' reports, and recent test results); and award letters, pay stubs, settlement agreements, or other proof of a benefit. The agency may also contact you by telephone or mail if it needs more information or documentation.

To apply for disability benefits for a child under age 18, you need to complete an Application for Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and a Child Disability Report. The report collects information about the child's disabling condition and how it affects his or her ability to function. At this time, only the Child Disability Report can be completed online; you should contact Social Security by phone or in person to schedule an appointment to complete the SSI application. The steps to apply are: (1) Review the Child Disability Starter Kit, which answers common questions about applying for SSI benefits for children and includes a worksheet to help gather the needed information; (2) Contact Social Security right away to find out whether the income and resources of the parents and the child are within the allowed limits, and to start the SSI application process; (3) Fill out the online Child Disability Report. At the end of the report, you will be asked to sign a form giving the child's doctor permission to give Social Security information about his or her disability, which is needed to make a decision on the child's claim. If you do not want to do the report online or need help, you can call toll-free at 1-800-772-1213, or if deaf or hard-of-hearing, call the toll-free TTY number at 1-800-325-0778; representatives are available Monday through Friday between 8 a.m. and 5:30 p.m.

Yes. Social Security provides benefits to you, your spouse, and other eligible family members when you retire, if you become disabled, and when you die. You can use the planners to better understand your Social Security protection as you plan your financial future, then choose a benefit calculator to get estimates of benefits you and your family may be eligible for. For information about benefits for your family, you can go to "Benefits For Your Family."

The Benefits Planner helps you understand your Social Security protection as you plan for your financial future, and you can then choose a benefit calculator to get estimates of benefits you and your family may be eligible for. Social Security can provide you, your spouse, and other eligible family members with benefits when you retire, if you become disabled, and when you die. If you are interested in information about benefits for your family, the planner directs you to the "Benefits For Your Family" section. You can also apply for retirement benefits, disability benefits, or Medicare online if you meet certain criteria, which requires agreeing to a Terms of Service Agreement and creating or logging in to your personal my Social Security account.

You can use the Social Security Benefits Planner to better understand your Social Security protection as you plan for your financial future, and then choose a benefit calculator to get estimates of benefits you and your family may be eligible for. If you want to apply for retirement benefits, disability benefits, or just Medicare and you meet certain criteria, you can complete your application online; you will be asked to agree to a Terms of Service Agreement and create or log in to your personal my Social Security account. Note that family benefits for a spouse or child generally become available when you start receiving Social Security retirement benefits, and if they qualify, your spouse or child may receive a monthly payment of up to one-half of your full retirement benefit amount.

If your spouse is applying for benefits under your record, they may be able to get benefits if they are at least 62 years of age and you are receiving or eligible for retirement or disability benefits. If your spouse qualifies for benefits on their own record, that amount is paid first; if the benefit on your record is higher, they will get an additional amount on your record so the combination equals the higher amount. If they begin receiving benefits between age 62 and their full retirement age, the amount will be permanently reduced by a percentage based on the number of months up to full retirement age. If your spouse is under full retirement age and works while receiving benefits, their benefits may be affected by the retirement earnings test. If they also qualify on their own record, their application will include both benefits. At full retirement age, the spouse's benefit cannot exceed one-half of your full retirement amount. Your spouse can also qualify for Medicare at age 65.

Yes, some family members may qualify to receive benefits on your record when you start receiving Social Security retirement benefits. If they qualify, your spouse or child may receive a monthly payment of up to one-half of your full retirement benefit amount, and these payments will not decrease your retirement benefit. There is a limit to the total amount payable to your family; it generally ranges from about 150 to 180 percent of your full retirement benefit, depending on your benefit amount and the number of qualifying family members. For example, your spouse may be able to get benefits even if they never worked under Social Security, if they are at least 62 years of age and you are receiving or eligible for retirement benefits.

If you die while receiving Social Security disability benefits, certain family members may be eligible for monthly survivor benefits. These can include a widow or widower age 60 or older (50 or older if disabled), a surviving divorced spouse under certain circumstances, a widow or widower at any age caring for the deceased's child who is under age 16 or disabled and receiving benefits on their record, and an unmarried child of the deceased who is younger than age 18 (or up to age 19 if a full-time student in an elementary or secondary school). Benefits can be paid to the worker's children and a surviving spouse caring for the children even if the worker doesn't have the required number of credits, provided the worker has credit for one and one-half years of work (6 credits) in the three years just before death. Because each person's situation is different, you should talk to a Social Security claims representative about your choices. Also, Social Security should be notified as soon as possible when a family member dies, and any funds received for the month of death or later should be returned.

Based on the evidence, if you die, survivors benefits may be payable to your family. Benefits can be paid to your children and to your spouse who is caring for the children even if you don't have the required number of credits, as long as you have credit for one and one-half years of work (6 credits) in the three years just before your death. There is a maximum family amount: the limit varies but is generally between 150 and 180 percent of the basic benefit rate, and if the sum of benefits payable to family members exceeds this limit, benefits are reduced proportionately. Benefits paid to a surviving divorced spouse based on disability or age don't count toward this maximum. There are also limits on how much survivors may earn while receiving benefits. Widows and widowers can receive reduced benefits as early as age 60, or full benefits at full retirement age or older, and benefits as early as age 50 if they're disabled. A widow, widower, or surviving divorced spouse who remarries before age 60 (age 50 if disabled) cannot receive benefits as a surviving spouse while married; if they remarry after that age, they continue to qualify on the deceased spouse's record. A widow, widower, or surviving divorced spouse receiving survivors benefits can switch to their own retirement benefit as early as age 62 if eligible and the retirement rate is higher.
