The evidence does not specifically address how a survivor's own Social Security disability income affects these survivors benefits.

Yes. When you start receiving disability benefits, certain members of your family may also qualify for benefits on your record. Benefits may be paid to your spouse, divorced spouse, children, disabled child, and adult child disabled before age 22. Each family member may be eligible for a monthly benefit of up to 50 percent of your disability benefit amount, though there is a family limit—generally the total you and your family can receive is between 150 and 180 percent of your disability benefit. If the sum payable exceeds the family limit, family members' benefits are reduced proportionately, but your benefit will not be affected. If qualified family members apply, Social Security will ask for their Social Security numbers and birth certificates, and for a spouse applying, possibly proof of marriage and dates of prior marriages.

If the deceased was receiving Social Security benefits, you must return the benefit received for the month of death and any later months. For example, if the person died in July, you must return the benefits paid in August. How you return the benefits depends on how the deceased received them: for funds received by direct deposit, contact the bank or other financial institution and request that any funds received for the month of death or later be returned to Social Security; benefits received by check must be returned to Social Security as soon as possible, and you should not cash any checks received for the month in which the person dies or later.

The evidence does not directly state that applying online is better than other methods, but it lists advantages of the online disability application process: you can start your claim immediately without waiting for an appointment, apply from home or any computer, stop and return to a saved application before submission, avoid trips to a Social Security office, and complete the process online even if you live outside the United States. Note that the online application is currently only available in English.

If you plan to continue working, you may still be able to receive some benefits. If you are under full retirement age and earn over a certain amount, the excess earnings will be deducted from your benefits. There are limits on how much you can earn each year between age 62 and full retirement age and still get all your benefits; depending on your benefit amount and earnings, you may have to give up some benefits, and if your earnings will be high you may decide to wait until full retirement age to start benefits. Once you reach full retirement age, there is no limit on how much you can earn, and if you delay receiving benefits until the month you reach full retirement age, you may receive your benefits with no limit on your earnings.

Yes. You can turn down Part B and decide to enroll later, but your coverage may be delayed and you may have to pay a higher monthly premium for as long as you have Part B. Your monthly premium will go up 10 percent for each 12-month period you were eligible for Part B but didn't sign up, unless you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. If you already have Part A and wish to sign up for Part B later, you can complete form CMS 40-B and take or mail it to your local Social Security office.

Yes, you may be able to get divorced spouse benefits. If you are divorced but your marriage lasted 10 years or longer, you can receive benefits on your ex-spouse's record even if they have remarried, provided that: you are unmarried; you are age 62 or older; your ex-spouse is entitled to Social Security retirement or disability benefits; and the benefit you are entitled to based on your own work is less than the benefit you would receive based on your ex-spouse's work. If you remarry, you generally cannot collect benefits on your former spouse's record unless your later marriage ends (by death, divorce, or annulment). If your ex-spouse has not applied for retirement benefits but can qualify for them, you can receive benefits on their record if you have been divorced for at least two years. If you are eligible for both your own retirement benefits and divorced spouse's benefits, the retirement benefit is paid first; if the benefit on your ex-spouse's record is higher, you will get an additional amount so the combination equals that higher amount.

Even if you do not qualify for benefits on someone else's record, some members of your family may qualify for benefits on your record. If you are interested in information about benefits for your family, go to "Benefits For Your Family." Family members who may qualify on your record include your spouse, divorced spouse, children, disabled child, and adult child disabled before age 22. When qualified family members apply, Social Security will ask for their Social Security numbers and birth certificates; if your spouse is applying, they may also ask for proof of marriage and dates of prior marriages, if applicable. Each family member may be eligible for a monthly benefit of up to 50 percent of your disability benefit amount, though there is a limit on the total amount payable to your family. For retirement benefits, even a spouse who has never worked under Social Security may be able to get benefits if they are at least 62 years of age and you are receiving or eligible for retirement benefits.

If you do not live in the U.S. or one of its territories, you can contact the nearest U.S. Social Security office, U.S. Embassy or consulate. You can also contact the Federal Benefits Unit for your country of residence to apply for retirement benefits.

The evidence provided does not contain a description of the lifetime benefits payable on your record. The available passages discuss related topics—such as divorced-spouse benefits, how lifetime earnings affect benefit amounts, survivor benefits, and spousal benefits—but none states what lifetime benefits will be paid on your record.

If your full retirement age is 66 and you decide to start your retirement benefits at age 65, your benefit will be 93.33 percent of your full benefit amount. In general, your monthly benefits will be reduced if you start them any time before full retirement age, and this reduction is usually permanent.

You must present original documents or copies certified by the issuing agency; photocopies, notarized copies, expired documents, and receipts showing you applied for a document are not accepted. For proof of U.S. citizenship, acceptable documents include a U.S. passport, Certificate of Naturalization N-550/N-570, Certificate of Citizenship N-560/N-561, Certificate of Report of Birth DS-1350, and Consular Report of Birth Abroad FS-240 (CRBA); for someone who has not already established citizenship with SSA, a U.S. birth certificate or U.S. passport is accepted. For age, you must present your foreign birth certificate if you have it or can get it within 10 days; otherwise other documents such as your passport may be considered. For a foreign-born U.S. citizen child, acceptable citizenship documents include Certification of Report of Birth DS-1350, Consular Report of Birth Abroad FS-240, U.S. passport, Certificate of Citizenship N-560/N-561, and Certificate of Naturalization N-550/N-570, and the child's foreign birth certificate is required for age if available or obtainable within 10 days.

Yes. You must present original documents or copies certified by the agency that issued them; photocopies and notarized copies are not accepted. All documents must be current and not expired, and a receipt showing you applied for the document is not accepted. You must provide at least two separate documents, though one document may serve two purposes (for example, a U.S. passport as proof of both citizenship and identity).

Yes, a person can choose to delay retirement: Social Security retirement benefits increase by a certain percentage depending on date of birth if you delay your retirement beyond full retirement age, though the increase no longer applies once you reach age 70. If you decide to delay your retirement, you should sign up for just Medicare at age 65, since not signing up may delay Medicare coverage and cost more. Regarding health insurance coverage expiring before the enrollment period, the evidence describes a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) in the context of Medicare Part B: if you have medical insurance coverage under a group health plan based on your or your spouse's current employment, you may not need to apply for Medicare Part B at age 65, and the late enrollment premium increase does not apply if you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. The evidence does not specifically state whether coverage expiring before the enrollment period makes you eligible for an SEP.

Since you were already receiving benefits on your spouse's record, you generally will not need to file an application for survivors benefits — Social Security will automatically change your monthly benefits to survivors benefits after receiving the report of death. You cannot report a death or apply for survivors benefits online; you can call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Monday through Friday, or visit your local Social Security office. An appointment is not required, but scheduling one ahead may reduce your wait. The evidence notes that documents may be needed when applying for certain benefits, but it does not specify whether all paperwork must be ready before you report the death or apply.
Yes. If you are not getting benefits, you should apply for survivors benefits promptly, because in some cases benefits may not be retroactive.

For help with low-income Medicare beneficiaries, contact your state or local welfare office or Medicaid agency, since only your state can decide if you qualify for assistance with Medicare premiums and other costs. For Extra Help with Medicare prescription drug costs, you can also visit the Extra Help with your Medicare prescription drug costs page. Additionally, your State Health Insurance Counseling and Assistance Program (SHIP) can help answer your Medicare questions, and you can find your local SHIP contact information in the back of your Medicare & You 2020 Handbook online or request it when you call.

The evidence does not specify a payment date based on an approval date. For Social Security disability benefits, the first benefit is paid for the sixth full month after the date the disability began, and benefits are paid in the month following the month for which they are due. For retirement benefits, benefits are paid the month after they are due; for example, if benefits start in April, the first payment arrives in May. Because your disability onset date or benefit start date is not provided, an exact first payment date cannot be determined.

For security reasons, there are time limits for viewing each page. You will receive a warning after 25 minutes without doing anything, and you can extend your time on the page. After the third warning, you must move to another page or your time will run out and your work on that page will be lost.

No. After the third warning, you must move to another page or your information will not be saved, and your work on that page will be lost. The evidence does not say that you can start a new session and complete the unsaved information; it only explains that you can start the application now and finish it later, or return to a saved application later without losing the information you entered.

The evidence does not state that applying for Medicare is mandatory. It explains that when you apply for Medicare you can sign up for Part A Hospital Insurance and Part B Medical Insurance, and that because you must pay a premium for Part B coverage, you can turn it down (though enrolling later may incur a late enrollment penalty). If you don't have Medicare but are within 3 months of age 65, you can use the retirement application to apply for both retirement and Medicare, or just Medicare if you aren't ready to receive retirement benefits yet. As for benefits, anyone who has Medicare can get Medicare prescription drug coverage, and some people with limited resources and income may be able to get Extra Help to pay for the costs.

Yes. Social Security offers many time-saving online services to help you stay in control, including checking your application status, setting up or changing direct deposit, getting a proof of income letter, getting a Social Security 1099 (SSA-1099) form, requesting a replacement Social Security card, opting out of certain mailed notices, and advanced designation of representative payee. You can visit the online services page for a complete list, search the comprehensive FAQs for help with specific retirement issues, or visit the contact us page for other ways to get support. A free my Social Security account also helps you manage your information and keep track of your records.

If you receive a suspicious call from someone claiming to be from Social Security, hang up and then report details of the call to the Office of the Inspector General by submitting a report online. If you receive a suspicious email claiming to be from Social Security or one of its marketing firms, do not respond or click any links; instead, report it by forwarding the suspicious email to the U.S. Computer Emergency Readiness Team (US-CERT) at phishing-report@us-cert.gov.

For security reasons, there are time limits for viewing each page. You will receive a warning after 25 minutes without doing anything, and you will be able to extend your time on the page. After the third warning, you must move to another page or your time will run out and your work on that page will be lost (your information will not be saved).

To help keep your personal information safe, you can confirm your email address or phone number by entering a one-time security code within 10 minutes of receiving it. You can also add NO-REPLY@ssa.gov to your contact list so security emails don't go into your spam or junk folder, and visit the Federal Trade Commission's OnGuard Online for additional tips to stay safe and secure online. You may also choose to add extra security when you create an online account, and you can create a my Social Security account to help keep track of your records. If you receive a suspicious call from someone claiming to be from Social Security, hang up and report the details of the call to the Office of the Inspector General by submitting a report online.

Pages expire due to security-related time limits for viewing each page, not necessarily because you were on it very long. You receive a warning after 25 minutes without doing anything, and you can extend your time on the page. After the third warning, you must move to another page or your time will run out and your work on that page will be lost.

Yes. You can complete the online retirement application and review your answers and make corrections before you submit it. When you're finished, you click "Submit Now" to send your application to Social Security. The evidence also mentions a "Return to a Saved Application" option, indicating you can save your application and return to it later before submitting.

The Disability Planner helps you find out how you and your family may qualify for benefits if you become severely disabled before you qualify for retirement benefits. It also helps you find out how you can qualify and apply for benefits, what happens if your application is approved, who can receive benefits on your earnings record, and what you need to know about receiving disability benefits.

You are protected through several measures. Social Security has a robust cybersecurity program and follows federal guidelines, using an identity verification process that requires signing in with a username and password, offers extra security, and complies with federal laws, regulations, and guidelines. Your personal my Social Security account is for your use only—no one can create or use an account on your behalf, even with written permission, and you should not share your account with anyone. You can also protect yourself by not routinely carrying your Social Security card, never saying your Social Security number aloud in public, being aware of phishing scams (emails, links, texts, and phone calls), and creating a my Social Security account to track your records.

Based on the evidence, creating an online account involves several protections: you verify your identity by providing personal information and answering questions only you are likely to know, you create a username and password, and you confirm your email address or phone number by entering a one-time security code within 10 minutes of receiving it to help keep your personal information safe. You can also choose to add extra security when you create an online account. If you are unable or unwilling to create an account online, you may still create an account in person by visiting your local Social Security office. For additional tips to help you stay safe and secure online, you can visit the Federal Trade Commission's OnGuard Online.

You can choose to add extra security when you create an online account. In addition to your username and password, you can choose either your cell phone or email address as your second identification method when you sign in or register; each time you sign in you enter your username and password and then the security code sent by text message or email. Two forms of identification help better protect your account from unauthorized use and potential identity fraud. Note that the policy has changed for this one service: we may now ask for the last eight digits of your Visa or MasterCard. If you are unable or unwilling to create an online account, you can still create one in person at your local Social Security office.

Yes, you can ask another question. To get a Social Security Benefit Verification Letter, log in to your my Social Security account for instant access. If you already have an account, sign in, go to Replacement Documents on the right side of the screen, and choose get a Benefit Verification Letter to view, save, and print your personalized letter. If you don't have an account, you can create a free my Social Security account in less than 10 minutes, which lets you download or print your letter. If you still have questions or need help, call 1-800-772-1213 or visit your Social Security office; for deaf or hard of hearing, call TTY 1-800-325-0778 between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Monday through Friday.

The Benefits Planner helps you better understand your Social Security protection as you plan for your financial future, and you can then choose a benefit calculator to get estimates of benefits you and your family may be eligible for. If you already have enough Social Security credits to qualify for benefits, you can use the Retirement Estimator to get a personalized, instant estimate of your retirement benefits, entering different dates and ages to determine the best time to retire. If you want an estimate for survivors or disability benefits, or you do not already have enough credits to qualify, use one of the benefit calculators. You can also apply for retirement benefits, disability benefits, or Medicare online if you meet certain criteria, which requires agreeing to a Terms of Service Agreement and creating or logging in to your personal my Social Security account.

Yes. If you continue to work while receiving benefits, the retirement benefit earnings limit still applies. There are limits on how much you can earn each year between age 62 and full retirement age and still get all your benefits; depending on your benefit amount and earnings, you may have to give up some benefits. If you are under full retirement age and earn over a certain amount, the excess earnings are deducted from your benefits. Once you reach full retirement age, there is no limit on how much you can earn.

To figure out the amount of your benefits, you can use the Retirement Estimator if you have enough Social Security credits to qualify and are not currently receiving benefits on your own record, waiting for a decision on an application for benefits or Medicare, age 62 or older and receiving benefits on another Social Security record, or eligible for a pension based on work not covered by Social Security. For the most accurate estimates, you can use the Detailed Calculator, which requires entering all your past earnings as shown on your online record.

The evidence describes requirements for filing for SSI online as an adult with a disability: you must be between the ages of 18 and 65, have never been married, not be blind, and be a U.S. citizen residing in one of the fifty states or the District of Columbia. More generally, SSI is for disabled adults and children who have limited income and resources, and people without enough work credits for Social Security Disability benefits may possibly qualify for SSI if they have limited income and resources.

Based on the evidence, the documents involved in a disability benefits application include medical records, doctors' reports, and recent test results; award letters, pay stubs, settlement agreements, or other proof of any temporary or permanent workers' compensation-type benefits received; and proof of birth such as a birth certificate. Photocopies of W-2 forms, self-employment tax returns, or medical documents are accepted, but the original of most other documents (such as a birth certificate) must be seen and will be returned. Applicants should not delay applying because they lack all documents, as help is available to obtain them. If documents are mailed, the Social Security number must be included (written on a separate sheet of paper, not on the original documents) so they can be matched with the correct application; alternatively, documents may be brought to a Social Security office. Foreign birth records and Department of Homeland Security documents should not be mailed but brought to a Social Security office.

Yes. People who have worked long enough may be able to receive Social Security disability or retirement benefits as well as SSI. The Social Security disability insurance program pays benefits if you worked long enough and paid Social Security taxes, while SSI pays benefits to disabled adults and children with limited income and resources.

Yes. If you have a security freeze on your credit report, you can still open a my Social Security account by temporarily lifting it. Contact the Identity Services Provider and request that they temporarily lift your security freeze, then create your account online after lifting it. You can reinstate the freeze afterward if needed; the provider may automatically reinstate it after your temporary lift expires. If you don't want to temporarily lift your freeze, you can visit your local Social Security office to open an account in person.

The evidence does not directly address whether receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) affects eligibility for a higher Social Security benefit based on your parents' work. It does state that if you have worked, you may be eligible for a higher retirement benefit or a higher disability benefit based on your own work. It also notes that if your parent is deceased or receiving Social Security benefits, you may be eligible for child benefits based on your parent's work, and that you may be able to get additional income through the SSI program. Additionally, certain life changes may affect eligibility for an increase in federal benefits, and you can find out whether you might be eligible for a benefit based on another person's work or a higher benefit based on your own work through the Social Security website. However, the evidence does not specifically confirm whether SSI receipt affects eligibility for a higher benefit based on a parent's work.

Yes. If your spouse or ex-spouse has died, you may be eligible for a higher survivor benefit based on his or her work. The death of an ex-spouse may allow you to be eligible for a higher survivor benefit even if you are already receiving a survivor benefit on another spouse. Certain life changes, such as the death of a spouse or ex-spouse, may affect eligibility for an increase in your federal benefits.

No. Your personal mySocial Security account is for your use only. You are the only one who can create it for your own exclusive use, and no one can create or use an account on your behalf, even with written permission. You should not share the use of your account with anyone else under any circumstances, as unauthorized use is a misrepresentation of your identity to the federal government and could subject you to criminal or civil penalties, or both.

No. Your personal my Social Security account is for your use only. You are the only one who can create your personal my Social Security account for your own exclusive use, and no one can create or use an account on your behalf, even with written permission. You should not share the use of your account with anyone else under any circumstances, as unauthorized use is a misrepresentation of your identity to the federal government and could subject you to criminal or civil penalties, or both.

To get your benefit verification letter online, sign in to your mySocial Security account, go to Replacement Documents on the right side of the screen, and choose get a Benefit Verification Letter to view, save, and print your personalized letter. If you don't have a mySocial Security account, you can create one for free in less than 10 minutes, which lets you download or print your benefit verification letter. If you have questions or need help understanding how to request your benefit verification letter online, call 1-800-772-1213 or visit your Social Security office; if you are deaf or hard of hearing, call the TTY number 1-800-325-0778 between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Monday through Friday.
You need 40 Social Security credits to qualify for retirement benefits (for people born after 1928, or 1929 or later). Typically, earning 40 credits represents about 10 years of work.

You earn Social Security credits when you work and pay Social Security taxes. Since 1978, you can earn up to a maximum of four credits per year. To qualify for retirement benefits, you generally need at least 40 credits (if you were born after 1928, or in 1929 or later), which usually represents about 10 years of work. The number of credits only determines eligibility, not the benefit amount; your benefit amount is based on the average of your earnings over your working years, not the total number of credits.

The evidence does not state whether you personally have a security freeze or fraud alert on your credit report; that is a question you would need to answer about your own situation. The evidence explains that if you have a security freeze, fraud alert, or both on your credit report, you can still open a my Social Security account by temporarily lifting it. You would contact the Identity Services Provider and request that they temporarily lift your security freeze or fraud alert, then create the account online after lifting it, and reinstate the freeze or alert if needed. The Identity Services Provider may automatically reinstate it after your temporary lift expires. If you don't want to temporarily lift your security freeze or fraud alert, you can visit your local Social Security office to open an account in person.

Yes, the evidence addresses this: if you are deaf or hard of hearing, you can call the TTY number at 1-800-325-0778. You can also visit your local Social Security office in person, and you should call first to make an appointment. If you do not live in the U.S. or one of its territories, you can contact the nearest U.S. Social Security office, U.S. Embassy, or consulate.

You may be able to request a replacement Social Security card online. The online service is described as a fast and secure way to get a replacement. If you are age 18 or older, have a U.S. mailing address, and have a my Social Security account, you can apply for a replacement card online. For more information about creating a my Social Security account and getting a replacement card online, visit the Social Security Number and Card website. Replacement cards are free if your card is lost or stolen, though you may not need a replacement since knowing your Social Security number is what's important. You are limited to three replacement cards per year and 10 during your lifetime; legal name changes do not count toward these limits, and the limits may not apply if you can prove you need the card to prevent a significant hardship.

Yes. For a person age 65 and older, the Social Security Administration says to call 1-800-772-1213. If the person is deaf or hard of hearing, the TTY number is 1-800-325-0778. You can also visit your local Social Security office, but call first to make an appointment.

Yes. Besides applying online, you can apply for retirement benefits by phone (call 1-800-772-1213; TTY 1-800-325-0778, from 7 AM to 7 PM Monday through Friday) or in person by visiting your local Social Security office (call first to make an appointment). If you do not live in the U.S. or one of its territories, you can also contact the nearest U.S. Social Security office, U.S. Embassy, or consulate.

You may be eligible for increased Social Security or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits if certain life changes occur. For example, if your spouse or ex-spouse dies, you may become eligible for a higher survivor benefit based on his or her work, even if you already receive a survivor benefit on another spouse. If you have worked, you may be eligible for a higher disability benefit based on your own work. If you are at least 62 and unmarried, you may be eligible for a benefit based on a former spouse's work if that marriage lasted 10 years or more. You may be eligible for spouse's benefits if you have in your care a child under age 16 or disabled prior to age 22, and your child may be eligible for benefits based on your work. If you served in the U.S. military, you may be eligible for benefits through the Veterans Administration. If you are unmarried and under age 18 or were disabled prior to age 22, and your parent is deceased or receiving Social Security benefits, you may be eligible for child benefits based on your parent's work. You can use the Benefit Eligibility Screening Tool (BEST) to find out which benefits you might be eligible for and how to qualify and apply.

Yes. There is a limit on the amount family members can receive each month. The limit varies, but it is generally equal to between 150 and 180 percent of the basic benefit rate. If the sum of benefits payable to family members exceeds this limit, the benefits are reduced proportionately. Benefits paid to a surviving divorced spouse based on disability or age do not count toward this maximum amount.

You or your family members may be eligible for increased benefits if you receive Social Security or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and certain life changes occur. For example, if your spouse or ex-spouse dies, you may become eligible for a higher Social Security benefit. You may also be eligible for a benefit based on another person's work, or a higher benefit based on your own work. Additionally, when you start receiving disability benefits, certain family members may qualify for benefits on your record, including your spouse, divorced spouse, children, disabled child, and adult child disabled before age 22.

To find out what benefits you qualify for, you can use the Social Security Administration's online tools. If you already have enough Social Security credits to qualify for benefits, you can use the Retirement Estimator to get a personalized, instant estimate of your retirement benefits, entering different dates and ages to determine the best time to retire. If you want an estimate for survivors or disability benefits, or you do not yet have enough credits to qualify, you can use one of the benefit calculators to estimate your future retirement, disability, and survivors benefits. You can also use the Retirement Planner to learn how you qualify for Social Security retirement benefits, about possible benefits you may be eligible for on someone else's record, and which family members may get benefits based on your earnings record. Additionally, you may qualify for spouse's benefits even if you never worked under Social Security if you are the spouse or divorced spouse of a retired or disabled worker, or the widow/widower or surviving divorced spouse of a deceased worker.

Social Security pays disability benefits to people who can't work because they have a medical condition expected to last at least one year or result in death. To find out if you qualify, you can use the Disability Planner, which helps you learn whether you qualify and how Social Security can help. To qualify, you must first have worked in jobs covered by Social Security and have a medical condition that meets Social Security's definition of disability; in general, monthly benefits are paid to people unable to work for a year or more because of a disability. You can apply for disability benefits online if you are age 18 or older, are not currently receiving benefits on your own Social Security record, are unable to work because of a medical condition expected to last at least 12 months or result in death, and have not been denied disability benefits in the last 60 days.

You or your family members may be eligible for increased benefits. If you or a family member receive Social Security or Supplemental Security Income (SSI), certain life changes may affect eligibility for an increase in your federal benefits—for example, if your spouse or ex-spouse dies, you may become eligible for a higher Social Security benefit. You can find out whether you or a family member might be eligible for a benefit based on another person's work, or a higher benefit based on your own work, through the information about benefits on the Social Security website. In addition, when you start receiving Social Security retirement benefits, some family members may also qualify to receive benefits on your record; if they qualify, your spouse or child may receive a monthly payment of up to one-half of your full retirement benefit amount, and these payments will not decrease your retirement benefit. When you start receiving disability benefits, certain family members may also qualify for benefits on your record—benefits may be paid to your spouse, divorced spouse, children, disabled child, and adult child disabled before age 22—and each family member may be eligible for a monthly benefit of up to 50 percent of your disability benefit amount, subject to a maximum family amount.

The evidence describes benefits under several different VA programs, but it doesn't identify which program applies to you, so I can't say specifically what benefits you get. The benefits listed include: under the VR&E Independent Living Track, services may include evaluation and counseling to identify your needs and goals, home consultations with specialists, referral to support resources, and guidance on eligibility for adaptive-housing programs (these services generally last up to 24 months); under Educational and Career Counseling (Chapter 36), counseling to help you decide which civilian or military jobs you want, help finding a training program or job, educational and career counseling, and academic and adjustment counseling; under VEAP, money for tuition; for survivors and dependents, education and training, money for tuition, money for housing, and money for books and supplies; and under Work Study, you can get paid to work a part-time job while you study.

You can contact the Social Security Administration by phone at 1-800-772-1213 from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Friday; if you are deaf or hard of hearing, call TTY 1-800-325-0778. You can also visit your local Social Security office in person, calling first to make an appointment. If you do not live in the U.S. or one of its territories, you can contact the nearest U.S. Social Security office, U.S. Embassy, or consulate.

Yes. Social Security Family Benefits are benefits that qualifying family members may receive on a worker's record, such as a spouse or children. There is a limit on how much a family can receive: the total depends on your benefit amount and the number of family members who qualify on your record, and generally the total you and your family can receive is about 150 to 180 percent of your full retirement benefit (or, for disability, between 150 and 180 percent of your disability benefit). If the sum of benefits payable is greater than the family limit, benefits to family members are reduced proportionately, while your own benefit is not affected. For survivors, the monthly family limit is generally equal to between 150 and 180 percent of the basic benefit rate, and benefits paid to a surviving divorced spouse based on disability or age do not count toward this maximum.

If you are not yet receiving Social Security or SSI benefits but plan to apply, tell the Social Security representative when you apply for benefits that you want to sign up for Direct Deposit. If you already have a bank account, bring your checkbook or a copy of your bank statement with you. If you don't have an account, you must open one before you can sign up for Direct Deposit; when you choose an account, let the representative at the financial institution know you are interested in signing up to receive your benefits by Direct Deposit.

For questions or help understanding how to set up or change direct deposit online, call the toll-free number at 1-800-772-1213 or visit your Social Security office. If you are deaf or hard of hearing, call the toll-free TTY number at 1-800-325-0778 between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Monday through Friday.
For more information about phishing, go to OnGuard Online. You can also keep your web browser up to date to help avoid security problems.

The evidence does not explain how to check whether you personally have a security freeze on your credit report. It only describes situations in which you would need to lift or remove a freeze: for a PLUS Loan application, you must lift or remove the freeze at each credit bureau before continuing, and the application will not be processed if you have a security freeze. For a my Social Security account, you can still open an account by temporarily lifting a security freeze or fraud alert through the Identity Services Provider, or you can visit your local Social Security office to open an account in person. For more information on security freezes and fraud alerts, the evidence points to the Federal Trade Commission's Credit Freeze FAQs.

Yes. After temporarily lifting your security freeze or fraud alert, you can create a my Social Security account online. If you don't want to temporarily lift it, you can visit your local Social Security office to open an account in person. Regarding someone else opening an account in your stead: for your protection, you're the only one who can create your personal my Social Security account for your own exclusive use. No one can create or use an account on your behalf, even with written permission, and you shouldn't share use of your account with anyone else under any circumstances, as unauthorized use is a misrepresentation of your identity to the federal government and could subject you to criminal or civil penalties, or both.

To set up direct deposit for your benefit payment, have your Social Security number, bank routing transit number, account type (checking or savings), and account number ready. If you already receive Social Security or SSI benefits and have a bank account, log in to or create a free my Social Security account. Once signed in, select the blue Benefits & Payment Details link on the right side of the screen, scroll down and select the Update Direct Deposit button, choose whether you are the owner or co-owner of the bank account, enter your bank account information and select Next, then review and verify your banking information and select Submit, then Done. You can also decide when your change will take effect using the My Profile tab within mySocial Security. Alternatively, you can contact your bank, credit union, or savings and loan association, call Social Security toll-free at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778), or consider the Direct Express debit card, which does not require a bank account.

If you already receive Social Security or SSI benefits and have a bank account, you can sign up for Direct Deposit by starting or changing Direct Deposit online (Social Security benefits only), by contacting your bank, credit union, or savings and loan association, or by calling Social Security toll-free at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). If you don't have a bank account, you can consider the Direct Express debit card, which lets you access your benefits without a bank account; your federal benefit payment is deposited directly into your card account. To set up direct deposit, have your Social Security number, bank routing transit number, account type (checking or savings), and account number ready.

If you plan to continue working, there are limits on how much you can earn each year between age 62 and full retirement age and still get all your benefits; depending on your benefit amount and your earnings for the year, you may have to give up some of your benefits. If your earnings will be high, you may decide to wait until full retirement age to start your benefits. Once you reach full retirement age, there is no limit on how much you can earn. Also, if you are under full retirement age and earn over a certain amount, the excess earnings will be deducted from your benefits, but if you delay receiving benefits until the month you reach full retirement age, you may receive your benefits with no limit on your earnings.

You can work while receiving Social Security retirement benefits, and doing so could mean a higher benefit for you in the future. Each year the records of all working Social Security recipients are reviewed; if your earnings for the prior year are higher than one of the years used to compute your retirement benefit, the benefit amount will be recalculated, with the increase paid retroactive to January of the year after you earned the money. Higher benefits can be important later in life and can increase future benefit amounts your family and survivors could receive. Whether you are under full retirement age matters: if you are under full retirement age and continue to work while receiving benefits, your benefits may be affected by the retirement earnings test, and if you are younger than full retirement age and make more than the yearly earnings limit, your earnings may reduce your benefits.

Yes. You can apply for retirement benefits before reaching full retirement age, but your benefits will be reduced because you are taking them earlier. You can start your retirement benefit at any point from age 62 up until age 70, and the benefit amount is higher the longer you delay starting it. For example, if your full retirement age is 66 and you start your retirement benefits at age 65, your benefit will be 93.33 percent of your full benefit amount.

The additional information provided is a link titled "What's the best time to start your retirement benefits?" The SSA does not recommend starting at age 62, full retirement age, age 70, or any age in between, and offers further resources to help you decide: "Early or Late Retirement?", "Retirement Information for Medicare Beneficiaries to Consider", and "Other Things".

If you have not signed up, the evidence addresses signing up for Medicare rather than retirement benefits: if you decide to delay your retirement, be sure to sign up for just Medicare at age 65, because if you do not sign up, in some circumstances your Medicare coverage may be delayed and cost more. The evidence does not state what happens to Social Security retirement benefits if you have not signed up for them.

You can start receiving retirement benefits at any point from age 62 up until age 70, and your benefit amount will be higher the longer you delay starting it (this adjustment is usually permanent). If you apply before full retirement age, your benefits will be reduced. Since you have not yet reached full retirement age but will in six months, starting now would mean reduced monthly benefits, while waiting until your full retirement age or later could increase your benefit through delayed retirement credits. Delayed retirement credits may be added if benefits start after full retirement age, and the increase no longer applies once you reach age 70. Also, if you elect to receive benefits before full retirement age, you should understand how continuing to work can affect your benefits. If you decide to delay, be sure to sign up for just Medicare at age 65, since failing to sign up could delay your Medicare coverage and cost more.

The evidence does not state an income percentage at full retirement age. It explains that if you delay receiving retirement benefits after reaching full retirement age, up to age 70, you can increase your benefit by accumulating Delayed Retirement Credits, and that the increase depends on your date of birth. For example, if your full retirement age is 66 and 2 months and you wait until age 70, your benefit will be 130.67 percent of your full retirement age benefit.

The evidence does not identify a single best age to start retirement benefits; it states that the SSA is not recommending starting at age 62, full retirement age, age 70, or any age in between, and suggests reviewing early versus late retirement information to decide what is right for you. Relevant considerations: you may start benefits as early as age 62 or as late as age 70; benefits are reduced if started before full retirement age; delayed retirement credits may be added if benefits start after full retirement age, with the increase depending on date of birth and no longer applying once you reach age 70; if you have reached full retirement age, you can choose to start benefits before the month you apply, but retroactive benefits cannot be paid for any month before you reached full retirement age or more than 6 months in the past; and if you delay retirement, be sure to sign up for just Medicare at age 65 to avoid possible delays and higher costs.

There is no single "best age" for everyone to start retirement benefits; it is your choice, and you should make an informed decision based on your individual and family circumstances. You can start retirement benefits as early as age 62 or as late as age 70. Your monthly benefit amount can differ substantially depending on the age you start: if you start before your full retirement age, your benefit will be smaller but you will receive it for a longer period of time; if you start at your full retirement age or later, you will receive a larger monthly benefit for a shorter period of time. The amount you receive when you first get benefits sets the base for the amount you will receive for the rest of your life. The SSA does not recommend starting at age 62, your full retirement age, age 70, or any age in between. Other things to consider include that some company pensions include a Social Security-equivalent supplement that stops automatically at age 62, and if your spouse or minor or disabled children also qualify for benefits from your record, the value of their benefits added to your own may help you decide whether taking benefits sooner is your best choice. To apply, you can apply four months before you want benefits to start; to start at age 62, you can apply at age 61 and eight months.

Yes. The evidence lists several retirement planning tools: the Benefit Eligibility Screening Tool (BEST) to identify other Social Security programs you may be eligible for; the Employee Benefit Research Institute's Ballpark E$timator calculator to get a basic idea of how much you need to save before you retire; Department of Labor publications and reports on health benefits and retirement planning; the Retirement Savings Toolkit with English and Spanish publications about retirement savings; the MyMoney.gov "Planning for Retirement / Retiring" page with various retirement planning tools, including a Medicare Eligibility Tool; the USA.gov Retirement Resources site with financial planning tools, including a Federal Employees Retirement Calculator; and the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation's Find an Unclaimed Pension tool if your defined benefit pension plan was terminated. Additionally, you can create a free my Social Security account to check your earnings history, and the Retirement Calculator within my Social Security provides personalized retirement benefit estimates based on your actual earnings, showing how the date or age you begin benefits affects your future income. Other tools are available on the Social Security Calculators page.

When you die, a one-time payment of $255 can be paid to your surviving spouse if he or she was living with you, or, if living apart, was receiving certain Social Security benefits on your record. If there is no surviving spouse, the payment is made to a child who is eligible for benefits on your record in the month of death. If you were receiving monthly Social Security benefits, the benefit received for the month of death and any later months must be returned; for example, if the person died in July, the benefits paid in August must be returned. How the benefits are returned depends on how they were received—for funds received by direct deposit, contact the bank or other financial institution and request that any funds received for the month of death or later be returned to Social Security. Survivors may also be eligible for other benefits: a child attending secondary school full time can be eligible to receive Social Security benefits when you die, and a child can get benefits at any age if they were disabled before age 22 and remain disabled; stepchildren, grandchildren, step grandchildren, or adopted children may also receive benefits under certain circumstances. Your parents may qualify if you were providing at least half of their support and they are not eligible for a higher retirement benefit, and generally a parent must not have married after your death, though there are exceptions.

No. Survivors' benefits for children are not automatic for all workers with children. A worker's protection is particularly important for young families with children, and even very young workers may have this protection, but eligibility depends on work credits and how they affect survivors benefits. Children may qualify only under certain circumstances: an unmarried child under 18 (up to age 19 if attending elementary or secondary school full time) of a worker who dies can be eligible, and benefits can be paid at any age if the child was disabled before age 22 and remains disabled. Besides natural children, stepchildren, grandchildren, or adopted children may receive benefits under certain circumstances.

There is no single "best age" for everyone to start retirement benefits; ultimately, it is your choice. The Social Security Administration does not recommend starting at age 62, your full retirement age, age 70, or any age in between. You should make an informed decision based on your individual and family circumstances. Your monthly benefit amount can differ substantially depending on when you start: starting before your full retirement age gives a smaller benefit but for a longer period, while starting at full retirement age or later gives a larger monthly benefit for a shorter period. You may start benefits as early as age 62 or as late as age 70.

Yes. Social Security retirement benefits are increased by a certain percentage depending on date of birth if you delay your retirement beyond full retirement age. The amount continues to increase up until age 70, and the benefit increase no longer applies once you reach age 70, even if you continue to delay taking benefits. For example, if your full retirement age is 66 and 2 months and you wait until age 70, your benefit will be 130.67 percent of your full benefit amount.

Not necessarily. If you are age 65 or older and your medical insurance coverage is under a group health plan based on your or your spouse's current employment, you may not need to apply for Medicare Part B at age 65. You may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) that lets you sign up for Part B during any month you remain covered under the group health plan and your (or your spouse's) employment continues, or during the 8-month period beginning the month after your group health plan coverage or the employment it is based on ends, whichever comes first. Otherwise, if you are eligible at age 65, your initial enrollment period begins three months before your 65th birthday, includes the month you turn 65, and ends three months after that birthday; if you don't enroll during that period, you can sign up during a general enrollment period from January 1 through March 31, with coverage beginning July 1 of the year you enroll. Also, your monthly premium will go up 10 percent for each 12-month period you were eligible for Part B but didn't sign up, unless you qualify for a special enrollment period.

If you choose not to enroll in Medicare Part B when you are eligible and then decide to enroll later, your coverage may be delayed and you may have to pay a higher monthly premium for as long as you have Part B. Specifically, your monthly premium will go up 10 percent for each 12-month period you were eligible for Part B but did not sign up, unless you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period.

Yes. You can apply online using the Social Security Retirement/Medicare Benefit Application for retirement, spouse's, divorced spouse's, or Medicare benefits, by phone at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778), or in person at your local Social Security office. If your spouse is already receiving benefits when you apply, or if you both apply at the same time, Social Security will also check your eligibility for benefits as a spouse, and if you qualify, your application will automatically serve as a request for spousal benefits. Regarding a maximum, if a child also qualifies for benefits there is a limit on the total your family can receive; it depends on the benefit amount and the number of family members qualifying on the record, but generally the total is about 150 to 180 percent of the worker's full retirement benefit.

You can find information about Social Security benefits for your family by going to the "Benefits For Your Family" section on the Social Security website. The evidence also notes that even if you do not qualify for benefits on someone else's record, some members of your family may qualify for benefits on your record.

Since you are married and have children, you can find information about benefits for your family by going to "Benefits For Your Family." If one of your children also qualifies for benefits, there is a limit to the total your family can receive; it generally ranges from about 150 to 180 percent of your full retirement benefit, depending on your benefit amount and the number of family members who qualify on your record. If qualified family members apply with you, you will be asked for their Social Security numbers and birth certificates.

Possibly. According to the evidence, you or your family members may be eligible for increased benefits. If you or a family member receive Social Security or Supplemental Security Income (SSI), certain life changes may affect eligibility for an increase in federal benefits—for example, if your spouse or ex-spouse dies, you may become eligible for a higher Social Security benefit. To find out whether you or a family member might be eligible for a benefit based on another person's work, or a higher benefit based on your own work, see the information about benefits on the Social Security website. The evidence does not determine eligibility for your specific family members; it directs you to check the Social Security website for an individual determination.

Yes. If you receive Social Security or Supplemental Security Income (SSI), certain life changes may affect eligibility for an increase in your federal benefits for you or a family member. For example, if your spouse or ex-spouse dies, you may become eligible for a higher Social Security benefit. To find out whether you or a family member might be eligible for a benefit based on another person's work, or a higher benefit based on your own work, see the information about benefits on the Social Security website.

Since you already receive SSI, certain life changes may affect your eligibility for an increase in your federal benefits. For example, if your spouse or ex-spouse dies, you may become eligible for a higher Social Security benefit. To find out if you might be eligible for a benefit based on another person's work, or a higher benefit based on your own work, see the information about benefits on the Social Security website. You can also contact a local Social Security office or call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., Monday through Friday.

Yes. You can apply for SSI at the same time as Social Security Disability Insurance, and in fact applying for SSDI at the same time as your SSI claim is one of the conditions for filing for SSI online. To file online for SSI you must: be between 18 and 65; have never been married; not be blind; be a U.S. citizen residing in one of the fifty states, the District of Columbia, or the Northern Mariana Islands; not have applied for or received SSI in the past; and be applying for Social Security Disability Insurance at the same time as your SSI claim. After you finish the online process, a Social Security representative will contact you by phone or mail for any additional information needed. You can also schedule an appointment with a local Social Security office to file an application. Note that people who have worked long enough may be able to receive Social Security disability benefits as well as SSI.

The evidence does not address SSDI disability criteria for a child who is not yet 18. The criteria described apply to an "adult child," who must be unmarried, age 18 or older, have a disability that started before age 22, and meet the adult definition of disability; benefits are paid on the parent's earnings record, and the adult child must not have substantial earnings (in 2019, earning more than $1,220 a month). For a child age 18 or older, disability is evaluated the same way as for any adult, with the application sent to the state Disability Determination Services. Separately, a child under age 18 may be disabled, but the child's disability is not considered when deciding if the child qualifies as a dependent, and the child's benefits normally stop at age 18 unless the child is a full-time elementary or high school student (benefits can continue until age 19) or is disabled.

To qualify for Social Security disability benefits, you must first have worked in jobs covered by Social Security. You must also have a medical condition that meets Social Security's definition of disability; in general, monthly benefits are paid to people who are unable to work for a year or more because of a disability. In addition to meeting the definition of disability, you must have worked long enough and recently enough under Social Security to qualify. Work credits are based on your total yearly wages or self-employment income, and you can earn up to four credits each year; the number of credits needed depends on your age when you become disabled. Benefits usually continue until you are able to work again on a regular basis, and if you are receiving disability benefits when you reach full retirement age, they automatically convert to retirement benefits, with the amount remaining the same.

Based on the evidence, you may start receiving retirement benefits as early as age 62 or as late as age 70. Full retirement age, also called normal retirement age, is the age at which you may first become entitled to full or unreduced retirement benefits; depending on your date of birth, this may be between age 66 and 67. You can retire at any time between age 62 and full retirement age, but if you start benefits early, your benefits are reduced a fraction of a percent for each month before your full retirement age. If you start benefits after your full retirement age, delayed retirement credits may be added. Also, if you elect to receive benefits before full retirement age, continuing to work can affect your benefits. The evidence does not specify benefits for a particular age because your age and year of birth were not provided.

The evidence does not address a special enrollment period for retirement benefits after full retirement age. It only describes a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) for Medicare Part B, which applies if you are age 65 or older and covered under a group health plan based on your or your spouse's current employment; you may qualify during any month you remain covered under the group health plan and the employment continues, or during the 8-month period beginning the month after the coverage or employment ends, whichever comes first. There is an exception if the coverage or employment ends during your initial enrollment period for Medicare Part B. The evidence also notes that a late enrollment penalty may apply unless you qualify for a special enrollment period, and that delaying retirement benefits past full retirement age up to age 70 can increase your benefit through Delayed Retirement Credits.

Yes. A spouse's current employment can matter for Medicare special enrollment period eligibility: if you are age 65 or older and your medical insurance coverage is under a group health plan based on your or your spouse's current employment, you may not need to apply for Medicare Part B at age 65 and may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. That SEP lets you sign up during any month you remain covered under the group health plan and your or your spouse's employment continues, or during the 8-month period beginning the month after the group health plan coverage or the employment it is based on ends, whichever comes first. There is an exception if that coverage or employment ends during your initial enrollment period for Medicare Part B. Regarding retirement benefits, if your spouse is under full retirement age and works while receiving benefits, their benefits may be affected by the retirement earnings test; at full retirement age, the spouse's benefit cannot exceed one-half of your full retirement amount. Also, benefits paid to you as a spouse will not decrease your spouse's retirement benefit.

There is a limit on the total amount that can be paid to your family. The total depends on your benefit amount and the number of family members who also qualify on your record. It varies, but generally the total amount you and your family can receive is between 150 and 180 percent of your benefit (about 150 to 180 percent of your full retirement benefit for retirement, or between 150 and 180 percent of your disability benefit for disability). If the sum of the benefits payable on your account is greater than the family limit, the benefits to the family members will be reduced proportionately, and your own benefit will not be affected. For survivors, the limit is generally equal to between 150 and 180 percent of the basic benefit rate, and any benefits paid to a surviving divorced spouse based on disability or age won't count toward this maximum amount.

If the deceased was receiving Social Security benefits, you must return the benefit received for the month of death and any later months. For example, if the person died in July, you must return the benefits paid in August. How you return the benefits depends on how the deceased received them; for funds received by direct deposit, contact the bank or other financial institution and request that any funds received for the month of death or later be returned to Social Security.

When someone starts receiving Social Security disability benefits, certain family members may also qualify for benefits on that person's record. Eligible family members may include: a spouse; a divorced spouse; children; a disabled child; and an adult child who became disabled before age 22. Each family member may be eligible for a monthly benefit of up to 50 percent of the disability benefit amount, though there is a limit on the total amount payable to the family, depending on the benefit amount and the number of qualifying family members.

When you qualify for Social Security disability benefits, your children may also qualify to receive benefits on your record. An eligible child can be your biological child, adopted child, or stepchild, and a dependent grandchild may also qualify. To receive benefits, the child must be unmarried and be: under age 18; or 18–19 years old and a full-time student no higher than grade 12; or 18 or older with a disability that started before age 22. Normally, benefits stop when children reach age 18 unless they are still in school or disabled. Survivor benefits may also be payable to your children when you die, and a child can get benefits at any age if they were disabled before age 22 and remain disabled; besides natural children, stepchildren, grandchildren, step-grandchildren, or adopted children may receive benefits under certain circumstances.

To qualify for Social Security disability benefits, you must first have worked in jobs covered by Social Security, and then you must have a medical condition that meets Social Security's definition of disability. In general, benefits are paid monthly to people who are unable to work for a year or more because of a disability. You must also have worked long enough and recently enough under Social Security to qualify. Work credits are based on your total yearly wages or self-employment income, and you can earn up to four credits each year. The number of credits needed depends on your age when you become disabled; generally you need 40 credits, 20 of which were earned in the last 10 years ending with the year you become disabled, though younger workers may qualify with fewer credits. Under Social Security rules, you are considered disabled if you cannot do the work you did before, you cannot adjust to other work because of your medical condition, and the disability has lasted or is expected to last for at least one year or to result in death. Social Security pays only for total disability; no benefits are payable for partial or short-term disability.

To qualify for Social Security disability benefits, you must meet the Social Security definition of disability and have worked long enough and recently enough under Social Security. Social Security pays only for total disability—no benefits are payable for partial or short-term disability. You are considered disabled if you cannot do the work you did before, you cannot adjust to other work because of your medical condition, and the disability has lasted or is expected to last for at least one year or to result in death. Regarding work credits: credits are based on your total yearly wages or self-employment income, and you can earn up to four credits each year (in 2019, one credit per $1,360 in wages or self-employment income, with four credits earned at $5,440). The number of credits needed depends on your age when you become disabled; generally you need 40 credits, 20 of which were earned in the last 10 years ending with the year you become disabled, though younger workers may qualify with fewer credits.

Yes. Social Security has special rules called "work incentives" that help you keep your cash benefits and Medicare while you test your ability to work. These rules provide continued benefits and health care coverage to help you make the transition back to work. For more information about Social Security work incentives, you can read the publication "Working While Disabled: How We Can Help."

Certain family members may be eligible for monthly survivors benefits, including: a widow or widower age 60 or older (age 50 or older if disabled); a surviving divorced spouse under certain circumstances; a widow or widower at any age who is caring for the deceased's child who is under age 16 or disabled and receiving benefits on their record; and an unmarried child of the deceased who is younger than age 18, or up to age 19 if a full-time student in an elementary or secondary school. Children, grandchildren, stepchildren, or adopted children may receive benefits under certain circumstances. A dependent parent age 62 or older of a worker who dies may also be eligible, if they were receiving at least half of their support from the working child and are not eligible for a higher retirement benefit; generally they must not have married after the deceased adult child's death, though there are some exceptions. The parent could be a natural parent, stepparent, or adoptive parent if they became the deceased worker's parent before age 16.

Yes. When you start receiving Social Security retirement benefits, some members of your family may also qualify to receive benefits on your record. If they qualify, your spouse or child may receive a monthly payment of up to one-half of your full retirement benefit amount, and these payments will not decrease your retirement benefit. There is also a family maximum limit on the total that can be paid to family members on the same record.

Yes. Under certain circumstances, family members other than your spouse may be eligible, including a stepchild, grandchild, step grandchild, or adopted child. In addition, parents age 62 or older who were dependent on the deceased for at least half of their support may be eligible.

Since you don't have computer access right now, you can apply for Medicare by phone or in person at a Social Security office instead of online. If applying by phone, gather the needed information and Social Security will walk you through the process on the phone. If applying in person, call your local Social Security office to ask what to bring when you schedule an appointment; they can help if you don't have all your documents right now.

The documents to provide depend on how you apply. For an online application, first gather the documents listed on the Checklist for Online Medicare, Retirement & Spouses Application; instructions on how to submit your documents will appear at the end of the online application. If applying by phone, gather the information above, and they will walk you through the process on the phone. If applying in person, ask your local Social Security office what you need to bring when you call to schedule your appointment; they can help if you don't have all your documents right now. Documents may include your original birth certificate or other proof of age (original or certified copy from the issuing agency), proof of U.S. citizenship if you were not born in the U.S. and have not submitted proof for an earlier Medicare or Social Security claim (original or agency-certified copies; expired, notarized, or photocopied documents are not accepted), a copy of your W-2 tax form and/or self-employment tax return from last year (photocopy acceptable), and a copy of your U.S. military service papers if you served before 1968 (photocopy acceptable).

The evidence lists documents that may be required when applying for benefits: your original birth certificate or other proof of age (original or certified copy from the issuing agency); proof of U.S. citizenship if you were not born in the U.S. and have not submitted proof for an earlier Medicare or Social Security claim (original or agency-certified copies; expired, notarized, or photocopied documents are not accepted); a copy of your W-2 tax form and/or self-employment tax return from last year (photocopy acceptable); and a copy of your U.S. military service papers if you served before 1968 (photocopy acceptable). For disability benefits, documents may include medical records, doctors' reports, and recent test results, as well as award letters, pay stubs, settlement agreements, or other proof of temporary or permanent workers' compensation-type benefits received. Photocopies of W-2 forms, self-employment tax returns, or medical documents are accepted, but the original of most other documents, such as your birth certificate, must be seen and will be returned. The evidence does not identify specific application fields that require supporting documentation beyond these document categories.

Yes. If you receive Social Security benefits (retirement, survivors, or disability) or are enrolled in Medicare, you can change your address online by logging in to or creating a free my Social Security account. The steps are: log in to my Social Security, select the My Profile link on the right side of the screen, select the Update Contact Information button and enter your address information, select when you would like to schedule the update and select Next, then review and verify your information and select Submit. Separately, if you move you must report a change of residence address on your license, permit, non-driver ID, or vehicle records to the DMV within 10 days, and changing your address with the USPS does not update your DMV records. You can change your DMV address online through MyDMV using the ID number and document number from your New York State driver license, learner permit, or Non-Driver ID, or by mail by sending a completed Address Change (MV-232) form to the NYS DMV License Production Bureau, PO Box 2895, Albany, NY 12220-0895.

If you still have questions or need help understanding how to change your address and telephone number online, you can call the toll-free number at 1-800-772-1213 or visit your Social Security office. If you are deaf or hard of hearing, you can call the toll-free TTY number at 1-800-325-0778 between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Monday through Friday.

If you still have questions or need help understanding how to change your address online, you can call the toll-free number 1-800-772-1213 or visit your Social Security office. If you are deaf or hard of hearing, you can call the toll-free TTY number 1-800-325-0778 between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Monday through Friday.

You can apply online, by phone, or in person at a Social Security office. Applying online is described as the easiest way: go to the Apply for Benefits page, read and agree to the Terms of Service, click Next, review the Getting Ready section, select Start A New Application, answer a few questions about who is filling out the application, then sign into your my Social Security account or create one, and complete the application. Before applying, gather the documents listed on the Checklist for Online Medicare, Retirement & Spouses Application; instructions on submitting documents appear at the end of the online application. If applying by phone, gather that information and they will walk you through the process. If applying in person, ask your local Social Security office what to bring when you call to schedule an appointment. In general, the process is: gather the information and documents you need, complete and submit your application, SSA reviews it and contacts you if more information is needed, mails you a decision letter, and you start receiving benefits.

Direct deposit information is not strictly required to apply, but it is recommended. When you apply for benefits, you can tell the Social Security representative that you want to sign up for Direct Deposit. If you already have a bank account, bring your checkbook or a copy of your bank statement. You should also bring along your bank information so you can sign up for Direct Deposit. If you do not have a bank account, you can sign up for the Direct Express card program, which deposits federal payments directly to the card.
Understood — no problem. Since you already know how, there's nothing further needed here.

For retirement planning, the evidence lists several sites and tools: the Social Security Administration's Benefit Eligibility Screening Tool (BEST), the Employee Benefit Research Institute's Ballpark E$timator calculator, the Department of Labor's Publications and Reports page and Retirement Savings Toolkit, the MyMoney.gov "Planning for Retirement / Retiring" page (which includes a Medicare Eligibility Tool), and the USA.gov Retirement Resources site (which includes a Federal Employees Retirement Calculator). The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) is also mentioned for those with defined benefit pensions.

Yes, it can be normal to get different benefit estimates at different times. The Online Calculator is updated periodically with new benefit increases and other benefit amounts, so it is likely that future benefit estimates will differ from those calculated today. Also, different calculators can produce different results: the Online Calculator allows you to estimate your benefit, but for the most accurate estimates you should use the Detailed Calculator. The evidence does not say which calculator you or the person who helped you used, so it cannot confirm whether a different calculator was involved.

If the online retirement benefits and Medicare applications do not apply to you, you can apply by phone, apply in person at your local Social Security office (calling first to make an appointment), or, if you do not live in the U.S. or one of its territories, contact the nearest U.S. Social Security office, U.S. Embassy, or consulate.

The evidence does not identify which benefit you are applying for, so the required documents cannot be determined. The available information covers different applications: for pre-need burial eligibility in a VA cemetery, you need your or your sponsor's Social Security number, date and place of birth, and military status and service history (such as service dates, discharge character, and rank, commonly found on the DD214); for Social Security retirement or Medicare, you should gather the documents listed on the Checklist for Online Medicare, Retirement & Spouses Application, and if applying in person, ask your local Social Security office what to bring; for survivors benefits, the documents depend on the specific benefit selected from the list. Please specify the benefit you are applying for so the relevant requirements can be identified.

Yes, you can apply online, but eligibility depends on the benefit type. For retirement benefits or benefits as a spouse, you can apply online if you are at least 61 years and 8 months old, are not currently receiving benefits on your own Social Security record, have not already applied for retirement benefits, and want your benefits to start no more than 4 months in the future. For adult disability benefits, you can apply online if you are age 18 or older, are not currently receiving benefits on your own Social Security record, are unable to work because of a medical condition expected to last at least 12 months or result in death, and have not been denied disability benefits in the last 60 days. The online application is currently only available in English.

If you are younger than full retirement age and earn more than the yearly earnings limit, your earnings may reduce your benefit amount.
