If you are under full retirement age for the entire year, $1 is deducted from your benefit payments for every $2 you earn above the annual limit; for 2019, that limit is $17,640. Once you reach full retirement age, there is no limit on how much you can earn.

The Social Security Benefits Planner provides planners to help you better understand your Social Security protection as you plan for your financial future, and you can then choose a benefit calculator to get estimates of benefits you and your family may be eligible for. If you already have enough Social Security credits to qualify for benefits, you can use the Retirement Estimator to get a personalized, instant estimate of your retirement benefits, entering different dates and ages to determine the best time to retire. If you want an estimate for survivors or disability benefits, or do not have enough credits to qualify, you can use one of the benefit calculators. You can also apply for retirement benefits online if you meet certain criteria, which requires agreeing to a Terms of Service Agreement and creating or logging in to your personal my Social Security account.

Yes. If you are within three months of age 65 or older and are not ready to start your monthly Social Security benefits yet, you can use the online retirement application to sign up just for Medicare and wait to apply for your retirement or spouse's benefits later. Similarly, if you don't have Medicare but are within 3 months of age 65, you can use the application to apply for just Medicare if you aren't ready to receive retirement benefits yet. Before deciding, be sure you understand how waiting until later will affect the lifetime benefits payable on your account and your health insurance coverage.

Yes. You can apply for retirement benefits or Medicare online, by phone, or in person at your local Social Security office. You must be at least 61 years and 9 months old to apply for retirement benefits, and you should apply no more than four months before the date you want benefits to start. If you already have Medicare, you can still use the application to apply for retirement benefits. You can also work while receiving retirement or survivors benefits, which could mean a higher future benefit; each year the SSA reviews records, and if prior-year earnings exceed one of the years used to compute your benefit, it recalculates and pays the increase retroactively to January of the year after you earned the money. Social Security credits work like this: you earn credits when you work and pay Social Security taxes, and you generally need at least 40 credits to qualify for Social Security benefits. Since 1978, you can earn up to a maximum of four credits per year. The number of credits does not affect the amount of benefits you receive; it only determines whether you are eligible, and you do not get extra benefits for earning more than the minimum number of credits. Credits are used to determine eligibility for retirement or disability benefits, as well as your family's eligibility for survivors benefits when you die. If you stop working before you have enough credits to qualify, the credits remain on your Social Security record, and if you return to work later, more credits may be added. For disability benefits, you must have worked long enough and recently enough under Social Security, and the number of work credits needed depends on your age when you become disabled. When you sign up for Medicare, you will be asked whether you want to enroll in Medical insurance Part B. Part B helps pay for doctors' services and many other medical services, and anyone eligible for free Medicare hospital insurance Part A can enroll in Part B by paying a monthly premium (some higher-income beneficiaries pay a higher premium). Because you must pay a premium for Part B, you can turn it down; however, if you decline Part B and decide to enroll later, your coverage may be delayed and you may have to pay a higher monthly premium (a late enrollment penalty) unless you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period. So the decision depends on your circumstances, but be aware of the potential delay and higher premium if you decline now and enroll later.

You may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period (SEP) if you are age 65 or older and your medical insurance coverage is under a group health plan based on your own or your spouse's current employment. The SEP lets you sign up for Part B during: any month you remain covered under the group health plan and your (or your spouse's) employment continues; or the 8-month period that begins with the month after your group health plan coverage or the employment it is based on ends, whichever comes first. Exception: if your group health plan coverage or the employment it is based on ends during your initial enrollment period for Medicare Part B, you do not qualify for a SEP.

Planning is the key to creating your best retirement, and you'll need to plan and save for years to achieve your retirement goals. Social Security should be just one part of your retirement plan—on average, retirement beneficiaries receive 40% of their (benefits from it). When thinking about retirement, be sure to plan for the long term: a man who turned 65 in 2014 can expect to live about another 19.3 years, and a woman who turned 65 the same year can expect to live about another 21.6 years; about one in four 65-year-olds today will live past age 90. You can also apply for just Medicare at age 65 and start receiving retirement benefits later. Several resources can help with planning: the Benefit Eligibility Screening Tool (BEST) to identify other Social Security programs you may be eligible for; the Employee Benefit Research Institute's Ballpark E$timator calculator to get a basic idea of how much you need to save before you retire; Department of Labor publications and consumer information on health benefits and retirement planning; the Retirement Savings Toolkit with English and Spanish publications about retirement savings; the MyMoney.gov "Planning for Retirement / Retiring" page with various retirement planning tools, including a Medicare Eligibility Tool; and USA.gov's financial planning tools, including a Federal Employees Retirement Calculator. If you have or had a job with a defined benefit pension, the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) may be protecting your pension, and if your plan was terminated you may be able to use its Find an Unclaimed Pension tool to check for unclaimed benefits.

Medicare is the country's health insurance program for people age 65 or older. It helps with the cost of health care, but it does not cover all medical expenses or the cost of most long-term care. Hospital insurance (Part A) helps pay for inpatient care in a hospital or skilled nursing facility following a hospital stay, some home health care, and hospice care. Medical insurance (Part B) helps pay for doctors' services and other medical services; you must pay a monthly premium for Part B coverage if you want it, and most people have both parts. People with Parts A and B can choose Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans offered by private companies and approved by Medicare, and Prescription Drug Coverage (Part D) helps pay for medications doctors prescribe. If you decline Part B and enroll later, your coverage may be delayed and your monthly premium may be higher (10 percent for each 12-month period you were eligible but didn't sign up), unless you qualify for a Special Enrollment Period, such as when you have group health plan coverage based on current employment.

You earn Social Security credits when you work and pay Social Security taxes. Since 1978, you can earn up to a maximum of four credits per year, based on your total wages and self-employment income for the year; you might work all year to earn four credits or earn enough for all four in much less time. The amount of earnings needed for a credit may change each year—for example, in 2020 you earn one credit for every $1,410 in covered earnings, and $5,640 gets you the maximum four credits for the year. You must earn at least 40 credits to qualify for Social Security benefits. The number of credits does not affect the amount of benefits you receive; it only determines eligibility, and extra credits beyond the minimum do not increase your benefit amount. Credits are used to determine eligibility for retirement or disability benefits, as well as your family's eligibility for survivors benefits when you die.

Social Security has special rules for people who are blind that recognize the severe impact of blindness on a person's ability to work. For example, the monthly earnings limit for people who are blind is generally higher than the limit that applies to non-blind disabled workers; in 2019 the monthly earnings limit is $2,040. In addition, if you are statutorily blind, you must only meet the duration of work test—there is no recent work test requirement when statutory blindness is involved. Note that you are considered legally blind under Social Security rules if your vision cannot be corrected to better than 20/200 in your better eye or if your visual field is 20 degrees or less, even with corrective lenses.

The number of Social Security credits you need to qualify for disability benefits depends on your age when you become disabled. Generally, you need 40 credits, 20 of which must have been earned in the last 10 years ending with the year you become disabled. However, younger workers may qualify with fewer credits. For example, workers under age 24 may qualify with 6 credits earned in the 3-year period ending when the disability starts; for ages 24 to 31, you generally need credit for working half the time between age 21 and the time you become disabled; and for age 31 or older, you generally need at least 20 credits in the 10-year period immediately before you become disabled.

Yes. The evidence indicates that you may be eligible for benefits on someone else's record. It refers to possible benefits you may be eligible for on someone else's record, and notes that you may qualify as a survivor on someone else's Social Security record.

The evidence does not state a specific benefit amount for you. It explains that a monthly disability benefit amount is based on your lifetime average earnings covered by Social Security, and that you can get an estimate through your personal my Social Security account or the Benefit Estimator. It also notes that Retirement Estimator figures are only estimates based on your actual earnings record. To determine your actual amount, you would need to obtain a personalized estimate or benefit statement.

If you need help with managing your benefits and cannot find the answer or service online, visit the contact us page for other ways to get support. You can also search the comprehensive FAQs section for help with specific retirement issues.

The Retirement Estimator gives estimates based on your actual Social Security earnings record, but these are just estimates. Your actual benefit amount can't be provided until you apply, and it may differ from the estimates because your earnings may increase or decrease in the future, benefits are adjusted for cost-of-living increases after you start receiving them, and your estimated benefits are based on current law, which may change. If you already have enough Social Security credits to qualify, you can use the Retirement Estimator to get a personalized, instant estimate, entering different dates and ages to determine the best time to retire. For survivors or disability estimates, or if you don't have enough credits, use one of the benefit calculators instead.

Yes, I can help point you to retirement planning resources. The evidence lists several tools and resources: the Benefit Eligibility Screening Tool (BEST) to identify other Social Security programs you may be eligible for; the Employee Benefit Research Institute's Ballpark E$timator calculator to get a basic idea of how much you need to save before you retire; Department of Labor publications and reports on health benefits and retirement planning; a Retirement Savings Toolkit with English and Spanish publications about retirement savings; the MyMoney.gov "Planning for Retirement / Retiring" page with various retirement planning tools, including a Medicare Eligibility Tool; and the USA.gov site with financial planning tools, including a Federal Employees Retirement Calculator. It also notes that if you have or had a job with a defined benefit pension, the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) may be protecting your pension, and if your pension plan was terminated you may be able to use the PBGC's Find an Unclaimed Pension tool to check for unclaimed benefits.

A free my Social Security account lets you manage your Social Security information and stay in control of your retirement benefits. It is a foundation for understanding what you are entitled to, and you can use it to check your earnings history online. The Retirement Calculator within my Social Security provides personalized retirement benefit estimates based on your actual earnings, making it easy to see how changes in the date or age you begin receiving benefits will affect your future income. If you do not want to create an account or cannot set one up, other tools and resources are available to help estimate your benefit amount.

If you are not currently receiving Social Security or SSI benefits but are planning to apply, tell the Social Security representative when you apply for benefits that you want to sign up for Direct Deposit. If you already have a bank account, have your checkbook or a copy of your bank statement with you. If you don't have an account, you must open one before you can sign up for Direct Deposit; shop around in your area to find an account with the features you want at a price you can afford, and let the representative at the financial institution know you are interested in signing up to receive your benefits by Direct Deposit.

No. An acceptable document used as proof of identity must be current, not expired, and must show your name, identifying information (date of birth or age), and preferably a recent photograph. This applies both to the specific documents Social Security must see (such as a U.S. driver's license, state-issued non-driver identification card, or U.S. passport) and to any other documents submitted if you don't have one of those or can't get a replacement within 10 days (for example, an employee identification card).

If your son lived outside the United States for an extended period, a current or previous passport, school and/or employment records, and any other record showing long-term residence outside the United States could be used to show that he does not have a Social Security number. This applies when applying for an original Social Security number for a child. The evidence does not address how long-term residence abroad affects eligibility for benefits or direct deposit.

A change in income can affect your Medicare premiums through the income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA). If you have higher income, you'll pay an additional premium amount for Medicare Part B and Medicare prescription drug coverage; this affects less than five percent of people with Medicare, and most people don't pay higher premiums. If your income has gone down due to certain situations—such as marrying, divorcing, or becoming widowed; you or your spouse stopping work or reducing work hours; losing income-producing property because of a disaster or other event beyond your control; or a scheduled cessation, termination, or reorganization of an employer's pension plan—and the change makes a difference in the income level considered, you should contact Social Security to explain that you have new information and may need a new decision about your income-related monthly adjustment amount. Social Security will update its records with the information you provide and correct or remove your income-related monthly adjustment amounts as appropriate.

Based on the evidence, if your income has gone down due to certain situations—such as marrying, divorcing, or becoming widowed; you or your spouse stopping work or reducing work hours; losing income-producing property because of a disaster or other event beyond your control; or a scheduled cessation, termination, or reorganization of an employer's pension plan—and the change makes a difference in the income level considered, you should contact Social Security to explain that you have new information and may need a new decision about your income-related monthly adjustment amount. Social Security will update its records with the information you provide and correct or remove your income-related monthly adjustment amounts as appropriate. The evidence also notes that you should tell Social Security whenever there is a change in your life circumstance that could affect your benefits, and that you can update much of your information if you already receive Social Security benefits. The evidence does not provide details on how an income change affects retirement benefit amounts generally beyond these Medicare premium adjustment and reporting points.

The standard Part B premium for 2020 is $144.60 per month. Higher-income beneficiaries pay a larger percentage of the total cost of Part B, with monthly Part B premiums equal to 35, 50, 65, 80, or 85 percent of the total cost depending on the income reported to the IRS. If you file taxes as married filing jointly and your MAGI is greater than $170,000, or if you file with a different status and your MAGI is greater than $85,000, you'll pay higher premiums for Part B and Medicare prescription drug coverage.

Direct Deposit is described as a simple, safe, and secure way to get Social Security or SSI benefits. If you already receive benefits and have a bank account, you can set up or change your direct deposit by logging in to or creating a personal and secure my Social Security account. To have payments sent to a bank or credit union account, you should have your Social Security number, bank routing transit number, account type (checking or savings), and account number ready when you apply. If you don't have an account, you must open one before you can sign up for Direct Deposit; you should shop around for an account with the features you want at a price you can afford, and let the financial institution representative know you want to receive benefits by Direct Deposit. If you don't yet receive Social Security or SSI benefits but plan to apply, tell the Social Security representative when you apply that you want to sign up for Direct Deposit, and if you already have an account, bring your checkbook or a copy of your bank statement. For those without a bank account, a Direct Express card is an option: your monthly benefits are available on your payment day on time, every time, and you can use the card to make purchases, pay bills, or get cash at thousands of locations; you can sign up by calling the toll-free Direct Express hotline at 1-800-333-1795, and Social Security can also help you sign up.

Social Security Direct Deposit is described as a simple, safe, and secure way to get benefits, with payments sent to a bank or credit union account. If you already receive Social Security or SSI benefits and have a bank account, you can set up or change your direct deposit by logging in to or creating a personal and secure my Social Security account. When applying, you should tell the Social Security representative that you want to sign up for Direct Deposit; if you already have an account, bring your checkbook or a copy of your bank statement. To have payments sent to a bank or credit union account, have your Social Security number, bank routing transit number, account type (checking or savings), and account number ready. If you don't have an account, you must open one before you can sign up for Direct Deposit, and you should shop around for an account with features you want at a price you can afford. If you don't get Social Security or SSI benefits yet but plan to apply, tell the representative when you apply that you want Direct Deposit.

Since you are not currently receiving benefits and do not yet have an account, you must open a bank account before you can sign up for Direct Deposit. You should shop around in your area to find an account with the features you want at a price you can afford. Once you choose an account, let the representative at the financial institution know you are interested in signing up to receive your benefits by Direct Deposit. Also, when you apply for benefits, tell the Social Security representative that you want to sign up for Direct Deposit. Alternatively, the Direct Express debit card is an option that does not require a bank account; you can call the toll-free Direct Express hotline at 1-800-333-1795, and Social Security can also help you sign up.

If you already receive Social Security or SSI benefits and have a bank account, you can sign up for Direct Deposit by starting or changing Direct Deposit online (Social Security benefits only), by contacting your bank, credit union, or savings and loan association, or by calling Social Security toll-free at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). Another option is the Direct Express debit card, which you can use to access your benefits and which does not require a bank account; with that program your federal benefit payment is deposited directly into your card account, and your monthly benefits are available on your payment day on time, every time. You can also set up or change Direct Deposit by logging in to or creating your personal and secure my Social Security account.

If you don't have the required original documents at hand, note that the SSA cannot accept photocopies or notarized copies, and it cannot accept a receipt showing you applied for the document. All documents must be originals or copies certified by the issuing agency and must be current (not expired). For proof of age, you must present your child's foreign birth certificate if you have it or can get it within 10 days; if not, the SSA will consider other documents such as your child's passport.

If you don't have one of the specific identity documents (such as a U.S. driver's license, State-issued non-driver identification card, or U.S. passport), or you cannot get a replacement for one of them within 10 days, Social Security will ask to see other documents. Any documents you submit must be current (not expired) and show your name, identifying information such as date of birth or age, and preferably a recent photograph. Examples of other acceptable documents include an employee identification card, school identification card, health insurance card (not a Medicare card), or U.S. military identification card. Note that one document may be used for two purposes—for example, a U.S. passport can serve as proof of both citizenship and identity.

Yes, a Certification of Report of Birth (DS-1350) is one of the documents accepted as proof of U.S. citizenship for a foreign-born U.S. citizen child. However, it must be an original or a copy certified by the issuing agency—photocopies, notarized copies, and receipts showing you applied for the document are not accepted, and the document must be current (not expired). Note that this document serves as citizenship proof; for age, you must present the child's foreign birth certificate if you have it or can get it within 10 days, otherwise other documents such as the child's passport may be considered.

Yes. Medicare prescription drug coverage (Part D) helps pay for medications doctors prescribe for treatment. For most beneficiaries, the government pays a major portion of the total costs for this coverage, and the beneficiary pays the rest. Prescription drug plan costs vary depending on the plan and whether you get Extra Help (the subsidy) with your portion of the costs. If you have limited resources and income, you may be eligible for Extra Help with Medicare Prescription Drug Plan Costs.

The evidence does not list the specific fields on the application. It states that to apply for a child you must complete an Application for Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and a Child Disability Report, and that the Child Disability Report collects information about the child's disabling condition and how it affects his/her ability to function. Only the Child Disability Report can be completed online; the SSI application is completed by phone or in person at a scheduled appointment. The Child Disability Starter Kit includes a worksheet to help gather the needed information, but the individual fields are not enumerated in the provided evidence.

If you do not want to complete the Child Disability Report online, or you need help, you can call Social Security toll-free at 1-800-772-1213. If you are deaf or hard-of-hearing, you can call the toll-free TTY number at 1-800-325-0778. Representatives are available Monday through Friday between 8 a.m. and 5:30 p.m.

The evidence does not identify specific fields on the SSI child disability application that require supporting documents. It states that you must complete an SSI application and a Child Disability Report, and that at the end of the report you will be asked to sign a form giving the child's doctor permission to share information about the disability. The only list of supporting-document details in the evidence relates to a VA pre-need burial eligibility application for an unmarried adult child of a Veteran, not the SSI child disability application.

The evidence does not list the specific documents to provide when applying for SSI benefits for a disabled child. It indicates you will need to complete an SSI application and a Child Disability Report, and that at the end of the online Child Disability Report you will be asked to sign a form giving the child's doctor permission to share information about the disability. The Child Disability Starter Kit includes a worksheet to help gather the information needed. General SSA disability evidence mentions medical records, doctors' reports, recent test results, and proof of other benefits, and notes originals of most other documents (such as a birth certificate) must be seen, but this is not specific to a child's SSI application.

After you request a temporary lift of your credit freeze or fraud alert from the Identity Services Provider, the provider may automatically reinstate it after your temporary lift expires. You can also reinstate the security freeze or fraud alert with the Identity Services Provider if needed. Once the freeze or fraud alert is lifted, you can create a my Social Security account online.

Under Social Security rules, you are considered legally blind if your vision cannot be corrected to better than 20/200 in your better eye, or if your visual field is 20 degrees or less, even with a corrective lens. Many people who meet the legal definition of blindness still have some sight and may be able to read large print and get around without a cane or guide dog. If you do not meet the legal definition of blindness, you may still qualify for disability benefits if your vision problems alone or combined with other health problems prevent you from working. There are special rules for people who are blind that recognize the severe impact of blindness on a person's ability to work; for example, the monthly earnings limit for people who are blind is generally higher than the limit for non-blind disabled workers (in 2019, $2,040). In addition, if you are statutorily blind, you must only meet the duration of work test—there is no recent work test requirement.

You can start receiving Social Security retirement benefits as early as age 62. However, if you begin benefits before your full retirement age, your monthly benefit is reduced. You can retire at any time between age 62 and your full retirement age, with benefits reduced a fraction of a percent for each month before full retirement age.

Based on the evidence provided, the clearest stated right is that you have a right to appeal any decision Social Security makes about whether you are entitled to benefits. You must request an appeal in writing within 60 days of receiving the decision, and there are four levels of appeal: reconsideration by Social Security staff, a hearing before an administrative law judge, a review by Social Security's Appeals Council, and a review by the federal courts. The evidence also notes that a solid foundation for retirement includes understanding what you are entitled to, staying up to date on program changes, and making sure Social Security has your current information. Other evidence addresses family benefits for a spouse (at least age 62, with Medicare at 65) and disability benefits, but does not state additional rights under the retiree benefits program.

The number of credits needed for survivor benefits depends on the worker's age when they die; the younger the person, the fewer credits needed. No one needs more than 40 credits (10 years of work). Under a special rule, benefits can be paid to the worker's children and a surviving spouse caring for the children even if the worker doesn't have the required number of credits, as long as the worker has credit for one and one-half years of work (6 credits) in the three years before death.

If you cannot use Social Security's online services, your local Social Security office can help you apply for retirement benefits. Although the offices are closed to the public, employees from those offices are assisting people by telephone. You can find the phone number for your local office using the Field Office Locator and looking under Social Security Office Information; the toll-free office number is your local office. You can also apply by phone by calling 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778) from 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., Monday through Friday. If you do not live in the U.S. or one of its territories, contact the Federal Benefits Unit for your country of residence to apply for retirement benefits.

Yes. You can contact Social Security by phone at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778 for those who are deaf or hard of hearing). You can also visit your local Social Security office in person, calling first to make an appointment; you can find your local office's phone number using the Field Office Locator. If you do not live in the U.S. or one of its territories, you can contact the nearest U.S. Social Security office, U.S. Embassy or consulate, or the Federal Benefits Unit for your country of residence.

The Early Retirement Age for Social Security retirement benefits is age 62. You can get Social Security retirement benefits as early as age 62, but your benefit is reduced if you start receiving benefits before your full retirement age. You may start receiving benefits as early as age 62 or as late as age 70.

You may help someone else fill out their retirement benefits application online, but you are not allowed to sign it for them. Only the person applying for benefits can legally sign the application; a legal representative or person helping cannot sign it. If the person applying is not able to sign online, Social Security will mail them a copy to sign.
Yes. If you change your mind after submitting your application, you have up to 12 months to withdraw it. You will be required to repay any benefits you've already received.

If you don't want to create a my Social Security account (or are unable to set one up), SSA offers other tools and resources to help you estimate your benefit amount—visit the Social Security Calculators page for more online and downloadable options. Note that applying online requires you to sign into your my Social Security account or be prompted to create one; however, you can also apply by phone or at a Social Security office instead of online.

The school's financial aid office determines how much aid you are eligible to receive. It starts by setting your cost of attendance (COA), then subtracts your Expected Family Contribution (EFC) to determine your financial need and therefore how much need-based aid you can get. You can't receive more need-based aid than your financial need—for example, if your COA is $16,000 and your EFC is $12,000, your financial need is $4,000, so you aren't eligible for more than $4,000 in need-based aid. For non-need-based aid, the school takes your cost of attendance and subtracts any financial aid you've already been awarded. Eligibility also depends on your year in school, your enrollment status, and the cost of attendance at the school you will be attending.

You can get help through VA if you're a Veteran who has experienced MST. You don't need a service-connected disability rating, you may be able to get MST-related care even if you don't qualify for other VA services, and you don't need to have reported the MST or have other proof that it happened. If you have a VA primary care provider, talk to that professional about what you've been through; all VA primary care providers are trained in MST and can help you figure out if you have related issues like PTSD or depression, and your provider will offer treatment and support as needed. If you don't have a VA primary care provider, call your nearest VA medical center and ask to speak to the MST coordinator. You can ask for a provider of a specific gender if that makes you more comfortable. If you'd prefer care outside of a medical setting, you can get free confidential counseling, alcohol and drug assessment, and other support at one of VA's community Vet Centers.

No. The evidence states that all VA primary care providers are trained in MST, but it does not say that all VA health care providers are trained in MST. It only indicates that providers knowledgeable about treating the aftereffects of MST are available at each facility and that specially trained professionals at Vet Centers can treat conditions related to sexual trauma.

To talk to someone right now, you can connect with the Veterans Crisis Line for confidential help from caring, qualified responders, many of whom are Veterans themselves. This service is private, free, and available 24/7. You can reach a responder anytime day or night by calling 800-273-8255 and then selecting 1, starting a confidential Veterans chat, or texting 838255. If you have hearing loss, call TTY: 800-799-4889. You can also call 911, go to the nearest emergency room, or go directly to your nearest VA medical center—it doesn't matter what your discharge status is or if you're enrolled in VA health care.

To prepare before starting your application, first find out if you're eligible for the benefits you're applying for, then gather the documents and information needed for the application. For VA health care, this means gathering documents such as your most recent tax return, Social Security numbers for yourself and your qualified dependents, and account numbers for any current health insurance. For GI Bill and other VA education benefits, you should find out if you're eligible for VA education benefits, gather the listed documents and information, and use the GI Bill Comparison Tool to see what benefits you'll get at the school you want to attend. To know if you're eligible, the evidence directs you to find out if you're eligible for the specific benefit—VA health care benefits or VA education benefits—before applying.

Yes. If you have a VA direct loan, VA loan technicians can work with you directly, and they can offer you financial counseling and help you deal with your servicer. You can contact a VA Loan Technician at 1-877-827-3702. Also, if you have a VA direct loan and it's 61 days past due, VA will automatically assign a VA Loan Technician to your loan. VA Loan Technicians can also help you figure out which foreclosure-avoidance option is best for you.

If your military records were destroyed in the 1973 fire at the National Personnel Records Center (NPRC) in St. Louis, Missouri, VA can help reconstruct them to support a VA disability compensation claim. Your records may have been destroyed if you were discharged from the Army between November 1, 1912, and January 1, 1960 (the fire destroyed 80% of records for Veterans discharged from the Army during that period), or from the Air Force between September 25, 1947, and January 1, 1964 (the fire destroyed 75% of records for Veterans discharged from the Air Force during that period with surnames beginning with Hubbard through the end of the alphabet). The fire did not involve records for retirees and Reservists who were alive on July 12, 1973. To reconstruct your records, VA submits a specific request to the NPRC for any additional service records they may have or can find; the NPRC searches for documents that may help reconstruct your records and may reach out to other government agencies, for example by trying to reconstruct portions of your service treatment records by reviewing unit records, morning reports, and hospital admission records from the surgeon general's office. If you're filing a VA disability compensation claim, you'll need to fill out the Request for Information Needed to Reconstruct Medical Data (NA Form 13055), giving as much information as you can about your assignments during service, such as unit, company, battalion, regiment, squadron, group, or wing. You should also gather or request supplemental records, such as statements from service medical personnel, certified buddy statements or affidavits from fellow service members who witnessed your injury or illness, military accident and police reports, examination reports related to employment or insurance, and letters or photographs from your time in the service. Make sure to include your NA Form 13055 and any supplemental records with your claim.

The evidence does not describe the specific requirements for care under the VA MISSION Act. It only indicates that the VA MISSION Act introduced new eligibility criteria for community care, without listing those criteria or requirements.

Yes. If you're the spouse, surviving spouse, dependent child, or family caregiver of a Veteran or service member, you may qualify for health care benefits, and in certain cases you may also qualify for benefits due to a disability related to your Veteran's service. If you're the family member of an active-duty, retired, or deceased service member, National Guard Soldier, Reservist, or Medal of Honor recipient, you may qualify for TRICARE, which provides comprehensive health coverage including health plans, prescription medicines, dental plans, and programs for people with special needs. In addition, fertility services using assisted reproductive technologies, including in vitro fertilization (IVF), are available to spouses of Veterans who have a service-connected disability that makes it impossible for them to have a baby without fertility treatment.

Yes, she may qualify for health care benefits. As the surviving spouse of a service member, she may qualify for health care benefits, and if she's the family member of a deceased service member, she may qualify for TRICARE, which provides comprehensive health coverage. She may also qualify for CHAMPVA as the surviving spouse of a service member who died in the line of duty, though in most of these cases family members qualify for TRICARE rather than CHAMPVA. The evidence does not address VA nursing homes, assisted living, or home health care specifically.

The evidence does not give a specific timeframe for when you'll hear back. It says VA will send you a letter in the mail to let you know if your application has been approved. If more than a week has passed since you gave your application and you haven't heard back, don't apply again—call the toll-free hotline at 877-222-8387 (Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET).

The evidence lists several ways to get more information and support about VA nursing homes, assisted living, and home health care: you can get help setting goals and priorities and making tough decisions about long-term care through the shared decision-making process; find services and resources to help with geriatric, elder, and long-term care; and visit the geriatrics section of VA.gov for more information about geriatric and long-term care and how to deal with diseases like Alzheimer's and dementia. The evidence also points to learning more about assisted living and residential care, home health care, and paying for long-term care (which may be covered through Medicaid, Medicare, or private insurance).

Since your husband is a Veteran and you're the dependent, you'll need your own Social Security number and VA file number, plus bank account direct deposit information. You'll also need basic information about your service history (if applicable), your education or training plans and goals, and your current or former school or training program and the new school or training program you plan to attend. Because you're the dependent of a Veteran, you'll also need your husband's Social Security number or VA file number and his basic service history information.

Yes. In addition to applying online, you can apply by mail, in person, or with the help of a trained professional. For Survivors' and Dependents' Educational Assistance, you can apply online or by mail using VA Form 22-5490, mailed to the regional processing office for your state.

Yes. You can get help applying for education benefits from a trained professional called an accredited representative. You can also apply online, by mail, in person at a VA regional benefit office where a VA employee can help you, or by working with your school's certifying official (usually in the Registrar or Financial Aid office).

Yes. The evidence confirms that you can submit your request by mail yourself: you download the form you need (VA Form 22-1995 for Veterans and service members, or VA Form 22-5495 for dependents) and mail it in. The evidence also notes that you have the option of submitting with the help of a trained professional, but doing it on your own by mail is described as a valid alternative way to submit the request.

The Affordable Care Act (ACA), also known as the health care law, was created to expand access to coverage, control health care costs, and improve health care quality and care coordination. Regarding penalties, you don't have to pay a penalty if you don't have health insurance in 2019 or any year after that; through the end of 2018, the ACA required all U.S. taxpayers to have health coverage meeting a minimum standard called the minimum essential coverage requirement unless they qualified for an exemption. The ACA does not change your VA health benefits or your out-of-pocket costs. Being signed up for VA health care meets the ACA requirement of having minimum essential health coverage, so you don't need other insurance to meet that requirement. Your current health insurance status does not affect whether you can get VA health care benefits. If you're not signed up for a VA or Department of Defense health care program, you may be able to get coverage through the Health Insurance Marketplace; open enrollment for 2019 is over, but you can still enroll or change plans with certain life changes or if you qualify for free or low-cost coverage through Medicaid or CHIP. Also, canceling your enrollment in VA health care may impact your health care coverage requirements under the ACA if you don't have other health care.

Yes. VA offers treatment and support for a range of mental health problems, including PTSD, depression, thoughts of suicide, issues related to military sexual trauma, substance use problems, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and anxiety-related conditions such as generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety, and specific phobias. VA provides a range of mental health services, including short-term inpatient care, outpatient care for serious mental illness, regular outpatient care (which may include care over the phone), rehabilitation and residential live-in programs, primary care for common mental and behavioral problems, and care for Veterans in crisis, including emergency mental health care 24 hours a day, 7 days a week and the Veterans Crisis Line. Services range from peer support with other Veterans to counseling, therapy, medication, or a combination of these options.

If you have an illness that isn't on the list of Agent Orange-related diseases but you believe it was caused by Agent Orange, you can still pursue a claim, but you'll need to provide scientific and medical evidence that the condition is related to Agent Orange exposure, or show that the problem started during or got worse because of your military service. Scientific proof may include an article from a medical journal or a published research study. When you file your claim, you'll need to submit a medical record showing that you have a current disability and that there's a connection between Agent Orange exposure and your condition. The evidence does not state whether this would be covered at no additional cost.

You can ask about how to access VA services for substance use problems (including applying for VA health care and talking with a VA primary care provider, or finding a Substance Use Disorder program or contacting your local VA medical center), what services VA provides for Veterans with substance use problems, and how to talk to someone right now through the Veterans Crisis Line.

Yes. The VA website offers several ways to find help. You can visit the Make the Connection website to hear Veterans' stories and get access to more resources and support, use the self-help resources guide for books, web resources, and mobile applications reviewed and recommended by VA experts, and visit the resources section of the VA website to find other trusted resources outside VA. You can also download the Guide to VA Mental Health Services PDF, and find your local Community Resource and Referral Center for non-VA resources in your community.

The evidence describes several VR&E tracks, but it does not specifically address options for someone enrolled in VR&E who does not want to return to their previous job. The Reemployment track requires that you would like to return to your former job, so it would not apply in that situation. Other tracks mentioned include help learning new skills, finding a new job, starting a business, getting educational counseling, and the Self-Employment track for those with a strong desire, skills, and drive to run a successful business. However, the evidence does not provide a complete list of options or eligibility details specifically for someone who does not want to return to their previous job.

After a Board decision you disagree with, you can file a Supplemental Claim if you have new and relevant evidence that supports your case. You can also appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims. A Veterans Service Organization or VA-accredited attorney or agent can help you request a decision review. While you wait, you don't need to do anything unless VA sends you a letter asking for more information, and if VA schedules exams for you, be sure not to miss them.

The evidence describes options after a Board decision only for situations where you disagree and have new and relevant evidence supporting your case: you can file a Supplemental Claim or appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims. The evidence does not state what you can do if you disagree but lack new and relevant evidence, so that specific question cannot be answered from the provided evidence.

The evidence describes a senior reviewer's second look only in the context of a Higher-Level Review, not a Board Appeal. In that context, a senior reviewer will take another look at your case and determine whether the decision can be changed based on a difference of opinion or an error that VA made. For a Board Appeal, the evidence says a judge at the Board of Veterans Appeals in Washington, D.C., will review your case, but it does not describe what a senior reviewer would do if a Board Appeal request were given a second glance.

If you volunteered for research involving chemical and biological testing between 1942 and 1975 and have an injury or disease directly caused by your participation in that testing, you can get medical care through the U.S. Army. For questions or help getting medical care, you can visit the U.S. Army web page or contact the VA by email at mustardgas@vba.va.gov.

Yes, you can still claim the impairment even if you're not sure it's in your military records. If you're claiming a disability for an injury or illness that you don't think is in your military records, you should upload statements that support your claim. These supporting statements should come from people who know about, or who you've talked to about, your claimed medical condition and how and when it occurred. You can ask for supporting statements from people such as those who served with you, service members, family and friends, clergy members, and law enforcement officers. If you saw a non-VA health care provider for diagnosis or treatment, you'll also need to upload copies of all medical records that provide information about the disability you're claiming, which may include doctor's reports, X-rays, and medical lab or test results.

Yes. Having depression does not by itself disqualify you from VA benefits. The evidence states that you may still be able to get care for mental health problems like depression, and VA mental health services cover depression and other needs—some services are available even if you're not enrolled in VA health care. General VA health care eligibility depends on factors such as serving in the active military, naval, or air service and not receiving a dishonorable discharge, along with minimum duty requirements in some cases. To find out what your specific care options are, you can call the general VA hotline at 800-827-1000, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. ET.

No. Contacting the VA is not the only step. For VA health care services, including treatment for depression, you first need to apply for VA health care. Once signed up, if you have a VA primary care provider, talk to them about your needs so they can screen you and offer treatment and support; if you don't have a VA primary care provider or have never been seen at a VA hospital, other steps apply. Some mental health services may be available even if you're not enrolled in VA health care.

If you want to know more about your VA health care benefits, your health care team, and where you'll go for care, VA can help, and you can learn more about your VA health care coverage. If you need help accessing services, call the toll-free hotline at 877-222-8387, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET. Separately, for help understanding your benefits or accessing services, you can call 877-827-1000, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. ET.

Yes. If you're signed up for the VA health care program, you can manage your VA health and benefits online through VA.gov. You can refill your prescriptions, send a message to your VA health care provider, and check the status of a disability or pension claim.

VA offers many services and programs for Veterans with specific needs, including women Veterans, Veterans with mental health problems, and elderly or disabled Veterans, and covers the cost of many of these under the VA health care program; other services like dental care may be available as an added benefit if you qualify. For women Veterans, VA provides primary care services such as general services (disease prevention, nutrition counseling), female-specific services (birth control, preconception counseling, menopausal support, hormone replacement therapy), screenings (cervical and breast cancer screens), and mental health services. VA also covers mental health services for conditions like PTSD, military sexual trauma, depression, and substance use problems; assisted living and home health care depending on needs, income, and program space; prescriptions written or approved by a VA doctor; and ancillary services such as diagnostic tests (blood work, X-rays, ultrasounds) and therapy and rehabilitation services (physical therapy, vision rehab). Mental health services include same-day services such as face-to-face visits, telehealth or video appointments, phone advice from a VA nurse, Secure Messaging, scheduling future appointments, and getting prescriptions filled. Long-term care services for sick or disabled Veterans include 24/7 nursing and medical care, physical therapy, help with daily tasks like bathing, dressing, making meals, and taking medicine, comfort care and pain management, and caregiver support, provided in various settings run by VA or by state or community organizations that VA inspects and approves.

Yes, you may be eligible for benefits as a family member caring for a disabled Veteran. VA provides information on what you may qualify for as a family member caring for a Veteran with disabilities. If you are caring for a Veteran with disabilities who was injured in the line of duty on or after September 11, 2001, you may qualify for health care benefits and other caregiver support through the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers. Eligibility for this program is based on the Veteran's qualifications: the Veteran must have a serious injury (including traumatic brain injury, psychological trauma, or other mental disorder) caused or made worse by active-duty service on or after September 11, 2001, and because of it cannot perform one or more activities of daily living and/or needs supervision or protection based on symptoms of lasting neurological damage or injury, and needs personal care services. Additionally, as a family member caring for a Veteran with disabilities, if you are not entitled to care or services through another health plan, you may qualify for CHAMPVA. As a family caregiver of a Veteran, you may also qualify for health care benefits in certain cases.

Yes, your wife may be eligible for CHAMPVA benefits if you don't qualify for TRICARE and you are a Veteran rated permanently and totally disabled for a service-connected disability by a VA regional benefit office. As the spouse of such a Veteran, she would meet one of the qualifying descriptions for CHAMPVA. Note that in most cases family members qualify for TRICARE rather than CHAMPVA. Additionally, as a dependent spouse, she may be considered a dependent for purposes of additional VA disability compensation if you are eligible for VA disability compensation and have a combined disability rating of at least 30%.

Yes. You can view your VA appointments online using the VA Appointments tools, which offer a secure, web-based way to schedule, view, and organize your VA appointments. You can view details about upcoming appointments, view appointments on your health calendar, print a list of your future appointments, and look up past appointments from the last 2 years. To use these tools, you must be enrolled in VA health care, be scheduling with a VA health facility that uses online scheduling, and have had an appointment at that facility within the last 2 years, plus have a Premium My HealtheVet account, a Premium DS Logon account, or a verified ID.me account. You can also call the VA health facility where you want to receive care, which is usually the fastest way to make appointments.

If your application is approved, VA will send you a letter in the mail letting you know your application has been approved. Next, wait for your welcome call from VA—they'll call to welcome you to the VA health care program, help you schedule your first doctor's appointment, and answer any questions about your health care benefits. You should also read your Veterans Health Benefits Handbook, which they'll send to you.

Yes. If you're signed up for the VA health care program, you can manage your VA health and benefits online through VA.gov. This includes refilling your prescriptions, sending a message to your VA health care provider (or a secure message to your health care team), and checking the status of a disability or pension claim.

The evidence describes online management only for people who are signed up for the VA health care program: those enrolled can use VA.gov to refill prescriptions, send a secure message to their health care team, and check the status of a disability or pension claim. It does not explain how someone who is not signed up can access or manage VA benefits and health care online. If you are not currently in the VA health care program, the evidence indicates you can apply for benefits, and it provides a toll-free hotline (877-222-8387, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET) for help accessing services.

If you don't meet the minimum service requirements for VA health care, the minimum duty requirement may not apply if you were discharged for a disability caused or made worse by your active-duty service, were discharged for a hardship or early out, or served prior to September 7, 1980. Separately, if you don't qualify for enhanced eligibility status but agree to pay copays for your care, you don't have to provide your financial information; however, if you don't provide it, VA may decline your enrollment and won't be able to consider your eligibility for free medications or beneficiary travel pay.

To qualify for ACA minimum essential coverage, you must have been enrolled in one of these programs: the VA health care program; the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA); CHAMPVA through the Program of Comprehensive Assistance to Family Caregivers; the Spina Bifida Health Care Benefits Program; or a Department of Defense TRICARE plan. Being signed up for VA health care meets the ACA requirement of having minimum essential health coverage, and you don't need any other insurance to meet this requirement.

You can search for documents sent to VA through the claim status tool: sign in, scroll to the "Track Claims" section, and click "View Status" for a specific claim to see details about that claim's status and supporting evidence. If you don't see a document you sent to VA as evidence, it may be because certain documents won't appear online—specifically, documents you sent by mail or fax, documents you brought in person, or documents VA has restricted to protect your or someone else's confidentiality/privacy.

Yes. VA offers disability compensation and other benefits for illnesses it believes are caused by contact with Agent Orange. You may qualify if you have an illness VA recognizes as a presumptive disease caused by Agent Orange and you came into contact with Agent Orange during military service. VA presumes contact if you served in Vietnam (including aboard a vessel on the inland waterways or within the 12-mile territorial seas) or in or near the Korean Demilitarized Zone during the Vietnam Era, or in certain related jobs. If you flew on or worked with C-123 aircraft in Vietnam or other locations, you may also have had contact with Agent Orange. In addition, VA has special health registries you can join that document Veterans' exposure to Agent Orange, depleted uranium, ionizing radiation, airborne hazards, and other hazardous materials.

Other things you should know include: you can use VA health care benefits along with other coverage such as a private insurance plan, Medicare, Medicaid, or TRICARE; VA asks for your health insurance information because it must bill your private health insurance provider for care, supplies, or medicine for non-service-connected conditions (it does not bill Medicare or Medicaid, but may bill Medicare supplemental insurance for covered services). Your VA medical benefits package is unique and covers care and services to treat illnesses and injuries, prevent future health problems, improve your ability to function, and enhance your quality of life; all Veterans receive coverage for most care and services, but only some qualify for added benefits like dental care, depending on your priority group, your VA primary care provider's advice, and medical standards. You may also be able to get help paying for other services like dental care if you qualify as an added benefit. Additional information covers the Million Veteran Program (a voluntary research study on genes and health), access and quality in VA health care (such as how quickly you can be seen and what other Veterans say), patient rights and responsibilities at VA health facilities or community living centers, and other VA benefits and services including disability compensation, life insurance, and aid and attendance benefits and housebound allowance.

I'm an AI assistant, not a real person. Regarding health care for depression: VA mental health services cover depression, and you can use some services even if you're not enrolled in VA health care. If you're a Veteran in crisis or concerned about one, you can contact the Veterans Crisis Line 24/7 by calling 800-273-8255 and selecting 1, starting a confidential chat, texting 838255, or (if you have hearing loss) calling TTY 800-799-4889. You can also call the general VA hotline at 800-827-1000, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. ET, to find out what your care options may be. If you have a VA primary care provider, talk to them; they can screen you for related issues like depression and offer treatment and support as needed. If you don't have a VA primary care provider, you can call your nearest VA medical center.

VA offers mental health services for depression, including treatment and support for depression, PTSD, thoughts of suicide, military sexual trauma (MST), substance use problems, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia, as well as anxiety-related conditions like generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety, and specific phobias. These services range from short-term inpatient care for severe or life-threatening mental illness to outpatient care for serious mental illness and regular outpatient care, which may include care provided over the phone. VA also provides free, confidential private counseling and treatment for mental and physical health conditions related to military sexual trauma, and covers mental health services to treat issues like PTSD, MST, depression, and substance use problems. You can find out how to access VA mental health services for PTSD, psychological effects of MST, depression, grief, anxiety, and other needs.

To get more information about non-VA emergency medical care and coverage, you can call your local VA medical center's enrollment coordinator, or get more details on emergency care coverage. You can also learn more about non-VA emergency medical care through VA's information resources.

To find out whether VA services can help with a specific need, you can look into how to access services for your specific needs, and VA provides guidance on finding out how to get health services for a specific condition or need. If you're not sure what kind of help you need, you can call 877-222-8387 to find the right resources for your needs (TTY: 800-877-8339), available Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET.

The evidence provides limited information about the costs of medical care. Medicare helps with the cost of health care but does not cover all medical expenses or the cost of most long-term care; Part A helps pay for inpatient hospital or skilled nursing facility care following a hospital stay, some home health care, and hospice care, and Part B helps pay for doctors' services and many other medical services. For VA health care, money collected goes back to VA medical centers to support health care costs for all Veterans, and income information is used to determine eligibility and whether copays will be required for certain types of care or medications. VA is committed to providing free health care for conditions related to military service and for Veterans with catastrophic disabilities and disability ratings of at least 50%, as well as for those who can't afford to pay for care.

Yes, in some cases. You can get free VA health care for any illness or injury that VA determines is related to your military service (service connected). VA also provides certain other services for free, including readjustment counseling and related mental health services, care for issues related to military sexual trauma (MST), and a registry health exam. VA is committed to providing free health care for conditions related to military service and for Veterans with catastrophic disabilities and disability ratings of at least 50%, as well as for those who can't afford to pay for care. Additionally, if you've just returned from service, you can receive free medical care for any condition related to your service in Iraq or Afghanistan for 5 years after discharge. Separately, you can get free mental health care for a year after separation no matter your discharge status, service history, or eligibility for VA health care.

The evidence does not describe specific care requirements under the VA MISSION Act. It only indicates that the VA MISSION Act introduced new eligibility criteria for community care, and that as a result of the VA MISSION Act of 2018, VA no longer needs permission to bill health insurance providers for care related to a sensitive diagnosis.

To qualify for a Veterans Pension, both of these must be true: you didn't receive a dishonorable discharge, and your yearly family income and net worth meet certain limits set by Congress. Your net worth includes all personal property you own except your house, your car, and most home furnishings, minus any debt you owe, and it includes your spouse's net worth. The program provides monthly payments to wartime Veterans who meet certain age or disability requirements and whose income and net worth are within certain limits.

To transfer unused Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits to a spouse or dependent children as an active duty service member, you must be on active duty or in the Selected Reserve and meet the requirements. At least one of the following must be true: (1) you have completed at least 6 years of service on the date your request is approved and you agree to add 4 more years of service, or (2) you have completed at least 10 years of service on the date your request is approved, can't commit to add 4 more years of service because of either a policy or statute, but agree to serve for the maximum amount. Note that the Department of Defense (DoD) decides whether you can transfer GI Bill benefits to your family.

The GI Bill and other VA education benefits help Veterans, service members, and their qualified family members pay for college tuition, find the right school or training program, and get career counseling. GI Bill benefits specifically help pay for college, graduate school, and training programs, and since 1944 have helped qualifying Veterans and their family members cover all or some of the costs for school or training. Eligibility extends to active-duty service members or Veterans, members of the National Guard or Reserves, and qualified survivors or dependents. For the Post-9/11 GI Bill, you may be able to get benefits if you served on active duty for at least 90 days—whether continuous or interrupted over shorter periods—after September 10, 2001. You can learn how the GI Bill works, check eligibility, and find out how to apply; tools like the GI Bill Comparison Tool and Veterans Service Organizations can help you explore options, and if awarded Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits, your GI Bill Statement of Benefits shows how much you've used and how much remains.

VA education benefits help Veterans, service members, and their qualified family members with needs like paying college tuition, finding the right school or training program, and getting career counseling. You can learn how to apply for and manage the education and training benefits you've earned. The page covers getting GI Bill and other education benefits (including how the GI Bill works, eligibility, and how to apply), managing your Veterans education benefits, and more information and resources. Specific resources include: the GI Bill Comparison Tool to learn about VA education benefits programs and compare GI Bill benefits by school; rate tables for the Post-9/11 GI Bill and other Veterans education benefits programs; guidance links for choosing GI Bill approved schools; the CareerScope assessment to help figure out your career path when transitioning to civilian life; answers to FAQs about GI Bill overpayments and VA education debt management; GI Bill questions and customer help to ask questions and get help online or by phone; the GI Bill School Feedback Tool; downloadable education benefits forms, fact sheets, and other resources; stories from Veterans and service members who used the Post-9/11 GI Bill; and links to non-VA resources and websites useful to student Veterans and those who support them.

Yes. You can transfer education benefits if you're on active duty or in the Selected Reserve and meet the requirements. One qualifying option is that you've completed at least 10 years of service on the date your request is approved, can't commit to add 4 more years of service because of either a policy or statute, but agree to serve for the maximum amount of time allowed. This must also be true: the person getting benefits has enrolled in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS). Note that the Department of Defense decides whether you can transfer GI Bill benefits to your family. If DoD approves the Transfer of Entitlement, your spouse or dependent children can apply for up to 36 months of benefits and may be able to get money for tuition, housing, books, and supplies.

Beyond education and training benefits, VA's other benefits and services include: VA transition assistance, which covers VA benefits available to you and your family as you transition out of active-duty, National Guard, or Reserve service; Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment, which helps you explore employment options, get any training you may need, and access other voc rehab services; home loan benefits, including options for Veterans home loans, applying for your Certificate of Eligibility (COE), and help if you're having trouble making mortgage payments; Veteran-owned small business support, including registering to do business with VA and getting support for your Veteran-owned small business; and jobs for Veterans, with help from the U.S. Department of Labor to find a job, get training, or explore career options.

VA education and training benefits help Veterans, service members, and their qualified family members with needs like paying college tuition, finding the right school or training program, and getting career counseling. You can learn how to apply for and manage the education and training benefits you've earned. The GI Bill is one of the main education benefits, and you can learn how it works and explore options to pay for school or training, check your eligibility, and find out how to apply. A GI Bill Comparison Tool is also available to help you learn about education programs.

Other VA benefits and services mentioned include transition assistance, Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (help exploring employment options, training, and other voc rehab services), home loan benefits (including applying for a Certificate of Eligibility and help with mortgage payments), Veteran-owned small business support, and jobs for Veterans through the U.S. Department of Labor. For education benefits, you submit an Application for VA Education Benefits (VA Form 22-1990), which can be done online, by mail, in person, or with the help of a trained professional. If you've already started training, take your VA Form 22-1990 application and the member copy of your DD214 to your school or employer, ask them to complete VA Form 22-1999 (Enrollment Certification), and send all the forms to VA. If you're not on active duty, you'll need to send copy 4 member copy of your DD214, Certificate of Release, or Discharge from Active Duty.

Besides paying for school or training, the Post-9/11 GI Bill can provide up to 36 months of benefits including money for housing if you're in school more than half time (a monthly housing allowance based on the cost of living where your school is located), money for books and supplies (up to $1,000 per school year), and a one-time payment of $500 to help you move from a rural area to go to school.

As you transition out of active duty, National Guard, or Reserve service, VA offers several benefits and services you can use: transition assistance to learn about VA benefits available to you and your family; Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment to find out if you qualify for help exploring employment options, training you may need, and other voc rehab services; home loan benefits, including applying for your Certificate of Eligibility (COE) and getting help if you're having trouble making mortgage payments; support for registering to do business with VA as a Veteran-owned small business; and help from the U.S. Department of Labor to find a job, get training, or explore career options. You can also use the GI Bill Comparison Tool to learn about education programs.
Yes. You can apply to have your GI Bill benefits restored if your school closed or your program ended because of a change in VA regulations or a new law.

VA education and training benefits help Veterans, service members, and their qualified family members with needs like paying college tuition, finding the right school or training program, and getting career counseling. They also include help exploring employment options, any training needed, and other vocational rehabilitation services, as well as free educational and career counseling (Chapter 36) for recently discharged Veterans or dependent family members. For survivors and dependents, benefits can include money for tuition, housing, and books and supplies.

The GI Bill helps pay for college, graduate school, and training programs, and since 1944 it has helped qualifying Veterans and their family members cover all or some of the costs for school or training. Under the Post-9/11 GI Bill (Chapter 33), you can receive up to 36 months of benefits, including tuition and fees (full in-state public tuition and fees if you qualify for the maximum benefit, with capped rates for private and foreign schools), a monthly housing allowance if you're in school more than half time based on the cost of living where your school is located, up to $1,000 per school year for books and supplies, and a one-time payment of $500 to help move from a rural area to go to school if you live in a county with 6 or fewer people per square mile. You can use these benefits to work toward undergraduate or graduate degrees, for tuition assistance top-up, tutorial assistance, vocational/technical training and non-college degree programs, on-the-job training and apprenticeships, and entrepreneurship training. You may also qualify for more than one VA education benefit, but you can't receive benefits under more than one program at a time. The evidence provided does not include the specific eligibility requirements for the GI Bill, so I can't confirm how to qualify beyond the general reference to qualifying Veterans and family members.

Yes. If you're a Guardsman, Reservist, or Veteran who doesn't qualify for the Post-9/11 GI Bill, you can see if you're eligible for other VA education benefits. Dependents who don't meet certain criteria may also still qualify for VA education benefits if the Veteran or service member transferred some or all of their Post-9/11 GI Bill entitlement to them while on active duty.

On the VA education and training benefits page, you can get GI Bill and other education benefits, manage your Veterans education benefits, and find more information and resources. Specifically, you can learn how the GI Bill works and explore options to pay for school or training, check your eligibility for GI Bill or other VA education benefits, learn how to prepare and apply, find out when to expect a decision after you apply and what to do next, see if you qualify for Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment help, get free educational and career counseling (Chapter 36), find out about education benefits for dependents and survivors, and explore other educational assistance programs for Guardsmen, Reservists, or Veterans who don't qualify for the Post-9/11 GI Bill.

To transfer Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits, the service member on active duty requests the transfer, change, or revocation of a Transfer of Entitlement (TOE) through milConnect; you can't apply for a TOE through VA. If DoD approves the TOE, the family members may then apply for benefits online or by mail by filling out and mailing an Application for Family Member to Use Transferred Benefits (VA Form 22-1990E) to the nearest VA regional benefit office. After leaving active duty, the service member can still provide a future effective date, change the number of months transferred, or revoke the TOE by submitting a written request to VA through milConnect.
Yes. If his school closed or his program ended because of a change in VA regulations or a new law, he can apply to have his GI Bill benefits restored.

As a friend helping a friend, you can download the guides from the VA Welcome Kit. The kit page says to feel free to share the guide with friends or family members who need help with their benefits, and you can print out copies for yourself and others. You can download the full VA Welcome Kit as a black-and-white PDF or a color PDF. There are also downloadable guides to VA benefits and services, including guides for Veterans (such as applying for VA health care, getting started with mental health services, applying for a disability rating, and applying for education benefits) and guides for family members (such as getting started with caregiver benefits and applying for survivor benefits).

The evidence does not describe the specific requirements for a VA pension for a National Guard member. The general Veterans Pension program provides monthly payments to wartime Veterans who meet certain age or disability requirements and whose yearly family income and net worth are within limits set by Congress; applicants also must not have received a dishonorable discharge. However, the evidence does not state how these pension requirements apply to National Guard service, so the specific requirements for a National Guard member cannot be determined from the provided evidence.

Available burial help includes a pre-need eligibility determination for burial in a VA national cemetery, which confirms eligibility and helps with pre-planning. If buried in a VA national cemetery, burial benefits at no cost to your family include opening and closing of the grave, a government-provided burial liner, a government-provided headstone or marker, and perpetual care of the gravesite. The person arranging the burial can also request additional honors and memorial items, and surviving spouses or other family members may qualify for survivor benefits, including help paying for funeral costs. VA also offers help planning a burial in a VA national cemetery, ordering a headstone or other memorial item, and applying for survivor and dependent benefits.

You can access and manage VA benefits and health care online through VA.gov.
