For health care, you can refill and track prescriptions, send a secure message to your health care team, schedule and view appointments, view lab and test results, and apply for VA health care. For disability, you can check your claim or appeal status, view payment history, upload evidence to support your claim, file for a VA disability increase, and file a claim for compensation. For education, you can check Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits, view payment history, change current education benefits, compare GI Bill benefits by school, and apply for education benefits. For records, you can get Veteran ID cards, get VA medical records, download benefit letters, change your address, and request military records (DD214). If you need help accessing services, call the toll-free hotline at 877-222-8387, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET. To update personal information such as income, address, and insurance, fill out a Health Benefits Update Form (VA Form 10-10EZR).

To transfer Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits to a spouse, you must be on active duty or in the Selected Reserve and meet at least one of these requirements: you have completed at least 6 years of service on the date your request is approved and agree to add 4 more years of service, or you have completed at least 10 years of service on the date your request is approved, can't commit to add 4 more years because of a policy or statute, but agree to serve for the maximum amount. The Department of Defense decides whether you can transfer benefits.

You don't need to already be enrolled in VR&E to be eligible for the program itself. For VR&E benefits and services as a Veteran, all of these must be true: you didn't receive a dishonorable discharge, you have a service-connected disability rating of at least 10% from VA, and you apply for VR&E services. However, to get help returning to your former job specifically through the VR&E Reemployment track, the requirements are that you have an employment barrier or handicap, are enrolled in VR&E, and would like to return to your former job. So enrollment in VR&E is required for the reemployment track, but it is something you apply for rather than a precondition for eligibility for VR&E overall.

If you're serving on active duty in the United States uniformed services, including active National Guard and Reserve with federal pay, you may be eligible for VA benefits both during service and after separation or retirement. Traditional or technical members of the National Guard and Reserve may also be eligible for some VA benefits. You'll learn about these benefits in your required Transition Assistance Program (TAP) briefing. Benefits you can use during and after service include GI Bill and other education benefits, which can help pay for school or training; if you qualify for the Post-9/11 GI Bill, you can learn how to transfer unused benefits to your spouse or dependent children. You can also get free mental health care for a year after separation.

You can get help with VA education benefits on VA.gov by applying online for education benefits, or by applying by mail, in person, or with the help of a trained professional. You can also go to a VA regional benefit office and have a VA employee help you, or work with your school's certifying official, who is usually in the Registrar or Financial Aid office. Additionally, you can work with an accredited representative to get help applying for education benefits. If you have questions about VA education benefits, call 888-442-4551 (888-GI-BILL-1), Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. ET.

To use VR&E as a Veteran, you must meet all of these requirements: you didn't receive a dishonorable discharge, you have a service-connected disability rating of at least 10% from VA, and you apply for VR&E services. More broadly, VR&E eligibility applies if you have a disability caused or made worse by your active-duty service that limits your ability to work or prevents you from working. If you're still on active duty, you may be eligible if you meet at least one of these: you have a 20% or higher pre-discharge disability rating memorandum rating and will soon leave the military, or you're participating in the Integrated Disability Evaluation System (IDES) process or awaiting discharge due to a medical condition from a serious injury or illness that occurred in the line of duty. For the reemployment track (returning to your former job), you must have an employment barrier or handicap, be enrolled in VR&E, and want to return to your former job.

If you're signed up for the VA health care program, you can manage your VA health and benefits online through VA.gov. Online options include refilling your prescriptions, sending a secure message to your VA health care team, and checking the status of a disability or pension claim. You can also schedule and view your VA appointments (by phone, online, or through Secure Messaging), view your VA lab and test results, order hearing aid batteries and prosthetic socks for home delivery, and get your VA medical records (also called "VA Blue Button"). For help accessing services, call the toll-free hotline at 877-222-8387, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET. To update your personal information, such as income, address, and insurance, fill out a Health Benefits Update Form (VA Form 10-10EZR).

If you're signed up for VA health care, you can manage your VA health and benefits online through VA.gov. Online options include refilling your prescriptions, sending a secure message to your VA health care team, and checking the status of a disability or pension claim. You can also call the toll-free hotline at 877-222-8387, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET, if you need help accessing services. To update your personal information, such as income, address, and insurance, you can fill out a Health Benefits Update Form (VA Form 10-10EZR) and mail it with any supporting materials.

To find women's health services near you, you can contact your local VA medical center and ask for the Women Veterans Program Manager, who will help coordinate all the services you may need, from primary care to specialized care. You can also call the Women Veterans Call Center at 855-829-6636 (Monday–Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. ET, and Saturday, 8:00 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. ET) and they'll connect you with your local manager, or chat online with a trained representative. Additionally, you can look for women's health services specific to your nearest VA medical center by going to the website of the VA health care system that the medical center is part of, clicking Health Care Services in the navigation, and selecting Women Veterans. If you're already signed up for VA health care, you can also contact your VA medical center and ask for the provider's phone number, or talk to your primary care provider, who will connect you with any services you may need.

If you're signed up for VA health care, you can manage your VA health and benefits online through VA.gov—for example, refilling your prescriptions, sending a secure message to your health care team, and checking the status of a disability or pension claim. If you need help accessing services, you can call the toll-free hotline at 877-222-8387, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET. To update your personal information such as income, address, and insurance, you can fill out a Health Benefits Update Form (VA Form 10-10EZR).

Yes. Through the VR&E Reemployment track, you may be eligible for help returning to the job you held before you deployed, and the track can help your employer accommodate your needs. To qualify, you must be a Veteran with a service-connected disability and meet all of these requirements: you have an employment barrier or handicap, you are enrolled in Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (VR&E), and you would like to return to your former job. An employment handicap means your service-connected disability limits your ability to prepare for, obtain, and maintain suitable employment. The benefits include help with the process of returning to your former job. To get these benefits, you first apply for VR&E benefits and then work with your Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC), who can provide a full range of rehabilitation services and refer you directly to the Department of Labor to begin the process.

To get VR&E Reemployment track assistance to return to a previous job, you must be a Veteran with a service-connected disability and meet all of these requirements: you have an employment barrier or handicap, you are enrolled in Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (VR&E), and you would like to return to your former job. An employment handicap means your service-connected disability limits your ability to prepare for, obtain, and maintain suitable employment. The benefit is help with the process of returning to the job you held before you deployed. To get these benefits, you first apply for VR&E benefits, then work with your Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC).

To get VR&E assistance to return to a previous job on the Reemployment track, you must be a Veteran with a service-connected disability and meet all of these requirements: you have an employment barrier or handicap, you are enrolled in Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (VR&E), and you would like to return to your former job. An employment handicap means your service-connected disability limits your ability to prepare for, obtain, and maintain suitable employment. To get these benefits, you first apply for VR&E benefits and then work with your Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC).

Yes. The VA life insurance resources include a life insurance needs calculator and a VGLI comparison questionnaire to help you decide how much life insurance you need. They also include information on common myths and rumors about SGLI/VGLI insurance, details about the SGLI Online Enrollment System (SOES), contact information for questions about your policy or filing a claim, VA life insurance forms, and downloadable publications and handbooks. You can also explore VA life insurance options and eligibility to find out which plans you may qualify for and the benefits you would receive with each plan.

Yes. The VA provides information on exposure to hazardous chemicals and materials, including whether you can get disability compensation monthly payments and other benefits for illnesses or conditions believed to be caused by contact with harmful chemicals or hazardous materials during military service. The information also covers specific exposures such as Agent Orange, asbestos, Project 112/SHAD chemical testing, radiation exposure, and toxic chemicals in the air, water, or soil for those who served in Iraq, Afghanistan, Djibouti, or near Atsugi, Japan. For volunteers in chemical and biological testing, medical care may be available through the U.S. Army, and you can visit the U.S. Army web page or call 800-984-8523 with questions.

Yes, you may be able to get VA disability benefits for an illness that VA believes is caused by Agent Orange exposure. These are called presumptive diseases. To qualify, you must have an illness VA believes is caused by Agent Orange (a presumptive disease), and at least one of the following must also be true: you came into contact with Agent Orange while serving in the military, or your military record shows qualifying service such as being aboard a U.S. military vessel that operated in certain waters between January 9, 1962, and May 7, 1975. If you have an illness VA believes is caused by Agent Orange, you won't need to show that the problem started during or got worse because of your military service. To get these benefits, you'll need to file a claim for disability compensation and submit your evidence and supporting documents. Benefits can include health care, compensation payments, and an Agent Orange Registry health exam.

Yes. VA may rate disability benefits for contaminated drinking water at Camp Lejeune. If you served at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River in North Carolina, you may have had contact with contaminants in the drinking water there, and scientific and medical evidence has shown an association between exposure to these contaminants during military service and development of certain diseases later on. You may be able to get disability benefits if you have qualifying service at Camp Lejeune and a current diagnosis of one of the listed conditions. Specifically, both of these must be true: you served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 cumulative days from August 1953 through December 1987, and you didn't receive a dishonorable discharge when you separated from the military. You must also have a diagnosis of one or more of these presumptive conditions: adult leukemia, aplastic anemia and other myelodysplastic syndromes, bladder cancer, kidney cancer, liver cancer, multiple myeloma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, or Parkinson's disease. The benefits available include health care and compensation payments, and you'll need to file a claim for disability compensation with supporting evidence such as your military records showing you served at Camp Lejeune.

Yes. VA pension benefits are available to some wartime Veterans and their survivors, and you can check whether you're eligible to apply. If you qualify as a Veteran, you can prepare and apply for a Veterans Pension, including completing VA Form 21P-527EZ online. If you need help with daily activities or are housebound, you can find out how to apply for extra VA pension benefits through Aid and Attendance benefits and Housebound allowance. Survivors can also find out if they're eligible and how to apply for VA Survivors Pension. For help applying for survivors pension benefits, you can work with a trained professional called an accredited representative. You can also manage your pension benefits, such as signing up for direct deposit or a pre-paid debit card, and get support by messaging online or calling the pension beneficiary support line at 877-294-6380 or the VA benefits hotline at 800-827-1000.

Yes. As a Veteran with a service-connected disability, you may be able to get help starting your own business through VA's VR&E Self-Employment track. Eligibility requires that you have an employment barrier or handicap, are enrolled in VR&E, and that your service-connected disability makes it hard for you to prepare for, obtain, or keep suitable employment. VA programs can also help you learn new skills, find a new job, start a new business, get educational counseling, or return to your former job, and you may be able to get entrepreneurship training to help start or improve a small business.

Yes. If you're a Veteran with a service-connected disability that impacts your ability to work, the Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (Voc Rehab, VR&E, or Chapter 31) program may be able to help. Specifically, if you want a job that matches your existing skills, the Rapid Access to Employment track may provide employment counseling and job-search support. You can explore the different tracks and find out how to apply for benefits and services.

Yes. The self-employment track is available to both service members and veterans with a service-connected disability, not only veterans. The evidence states that if you're a service member or Veteran with a service-connected disability, you can find out how VA can help you start your own business, and the VR&E Self-Employment track similarly applies to service members or Veterans with a service-connected disability who want help starting a business.

You can use only one of the benefits you qualify for, so you'll have to pick one when you apply. Once you've made that decision, you can't switch to the other program. To help you decide, you may be able to get free educational and career counseling (Chapter 36), which can help you explore options and choose a training program or job.

VA education benefits help Veterans, service members, and their qualified family members with needs like paying college tuition, finding the right school or training program, and getting career counseling. For survivors and dependents, benefits can include money for tuition, housing, and books and supplies. Regarding exceptions, for studying at a foreign school, family members who qualify for Survivors and Dependents Educational Assistance can get VA benefits while in approved postsecondary after high school non-college degree programs (the evidence text is cut off at this point).

Under the Montgomery GI Bill Active Duty (MGIB-AD) program, Category III applies when all of these are true: you have a high school diploma, GED, or 12 hours of college credit; you don't qualify for MGIB under categories I or II; and your military pay was reduced by $1,200 before separation. In addition, one of these must be true: you were on active duty on September 30, 1990, and were involuntarily separated not by your choice after February 2, 1991; or you were involuntarily separated on or after November 30, 1993; or you chose to voluntarily separate under either the Voluntary Separation Incentive (VSI) program or the Special Separation Benefit (SSB) program.

To get a Fry Scholarship, follow these steps: First, choose a school—the GI Bill Comparison Tool can help you pick one, and you should contact your school's certifying official to make sure your program is approved for VA benefits. Next, apply for benefits: apply online, or fill out a Dependents Application for VA Education Benefits (VA Form 22-5490) and send it to the VA regional benefit office where you want to go to school. If you aren't legally an adult, your parent or guardian must sign the application. If you've already started your educational program, ask a certifying official from your school or your employer to fill out a VA Enrollment Certification (VA Form 22-1999) and submit it online using VA Online Certification (VA-ONCE). Also, if you qualify for both the Fry Scholarship and DEA, you'll need to choose which program you want to use, and once you choose you can't change your mind (with an exception if your parent died in the line of duty before August 1, 2011).

To get a Fry Scholarship, follow these steps: (1) Choose a school — the GI Bill Comparison Tool can help you pick one, and you should contact your school's certifying official to make sure your program is approved for VA benefits. (2) Apply for benefits — apply online, or fill out a Dependents Application for VA Education Benefits (VA Form 22-5490) and send it to the VA regional benefit office where you want to go to school; if you aren't legally an adult, your parent or guardian must sign the application. If you've already started your educational program, ask a certifying official from your school or your employer to fill out a VA Enrollment Certification (VA Form 22-1999) and submit it online using VA Online Certification (VA-ONCE). (3) Choose your program — if you qualify for both the Fry Scholarship and DEA, you'll need to choose which program you want to use, and once you choose you can't change your mind (with an exception if your parent died in the line of duty before August 1, 2011, in which case you can use both, up to 81 months of full-time training, but only one program at a time).

Yes. If your parent died in the line of duty before August 1, 2011, you may qualify for both the Fry Scholarship and the Survivors' and Dependents' Educational Assistance (DEA) program, though you can use only one program at a time. Combined benefits are capped at 81 months of full-time training. Normally, if you qualify for both the Fry Scholarship and DEA, you must choose one and cannot change your mind, but the exception for children of service members who died in the line of duty before August 1, 2011 allows you to use both programs, one at a time, for up to 81 months of education and training. Note that if you're receiving Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC), you'll need to give up those payments when you start using the Fry Scholarship.

Since you already have a VA disability rating, you can apply online: sign in to your eBenefits account, select Apply, click Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment Benefits, and select the Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment benefit you're applying for. If you're eligible, VA will invite you to an orientation session at your nearest VA regional benefit office. If you're a service member who hasn't yet received a service-connected disability rating, you don't need to wait for a rating—instead, fill out VA Form 28, "VA Vocational Rehabilitation - Getting Ahead After You Get Out."

Yes. If you have VA life insurance, the easiest way to manage your policy is online through your online portal, where you can check your policy's status, pay your premium, learn about plan and renewal options, and update your beneficiary. How you access it depends on your policy: if your VA life insurance policy has a file number starting with V, RH, J, RS, K, or W (or if you want to apply for service-disabled life insurance), access your policy online through VA. If you have a Veterans Group Life Insurance (VGLI) policy with a VGLI control number, access your policy online through the Office of Servicemembers Group Life Insurance at Prudential Insurance Company of America.

The evidence does not contain any information about appointments related to VA life insurance. It covers topics such as accessing your policy online, updating beneficiaries, filing claims, checking appeal status, and converting to a commercial policy, but it does not say what to do with appointments.

If you have a disability rating of 30% or higher, you may be able to add eligible dependents to your VA disability compensation to get a higher payment, also called a benefit rate. Additionally, if you receive a combined disability rating of at least 30%, VA will automatically consider your eligibility for additional compensation for your dependents. If you have a combined disability rating of at least 30% and didn't claim dependents when you originally filed, you can file a claim for additional disability compensation now. Also, if your disability gets worse, you can file a claim for an increase in benefits.

Yes. You can sign in to VA.gov and change your address and other contact information in your VA.gov profile. This updates your information across disability compensation, pension benefits, claims and appeals, Vocational Rehabilitation & Employment (VR&E), and VA health care.

The Affordable Care Act (ACA), also known as the health care law, is the law referenced in connection with VA health care coverage. Being signed up for VA health care meets the ACA requirement of having minimum essential health coverage, and the ACA does not change your VA health benefits or your out-of-pocket costs.

If you're late with a mortgage payment or think you might be late with your next payment, contact your loan servicer right away—the sooner you contact them, the sooner they can help you find a solution. If you're nervous about contacting your servicer or would like help and advice, contact a VA Loan Technician at 1-877-827-3702. If you fall far behind, your servicer can take your house to cover the money owed (foreclosure), but VA loan technicians can help you avoid foreclosure and keep your house. If you're a Veteran or surviving spouse of a Veteran, VA provides financial counseling even if your loan isn't VA direct or VA-backed. There are 6 general ways to try to avoid foreclosure, including a repayment plan (added monthly amount to cover missed payments), special forbearance (extra time to repay missed payments), loan modification (adding missed payments and related legal costs to your loan balance with a new payment schedule), extra time to arrange a private sale, and short sale. For substance use, VA health care covers treatment services; apply for VA health care, and if you have a VA primary care provider, talk to them about your substance use so you can be screened and get treatment and support. If you're in crisis, you can contact the Veterans Crisis Line 24/7 by calling 800-273-8255 and selecting 1, starting a confidential chat, or texting 838255.

Yes. If you're signed up for the VA health care program, you can manage your VA health and benefits online through VA.gov—for example, refilling prescriptions, sending a message to your VA health care provider, and checking the status of a disability or pension claim. You can also use VA Appointments tools to schedule, view, and organize some VA appointments online, though eligibility for those tools requires meeting certain requirements (such as being enrolled in VA health care, using a facility that offers online scheduling, and having an appropriate account).

For a veteran who just returned from a deployment or combat mission, it's never too late to get help for PTSD, and getting counseling or treatment can help manage symptoms and keep them from getting worse. A veteran who has just returned from service can receive free medical care for any condition related to service in Iraq or Afghanistan for 5 years after discharge. Combat veterans can also visit a Vet Center for free individual and group counseling for themselves and their family, even if not enrolled in VA health care or receiving disability compensation; Vet Center services include readjustment counseling, bereavement grief counseling, employment counseling, and substance abuse assessment and referral. If the veteran has PTSD symptoms and suffered a serious injury, personal trauma, sexual trauma, or was threatened with injury, sexual assault, or death while serving, they may be able to get disability compensation or benefits. For immediate help, the Veterans Crisis Line offers confidential, private, free support 24/7 by calling 800-273-8255 and selecting 1.

Yes. In addition to PTSD specialists providing regular outpatient care at each VA medical center and special residential or inpatient care programs in each region, providers offer added PTSD care in some large community-based outpatient clinics. If you don't live near a VA medical center or clinic, VA mental health providers can counsel you over the phone through telemental health care, or VA can refer you to a Vet Center or health care provider near you. Also, if you've served in a combat zone, you may be able to get free private counseling, alcohol and drug assessment, and other support at one of VA's 300 community Vet Centers, even without VA health benefits.

Your VA care team's goal is to plan for all the care you need to help you stay healthy and well throughout your life. Your team will build a partnership with you, and you'll be an active member who works with the team to plan and make decisions to meet your personal health goals. The team will offer wellness care, education, and lifestyle coaching, and will provide or arrange preventive care such as immunizations (like flu shots) and screenings to find diseases like cancer in their earliest stages. They'll help you get care in ways that work best for you, which may include personal visits with your primary care provider, group clinics, and 24/7 telephone care. You can also get online educational information and secure messaging with your health care team through the My HealtheVet portal. Team members will meet often to talk with you and each other about your progress and goals, and they'll coordinate any care you may need from specialists outside the team. You'll choose the main VA location where you'd like to get care, and VA will assign you a health care team including your primary care provider based on that location; if you want to change to a different primary care doctor, you'll need to talk to your health care team leader. If you're signed up for VA health care, you can manage your VA health and benefits online through VA.gov, including sending a secure message to your health care team.

Your VA care team is a Patient Aligned Care Team (PACT), which includes you, your family members and caregivers who support you, and your health care providers. Your team includes a primary care provider (your main doctor, nurse practitioner, or physician's assistant), a clinical pharmacist who works with you and your provider to make sure you're taking the right medicines, a registered nurse care manager who makes sure your care is coordinated across all providers and services, and licensed practical nurse or medical assistant and clerk team members who support you and the other providers. When you need other services, your team may call other providers like social workers or specialists. Your team's goal is to plan all the care you need to help you stay healthy and well throughout your life. Your team will build a partnership with you, offering wellness care, education, and lifestyle coaching; provide or arrange preventive care such as immunizations and screenings; help you get care in ways that work best for you, including personal visits, group clinics, and 24/7 telephone care; and coordinate your care, meeting often to discuss your progress and goals and coordinating any care from specialists outside the team. You can also get online educational information and secure messaging with your health care team through the My HealtheVet portal.

Under the Post-9/11 GI Bill, VA pays tuition and fees directly to the school, not to you. Money for books is paid to you at the beginning of the term, and the housing allowance is paid to you at the end of each month. Payments are issued after each month's classes—for example, the payment for November classes comes in December.

Yes. Tutorial assistance is one of the ways you can use your Post-9/11 GI Bill (Chapter 33) benefits, and if you're using the Post-9/11 GI Bill, VA won't charge your GI Bill benefits for it. To get it: your course instructor or teacher at your school must agree you need a tutor and write a letter on your behalf; the instructor should send the letter to your school's certifying official and add a copy to your VA student file. If your school approves your need for a tutor, it will assign you a tutor and confirm the tutor's hourly pay. After you get tutoring, you, your tutor, and your school's certifying official must fill out and sign VA Form 22-1990t (Application for Individualized Tutorial Assistance). If you're using the Post-9/11 GI Bill, your instructor must also sign section 18 of this form. The form must be signed and dated on or after the date of the last certified tutoring session (item 12b on the form).

To get a disability rating, you file a claim for disability compensation. VA assigns you a disability rating based on the severity of your disability, expressed as a percentage representing how much your disability decreases your overall health and ability to function. VA then uses your disability rating to determine your disability compensation rate and to help determine your eligibility for other benefits, like VA health care. After you get a decision notice confirming your disability rating, you may be able to get disability compensation or benefits; if your decision notice shows at least a 10% disability rating, you'll get your first payment within 15 days. If you haven't gotten your decision notice, you can check your status, contact your nearest VA regional benefit office, call 800-827-1000, or contact VA online. If you disagree with your disability rating, you can file an appeal within 1 year of getting your decision notice.

After you apply for VA health care, VA will send you a letter in the mail letting you know whether your application was approved. If more than a week has passed since you submitted your application and you haven't heard back, don't apply again—call the toll-free hotline at 877-222-8387. If your application is approved, wait for your welcome call from VA, which will help you schedule your first doctor's appointment and answer questions about your health care benefits. You'll also receive your Veterans Health Benefits Handbook by mail, explaining your specific benefits based on your assigned priority group and your copay amounts. You'll also need to get your Veterans Health Identification Card (VHIC) by contacting your local VA medical center and speaking with the enrollment coordinator, or you can request it at your next VA health care appointment.

With a 100% disability rating, you may be able to get dental care and access to commissaries and exchanges. Separately, if you can't work because of a service-connected disability, you may qualify for Individual Unemployability, which can provide disability compensation or benefits at the same level as a Veteran with a 100% disability rating.

If you had surgery or received other treatment at a VA hospital, approved hospital, or outpatient center for a service-connected disability, you may be able to get a temporary 100% disability rating and disability compensation or benefits. To get these benefits, you'll need to file a claim for disability compensation. Recovery time from surgery or from immobilization of a joint by a cast without surgery requires a temporary 100% disability rating for a service-connected disability, and the temporary 100% rating may continue for 1 to 3 months depending on your unique case, with a possible extension of up to 3 more months if your case is severe.

Based on the evidence, you can learn more about your disability rating and related benefits by filing a claim for disability compensation. If you had surgery or received other treatment at a VA hospital, approved hospital, or outpatient center for a service-connected disability, you may be able to get a temporary 100% disability rating, health care while you recover, and added compensation payments. The temporary 100% rating may continue for 1 to 3 months depending on your case, with a possible extension of up to 3 more months if your case is severe. You can also check with your local or state VA offices for other benefits, such as help with buying a home, making home changes for accessibility, or getting a job, and find your state's Veterans Affairs website.

No. Having surgery by itself is not enough. To qualify for VA disability benefits after surgery, the surgery must have been for a service-connected disability, and both of these must be true: the surgery required a recovery time of at least one month (or reports show the surgery or treatment was for a service-connected disability), and the surgery resulted in severe issues such as unhealed surgical wounds, recent amputation stumps, therapeutic immobilization (splints or casts), house confinement, or being required to use a wheelchair or crutches. If you qualify, possible benefits include health care while you recover, added compensation payments, and a temporary 100% disability rating, which may last 1 to 3 months depending on your case, with a possible extension of up to 3 more months if severe. You get these by filing a claim for disability compensation.

For a Veteran in a mental health crisis, the Veterans Crisis Line offers confidential help that is private, free, and available 24/7: call 800-273-8255 and select 1, start a confidential Veterans chat, text 838255, or if you have hearing loss call TTY 800-799-4889. You can also call 911, go to the nearest emergency room, or go directly to your nearest VA medical center, regardless of discharge status or VA health care enrollment. For ongoing support, specially trained suicide prevention coordinators at each VA medical center can help you get counseling and services, Vet Centers can help you and your family readjust to life at home after returning from a combat zone, and Veterans Benefits Administration offices can help you access benefits such as disability compensation, job training, and home loans. Additional information and support are available on the VA suicide prevention website and the Make the Connection website, and family members or friends can get free, confidential help through the national Coaching Into Care program.

If you request an informal conference with a senior reviewer on the Higher-Level Review option, the senior reviewer will call the phone number that you or your representative provided on the Higher-Level Review form to schedule a time to discuss your case with you. The senior reviewer will try to reach you or your representative by phone twice. If no one answers, they'll leave a voice mail. During the call, you and/or your representative can talk about why you think the decision should be changed and identify errors. There won't be transcripts of this call.

To use VA health care benefits and services, you must be enrolled in VA health care and you must have received care from VA within the past 24 months. For urgent care, you also need to tell the urgent care provider that you're using the VA urgent care benefit when you arrive. For non-VA emergency care for a non-service-connected condition, you must meet several requirements. The full list of your covered benefits depends on your priority group, the advice of your VA primary care provider, and the medical standards.
The evidence says to "Learn more about priority groups" and points to a "Priority groups" resource that explains what VA priority groups are, how they work, and how they may affect you.

You may be able to get a COE as the surviving spouse of a Veteran, or as the spouse of a Veteran who is missing in action or being held as a Prisoner of War (POW). More specifically, you may qualify if you're the spouse of a Veteran and at least one of these is true for the Veteran: they are missing in action, are a Prisoner of War, or died while in service or from a service-connected disability and you didn't remarry (or didn't remarry before you were 57). Keep in mind you'll also need to meet your lender's credit and income requirements to get a loan. To apply, you can apply online through eBenefits, through the Web LGY system (in some cases via your lender), or by mail using VA Form 26-1880.

Yes. A surviving spouse may be able to get a COE if the Veteran is missing in action or is a Prisoner of War (POW). The spouse of a Veteran who is missing in action or being held as a POW may also be able to get a COE. Note that you'll also need to meet your lender's credit and income requirements to get a loan.

You can schedule and view VA health care appointments online using the VA Appointments tools on the My HealtheVet health management portal. These tools offer a secure, web-based way to schedule, view, and organize your VA appointments. With them you can schedule some VA medical appointments online, reschedule and cancel appointments made online, view appointments on your health calendar, find the location of the VA facility for your appointments, set up email reminders, print a list of future appointments, look up past appointments from the last 2 years, and add non-VA appointments to your health calendar. Eligibility depends on meeting certain requirements, and online scheduling availability and the types of appointments you can schedule depend on your VA health facility. For more questions, you can read the VA Appointments FAQs in the My HealtheVet portal or contact the My HealtheVet Help Desk at 877-327-0022 (TTY: 800-877-8339), Monday through Friday, 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. CT.

Yes, you may be able to keep your SGLI coverage for up to 2 years after the date you left the military through the SGLI Disability Extension, but you must qualify. You must be within 2 years of your separation date and meet the disability requirements—for example, being totally disabled at the time of discharge and unable to work, or having certain specified conditions such as total loss of hearing in both ears, loss of speech, or permanent loss of use of both hands, feet, or eyes. Since you previously indicated your condition doesn't prevent you from working, you would need to meet one of the specified conditions to qualify.

For housebound benefits based on a disability that is not 100% disabling, the evidence shows that you may qualify if you have a disability rated 60% or higher in addition to the disability that qualifies you for a pension. Housebound benefits may also be available if you get a VA pension and spend most of your time in your home because of a permanent disability that doesn't go away. Note that you can't get Aid and Attendance benefits and Housebound benefits at the same time.

Yes—if your PTSD resulted from a traumatic event, you may be able to get VA disability benefits. VA considers a traumatic event to include suffering a serious injury, personal or sexual trauma, or sexual violation, or being threatened with injury, sexual assault, or death. To qualify, all of these must be true: the stressor happened during your service, you can't function as well as you once could because of your symptoms, and a doctor has diagnosed you with PTSD. Covered beneficiaries are Veterans, and the benefits can include health care, compensation payments, and treatment for PTSD. To get these benefits, you'll need to file a claim for disability compensation, along with VA Form 21-0781 (Statement in Support of Claim for Service Connection for PTSD) or, for claims secondary to personal assault, VA Form 21-0781a.

If you're a Veteran in crisis or concerned about one, you can connect with the Veterans Crisis Line for confidential help. This service is private, free, and available 24/7. To reach a responder anytime, day or night: call 800-273-8255 and select 1, start a confidential Veterans chat, or text 838255. If you have hearing loss, call TTY: 800-799-4889.

If you served in Vietnam or in or near the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) during the Vietnam Era, or in certain related jobs, you may have had contact with Agent Orange—referred to as a presumption of contact. You can find out if you can get disability compensation and other benefits for illnesses VA believes are caused by Agent Orange. To qualify for disability benefits, you must have an illness VA believes is caused by Agent Orange (a presumptive disease), and at least one of the following must also be true: you came into contact with Agent Orange while serving in the military; you served in or near the DMZ for any length of time between September 1, 1967, and August 31, 1971; or you served in the Republic of Vietnam for any length of time between January 9, 1962, and May 7, 1975 (which may include serving aboard a vessel on the inland waterways or within 12 nautical miles seaward as detailed in the Blue Water Navy Vietnam Veterans Act of 2019). You can file a claim for disability compensation, and you may need to submit a medical record showing a current disability and a connection between Agent Orange exposure and that disability, plus a military record showing your qualifying service or other Agent Orange contact. For help filing your claim, you can call 800-827-1000 or TTY 800-877-8339, go to your nearest VA regional benefit office, or get help from a VA representative.

Having a severe disability that VA concluded was caused or made worse by your service is one requirement, but it isn't enough on its own. To be eligible for VMLI, all of these must also be true: you received a Specially Adapted Housing (SAH) grant to buy, build, or adapt a home for independent living, you have the title of the home, and you have a mortgage on the home.

To be eligible for VA Aid and Attendance benefits, you must first be receiving a VA pension and meet at least one of the following requirements: you need another person to help you perform daily activities like bathing, feeding, and dressing; you have to stay in bed or spend a large portion of the day in bed because of illness; you are a patient in a nursing home due to the loss of mental or physical abilities related to a disability; or your eyesight is limited even with glasses or contact lenses to 5/200 or less in both eyes, or concentric contraction of the visual field to 5 degrees or less. Note that you can't get Aid and Attendance benefits and Housebound benefits at the same time.

To be eligible for VA Aid and Attendance benefits, you must first be receiving a VA pension and meet at least one of the following requirements: you need another person to help you perform daily activities like bathing, feeding, and dressing; you have to stay in bed or spend a large portion of the day in bed because of illness; you are a patient in a nursing home due to the loss of mental or physical abilities related to a disability; or your eyesight is limited even with glasses or contact lenses to 5/200 or less in both eyes, or concentric contraction of the visual field to 5 degrees or less. Note that you cannot receive Aid and Attendance benefits and Housebound benefits at the same time.

You may qualify for enhanced eligibility status—placing you in a higher priority group and making you more likely to get benefits—if you meet at least one of these requirements: receiving financial compensation payments from VA for a service-connected disability; being discharged for a disability resulting from something that happened in the line of duty; being discharged for a disability that got worse in the line of duty; being a recently discharged combat Veteran; getting a VA pension; being a former prisoner of war; or having received a Purple Heart. Separately, for OEF/OIF/OND combat Veterans, enhanced eligibility requires meeting all of these: serving in a theater of combat operations after November 11, 1998; being discharged or released from active service on or after January 29, 2003; and not receiving a dishonorable discharge.

Based on the evidence, you can request an appointment to apply for survivor benefits by calling 1-800-772-1213; if you are deaf or hard of hearing, call the TTY number at 1-800-325-0778. If you wish to apply for disability benefits as a survivor, you can speed up the process by completing an Adult Disability Report and having it available at your appointment.

You can use the VA life insurance online portal to check your policy's status to make sure it's up to date, pay your premium (the amount you pay each month to keep your coverage), and find out about your plan and renewal options, which depend on the type of plan you have. You can also update your beneficiary information through the portal. To access your policy online, you can use VA if your policy has a file number starting with V, RH, J, RS, K, or W, or if you'd like to apply for service-disabled life insurance; if you have a VGLI policy with a VGLI control number, you access it through the Office of Servicemembers Group Life Insurance at Prudential Insurance Company of America.

To apply for Service-Disabled Veterans Life Insurance (S-DVI), you must meet all of these requirements: you were released from active duty on or after April 25, 1951, and didn't receive a dishonorable discharge; you were rated for a service-connected disability even if only 0%; you are in good health except for any service-connected conditions; and you apply within 2 years from the date VA grants your new service-connected disability. Note that an increase of a rating you had before, or a rating of Individual Unemployability, doesn't qualify you for S-DVI.

You can get help with your claim from an accredited representative or a Veterans Service Organization (VSO). These trained professionals can help you understand and apply for VA benefits, help you gather supporting documents like a doctor's report or medical test results, and file a claim or appeal on your behalf. They can also provide added support, such as help with transportation to medical appointments or emergency funds. In general, no individual or organization may charge you a fee to help you file your initial application for benefits, though they may charge for unusual expenses; only after VA has made a decision on your original claim may VA-accredited claims agents and attorneys charge for their services, so ask up front about any fees. To set up representation, you can use eBenefits or fill out and mail a form: VA Form 21-22 to have a VSO help you, or VA Form 21-22a to have a claims agent or attorney help you, mailing it to your nearest VA regional office. For decision reviews, a VSO or VA-accredited attorney or agent can help you request a decision review.

To qualify for Veterans Mortgage Life Insurance (VMLI), you must meet all of these requirements: you have a severe disability that VA has concluded was caused or made worse by your service; you received a Specially Adapted Housing (SAH) grant to buy, build, or modify a home (such as installing ramps or widening doorways) so you can live more independently; you have the title of the home; you have a mortgage on the home; and you are under 70 years old. VMLI provides mortgage protection insurance to families of Veterans with severe service-connected disabilities who have adapted a home to fit their needs, and you apply for VMLI in connection with the SAH grant process.

Yes. To qualify for S-DVI, all of the following must be true: you were released from active duty on or after April 25, 1951, and didn't receive a dishonorable discharge; you were rated for a service-connected disability, even if only 0%; you are in good health except for any service-connected conditions; and you apply within 2 years from the date VA grants your new service-connected disability. Note that an increase of a rating you had before, or a rating of Individual Unemployability, doesn't qualify you for S-DVI.

The evidence does not address whether a disability sustained after honorable discharge in 1963 qualifies for S-DVI. The listed S-DVI requirements state that you must have been released from active duty on or after April 25, 1951 without a dishonorable discharge, be rated for a service-connected disability, be in good health except for service-connected conditions, and apply within 2 years from the date the new service-connected disability is granted. The evidence does not specify whether the disability must have been incurred during service, so the question cannot be answered from the provided evidence.

Service-Disabled Veterans Life Insurance (S-DVI) provides low-cost coverage to eligible service members. You can apply for S-DVI if you meet all of these requirements: you were released from active duty on or after April 25, 1951, and didn't receive a dishonorable discharge; you were rated for a service-connected disability, even if only 0%; you are in good health except for any service-connected conditions; and you apply within 2 years from the date VA grants your new service-connected disability. S-DVI lets you continue your life insurance beyond 2 years after you leave the military if you're disabled because of an injury or illness caused or made worse by your active service.

Not automatically. Meeting the release-from-active-duty condition (released on or after April 25, 1951, without a dishonorable discharge) is only one of several requirements. You must also have been rated for a service-connected disability (even 0%), be in good health except for service-connected conditions, and apply within 2 years from the date VA grants your new service-connected disability. Since you indicated you do not have a service-connected disability, you would not currently meet all the requirements.

To apply for Service-Disabled Veterans Life Insurance (S-DVI) with a service-connected disability, you must meet all of these requirements: you were released from active duty on or after April 25, 1951, and didn't receive a dishonorable discharge; you were rated for a service-connected disability, even if only 0%; you are in good health except for any service-connected conditions; and you apply within 2 years from the date VA grants your new service-connected disability. Note that an increase of a rating you had before, or a rating of Individual Unemployability, doesn't qualify you for S-DVI. You can apply online or by mail using VA Form 29-4364 (fax it to 888-748-5822 or mail it to the Department of Veterans Affairs Regional Office and Insurance Center, RH, PO Box 7208, Philadelphia, PA 19101).

Based on the evidence, you can tell whether S-DVI is right for you by checking the eligibility requirements. S-DVI is for service members or Veterans who have a service-connected disability, and it lets you continue life insurance beyond 2 years after you leave the military. To apply, all of these must be true: you were released from active duty on or after April 25, 1951, and didn't receive a dishonorable discharge; you were rated for a service-connected disability, even if only 0%; you're in good health except for any service-connected conditions; and you apply within 2 years from the date VA grants your new service-connected disability. Note that an increase of a rating you had before, or a rating of Individual Unemployability, doesn't qualify you for S-DVI. If you're ending your military tour of duty soon, you'll need to get new coverage quickly, and in some cases you must act within a certain time. S-DVI offers up to $10,000 of basic coverage and up to $30,000 of supplemental coverage.

To determine which life insurance coverage is right for you as an Army service member, the evidence indicates that different VA programs cover different groups: VGLI for Veterans, SGLI for service members, and FSGLI for family members. You may also be able to get short-term financial coverage through TSGLI to help recover from a traumatic severe injury. If you're disabled because of an injury or illness caused or made worse by your active service, you may be able to get coverage through S-DVI to continue your life insurance beyond 2 years after you leave the military. As an active-duty member of the Army, you may be eligible for full-time SGLI coverage, and if you meet certain criteria you'll be automatically signed up through your service branch. You can choose your level of coverage or refuse coverage completely, and you can choose and change your beneficiaries; Army members can submit changes online through the SGLI Online Enrollment System (SOES) via milConnect. Note that if you're ending your military tour of duty soon, you'll need to get new coverage quickly, and in some cases you must act within a certain timeframe.

Yes. Besides SGLI, servicemembers may have other VA insurance options. Family Servicemembers Group Life Insurance (FSGLI) adds coverage for a spouse and dependent children, and Traumatic Injury Protection (TSGLI) provides short-term financial support to help recover from a severe injury. Veterans Group Life Insurance (VGLI) provides group life insurance once service has ended, and Service-Disabled Veterans Insurance (S-DVI) lets those disabled by an injury or illness caused or made worse by active service continue life insurance beyond 2 years after leaving the military. Veterans Mortgage Life Insurance (VMLI) offers mortgage protection for those with a severe service-connected disability for a home adapted to their needs.

Service-Disabled Veterans Life Insurance (S-DVI) provides low-cost coverage to eligible service members. You can apply for S-DVI if you meet all of these requirements: you were released from active duty on or after April 25, 1951, and didn't receive a dishonorable discharge; you were rated for a service-connected disability, even if only 0%; you are in good health except for any service-connected conditions; and you apply within 2 years from the date VA grants your new service-connected disability. An increase of a rating or a rating of Individual Unemployability does not qualify you for S-DVI. If you carry basic S-DVI coverage and become totally disabled and unable to work, you can apply for up to $30,000 more in coverage, called supplemental S-DVI coverage. Under certain conditions, the basic S-DVI policy provides for a waiver of premiums for Veterans who are totally disabled, but you must pay premiums for supplemental S-DVI. To apply, you can apply for basic S-DVI online or fill out VA Form 29-4364 and fax it to 888-748-5822 or mail it to the Department of Veterans Affairs Regional Office and Insurance Center RH, PO Box 7208, Philadelphia, PA 19101.

Yes. Under the Records section, you can apply for a printed Veteran ID card, get your VA benefit letters and medical records, and learn how to apply for a discharge upgrade. Separately, the Veteran Health Identification Card (VHIC) is used for VA health care appointments and gives access to your VA health record.

To use all the features of VA Blue Button, both of these must be true: you're enrolled in VA health care, and you're registered as a patient in a VA health facility. You must also have one of these free accounts: an Advanced or Premium My HealtheVet account, a Premium DS Logon account (used for eBenefits and milConnect, or that you can create on VA.gov), or a verified ID.me account.

Yes. If you can't get VA dental care benefits, you may be able to buy dental insurance at a reduced cost through the VA Dental Insurance Program (VADIP). To qualify, at least one of these must be true: you're signed up for VA health care, or you're signed up for CHAMPVA (the Civilian Health and Medical Program, a health insurance program for dependents of Veterans). VADIP can help you buy private dental insurance at a reduced cost, and signing up for VADIP won't affect your ability to get free VA dental care. If you're not eligible for free VA dental care, VADIP can help you buy private dental insurance at a reduced cost.

The evidence provided doesn't include information on how to get more questions answered about VADIP. It covers eligibility, benefits, costs, and how to enroll (through Delta Dental or MetLife), but not a contact or resource for additional questions.

VADIP plans cover many common dental procedures. These may include diagnostic services; preventive dental care to manage oral health problems and restore function, called endodontic or restorative services; root canals and other services; dental surgery; and emergency dental care. The cost of coverage depends on the insurance company and plan you choose; based on your plan, you'll pay the full insurance premium for each individual on your plan and any required copays when you get care.

Beyond education benefits, VA resources for survivors and dependents include: benefits for spouses, dependents, survivors, and family caregivers, including added support if you're caring for a Veteran with a service-connected disability; pension payments for wartime Veterans and survivors with limited or no income who meet certain age and disability requirements; burial and memorial help, including applying for survivor and dependent benefits; and records access, such as applying for a printed Veteran ID card, getting your VA benefit letters and medical records, and learning how to apply for a discharge upgrade. Other resources include housing assistance (VA home loan programs and housing grants for service-connected disabilities), careers and employment support (vocational rehabilitation services and Veteran-owned small business support), life insurance options for Veterans, service members, and families, and education and training benefits.

For dependent children, the service member pays nothing—dependent coverage is provided at no cost until the child is 18 (or sometimes longer if the child is a full-time student or became permanently and totally disabled before turning 18). For spousal coverage, the service member pays a premium that increases as the spouse ages; the specific monthly rates depend on the spouse's age and the amount of coverage chosen.

Nothing. Dependent coverage is provided at no cost until the child is 18 years old, or sometimes longer if the child meets certain requirements (for example, being a full-time student or becoming permanently and totally disabled before turning 18 and unable to support themselves).

Yes. Under the FSGLI dependent coverage rules, coverage is provided at no cost until the child is 18, but it can sometimes continue longer if the child meets certain requirements. One of those requirements is that the child becomes permanently and totally disabled before turning 18 and can no longer support themselves. In that situation, the coverage may be extended, in some cases indefinitely.

Within 240 days of leaving the military, you can sign up for Veterans' Group Life Insurance (VGLI) without needing to prove you're in good health. If you sign up after the 240-day period, you'll need to submit evidence of good health. You must apply for VGLI within one year and 120 days of leaving the military, and coverage amounts range from $10,000 to $400,000 based on the SGLI coverage you had when you left the military.

To continue receiving dependent coverage after age 18, one of these must be true: the child is a full-time student, or the child becomes permanently and totally disabled before turning 18 and can't support themselves. Coverage may also be extended if the child is a full-time student between 18 and 22 years old.

FSGLI covers the spouses and dependent children of service members who are covered under full-time SGLI. This includes spouses of service members covered under SGLI and dependent children of service members covered under SGLI. The service member must be on active duty and covered by full-time SGLI, or a member of the National Guard or Ready Reserve covered by full-time SGLI.
VGLI covers veterans (former service members).

For a dependent child who is a full-time student between 18 and 23 years old, you'll need to fill out both VA Form 21-686c (Declaration of Status of Dependents) and VA Form 21-674 (Request for Approval of School Attendance). You can mail the completed forms to the Department of Veterans Affairs Evidence Intake Center, PO Box 4444, Janesville, WI 53547-4444, or fax them to 844-531-7817 if you live in the U.S.

For dependent children, the service member pays nothing—dependent coverage is provided at no cost until the child is 18 (or sometimes longer if the child is a full-time student or became permanently and totally disabled before age 18). Note that a premium does apply for spousal coverage, which increases with the spouse's age.

The evidence doesn't say what happens if you don't take a specific action regarding Veterans Group Life Insurance (VGLI). It only explains that with VGLI you may be able to keep your life insurance coverage after leaving the military for as long as you continue to pay the premiums, and lists eligibility requirements. The consequences of not acting (for example, not paying premiums or not applying within the eligibility window) aren't described, so this can't be answered from the provided evidence.

To continue receiving dependent coverage after age 18, one of these must be true: the child is a full-time student, or the child becomes permanently and totally disabled before turning 18 and can't support themselves. In some cases coverage may be extended if the child is a full-time student between 18 and 22 years old.

VA Individual Unemployability (IU) is a benefit for Veterans who can't hold down a steady job because of a service-connected disability. If you qualify, you may receive disability compensation or benefits at the same level as a Veteran with a 100% disability rating. To qualify, both of these must be true: you have at least one service-connected disability rated at 60% or more disabling, or two or more service-connected disabilities with at least one rated at 40% or more disabling and a combined rating of 70% or more; and you can't hold down a steady job that supports you financially (substantially gainful employment) because of your service-connected disability. Odd jobs or marginal employment don't count. In certain cases, such as if you need to be in the hospital often, you may qualify at a lower disability rating. Covered beneficiaries are Veterans, and the benefits can include health care and compensation payments. To get these benefits, you file a claim for disability compensation and provide evidence, such as a doctor's report or medical test results, showing your disability prevents you from holding down a steady job; VA will also review your work and education history. Along with your disability claim, you'll need to fill out VA Form 21-8940 (Veteran's Application for Increased Compensation Based on Unemployability) and VA Form 21-4192 (Request for Employment Information in Connection with Claim for Disability Benefits).

The evidence describes application procedures for specific VA benefits rather than a single general VA benefits process. For VA health care, you first check whether you're eligible and gather the documents needed to complete an Application for Health Benefits (VA Form 10-10EZ), including your most recent tax return, Social Security numbers for yourself and qualified dependents, and account numbers for any current health insurance. You or someone with power of attorney must sign and date the form; if using a power of attorney, submit a copy of that form, and if you sign with an X, two people you know must witness your signature and sign and print their names. You can send the completed application to the Health Eligibility Center in Atlanta, GA, or apply in person by bringing the signed form to your nearest VA medical center or clinic. You can also get help through your state's Department of Veterans Affairs or from an accredited representative. After applying, you can check the status of related pension or disability claims online, and if more than a week has passed without hearing back, call the toll-free hotline rather than applying again. For a VA home loan, the first step is applying for a Certificate of Eligibility, which confirms to your lender that you qualify; Veterans need a copy of their discharge or separation papers (DD214), while active-duty service members need a statement of service signed by their commander, adjutant, or personnel officer. For education benefits, you can apply in person at a VA regional benefit office, work with your school's certifying official, or get help from an accredited representative.

The evidence does not explain what to do with appointments in connection with VGLI. The only appointment-related guidance is for VA health care: if you're enrolled in VA health care, you use your Veteran Health Identification Card (VHIC) to check in to your appointments at VA medical centers.

CHAMPVA (Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs) is a health insurance program for spouses or surviving spouses and children of Veterans with disabilities or of Veterans who have died, available to those who don't qualify for TRICARE. Through CHAMPVA, VA covers the cost of some health care services and supplies (cost sharing). Covered services include ambulance service, ambulatory surgery, durable medical equipment (DME), family planning and maternity, hospice, inpatient services, mental health services, outpatient services, pharmacy prescription medicines, skilled nursing care, and transplants, when determined medically necessary and received from an authorized provider. Family members caring for a Veteran with disabilities who aren't entitled to care through another health plan may also qualify. CHAMPVA is always the second payer to Medicare.

Beyond the active duty service requirement, the evidence lists additional ways to qualify for Post-9/11 GI Bill (Chapter 33) benefits. You can get these education benefits if you meet at least one of the requirements: served at least 90 days on active duty (all at once or with breaks in service) on or after September 11, 2001; received a Purple Heart on or after September 11, 2001, and were honorably discharged after any amount of service; served for at least 30 continuous days all at once, without a break in service, on or after September 11, 2001, and were honorably discharged with a service-connected disability; or are a dependent child using benefits transferred by a qualifying Veteran or service member. Additionally, if you're a member of the Reserves who lost education benefits when the Reserve Educational Assistance Program (REAP) ended in November 2015, you may qualify to receive restored benefits under the Post-9/11 GI Bill.

The evidence does not contain enough information to answer this question. It does not describe how to plan a burial for a father or what specific burial planning assistance is available, and it does not identify dependent benefits specifically available to a surviving child after a father's death. The evidence only mentions generally that help is available for planning a burial in a VA national cemetery and for applying for survivor and dependent benefits, and it describes application forms and certain survivor benefits without addressing burial planning for a father.

If you take fewer courses, VA will pay less toward your tuition and fees, and your school will also reduce the amount they pay. Refunds are based on each school's refund policy, and you'll need to pay back any overpayments VA made to the school that the school doesn't refund.

To get a VA-backed home loan, the first step is applying for a VA home loan Certificate of Eligibility (COE), which confirms to your lender that you qualify for the VA home loan benefit. To apply for the COE, you'll need to gather certain information depending on your status: if you're a Veteran, a copy of your discharge or separation papers (DD214); if you're an active-duty Servicemember, a statement of service signed by your commander, adjutant, or personnel officer. You may be able to get a COE if you didn't receive a dishonorable discharge and you meet the minimum active-duty service requirement based on when you served. Keep in mind that for a VA-backed home loan, you'll also need to meet your lender's credit and income loan requirements to receive financing. After getting your COE, your next steps will depend on the type of loan you're looking to get and on the private bank or mortgage company serving as your lender.

Yes. The Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers supports family members caring for a Veteran with disabilities, and you can find out if you qualify and how to apply. Eligibility depends on the Veteran's qualifications, such as having a serious injury (including traumatic brain injury, psychological trauma, or other mental disorder) caused or made worse by active-duty service on or after September 11, 2001, and needing personal care services. Additionally, if you are a family member caring for a Veteran with disabilities and are not entitled to care or services through another health plan, you may qualify for CHAMPVA, which covers cost sharing for some health care services and supplies.

In addition to the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers, VA resources include benefits for spouses, dependents, survivors, and family caregivers, including added support if you're caring for a Veteran with a service-connected disability. Other resources listed include pension payments for wartime Veterans and survivors with limited or no income, burials and memorials (including survivor and dependent benefits), and records services such as applying for a printed Veteran ID card, getting VA benefit letters and medical records, and applying for a discharge upgrade. Additional VA benefits and services include housing assistance (VA-backed home loans and housing grants for service-connected disabilities), life insurance, education and training (GI Bill and other education benefits), and career resources for spouses and other family members of Veterans and service members.

Through the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers, family caregivers of a Veteran with disabilities may get health care benefits through CHAMPVA if they don't already qualify for care or services under another health care plan, along with mental health services and counseling and up to 30 days per year of respite care. To get these benefits, you apply by filling out VA Form 10-10CG, which requires identification and health coverage information for both you and your Veteran, and both of you must sign and date the form.

If you are the child or spouse of a Veteran or service member who died, is captured or missing, or has disabilities, you may be able to get help paying for school or job training through the Survivors' and Dependents' Educational Assistance (DEA) program, also called Chapter 35. The benefits include education and training, money for tuition, money for housing, and money for books and supplies. Eligibility can apply where the service member died in the line of duty after September 10, 2001, is missing in action or was captured in the line of duty by a hostile force, or was detained/held by force in the line of duty by a foreign government or power; for a Veteran, where the Veteran is permanently and totally disabled due to a service-connected disability or died while on active duty or as a result of a service-connected disability.

To manage your VA education benefits, you can: view your VA payment history (including education and other benefits like disability compensation and pension); check how much of your Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits you have left to help pay for school or training; transfer your unused Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits to your spouse or other dependents; and request a change to use a different GI Bill program or to transfer your benefits to a new school or training program.

Under the Veterans work-study program, you'll earn an hourly wage equal to the federal minimum wage or your state minimum wage, whichever is greater; if your school usually pays students more for the job, they may pay you the difference between the VA amount and their usual rate. For payment timing, you may elect to be paid in advance for 40% of the hours in your work-study agreement, or for 50 hours, whichever is fewer. After you've worked the hours covered by your first payment, you'll be paid each time you finish 50 hours of service or every other week, whichever comes first.

Besides refilling and tracking prescriptions, VA health care covers other services and needs, including mental health services (such as for PTSD, military sexual trauma, depression, and substance use problems), assisted living and home health care depending on your needs and income as well as space in the programs, and prescriptions written or approved by a VA doctor. It may also cover ancillary services your VA primary care provider concludes you need to support your treatment, such as tests used to diagnose health conditions (including blood work, X-rays, and ultrasounds) and therapy and rehabilitation services (including physical therapy, vision rehab, and therapy for trauma). You can also manage your health and benefits through tools like VA Secure Messaging, scheduling and viewing VA appointments, viewing your VA lab and test results, ordering hearing aid batteries and prosthetic socks online for home delivery, and getting your VA medical records (VA Blue Button). Family and caregiver health benefits may also be available if you qualify as a spouse, surviving spouse, dependent child, or caregiver.

The evidence does not describe any records you need to keep for the VA work-study program. It only explains how to apply: you apply by filling out an Application for Work-Study Allowance (VA Form 22-8691), and you can contact the VA regional processing office that handles your claim with questions.

Under the Montgomery GI Bill Active Duty (MGIB-AD), Category III applies when all of these are true: you have a high school diploma, GED, or 12 hours of college credit; you don't qualify for MGIB under categories I or II; and your military pay was reduced by $1,200 before separation. In addition, at least one of these must be true: you were on active duty on September 30, 1990, and were involuntarily separated not by your choice after February 2, 1991; or you were involuntarily separated on or after November 30, 1993; or you chose to voluntarily separate under the Voluntary Separation Incentive (VSI) program or the Special Separation Benefit (SSB) program.

The evidence does not describe any appointment steps specific to the Veteran work-study program. It only explains general VA health care appointment tools: you can schedule some VA health care appointments online through the VA Appointments tools on My HealtheVet, or by phone or through the online scheduling tool. To use the online tools, you must be enrolled in VA health care, be scheduling with a VA health facility that uses online scheduling, have had an appointment at that facility within the last 2 years, and have a Premium My HealtheVet account, a Premium DS Logon account, or a verified ID.me account. These tools let you schedule, reschedule, cancel, view, and set reminders for VA appointments.

To request information about the Veterans work-study program, contact the VA regional processing office that handles your claim if you have questions about the program. To apply for the program, fill out an Application for Work-Study Allowance (VA Form 22-8691).

The evidence does not explain how to participate if you do not already have an open job at a VA facility or in a VA-related role at your school. It states that taking part requires meeting all listed requirements, including having found an open job either at a nearby VA facility or in a VA-related role at your school. It also says you apply by filling out VA Form 22-8691, and that you can contact the VA regional processing office handling your claim with questions.

If you're serving on active duty in the United States uniformed services, including active National Guard and Reserve with federal pay, you may be eligible for VA benefits both during service and after separation or retirement. Traditional or technical members of the National Guard and Reserve may also be eligible for some VA benefits. You can find out which benefits you may qualify for and when to apply, and you'll also learn about these benefits in your required Transition Assistance Program (TAP) briefing. The page covers benefits you can use during and after service, time-sensitive benefits to consider when separating or retiring, and other VA benefits. Specific benefits mentioned include free mental health care for a year after separation, vocational rehabilitation and employment (for those with a service-connected disability that limits or prevents work, applicable up to 12 years from notice of separation or first VA disability rating), disability compensation, Veterans Pension, aid and attendance or housebound allowance, disability housing grants, life insurance options, and pre-need eligibility determination for burial in a VA national cemetery.

If you qualify for burial in a VA national cemetery, you'll receive burial benefits at no cost to your family. These benefits include opening and closing of the grave, a burial liner provided by the government, a headstone or marker provided by the government, and perpetual ongoing care of the gravesite. The person arranging your burial can also request additional honors and memorial items. If you're a Veteran, your surviving spouse or other family members may also qualify for survivor benefits, including help paying for funeral costs. You can also apply for a pre-need eligibility decision letter to confirm that you qualify for burial in a VA national cemetery, which can help you pre-plan and make the process easier for your family members in their time of need.
If you have questions about other sources of financial assistance, contact your school's financial aid office.
