To take part in the VA Veterans work-study program, all of the following must be true: you are enrolled at least three-quarter time in a college degree, vocational, or professional program; you have found an open job either at a nearby VA facility or in a VA-related role at your school; you can finish the work-study contract while you still qualify for education benefits; and you are using an approved VA education benefits program to pay for your education or training. Approved programs include the Post-9/11 GI Bill for Veterans, Post-9/11 GI Bill for family members using transferred benefits, Montgomery GI Bill Active Duty (MGIB-AD), Montgomery GI Bill Selected Reserve (MGIB-SR), Veterans Educational Assistance Program (VEAP), Survivors and Dependents Educational Assistance (DEA) (with the note that dependents who qualify under 38 U.S.C. Chapter 35 may use work study only while enrolled at a school in one of the 50 states), National Call to Service, and vocational rehabilitation and employment.

Yes. The VA offers a Veterans work-study program that lets you earn money while you're enrolled in a college, vocational school, or professional training program. You can get paid to work a part-time job while you study. To take part, all of these must be true: you're enrolled at least three-quarter time in a college degree, vocational, or professional program; you've found an open job either at a nearby VA facility or in a VA-related role at your school; you can finish the work-study contract while you still qualify for education benefits; and you're using an approved VA education benefits program to pay for your education or training. To apply, fill out VA Form 22-8691 (Application for Work-Study Allowance).

To take part in the VA work-study program, all of these must be true: you are enrolled at least three-quarter time in a college degree, vocational, or professional program; you have found an open job either at a nearby VA facility or in a VA-related role at your school; you can finish the work-study contract while you still qualify for education benefits; and you are using an approved VA education benefits program to pay for your education or training. Approved programs include Post-9/11 GI Bill for Veterans, Post-9/11 GI Bill for family members using transferred benefits, Montgomery GI Bill Active Duty (MGIB-AD), Montgomery GI Bill Selected Reserve (MGIB-SR), Veterans Educational Assistance Program (VEAP), Survivors' and Dependents' Educational Assistance (DEA), National Call to Service, and vocational rehabilitation and employment. You apply by filling out an Application for Work-Study Allowance (VA Form 22-8691).

Yes. The Veterans work-study program lets you earn money while you're enrolled in a college, vocational school, or professional training program, and you can get paid to work a part-time job while you study. Separately, Federal Work-Study jobs help students earn money to pay for college or career school, and the program allows students with financial need to earn money to help pay education expenses.

Based on the evidence, eligibility for VA VR&E Independent Living services requires that you be a service member or Veteran with a service-connected disability who is eligible for VR&E benefits, and that all of the following be true: you have a serious employment handicap (SEH), your disabilities prevent you from looking for or returning to work, and you are in need of services to live as independently as possible. Because a serious employment handicap is listed as a required condition, the evidence does not describe eligibility for Independent Living services for someone who does not have a serious employment handicap. General VR&E eligibility requires a discharge that was not dishonorable, a VA service-connected disability rating of at least 10%, and applying for VR&E services.

The evidence describes eligibility based on service during January 9, 1962 to May 7, 1975. It states that Veterans who served on a Blue Water Navy vessel offshore of the Republic of Vietnam, or on another U.S. Navy or Coast Guard ship operating in the coastal waterways of Vietnam during that period are entitled to a presumption of service connection for illnesses related to Agent Orange exposure under Public Law 116-23, the Blue Water Navy Vietnam Veterans Act of 2019. It also states that to support a claim you must show that during that period you were aboard a U.S. military vessel that operated in the inland waterways of Vietnam, or served on a vessel not more than 12 nautical miles seaward from the demarcation line of the waters of Vietnam and Cambodia as detailed in Public Law 116-23. The evidence does not state separate eligibility rules specifically for someone who did not serve in the coastal waterways of Vietnam during that period.

To transfer Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits, the Department of Defense (DoD) decides whether you can transfer benefits to your family. You can transfer education benefits if you're on active duty or in the Selected Reserve and you meet the requirements below. At least one of these must be true: (1) you have completed at least 6 years of service on the date your request is approved and you agree to add 4 more years of service, or (2) you have completed at least 10 years of service on the date your request is approved, can't commit to add 4 more years of service because of either a policy or statute, but agree to serve for the maximum amount of time allowed. Additionally, the person getting benefits must have enrolled in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS).

If you're signed up for VA health care, you can manage your VA health and benefits online through VA.gov—refilling prescriptions, sending a message to your VA health care provider, and checking the status of a disability or pension claim. You can also apply for and manage your GI Bill and other education benefits, and manage your VA life insurance policy online. Other benefits and services available include housing assistance (VA home loan programs and, for service-connected disabilities, housing grants), careers and employment support (vocational rehabilitation services, support for Veteran-owned small businesses, and other career resources), life insurance options, and pension payments for wartime Veterans and survivors with limited or no income.

To transfer your unused Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits to your spouse or dependent children, the Department of Defense decides whether you can transfer benefits. You must be on active duty or in the Selected Reserve and meet the requirements below. At least one of these must be true: (1) you have completed at least 6 years of service on the date your request is approved and you agree to add 4 more years of service, or (2) you have completed at least 10 years of service on the date your request is approved, can't commit to add 4 more years of service because of either a policy or statute, but agree to serve for the maximum amount of time allowed. This must also be true: the person getting benefits has enrolled in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS).

To transfer your unused Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits to your spouse or dependent children, the Department of Defense decides whether you can transfer benefits. You must be on active duty or in the Selected Reserve and meet the requirements. At least one of these must be true: you have completed at least 6 years of service on the date your request is approved and you agree to add 4 more years of service, or you have completed at least 10 years of service on the date your request is approved, can't commit to add 4 more years of service because of a policy or statute, but agree to serve for the maximum amount of time allowed. Also, the person getting benefits must be enrolled in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS). With 8 years of service, you would meet the 6-year requirement if you agree to add 4 more years of service. If the DoD approves the Transfer of Entitlement, your spouse or dependent children can apply for up to 36 months of benefits.

To get a VA-backed home loan, the first step is to apply for a Certificate of Eligibility (COE), which confirms for your lender that you qualify for the VA home loan benefit. You can apply online right now through eBenefits. Before starting, gather the information you'll need for your COE application—for example, Veterans need a copy of their discharge or separation papers (DD214), and active-duty Servicemembers need a statement of service signed by their commander, adjutant, or personnel officer. After getting your COE, choose your loan type and learn about the rest of the loan application process. Keep in mind that you'll also need to meet your lender's credit and income requirements to get a loan.

I can guide you on these education benefits topics: how the GI Bill works and your options to pay for school or training; eligibility for GI Bill or other VA education benefits; how to prepare and apply for the GI Bill or other VA education and training benefits; and how to manage your Veterans education benefits. I can also cover approved VA education benefits programs, including the Post-9/11 GI Bill for Veterans and for family members using transferred benefits, the Montgomery GI Bill Active Duty (MGIB-AD), the Montgomery GI Bill Selected Reserve (MGIB-SR), the Veterans Educational Assistance Program (VEAP), Survivors and Dependents Educational Assistance (DEA), National Call to Service, and vocational rehabilitation and employment. In addition, I can help with work-study (getting paid to work a part-time job while you study) and with education benefits for survivors and dependents, including money for tuition, housing, and books and supplies.

Besides education benefits, VA offers other benefits and services, including: VA transition assistance (help learning about VA benefits available to you and your family as you transition out of active-duty, National Guard, or Reserve service); Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (help exploring employment options, any training you may need, and other voc rehab services); home loan benefits (options for Veterans home loans, applying for your Certificate of Eligibility, and help if you're having trouble making mortgage payments); Veteran-owned small business support (registering to do business with VA and getting support for your Veteran-owned small business); and Jobs for Veterans (help from the U.S. Department of Labor to find a job, get training, or explore career options). Other sources also list life insurance options for service members, Veterans, or family members.

If the Department of Defense approves the Transfer of Entitlement (TOE), your dependent children can apply for up to 36 months of benefits and may be able to get money for tuition, housing, and books and supplies. The person receiving benefits must also be enrolled in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS).

Yes. VA offers career and employment assistance to help you build your career and find opportunities that are right for you, including resources for managing your career. VA also offers a CareerScope assessment to help you figure out your career path when transitioning to civilian life, and VetSuccess on Campus counselors may help with the transition from military to college life. Additionally, VA provides links to external resources that can help in your job search.

Yes, in some cases. If you haven't used all of your Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits, you may be able to transfer up to 36 months of benefits to your spouse or a dependent child. The Department of Defense approves the transfer of benefits. A spouse may use the benefit right away, may use it while you're on active duty or after you've separated from service, doesn't qualify for the monthly housing allowance while you're on active duty, and may use the benefit for up to 15 years after your separation from active duty. While you're still on active duty, you'll request to transfer, change, or revoke a Transfer of Entitlement through milConnect.

If you haven't used all of your Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits, you may be able to transfer up to 36 months of benefits to your spouse or a dependent child. The Department of Defense decides whether you can transfer GI Bill benefits to your family. If the DoD approves the Transfer of Entitlement, your spouse or dependent children can apply for up to 36 months of benefits and may be able to get money for tuition, housing, and books and supplies. Spouses may use the benefit right away, and may use it while you're on active duty or after you've separated from service. In some cases, the dependent or surviving spouse and children of a Veteran can get educational assistance through a GI Bill program (Survivors and Dependents Assistance).

Veterans may qualify for burial in a VA national cemetery, which includes burial benefits at no cost to the family: opening and closing of the grave, a government-provided burial liner, a government-provided headstone or marker, and perpetual care of the gravesite. The person arranging the burial can also request additional honors and memorial items. Surviving spouses or other family members may also qualify for survivor benefits, including help paying for funeral costs. Veterans can apply for a pre-need eligibility decision letter to confirm they qualify for burial in a VA national cemetery, which can help with pre-planning and make the process easier for family members. If a Veteran changes their mind, family members can make arrangements for burial at a private cemetery even if a pre-need decision was already sent.

VA Vocational Rehabilitation, also called the Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (VR&E) program or Chapter 31, helps service members and Veterans with a service-connected disability that limits or prevents their ability to work. It offers support-and-services tracks to help you learn new skills, find a new job, start a business, get educational counseling, or return to your former job, and to help you find and keep a job and live as independently as possible. The tracks include a Reemployment track (help returning to the civilian job you held before deployment) and a Rapid Access to Employment track (employment counseling and job-search support if you want a job matching your existing skills), among others. You can check eligibility and find out how to apply, and in some cases family members may also be eligible for certain counseling, training, and education benefits.

To add your daughter as a dependent to your VA disability benefits, you can file a claim for additional disability compensation online through the eBenefits website. You may need to provide more information or forms along with your claim. If your daughter is between 18 and 23 years old and attending school full time, you'll also need to submit a Request for Approval of School Attendance (VA Form 21-674) with your application. If you're claiming a child who became permanently disabled before turning 18, you'll need to turn in all private medical records relating to the child's disabilities with your application. Note that you can add a dependent if you have or adopt a child, and eligibility for additional compensation generally requires that you are eligible for VA disability compensation and have a combined disability rating of at least 30%.

To be eligible for additional VA disability compensation for a dependent child, both of these must be true: you are eligible for VA disability compensation, and you have a combined disability rating of at least 30%. VA considers an unmarried child (including an adopted child or stepchild) a dependent if one of these is true: they are under 18 years old, or they are between 18 and 23 years old and enrolled in school full time, or they became permanently disabled before turning 18. To file, you can submit a claim for additional compensation for a child online through eBenefits. If claiming a child who became permanently disabled before age 18, you'll need to turn in all private medical records relating to the child's disabilities with your application. If the child is between 18 and 23 and attending school full time, you'll also need to submit a Request for Approval of School Attendance (VA Form 21-674) with your application.

You can view details about your upcoming VA appointments online using the VA Appointments tools on the My HealtheVet health management portal. These tools let you view appointments on your health calendar, set up email reminders for upcoming appointments, print a list of your future appointments, and look up past appointments from the last 2 years. To use them, you must be enrolled in VA health care, be scheduling with a VA health facility that uses online scheduling, and have had an appointment at that facility within the last 2 years, plus have a Premium My HealtheVet account, a Premium DS Logon account, or a verified ID.me account. Note that the fastest way to make all VA appointments is usually to call the VA health facility where you want to receive care.

The VR&E Reemployment track helps Veterans with a service-connected disability return to the job they held before they deployed. It is available to Veterans who are protected under USERRA, so they can't be disadvantaged in their civilian career because of their service. The track can help an employer accommodate the Veteran's needs, and the Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC) can provide a full range of rehabilitation services and refer the Veteran directly to the Department of Labor to begin the process. To be eligible, a Veteran must have an employment barrier or handicap, be enrolled in VR&E, and want to return to their former job. The benefit provided is help with the process of returning to the pre-deployment job. To get these benefits, a Veteran first applies for VR&E benefits and then works with their VRC.

Based on the evidence, your wife may be able to enjoy certain VA-related benefits as the spouse of a disabled Veteran, though eligibility depends on the specific program. As the spouse of a Veteran, she may qualify for health care benefits, and in certain cases may also qualify for health care benefits due to a disability related to your service (E1). If she is the current or surviving spouse of a Veteran with disabilities and doesn't qualify for TRICARE, she may be able to get health insurance through CHAMPVA, which covers cost sharing for some health care services and supplies (E4). Separately, if she is serving as your family caregiver, the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers may apply; eligibility is based on your qualifications as the Veteran, including having a serious injury caused or made worse by active-duty service on or after September 11, 2001, and needing personal care services (E5). Under that program, a primary caregiver may receive caregiver education and training, a monthly stipend, travel and lodging assistance when traveling with the Veteran to receive care, and access to health care benefits through CHAMPVA (E2). The evidence does not specify exact eligibility determinations for her individual circumstances, so she should review the criteria and apply for the relevant programs.

To find out which VR&E track options are available to you, first apply for VR&E benefits. After you apply, you'll work with your Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC), who can provide a full range of rehabilitation services and help direct you to the appropriate support. If you're eligible, VA will invite you to an orientation session at your nearest VA regional benefit office. If you have your VA disability rating, you can apply by signing in to your eBenefits account, clicking Additional Benefits on your dashboard, choosing Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment Program, and applying for the program. The VR&E program offers 5 support-and-services tracks, including the Reemployment track, Rapid Access to Employment track, and Self-Employment track, which you can explore to see which fits your situation.

Yes. Beyond the VR&E Reemployment track and USERRA protections, the evidence describes other VR&E support-and-services tracks, including help learning new skills, finding a new job, starting a business, getting educational counseling, and returning to a former job. It also mentions a Rapid Access to Employment track for those wanting a job matching existing skills (with employment counseling and job-search support), a Self-Employment track, and that in some cases family members may also be eligible for certain benefits. The evidence does not provide a complete list of all other VA benefits.

Yes. For emotional help, veterans can contact the Veterans Crisis Line for confidential, private, free support available 24/7: call 800-273-8255 and select 1, start a confidential online chat, text 838255, or if you have hearing loss call TTY 800-799-4889. You can also contact your nearest VA medical center and ask to speak with the VA social worker (female veterans can ask for the Women Veterans Program Manager), or call the National Call Center for Homeless Veterans at 877-424-3838 for free, private help 24/7 with a trained VA counselor. Caregivers can call the Caregiver Support Line at 855-260-3274 (Monday–Friday, 8:00 a.m.–8:00 p.m.), and the Coaching into Care program lets you speak directly with a licensed psychologist or social worker free of charge.

The VR&E Reemployment track helps Veterans with service-connected disabilities return to the job they held before deploying, and can help employers accommodate their needs. As a Veteran, you're protected under USERRA, so you can't be disadvantaged in your civilian career because of your service. Your Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC) can provide a full range of rehabilitation services and can refer you directly to the Department of Labor to begin the process. To be eligible, you must have an employment barrier or handicap, be enrolled in VR&E, and want to return to your former job; an employment handicap means your service-connected disability limits your ability to prepare for, obtain, and maintain suitable employment. To get these benefits, first apply for VR&E benefits, then work with your VRC. If you have your VA disability rating, you can apply by signing in to your eBenefits account, clicking Additional Benefits on your dashboard, choosing Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment Program, and applying; if eligible, you'll be invited to an orientation session at your nearest VA regional benefit office. Related opportunities include the Special Employer Incentives (SEI) and Non-Paid Work Experience (NPWE) programs, VR&E employment coordinators at VA regional offices, and VetSuccess on Campus counselors.

If you're serving on active duty in the United States uniformed services, including active National Guard and Reserve with federal pay, you may be eligible for VA benefits both during service and after separation or retirement. Traditional or technical members of the National Guard and Reserve may also be eligible for some VA benefits. You can find out which benefits you may qualify for and when to apply, and you'll also learn about these benefits in your required Transition Assistance Program (TAP) briefing. Specific benefits mentioned include free mental health care for a year after separation, and Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment for those with a service-connected disability that limits or prevents work (open to service members and Veterans in active duty, Guard, and Reserve).

If you're buried in a VA national cemetery, you'll receive burial benefits at no cost to your family. These include opening and closing of the grave, a government-provided burial liner, a government-provided headstone or marker, and perpetual ongoing care of the gravesite. The person arranging your burial can also request additional honors and memorial items. Your surviving spouse or other family members may also qualify for survivor benefits, including help paying for funeral costs. You can also apply for a pre-need eligibility determination for burial in a VA national cemetery to confirm you qualify and make pre-planning easier for your family. If you change your mind, your family can make arrangements for burial at a private cemetery even if a pre-need decision was already sent.

The evidence describes VR&E reemployment eligibility only for a Veteran with a service-connected disability. To get help returning to a former job through VR&E, all of these must be true: you have an employment barrier or handicap, you are enrolled in Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (VR&E), and you would like to return to your former job. An employment handicap means your service-connected disability limits your ability to prepare for, obtain, and maintain suitable employment. The evidence does not address whether a military spouse (a non-veteran) can receive VR&E assistance to return to a previous job, so that part of the question cannot be answered from the provided evidence.

For a Marine veteran with a service-connected disability, the VR&E Reemployment track can help your employer accommodate your needs, and your Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC) can provide a full range of rehabilitation services and refer you directly to the Department of Labor to begin the process. The specific benefit is help with the process of returning to the job you held before you deployed. To be eligible, you must have an employment barrier or handicap, be enrolled in VR&E, and want to return to your former job. To get these benefits, you first apply for VR&E benefits and then work with your VRC; if you have your VA disability rating, you can apply through your eBenefits account by choosing the Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment Program. Additional opportunities include the Special Employer Incentives (SEI) program and the Non-Paid Work Experience (NPWE) program, as well as VR&E employment coordinators at VA regional offices who can help you access employment services.

A Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC) can provide a full range of rehabilitation services and refer the Veteran directly to the Department of Labor to begin the process. To be eligible, you must be a Veteran with a service-connected disability and meet all of these requirements: you have an employment barrier or handicap, are enrolled in VR&E, and would like to return to your former job. To get these benefits, first apply for VR&E benefits, then work with your VRC; if you have your VA disability rating, you can apply through eBenefits by signing in, clicking Additional Benefits, choosing Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment Program, and applying.

If you qualify for burial in a VA national cemetery, you'll receive burial benefits at no cost to your family. These benefits include opening and closing of the grave, a burial liner provided by the government, a headstone or marker provided by the government, and perpetual ongoing care of the gravesite. The person arranging your burial can also request additional honors and memorial items. If you're a Veteran, your surviving spouse or other family members may also qualify for survivor benefits, including help paying for funeral costs. You can also apply for a pre-need eligibility decision letter to confirm that you qualify for burial in a VA national cemetery, which can help you pre-plan and make the process easier for your family members in their time of need.

Yes, you may be eligible. As a family member caring for a disabled veteran, you may qualify for VA health care benefits, and in certain cases you may also qualify for health care benefits due to a disability related to the veteran's service. Specifically, if you are a family member caring for a veteran with disabilities and you are not entitled to care or services through another health plan, you may qualify for CHAMPVA. If the veteran you are caring for was seriously injured in the line of duty on or after September 11, 2001, you may qualify for health care benefits and other caregiver support through the Program of Comprehensive Assistance to Family Caregivers. Eligibility depends on meeting the program's requirements, so you should check whether you qualify and how to apply.

Based on the evidence, your wife may qualify for certain VA family member benefits. As a spouse, she can learn about benefits she may qualify for as a spouse, dependent, or survivor, including as a family member caring for a Veteran with disabilities. If she is the spouse of a Veteran, she may qualify for health care benefits, and in certain cases may also qualify for health care benefits due to a disability related to your service. Specifically, under CHAMPVA, the spouse of a Veteran rated permanently and totally disabled for a service-connected disability by a VA regional benefit office may qualify, provided she doesn't qualify for TRICARE. Eligibility depends on meeting these conditions, so she should check whether she qualifies and how to apply.

Yes. You can view your VA appointments online using the VA Appointments tools, which offer a secure, web-based way to schedule, view, and organize your VA appointments. These tools let you view appointments on your health calendar, print a list of your future appointments, and look up past appointments from the last 2 years. You can also call the VA health facility where you want to receive care, which is usually the fastest way to make appointments.

The VR&E Reemployment track helps a Veteran with a service-connected disability return to the job they held before deploying, and can help the employer accommodate their needs. A Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor can provide a full range of rehabilitation services and refer the Veteran directly to the Department of Labor to begin the process. Based on the evidence, being in an approved hospital that is not a VA hospital does not by itself make you approved or eligible. For the increased disability rating for time in a hospital, one of these must be true: you spent more than 21 days in a VA hospital or other approved hospital for a service-connected disability, or you were under hospital observation for more than 21 days at VA's expense for a service-connected disability. If you weren't in a VA hospital, you'll need to give VA your hospital discharge summary showing the length and cause of your hospital stay when filing your claim. Separately, general VA disability compensation eligibility requires that you served on active duty (or active duty for training or inactive duty training) and have a disability rating for your service-connected condition, plus at least one other listed requirement. The evidence does not establish your specific eligibility, so whether you are approved or eligible depends on meeting these requirements.

Scientific and medical evidence has shown an association between exposure to Camp Lejeune water contaminants during military service and the development of certain diseases later on. The 15 conditions for which VA may reimburse out-of-pocket health care costs are: bladder cancer, breast cancer, esophageal cancer, female infertility, hepatic steatosis, kidney cancer, leukemia, lung cancer, miscarriage, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndromes, neurobehavioral effects, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, renal toxicity, and scleroderma. Veterans with qualifying service at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River and a current diagnosis of one of the listed conditions may be able to get disability benefits.

To get these benefits, you'll need to file a claim for disability compensation and provide supporting evidence documents, including your military records showing you served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River. You may be able to get disability benefits if you served there for at least 30 cumulative days from August 1953 through December 1987, didn't receive a dishonorable discharge, and have a diagnosis of one or more of the listed presumptive conditions. When applying for one or more of the presumed Camp Lejeune illnesses, upload evidence like a doctor's report or medical test results. The benefits available include health care and compensation payments.

If you served at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune or Marine Corps Air Station MCAS New River in North Carolina, you may have had contact with contaminants in the drinking water there. Scientific and medical evidence has shown an association between exposure to these contaminants during military service and development of certain diseases later on. Two on-base water wells that were shut down in 1985 had these chemicals: trichloroethylene (TCE), perchloroethylene (PCE), benzene, vinyl chloride, and other compounds. You may be able to get disability benefits if you served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 cumulative days and have a current diagnosis of one of the qualifying conditions. Veterans who served there for at least 30 cumulative days from August 1953 through December 1987, and their family members, can get health care benefits, and VA may reimburse out-of-pocket health care costs related to 15 conditions: bladder cancer, breast cancer, esophageal cancer, female infertility, hepatic steatosis, kidney cancer, leukemia, lung cancer, miscarriage, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndromes, neurobehavioral effects, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, renal toxicity, and scleroderma.

To get VA disability benefits for the Camp Lejeune water contamination issue, you must meet all of these requirements: (1) you served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 cumulative days from August 1953 through December 1987; (2) you didn't receive a dishonorable discharge when you separated from the military; and (3) you have a current diagnosis of one or more of the presumptive conditions, which include adult leukemia, aplastic anemia and other myelodysplastic syndromes, bladder cancer, kidney cancer, liver cancer, multiple myeloma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, and Parkinson's disease. To apply, you file a claim for disability compensation and provide supporting documents, such as your military records showing you served at Camp Lejeune.

You can check the status of a VA disability compensation claim or appeal online using the VA claim or appeal status tool. You can also view your VA disability payments history to check the status of your VA disability and pension payments.

Camp Lejeune water contamination health issues: If you served at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune or Marine Corps Air Station (MCAS) New River in North Carolina, you may have had contact with contaminants in the drinking water there. Scientific and medical evidence has shown an association between exposure to these contaminants during military service and development of certain diseases later on. If you have qualifying service at Camp Lejeune and a current diagnosis of one of the listed conditions, you may be able to get disability benefits. To qualify, you must have served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 cumulative days (the evidence text is cut off at this point). You can also sign up for Marine Corps notifications for the latest updates, download a fact sheet about Camp Lejeune-related benefits, and learn more about the Camp Lejeune Family Member program; for help with an application, call the Camp Lejeune Family Member program staff at 866-372-1144.

If you served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 cumulative days from August 1953 through December 1987 and did not receive a dishonorable discharge, you may be able to get VA disability benefits if you have a current diagnosis of one of these presumptive conditions: adult leukemia; aplastic anemia and other myelodysplastic syndromes; bladder cancer; kidney cancer; liver cancer; multiple myeloma; non-Hodgkin's lymphoma; or Parkinson's disease. The benefits available include health care and compensation payments. To get them, you file a claim for disability compensation and provide supporting documents, such as your military records showing you served at Camp Lejeune, and evidence like a doctor's report or medical test results, stating that you're applying for one or more of the presumed Camp Lejeune illnesses. Veterans who served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 cumulative days from August 1953 through December 1987, and their family members, can also get health care benefits, and VA may reimburse out-of-pocket health care costs related to any of these 15 conditions: bladder cancer, breast cancer, esophageal cancer, female infertility, hepatic steatosis, kidney cancer, leukemia, lung cancer, miscarriage, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndromes, neurobehavioral effects, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, renal toxicity, and scleroderma.

If you served at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune or Marine Corps Air Station MCAS New River in North Carolina, you may have had contact with contaminants in the drinking water there. Scientific and medical evidence has shown an association between exposure to these contaminants during military service and the development of certain diseases later on. If you have qualifying service at Camp Lejeune and a current diagnosis of one of the listed conditions, you may be able to get disability benefits. Veterans who served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 cumulative days from August 1953 through December 1987, and their family members, can get health care benefits, and VA may reimburse out-of-pocket health care costs related to any of these 15 conditions: bladder cancer, breast cancer, esophageal cancer, female infertility, hepatic steatosis, kidney cancer, leukemia, lung cancer, miscarriage, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndromes, neurobehavioral effects, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, renal toxicity, and scleroderma.

To be eligible for VA disability benefits related to Camp Lejeune water contamination, you must meet all of these requirements: (1) you served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 cumulative days from August 1953 through December 1987; (2) you didn't receive a dishonorable discharge when you separated from the military; and (3) you have a current diagnosis of one or more of these presumptive conditions: adult leukemia, aplastic anemia and other myelodysplastic syndromes, bladder cancer, kidney cancer, liver cancer, multiple myeloma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, or Parkinson's disease. Covered groups include veterans, reservists, and guardsmen, and the benefits available include health care and compensation payments. To apply, you file a claim for disability compensation and provide supporting documents, including your military records showing you served at Camp Lejeune.

The available information covers several VA health care topics: special VA health registries you can join that document Veterans' exposure to Agent Orange, depleted uranium, ionizing radiation, airborne hazards, and other hazardous materials; VA programs for health and wellness; community care for enrolled Veterans; the Affordable Care Act and VA health care coverage; and the Million Veteran Program research study. It also notes that if you were exposed to Agent Orange in or near Vietnam, ionizing radiation in certain service locations or jobs, or environmental contaminants in the Persian Gulf, you don't have to provide income information to qualify for free care related to your exposure. For Agent Orange specifically, benefits include health care, compensation payments, and an Agent Orange Registry health exam, obtained by filing a claim for disability compensation; certain illnesses are treated as presumptive diseases, so you won't need to show the problem started during or got worse because of your service. Additional resources include copay rates, mental health services, and care for specific health needs and conditions such as Agent Orange-related diseases or Camp Lejeune water contamination.

The Veterans Educational Assistance Program (VEAP) is a $2-to-$1 government-match program for educational assistance, letting you use part of your military pay to help cover the cost of school. To be eligible, all of these must be true: you entered service for the first time between January 1, 1977, and June 30, 1985; you opened and put money into your VEAP account before April 1, 1987; you contributed between $25 and $2,700 on your own; and you finished your first period of service without receiving a dishonorable discharge. If you're currently on active duty, you must have at least 3 months of contributions available to use your VEAP benefits. The benefit provides money for tuition. Covered training, programs, and fees include undergraduate and graduate degree programs, co-op training, non-college degree programs (technical or vocational courses), flight training, on-the-job training and apprenticeships, test fees, entrepreneurship training, and correspondence training; in some cases remedial courses are also covered. To get benefits, first make sure VA has approved your selected program, then apply by submitting VA Form 22-1990 online, by mail, in person, or with the help of a trained professional. If you're on active duty, your Education Services Officer must approve your enrollment and your Commanding Officer must verify your service; if you're not on active duty, you'll need to send the member copy 4 of your DD214. If you've already started training, take your VA Form 22-1990 and DD214 to your school or employer and ask them to complete VA Form 22-1999, Enrollment Certification, and send all forms to VA. Your school or training official must then verify your enrollment.

To be eligible for VEAP benefits, all of the following must be true: you entered service for the first time between January 1, 1977, and June 30, 1985; you opened and put money into your VEAP account before April 1, 1987; you contributed between $25 and $2,700 on your own; and you finished your first period of service and didn't receive a dishonorable discharge. Additionally, if you're currently on active duty, you must have at least 3 months of contributions available to use your VEAP benefits.

Based on the evidence, you meet two of the VEAP eligibility requirements: you entered service for the first time between January 1, 1977, and June 30, 1985, and you opened and put money into your VEAP account before April 1, 1987. However, VEAP eligibility requires meeting all of the listed requirements, and the evidence also requires that you put in $25 to $2,700 on your own and that you finished your first period of service and didn't receive a dishonorable discharge. The evidence does not confirm whether you meet those additional requirements, so eligibility cannot be fully confirmed from the information provided.

VADIP is the VA Dental Insurance Program, which offers discounted private dental insurance for Veterans and family members who meet certain requirements. You may be eligible if you're a Veteran enrolled in VA health care, or the current or surviving spouse or dependent child of a Veteran or service member enrolled in CHAMPVA (insurance carriers may offer separate coverage options for dependents who aren't CHAMPVA beneficiaries). VADIP provides coverage throughout the United States and its territories, including Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. If you're not eligible for free VA dental care, VADIP can help you buy private dental insurance at a reduced cost; if you're eligible for free VA care for some of your dental needs, you can buy a VADIP plan for added insurance, and signing up won't affect your ability to get free VA dental care. VADIP plans cover many common dental procedures, which may include diagnostic services, preventive dental care, endodontic or restorative services, root canals and other services, dental surgery, and emergency dental care. Costs depend on the insurance company and plan you choose; based on your plan, you'll pay the full insurance premium for each individual on your plan and any required copays when you get care. You can read coverage details and compare VADIP plans and premium rates from Delta Dental and MetLife, and once you've chosen a plan you can enroll online with Delta Dental or MetLife. If you were covered under the VADIP pilot program (2013 to 2017), you'll need to enroll again to get new coverage, and some plan options and fees may have changed. At this time, the program is allowed by law to continue until December 31, 2021. For questions about Delta Dental, call 855-370-3303; for questions about MetLife, call 888-310-1681.

To find out whether you qualify for VA dental care, note that eligibility depends on factors such as your military service history and your current health and living situation; VA places you into a benefits class based on these factors, and you receive the specific benefits assigned to that class. You can click on the statement that describes you best to find out your benefits class and the dental benefits you may qualify for. To apply for VA dental care benefits, you can apply online by filling out the 10-10EZ health care application. VA provides dental care to qualified Veterans at over 200 dental clinics across the country, including Alaska and Puerto Rico, and you can find a VA dental clinic near you. If you can't get VA dental care benefits, you may be able to buy dental insurance at a reduced cost through the VA Dental Insurance Program (VADIP) if you meet at least one requirement: you are signed up for VA health care, or you are signed up for CHAMPVA (a health insurance program for dependents of Veterans). VADIP offers discounted private dental insurance for Veterans and family members who meet certain requirements, and you can find out if you're eligible and how to enroll in a plan that meets your needs and budget.

VA offers help to build your career and find opportunities that are right for you. Specific career and employment resources mentioned include: attending a Transition Assistance Program (TAP) briefing to explore career options as you separate from the military; using the CareerScope assessment to get recommendations for careers you may enjoy and succeed in, along with training programs to get started; and searching for jobs through the Department of Labor, including help translating military skills and experience to civilian jobs. VA also offers programs that can help you learn new skills, find a new job, start a new business, get educational counseling, or return to your former job, including vocational rehabilitation for Veterans and service members with service-connected disabilities, Chapter 36 educational and career counseling for recently discharged Veterans or dependent family members, support for Veteran-Owned Small Businesses, and educational and vocational counseling for dependent spouses or children of Veterans or service members.

You can find out if you're eligible by checking the VADIP eligibility criteria: you may be eligible if you're a Veteran enrolled in VA health care, or if you're the current or surviving spouse or dependent child of a Veteran or service member and you're enrolled in CHAMPVA. The evidence describes Veterans Pension eligibility rather than VA MISSION Act care requirements. For Veterans Pension, both of these must be true: you did not receive a dishonorable discharge, and your yearly family income and net worth meet limits set by Congress. Net worth includes all personal property you own except your house, your car, and most home furnishings, minus any debt you owe, and it includes your spouse's net worth. The program provides monthly payments to wartime Veterans who meet certain age or disability requirements and whose income and net worth are within certain limits. For non-service-connected pension benefits, the evidence must show that your net worth and income are within certain limits, and at least one service condition must be true, such as serving on active duty for any length of time during a period of war and being discharged due to a service-connected disability, or starting active duty before September 8, 1980.

If you're buried in a VA national cemetery, you'll receive burial benefits at no cost to your family, including opening and closing of the grave, a government-provided burial liner, a government-provided headstone or marker, and perpetual ongoing care of the gravesite. The person arranging your burial can also request additional honors and memorial items. If you're a Veteran, your surviving spouse or other family members may also qualify for survivor benefits, including help paying for funeral costs. You can also get help planning a burial in a VA national cemetery, order a headstone or other memorial item, and apply for survivor and dependent benefits. Additionally, you can apply for a pre-need eligibility decision letter to confirm that you qualify for burial in a VA national cemetery, which can help you pre-plan and make the process easier for your family.

Yes. If you volunteered for research involving chemical and biological testing between 1942 and 1975 and have an injury or disease directly caused by your participation in that testing, you can get medical care through the U.S. Army. Both conditions must be met.

To prepare before starting your application, first find out if you're eligible for the benefits you're applying for, then gather the required documents. For VA health care, you'll need your most recent tax return, Social Security numbers for yourself and your qualified dependents, and account numbers for any current health insurance you already have (such as Medicare, private insurance, or employer insurance). For VA education (GI Bill) benefits, you should find out if you're eligible for VA education benefits, gather the documents and information needed to apply, and see what benefits you'll get at the school you want to attend using the GI Bill Comparison Tool. Note that applying for Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment (Chapter 31) or educational and career counseling (Chapter 36) requires a different application. Regarding eligibility, the evidence indicates you should find out if you're eligible for the relevant benefit (VA health care or VA education benefits) before starting your application; however, the evidence does not provide the specific eligibility criteria.

To apply for Survivors' and Dependents' Educational Assistance (DEA, also called Chapter 35), you must first contact your school's certifying official to make sure your program is approved for VA benefits. Then you can apply online or apply by mail by filling out a Dependents Application for VA Education Benefits (VA Form 22-5490) and mailing it to the regional processing office for your state; the address is on the last page of the form. Eligibility depends on both you and the Veteran or service member meeting certain requirements, with at least one of these being true: the Veteran or service member is permanently and totally disabled due to a service-connected disability, died while on active duty, or died as a result of a service-connected disability. A dependent who doesn't meet those criteria may still qualify if the Veteran or service member transferred some or all of their Post-9/11 GI Bill entitlement to them while on active duty.

You can work during or between enrollment periods. You can't work more hours total than 25 times the number of weeks in your enrollment period. For example, if you're enrolled for a semester that lasts 15 weeks, you can work up to 375 hours for that enrollment period.

To be eligible for a Veteran ID Card (VIC), you must meet both of these requirements: (1) you served on active duty, in the Reserves, or in the National Guard (including the Coast Guard), and (2) you received an honorable or general discharge under honorable conditions. If you received an other than honorable, bad conduct, or dishonorable character of discharge, you're not eligible. If your discharge status is uncharacterized or unknown, VA will need to verify your eligibility. When applying, you'll also need to submit a valid ID (driver's license or passport) and a photo that meets the photo requirements (for example, a square-size photo with a white or plain-color background, no scenery or other people, showing what you look like now and taken within the last 10 years, uploaded as a .jpeg, .png, .bmp, or .tiff file).

To be eligible for a Veteran ID Card (VIC), both of these must be true: you served on active duty, in the Reserves, or in the National Guard (including the Coast Guard), and you received an honorable or general discharge under honorable conditions. If you received an other than honorable, bad conduct, or dishonorable character of discharge, you're not eligible for a VIC. If you have an uncharacterized or unknown discharge status, VA will need to verify your eligibility before approving your application.

Yes. To be eligible for a Veteran ID Card, you must have served on active duty, in the Reserves, or in the National Guard (including the Coast Guard), and you must have received an honorable or general discharge under honorable conditions. Both requirements must be met.

To get education benefits for co-op training, you must meet all of these requirements: you're using VA educational assistance, you're enrolled at an approved Institution of Higher Learning (IHL), and you're in an educational program that requires part-time study and part-time work or training. Co-op training is covered under VA education benefits such as VEAP, and the amount covered depends on the benefit you use—for example, under the Post-9/11 GI Bill at a public IHL, VA pays the actual costs for public in-state tuition and fees, plus some housing and book costs.

The evidence does not identify any exceptions to the co-op training requirement that the educational program include part-time study and part-time work or training. The only exception mentioned in the evidence concerns foreign programs, where family members who qualify for Survivors and Dependents Educational Assistance can get VA benefits while in approved postsecondary after high school non-college degree programs.

The evidence does not list specific application questions. It states that to get disability benefits you must meet both requirements: (1) you were part of Projects 112 or SHAD testing from 1962 to 1974, and (2) you have an illness believed to be caused by the testing. To apply, you file a claim for disability compensation; you can call the VA Special Issues Helpline at 800-749-8387 or file a claim online. If you have questions about the tests or information showing you were part of them, you can contact the Department of Defense at 800-497-6261.

Based on the evidence, you may be able to get VA disability benefits if you meet both of these requirements: (1) you were part of Projects 112 or SHAD testing from 1962 to 1974, and (2) you have an illness believed to be caused by the testing. Both must be true. If you were not part of that testing, the evidence does not establish that you would qualify under these Project 112/SHAD criteria. The evidence also notes that if you received an other than honorable, bad conduct, or dishonorable discharge, you may not be eligible for VA disability benefits, though there are ways to try to qualify such as applying for a discharge upgrade or a VA Character of Discharge review. Covered beneficiaries include Veterans and qualified survivors, and benefits may include health care and compensation payments; you would file a claim for disability compensation.

You would use your stepparent's information because, if you have a stepparent currently married to your legal parent whose information you are reporting, you generally must provide information about that stepparent as well. Including your stepparent's information on the FAFSA form helps create an accurate picture of your family's total financial strength. One exception: for the questions about your parents' education level, your stepparent is not considered your parent.

The evidence doesn't list specific career fields, but it describes how to explore career options. A college or career school education can give you the skills needed to pursue a career that interests you, and you can find possible careers that match your interests (for example, working with animals or computers). Understanding your career goals and options, along with their earning potential, will help you choose a college or career school that meets your needs, and a Career Search can help match your skills and interests with potential careers. You can also research the types of schools available, such as two- and four-year colleges and universities, vocational, trade, and career schools, online schools, and graduate schools, since different schools serve different purposes. For Veterans, Reservist, or National Guard members, VA resources include help transitioning to a civilian career and career resources for spouses and family members.

The evidence does not provide a list of specific career options for someone who uses computers but does not want to work on computer-related things. To explore options beyond computers, you could research possible colleges or career schools and the types of schools available, such as two- and four-year colleges, vocational, trade, and career schools, online schools, and graduate schools, choosing the type that helps you achieve your goals.

For parents planning ahead for a child's higher education, resources are available covering saving early, finding tax breaks, and understanding parent loans to help support the child's college journey. Checklists from elementary school through high school include items for parents, such as how to support a child in his or her studies, where to set up a college savings account, and what to do when it's time to apply for financial aid. A College Preparation Checklist helps parents (as well as students and adults) prepare financially and academically for college. Information on Direct PLUS Loans for parents includes an overview of eligibility, the application process, and repayment.

For new applicants to an income-driven repayment (IDR) plan, the available information indicates that if you are not currently on an income-driven plan and want to apply, you can apply for an income-driven repayment plan that limits your payments to a percentage of your income. The process must be completed in a single session, and most people complete it in 10 minutes or less. You will need a verified FSA ID to apply. Separate guidance is provided for returning IDR applicants, who submit annual re-certification of income and family size.

A general forbearance (sometimes called a discretionary forbearance) may be requested when you are temporarily unable to make your scheduled monthly loan payments for reasons such as financial difficulties, medical expenses, a change in employment, or other reasons acceptable to your loan servicer. Your loan servicer decides whether to grant a general forbearance.

Yes. The evidence identifies income-driven repayment as an alternative to deferment: it bases your monthly payment on your income and family size, and may be a better option if your repayment trouble may continue for an extended period or you're unsure when you can afford payments again. Forbearance is another option that lets you temporarily stop making payments or make smaller payments, though interest still accrues during deferment or forbearance and both can affect potential loan forgiveness.

To consolidate a loan, the loans you consolidate must be in repayment or in the grace period. Generally, you cannot consolidate an existing consolidation loan unless you include an additional eligible loan in the consolidation, though under certain circumstances you may reconsolidate an existing FFEL Consolidation Loan without including any additional loans. If you want to consolidate a defaulted loan, you must either make satisfactory repayment arrangements (defined as three consecutive monthly payments on the loan before you consolidate) or agree to repay your new Direct Consolidation Loan under the Income-Based Repayment Plan. Generally, you are eligible to consolidate after you graduate, leave school, or drop below half-time enrollment.

To get started with the Loan Simulator, select the option 'I Want to Find the Best Repayment Strategy.' The simulator will guide you through a series of questions based on your selection, then recommend a repayment plan based on your needs and goals and help you explore options like making extra payments or consolidating your loans. You can either log in and start or start from scratch. To get the most realistic results, provide complete and accurate information when using the simulator. You can also use it before contacting your loan servicer to get an early look at which plans you may be eligible for and to compare estimated monthly payment amounts across federal student loan repayment plans.

After you submit your consolidation application electronically or by mailing a paper application, the consolidation servicer you selected will complete the actions required to consolidate your eligible loans, and that servicer will be your point of contact for questions about your application. Unless the loans you want to consolidate are in a deferment, forbearance, or grace period, you should continue making payments on those loans until your consolidation servicer tells you they have been paid off by your new Direct Consolidation Loan. For questions after you have submitted your application, contact the servicer for your new Direct Consolidation Loan; if you applied online, the servicer's contact information was provided at the end of the online process, and if you mailed a paper application, it was available when you downloaded or printed the application.

If you disagree with a Federal Student Aid decision, you can ask ED to reconsider your borrower defense application. You can do so in one of two ways: send a new email with the subject line "Request for Reconsideration" to BorrowerDefense@ed.gov, including the number that appears with the words "Request for Reconsideration" in the "What if I don't agree with this decision?" section of your notification email, or mail your request to U.S. Department of Education, P.O. Box 1854, Monticello, KY 42633. In your request for reconsideration, provide what you think was decided incorrectly, why you believe the decision was incorrect, and any evidence that you believe establishes that you are eligible for a different decision. Note that requests including new allegations of misconduct by your school will not be accepted. Separately, if you previously submitted a complaint and Federal Student Aid gave you a response you don't agree with or believe is incorrect, you can follow the procedure for resolving disputes before contacting the Federal Student Aid Ombudsman Group, a neutral, informal, and confidential resource to help resolve disputes about your federal student aid.

To receive a parent PLUS loan, you must meet the eligibility requirements: you must be the biological or adoptive parent (or in some cases, the stepparent) of a dependent undergraduate student enrolled at least half-time at an eligible school; you must not have an adverse credit history unless you meet certain additional requirements; and you must meet the general eligibility requirements for federal student aid. Your child must also meet these requirements. Before you apply, make sure your child has already filled out the FAFSA form. If you are eligible, you will be required to sign a Direct PLUS Loan Master Promissory Note (MPN) agreeing to the terms of the loan, and you should contact the financial aid office at the school your child plans to attend for details about that school's process. If you are taking out parent PLUS loans for more than one child, you will need to sign separate Direct PLUS Loan MPNs for each child. If you have an adverse credit history, you may still receive a parent PLUS loan by obtaining an endorser who does not have an adverse credit history (the endorser cannot be the child on whose behalf you are borrowing) or by documenting to the satisfaction of the U.S. Department of Education that there are extenuating circumstances relating to your adverse credit history; with either option, you also must complete credit counseling for parent PLUS loan borrowers.

To receive a parent PLUS loan, you must be the biological or adoptive parent (or in some cases, the stepparent) of a dependent undergraduate student enrolled at least half-time at an eligible school; you must not have an adverse credit history unless you meet certain additional requirements; and you must meet the general eligibility requirements for federal student aid. Your child must also meet these requirements. A credit check is required, and borrowers with an adverse credit history must meet additional requirements to qualify—for example, by obtaining an endorser who does not have an adverse credit history or documenting extenuating circumstances, and in either case completing credit counseling for parent PLUS loan borrowers. Before applying, your child should have already completed the FAFSA, and before receiving a Direct PLUS Loan you must complete a Direct PLUS Loan Master Promissory Note.

Yes. According to the evidence, a college or career school education means more money, more job options, and more freedom, and as you get more education you make more money. A college education is described as a long-term investment, and with careful planning you can find the school and funding options that work best for your situation and put you on the path to success. A college or career school education can also give you the skills needed to pursue a career that really interests you, and getting the right education and training will help you get a better-paying job.

You can learn more about paying for college by exploring your options early—it's never too early or too late to research and understand them. Districts appear blank (white) on the maps when they are listed as missing or insufficient data. This happens if any of the following is true: the regulatory adjusted cohort graduation rate is missing (for example, if districts merged or a new district was created after 2009–10); a district has fewer than 15 students in the regulatory adjusted cohort graduation rate data; there is an unpredicted increase in the number of district graduating seniors (for example, a dramatic increase in the graduation rate, or two districts merging under one district's name); a district has fewer than 10 projected graduates; a district has fewer than five completed FAFSA forms; or the National Center for Education Statistics Local Education Agency (LEA) code does not match the LEA code found in the Tiger/Line shapefile for the state.

The Federal Student Aid Specific Resources section of the IT Standards Library includes documents that are specific to the Federal Student Aid IT lifecycle for all projects and lists other pertinent references that an IT project may be required to comply with depending on the contract. Its listed references are General References, IT Security, Data Management, Testing Services, and Program Quality Assurance. Within these, General References includes the Lifecycle Management Methodology, IT Security contains IT Security documents used by FSA such as the Interconnection Security Agreement Template, Data Management includes resources such as the Data Migration Roadmap, Data Model Standards and Guidelines, and Data Standardization Policies and Procedures, and Testing Services includes the Enterprise Test Management Standards.

To seek credit using an endorser, the endorser must not have an adverse credit history and must agree to repay the loan if the borrower does not repay it. The endorser may not be the student on whose behalf the Direct PLUS Loan is requested, and for a parent PLUS loan the endorser cannot be the child on whose behalf the borrower is borrowing. In addition, the borrower must complete PLUS Credit Counseling (credit counseling for parent PLUS loan borrowers).

If the IDR request was completed as part of a Direct Consolidation Loan Application, the applicant should log in to StudentAid.gov, click on "Direct Consolidation Loan Applications" under "My Loan Documents," and locate the Co-sign Code there to provide to the co-signer. If you are the co-signer and do not have the code, contact the IDR applicant; an email containing the Reference Number/Co-sign Code was sent to the applicant, who can also access it by logging in to StudentAid.gov and clicking the appropriate link.

The earlier statement was that, as a primary requirement, you must fill out various documents related to the topic. The evidence describes specific documentation required to prove extenuating circumstances in a credit appeal: for a timing issue regarding bankruptcy, discharge paperwork showing the bankruptcy was discharged over 5 years ago; for bankruptcy chapter conversion, discharge paperwork or paperwork showing a Chapter 7, 11, or 12 bankruptcy was converted into a Chapter 13 bankruptcy; for an account or debt included in a Chapter 13 Bankruptcy, a Final Order from the bankruptcy court indicating the account in question is included in the bankruptcy; for debt consolidation, a letter from the debt consolidation company on company letterhead showing all accounts included in the debt consolidation, plus proof that six months of voluntary, consecutive, on-time, full monthly payments have been made; for divorce, a Final Divorce Decree showing the borrower is not responsible for repayment of the debt in question; and for a lien incorrectly filed, a letter on official letterhead showing the lien was filed in error, sometimes in the form of a release, or a copy of the actual release if the lien has been released. For collection accounts or debts 90 or more days delinquent, proof can include documentation on creditor company letterhead showing the borrower is an authorized user on the account, the account has been paid in full, or a satisfactory repayment arrangement has been established with six months of voluntary, consecutive, on-time, full monthly payments. If you no longer wish to document extenuating circumstances, options include obtaining an endorser and completing PLUS Credit Counseling, or notifying the school's financial aid office.

To apply for a Direct PLUS Loan for graduate or professional students, select the Direct PLUS Loan Application for Graduate/Professional Students. Note that if you have placed a security freeze on your credit file, you must lift or remove the freeze at each credit bureau before you continue, because your application will not be processed if you have a security freeze. The information you provide will be sent to the school you select, which will use it to determine your eligibility and process your application. Before you can receive a Direct PLUS Loan, you must complete a Direct PLUS Loan Master Promissory Note (MPN), which explains all terms and conditions and is your legally binding agreement to repay all Direct PLUS Loans you receive under the MPN; you will have an opportunity to complete the MPN after you complete the Direct PLUS Loan Request.

Aidan is a virtual assistant (in beta) from Federal Student Aid that can answer questions about federal student aid. It uses artificial intelligence and natural language processing to answer common questions, such as finding your loan account balance, learning about grants, or getting help contacting your loan servicer. It can also help find pages on the website, retrieve your loan balance, make a payment, explain your repayment plan, find customer support information, and find your loan servicer. Aidan is still in early development (beta mode) and is always learning new skills. Currently, Aidan speaks only English and is available only to a pilot group of users when logged in to their accounts, accessible via the Aidan owl icon in the bottom right-hand corner of the site.

A co-signer is the spouse of an applicant who initiated an Income-Driven Repayment Plan Request. As a co-signer, you are not obligated to repay the loan by signing a borrower's IDR application. The IDR applicant should have provided you with a Reference Number/Co-sign Code; if you don't have it, contact the IDR applicant, who can also access it by logging in to StudentAid.gov. To complete the co-sign process, you must be logged in with your own unique FSA ID, and you'll need the Reference Number/Co-sign Code, the IDR applicant's SSN, and financial information (only if you file income taxes separately from your spouse). The entire co-sign process must be completed in a single session, and most people complete it in about 10 minutes.
Most people complete the Co-Sign process in 10 minutes, and the entire process must be completed in a single session.

The evidence does not define "bad credit" directly, but it describes what counts as adverse credit: charged-off accounts (accounts charged off or written off in the two years before the credit report with a balance greater than zero) and collection accounts (accounts placed in collection in the two years before the credit report with a balance greater than zero). Debts are not considered adverse credit if their combined total outstanding balance is less than $2,085. To appeal a credit decision, you may take one of the following actions: show that the information causing the adverse credit decision is incorrect, or show extenuating circumstances relating to the adverse credit history (endorsers are not eligible for this option), and complete PLUS Credit Counseling. You must provide a statement explaining your extenuating circumstances with supporting documentation. The Secretary may use discretion to consider whether your circumstances allow you to qualify for a loan, though review does not guarantee approval. If you no longer wish to document extenuating circumstances, your options include obtaining an endorser and completing PLUS Credit Counseling, notifying the school's financial aid office of your decision, or not pursuing a Direct PLUS Loan at this time and contacting the school's financial aid office to discuss other options.

Yes. If you are appealing an adverse credit decision, you may become eligible for a Direct PLUS Loan by showing there are extenuating circumstances relating to your adverse credit history. You would provide a statement explaining your extenuating circumstances along with documentation supporting your claim, and the Secretary may use discretion to consider whether those circumstances allow you to qualify for a loan. Examples of extenuating circumstances are provided in a non-exhaustive list, and you should review the Proof of Extenuating Circumstances information to see if your situation could qualify for review. Note that review does not guarantee approval, and additional documentation may be required beyond the basic requirements. Also, loss of a job or a poor economy alone are generally not considered extenuating circumstances. If you decide not to document extenuating circumstances, you have options such as obtaining an endorser and completing PLUS Credit Counseling.
To obtain funds from the Direct Loan Program, you must be enrolled at least half-time. You must also maintain satisfactory academic progress in college or career school.

Yes.
