Financial aid can come from federal, state, school, and private sources.

Financial aid can come from federal, state, school, and private sources. Other places to look include aid from your state government, aid from your college or career school, and aid and other resources from the U.S. federal government. For scholarships specifically, you can contact the financial aid office at the school you plan to attend, check a public library or online, use free sources such as a high school or TRIO counselor, the U.S. Department of Labor's free scholarship search tool, your state grant agency, your library's reference section, and foundations, religious or community organizations, local businesses, or civic groups. Be careful to make sure scholarship information and offers are legitimate, and remember you don't have to pay to find scholarships or other financial aid.

A school calculates non-need-based federal student aid by taking your cost of attendance (COA) and subtracting any financial aid you've already been awarded; the result is your eligibility for non-need-based aid. The aid already awarded includes aid from all sources, such as the school and private scholarship providers. Non-need-based aid is aid that is not based on your Expected Family Contribution (EFC); what matters is your COA and how much other assistance you've been awarded so far. The cost of attendance example illustrates this: if your COA is $16,000 and you've been awarded a total of $4,000 in need-based aid and private scholarships, you can get up to $12,000 in non-need-based aid. Non-need-based federal student aid programs include the Direct Unsubsidized Loan, Federal PLUS Loan, and TEACH Grant.

To figure out your net price (net cost) for a school, follow these steps: First, find the cost of attendance for your program on the aid offer; if the school doesn't list it on the aid offer, ask the financial aid office for the figure. Make sure it includes amounts you'll pay the school directly, such as tuition and fees, as well as other costs like living expenses, books and supplies, and transportation. Next, subtract the grant and scholarship amounts on your aid offer from the cost of attendance amount. Also subtract any savings you have available to put toward your school costs for the school year. The remaining amount is your net or out-of-pocket cost. You can then compare the net costs for the schools you're considering; the net cost is the amount you'll have to pay out of your pocket, using earnings from work or loan funds you borrow. If you have questions or don't understand what's in your aid offer, contact the school's financial aid office. Separately, schools that participate in federal student aid programs are required to offer a net price calculator on their website, which can give you an idea of how much a program may cost after subtracting financial aid.

The evidence does not address whether the same benefit can be received for both a professional school and a university. On the second question, it is advisable to compare each school's costs: aid offers should be compared to see which school is most affordable, and because each school may offer different financial aid packages and aid amounts vary from school to school, you should figure out the net cost for each school and compare those net costs to determine which is most affordable.

If the school doesn't list the cost of attendance on the aid offer, ask the financial aid office for this figure. Make sure it includes amounts you will pay to the school directly, such as tuition and fees, as well as other costs such as living expenses, books and supplies, and transportation.

If you withdrew from school and the school did not make a required return of loan funds to your loan servicer, you might be eligible for an unpaid refund discharge of your federal student loans. Under federal regulations, the school may have been required to return some or all of the loan money to your loan servicer, and if it failed to do so, you might be eligible for a discharge of the portion of your loan that the school failed to return. To apply: if the school is still open, contact the school and try to resolve the issue before applying; if the school has closed, first determine whether you may be eligible for a closed school discharge instead. You can contact your loan servicer for more information (and find your servicer by logging in to My Federal Student Aid). To apply for the unpaid refund discharge, complete the Loan Discharge Application: Unpaid Refund and send it to your loan servicer. If approved, only the portion of your loan that your school should have returned will be discharged.

Attending a school that closed less than three years ago does not by itself make you eligible for a closed school discharge. You may be eligible for a 100 percent discharge of your Direct Loan (or FFEL or Perkins) loans if you were unable to complete your program because your school closed and you were enrolled when it closed, were on an approved leave of absence when it closed, or your school closed within 120 days after you withdrew. You are not eligible if, except in exceptional circumstances, you withdrew more than 120 days before the school closed, or if you are completing a comparable educational program at another school through a teach-out or by transferring credits. If you attended a school that closed less than three years ago, meet the eligibility requirements, and want your loans discharged, you can contact your loan servicer about applying now rather than waiting for an automatic discharge after three years.

The Loan Simulator is a tool to help you make decisions about your student loans. It can be used to find a repayment plan that meets your needs and goals, or to decide whether to consolidate. It also helps you explore options such as making extra payments or consolidating loans, see how you can lower your payment, see how you can pay off your loans faster, and get an early look at what repayment plans you may be eligible for along with a comparison of estimated monthly payment amounts for all federal student loan repayment plans. Results are for informational purposes only and should not be considered financial advice.

To use Loan Simulator, start by choosing the option that matches your situation: if you want to find the best repayment strategy, it will guide you through a series of questions and recommend a repayment plan based on your needs and goals, and help you explore options like making extra payments or consolidating your loans; you can log in and start or start from scratch. If you're struggling with payments, it helps you decide whether to temporarily stop payments or lower your monthly payment instead, and you can log in and start or start from scratch. You can also use it to simulate borrowing more money, though that feature is listed as coming soon. To get the most realistic results, provide complete and accurate information; the tool can't predict your future payments with 100% accuracy and makes several assumptions when calculating monthly repayment amounts. Results are for informational purposes only and should not be considered financial advice. You can also use Loan Simulator to get an early look at what repayment plans you may be eligible for and to compare estimated monthly payment amounts across federal student loan repayment plans before contacting your loan servicer.

It can also help you simulate borrowing more money, explore impacts when you borrow more, find out about federal loan limits, and see how choice of school affects how much you may need to borrow. Additionally, you can use it to get an early look at repayment plans you may be eligible for and compare estimated monthly payment amounts across federal student loan repayment plans.

To be eligible for a parent PLUS loan, you must be the biological or adoptive parent (or in some cases, a stepparent) of a dependent undergraduate student enrolled at least half-time at an eligible school; you must not have an adverse credit history unless you meet certain additional requirements; and you must meet the general eligibility requirements for federal student aid. Your child must also meet these requirements. Grandparents (unless they have legally adopted the dependent student) and legal guardians are not eligible. To get one, your child must first complete the FAFSA form. You then apply through the online Direct PLUS Loan Application for Parents, though some schools have different application processes, in which case you should check with the school's financial aid office. If eligible, you will be required to sign a Direct PLUS Loan Master Promissory Note (MPN) agreeing to the loan terms; if you take out loans for more than one child, you'll need separate MPNs for each child.

To receive a parent PLUS loan, you must be the biological or adoptive parent (or in some cases, the stepparent) of a dependent undergraduate student enrolled at least half-time at an eligible school; not have an adverse credit history unless you meet certain additional requirements; and meet the general eligibility requirements for federal student aid. Your child must also meet these requirements. Grandparents (unless they have legally adopted the dependent student) and legal guardians are not eligible. Eligibility is not based on financial need, but a credit check is required, and borrowers with an adverse credit history must meet additional requirements to qualify.

To decide which income-driven repayment plan to choose, pick the plan that provides the most benefit based on your individual circumstances. Although all four income-driven plans base your monthly payment on your income, they differ in who qualifies, how much you pay each month, the length of the repayment period, and the types of loans that can be repaid under the plan. If you have only Direct Loans, you can choose from all four plans. If you're not sure which to choose, you can request the income-driven plan that provides the lowest payment amount; your servicer will determine which plans you qualify for and place you on the plan with the lowest monthly payment. If you have FFEL Program loans, your only income-driven option is the IBR Plan, though consolidating them into a Direct Consolidation Loan gives you access to REPAYE, PAYE, and ICR. You can also contact your loan servicer before applying; they will help you decide whether one of these plans is right for you.

Yes. You can help improve the Loan Simulator by contacting the tool's team to share your feedback, ask questions, and request new features. You can also share the Loan Simulator tool with friends and family.

Loans that are not eligible for income-driven repayment plans include private student loans (only federal student loans can be repaid under income-driven plans) and defaulted loans, which are not eligible for repayment under any of the income-driven plans. In addition, PLUS loans made to parents cannot be repaid under any of the income-driven repayment plans, including the ICR Plan, unless the parent borrower consolidates the Direct PLUS Loans or Federal PLUS Loans into a Direct Consolidation Loan and then repays the new consolidation loan under the ICR Plan (though not under any other income-driven plan).

Loan forgiveness refers to having some or all of your federal student loans forgiven. The evidence describes several types: Borrower Defense to Repayment, which may forgive federal student loans used to attend a school that misled borrowers or engaged in other misconduct in violation of certain laws; Teacher Loan Forgiveness, which may provide up to $17,500 in forgiveness for teaching full-time for five complete and consecutive academic years in a low-income school or educational service agency and meeting other qualifications; and Public Service Loan Forgiveness, which forgives the remaining balance on Direct Loans after 120 qualifying monthly payments under a qualifying repayment plan while working full-time for a qualifying employer.

Yes, federal student loans may be forgiven for teaching service under the Teacher Loan Forgiveness Program. If you teach full-time for five complete and consecutive academic years in a low-income school or educational service agency and meet other qualifications, you may be eligible for forgiveness of up to $17,500 on your Direct Subsidized and Unsubsidized Loans and your Subsidized and Unsubsidized Federal Stafford Loans. If you have a Direct Consolidation Loan or Federal Consolidation Loan, you may be eligible for forgiveness of the outstanding portion that repaid an eligible Direct Subsidized Loan, Direct Unsubsidized Loan, or Subsidized Federal Stafford Loan. You must have been employed at an elementary school, secondary school, or educational service agency that serves low-income students, and the loan for which you seek forgiveness must have been made before the end of your five academic years of qualifying teaching service. You apply by submitting a completed Teacher Loan Forgiveness Application to your loan servicer after completing the required five consecutive years of qualifying teaching, with the chief administrative officer of the school or agency certifying your qualifying teaching service.

To apply for cancellation or discharge of a Perkins Loan, you must submit an application to the school that made the loan or to the school's Perkins Loan servicer; the school or its servicer can provide the forms and instructions specific to your type of cancellation or discharge. Regarding the purpose of the loan application, the evidence describes the federal student loan application process: you must first complete and submit a Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) form, after which your school sends a financial aid offer that may include federal student loans and tells you how to accept all or part of the loan. The evidence does not state a separate stated purpose for the loan application beyond this process.

The Graduated Repayment Plan starts with lower payments that increase every two years. Payments are made for up to 10 years (between 10 and 30 years for consolidation loans). It may be right for you if your income is low now but you expect it to increase steadily over time. Eligible loans include Direct Subsidized, Direct Unsubsidized, Direct PLUS, and Direct Consolidation Loans, as well as Subsidized and Unsubsidized Federal Stafford Loans, FFEL PLUS Loans, and FFEL Consolidation Loans. Your loan servicer can help you choose a plan, and you can use the Loan Simulator to get an early look at eligibility and compare estimated monthly payment amounts across plans; the Graduated Plan may not provide the lowest payment for your circumstances. Note that choosing a plan that lowers your monthly payment may increase the total interest you pay over time, sometimes significantly more.

The following loans from the William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan Program and the Federal Family Education Loan (FFEL) Program are eligible for the Graduated Repayment Plan: Direct Subsidized Loans, Direct Unsubsidized Loans, Direct PLUS Loans, Direct Consolidation Loans, Subsidized Federal Stafford Loans, Unsubsidized Federal Stafford Loans, FFEL PLUS Loans, and FFEL Consolidation Loans.

Yes. You can change your repayment plan at any time, and doing so is free. If your financial situation changes, you can change your repayment plan at any time; contact your loan servicer to discuss repayment plan options or to change your plan. You may also use Loan Simulator before contacting your servicer to get an early look at which plans you might qualify for.

To choose the Direct Loan MPN you want to preview or complete, select the option that matches your role: undergraduate students use the MPN for Direct Subsidized or Direct Unsubsidized Loans; graduate/professional students select the MPN type they need (they may be eligible for Direct Unsubsidized Loans, Direct PLUS Loans, or both, and must complete an MPN for each loan type); parents of undergraduate students use the MPN for Direct PLUS Loans.

As a graduate/professional student, select the "I'm a Graduate/Professional Student" option to find and use the MPN you need to borrow federal student loans. Graduate/professional students may be eligible for Direct Unsubsidized Loans, Direct PLUS Loans, or both, and you need to complete an MPN for each loan type you intend to receive. You should request Direct Unsubsidized Loans up to your full eligibility before borrowing Direct PLUS Loans. To proceed, use the "Log In to Select MPN Type" option.

The Master Promissory Note (MPN) is a legal document in which you promise to repay your loan and any accrued interest and fees to the U.S. Department of Education, and it also explains the terms and conditions of your loan. For graduate/professional students, you may be eligible for both Direct Unsubsidized Loans and Direct PLUS Loans, which have different MPNs, and you need to complete an MPN for each loan type you intend to receive. You may receive more than one loan under an MPN over a period of up to 10 years to pay for your educational costs, as long as the school is authorized to use the MPN in this way and chooses to do so; your school will tell you which loans, if any, you are eligible to receive.

Entrance counseling is required by the Federal Government if you have not previously received a Direct Loan or Federal Family Education Loan (FFEL); it ensures you understand the responsibilities and obligations you are assuming. For undergraduate borrowers, entrance counseling fulfills the counseling requirements for Direct Subsidized Loans and Direct Unsubsidized Loans; for graduate or professional student borrowers, it fulfills requirements for Direct Subsidized Loans, Direct Unsubsidized Loans, and Direct PLUS Loans. Your school may have alternate entrance counseling requirements, so check with your school's financial aid office. The entire counseling process must be completed in a single session, and most people complete it in 20–30 minutes.

The evidence offers some tools and tips, though not a comprehensive list. For tools, Federal Student Aid's Financial Aid Toolkit provides federal student aid information and outreach tools for counselors, college access professionals, nonprofit mentors, and others, including tips on hosting events, sample PowerPoint presentations, and suggested messages for social media and email outreach. FAFSA4caster is a helpful tool for anyone not yet ready to submit a FAFSA form, providing early estimates of federal student aid eligibility. There is also a tool to search for your school's Federal School Code. For keeping your federal student aid qualification, the evidence indicates you need to make satisfactory academic progress in college or career school in order to keep getting federal student aid, and if your grades slipped or you haven't completed enough credits, you should talk to your school about whether you can appeal the decision. It also notes that if you defaulted on your student loan, you'll need to get out of default before you can receive aid again, and if you were an eligible noncitizen whose status expired or was revoked, you'll need to reinstate that status. Other general tips include starting early, doing your research, keeping a to-do list, keeping track of everything required of you, making copies or scanning paper documents and filing them safely, and meeting deadlines.

Based on the evidence, several things can make you ineligible for federal student aid. Undocumented students, including DACA recipients, are not eligible for federal student aid. You are also NOT an eligible noncitizen and cannot receive federal student aid if you have only a Notice of Approval to Apply for Permanent Residence (I-171 or I-464), are in the U.S. on an F-1 or F-2 nonimmigrant student visa, are on a J-1 or J-2 nonimmigrant Exchange Visitor Visa, or hold a G series visa pertaining to international organizations. In addition, if you were an eligible noncitizen but your status expired or was revoked, you must reinstate that status or become a citizen or permanent resident before you can receive federal student aid. Eligibility can also be affected by incarceration, having a conviction for a drug offense, or being subject to an involuntary civil commitment after completing a period of incarceration for a sexual offense.

You would be ineligible for federal student aid if you have only a Notice of Approval to Apply for Permanent Residence I-171 or I-464, or if you are in the U.S. on an F-1 or F-2 nonimmigrant student visa, on a J-1 or J-2 nonimmigrant Exchange Visitor Visa, or hold a G series visa pertaining to international organizations. Since you are not on an F-1 or F-2 visa and do not have the I-171 or I-464 documentation, those specific grounds do not apply to you; however, the J-1/J-2 and G series visa categories would still make you ineligible if they apply. If you are not an eligible noncitizen, you may still find some scholarships and other aid, such as by checking with your country's embassy or consulate or the appropriate government office.

The purpose of federal student aid is to help students pay for college or career school. The U.S. Department of Education's office of Federal Student Aid provides grants, loans, and work-study opportunities to eligible students attending participating colleges or career schools, and it is the largest source of financial aid in the U.S.

If you have not received your school's financial aid offer yet, you cannot yet indicate which aid you want to accept, because your school's financial aid office sends the aid offer and asks you to indicate which financial aid you want. Once you receive the offer, review your options carefully and make an informed decision, prioritizing free money first (scholarships, grants), earned money second (work-study), and borrowed money last (federal student loans). Your aid offer will include directions on accepting aid, which you should follow carefully—this may involve entering amounts in an online form, signing and mailing a paper offer, or additional steps such as signing a promissory note or completing entrance counseling for a first federal loan. If you have not received your financial aid and need to pay for textbooks and other course materials, schools participating in federal student aid programs must provide a way for you to obtain books and supplies by the seventh day of the term if you are eligible for disbursement and will have a credit balance. You can also contact your school's financial aid office, which can explain how your aid was determined.

The Income-Sensitive Repayment Plan is available to low-income borrowers who have Federal Family Education Loan (FFEL) Program loans; the eligible loans listed are Subsidized Federal Stafford Loans, Unsubsidized Federal Stafford Loans, FFEL PLUS Loans, and FFEL Consolidation Loans, and William D. Ford Federal Direct Loans are not eligible. Perkins Loan repayment plan options are not the same as those for Direct Loan Program or FFEL Program loans, so you should check with your school for more information on Perkins Loan repayment plans. Note also that you may lose certain loan benefits if you consolidate a Federal Perkins Loan.

Yes. After you select or are assigned a repayment plan when you first begin repaying your student loan, you can change repayment plans at any time for free. You can also change your repayment plan at any time if your financial situation changes. To discuss repayment plan options or change your plan, contact your loan servicer. If you want to switch from one income-driven repayment plan to another, you can apply to switch at any time without waiting for your annual recertification.

Yes, you can ask another question. The FSA's Loan Simulator is a tool to help you make decisions about your student loans—for example, to find a repayment plan that meets your needs and goals or to decide whether to consolidate. It can also give you an early look at what repayment plans you may be eligible for and a comparison of estimated monthly payment amounts across all federal student loan repayment plans. Results are for informational purposes only and should not be considered financial advice.

Yes, you may be able to combine your multiple federal student loans into a single Direct Consolidation Loan to simplify repayment, and this can also affect your access to income-driven repayment plans. Consolidation is not the right choice for all borrowers or all loan types, and there may be tradeoffs, so you should understand the advantages and possible disadvantages before you apply. For example, if you have FFEL Program loans, your only income-driven repayment option is the IBR Plan, but consolidating them into a Direct Consolidation Loan gives you access to the REPAYE, PAYE, and ICR plans. You may also lose certain loan benefits if you consolidate a Federal Perkins Loan. Keep in mind that income-driven plans usually lower your monthly payments, but making lower payments or extending your repayment period will likely mean you pay more in interest over time, sometimes significantly more. Only federal student loans can be repaid under income-driven plans; private student loans are not eligible.

If you have multiple federal student loans, you can consolidate them into a single Direct Consolidation Loan, which may simplify repayment by giving you one monthly payment to one servicer instead of separate payments to different holders or servicers. There may be tradeoffs, so you should learn about the advantages and possible disadvantages before consolidating. Regarding FFEL program loans owned by the U.S. Department of Education: ED uses several loan servicers to handle billing and other services for loans made under the FFEL Program that ED later purchased, and your loan servicer will set you up under a repayment plan. The evidence does not describe any special additional consequence of consolidating FFEL loans owned by ED beyond this servicer arrangement.

To choose a federal student loan repayment plan, start by deciding whether you want to repay your loans quickly or pay as little as possible per month—you can't choose both, since lowering your payment means a longer repayment period and more interest over time. You can use Loan Simulator for an early look at which plans may fit your goal before contacting your loan servicer, and you can change repayment plans at any time for free. For the most affordable options: if you want the lowest monthly payment or can't afford payments under the Standard Repayment Plan, select an income-driven repayment plan, which sets your payment at a percentage of your income and usually has a lower monthly payment. If you have only Direct Loans, you can choose from all four income-driven plans, and if unsure which to pick you can request the income-driven plan with the lowest payment amount; your servicer will determine which plans you qualify for and place you on the one with the lowest monthly payment. If you have FFEL Program loans, your only income-driven option is the IBR Plan, though consolidating into a Direct Consolidation Loan gives access to REPAYE, PAYE, and ICR. Note that choosing a plan with a lower monthly payment may increase the interest you pay over time, sometimes significantly.

Under the Graduated Repayment Plan, monthly payments for Direct Consolidation Loans and FFEL Consolidation Loans start out low and increase every two years, are made over a period of between 10 and 30 years, will never be less than the amount of interest that accrues between your payments, and won't be more than three times greater than any other payment.

Several repayment options are available to meet individual borrower needs. These include standard, graduated, and extended repayment plans, which base your payment on your loan balance and interest rate, as well as income-driven repayment plans, which base your payment on your income. Income-driven plans set your payment at a percentage of your income, usually have a lower monthly payment than other plans, and can have payments as low as $0 per month, with repayment over up to 20 or 25 years and forgiveness of any remaining balance afterward. You can change repayment plans at any time for free by contacting your loan servicer, and your loan servicer can help you understand which options are available to you. You can also use the Loan Simulator for an early look at which plans you might qualify for. Note that choosing a plan that lowers your monthly payment may increase the amount of interest you pay over time.

You can use the Loan Simulator to get an early look at which repayment plans you may be eligible for and see estimates for how much you would pay monthly and overall. You can also contact your loan servicer to discuss repayment plan options.

The Income-Sensitive Repayment Plan is available to low-income borrowers with Federal Family Education Loan (FFEL) Program loans, and payments increase or decrease based on your annual income. Eligible FFEL loans are Subsidized Federal Stafford Loans, Unsubsidized Federal Stafford Loans, FFEL PLUS Loans, and FFEL Consolidation Loans. William D. Ford Federal Direct Loans are not eligible. Payments are made for a maximum period of 10 years. Separately, if you have FFEL Program loans, your only income-driven repayment plan option is the IBR Plan; consolidating FFEL loans into a Direct Consolidation Loan gives access to REPAYE, PAYE, and ICR.

You can contact your loan servicer to discuss repayment plan options or change your repayment plan. You can also use the Loan Simulator before contacting your loan servicer to get an early look at which plans you may be eligible for and estimates of what you would pay monthly and overall. To find the loan servicer for your loans, log in to My Federal Student Aid.

Yes. When you apply for an income-driven repayment plan, you'll be asked to provide income information that is used to calculate your monthly payment amount under all income-driven repayment plans. Generally, your payment is a percentage of your discretionary income, and depending on your income and family size you may have no monthly payment at all.

If you have FFEL Program loans owned by the U.S. Department of Education (ED), contact your loan servicer to modify your payment plan. To discuss repayment plan options or change your repayment plan, contact your loan servicer; before contacting them, you can use the Loan Simulator to get an early look at which plans you may be eligible for and estimates of your monthly and overall payments. You can also change your repayment plan at any time if your financial situation changes.

Under the Graduated Repayment Plan, monthly payments for Direct Consolidation Loans and FFEL Consolidation Loans start out low and increase every two years, and are made over a period of between 10 and 30 years. These payments will never be less than the amount of interest that accrues between payments and won't be more than three times greater than any other payment.

You can find information on federal student loan repayment options and making payments through Federal Student Aid resources. The resource 'Federal Student Loans: Repaying Your Loans' provides information about federal student loan repayment plan options, finding loan history and loan servicers, and making payments. You can also visit StudentAid.gov/plans for more information about student loan repayment options. Additionally, you can contact your loan servicer to discuss repayment plan options, and you can use the Loan Simulator to get an early look at which plans you may be eligible for and see estimates for how much you would pay monthly and overall.

Under the evidence provided, for a loan made under the Federal Perkins Loan Program, the holder of the loan may declare the loan to be in default if you don't make your scheduled payment by the due date. The evidence does not identify any other party required to make such a declaration.

If you are having trouble making your student loan payments, contact your loan servicer as soon as possible. Your servicer can explain your options, such as changing to a repayment plan that lowers your monthly payment (in some cases based on your income), or applying for deferment, forbearance, or loan consolidation. Staying in touch with your servicer helps you stay on track or get back on track and avoid default.

The evidence explains that loans must be repaid, and if you've missed a payment or are having trouble making payments, you should immediately contact the organization that handles billing and other services for your loan to avoid defaulting. For the William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan Program or the Federal Family Education Loan Program, contact your loan servicer; for the Federal Perkins Loan Program, contact the school where you received the loan. If you don't know who your loan servicer is, call the Federal Student Aid Information Center (FSAIC) at 1-800-433-3243. Regarding delinquency: the first day after you miss a student loan payment, your loan becomes past due, or delinquent, and your account remains delinquent until you repay the past due amount or make other arrangements such as deferment, forbearance, or changing repayment plans. If you are delinquent for 90 days or more, your loan servicer will report the delinquency to the three major national credit bureaus. Regarding default: if your loan continues to be delinquent, it may go into default, and the point of default varies by loan type. For Direct Loans or FFEL Program loans, you're considered in default if you don't make scheduled payments for at least 270 days; for a Perkins Loan, the holder may declare the loan in default if you don't make your scheduled payment by the due date. If you defaulted on any federal student loans, contact the organization that notified you of the default as soon as possible to explain your situation and discuss options; making repayment arrangements soon enough may allow you to resolve the default quickly. Consequences of default can impact your ability to borrow and your finances, including that the entire unpaid balance of your loan and any interest owed becomes immediately due. The evidence also notes that during the COVID-19 national emergency, federal student loan borrowers were automatically placed in an administrative forbearance allowing temporary suspension of monthly payments, with interest temporarily set at 0% from March 13, 2020, through Sept. 30, 2020.

If you are having trouble making payments on your student loans, you should immediately contact the organization that handles billing and other services for your loan to avoid defaulting. For Direct Loans or Federal Family Education Loan Program loans, contact your loan servicer; for Perkins Loans, contact the school where you received the loan, or the ECSI Federal Perkins Loan Servicer if the loan has been assigned to the U.S. Department of Education. If you don't know who your servicer is, call the Federal Student Aid Information Center at 1-800-433-3243. Staying in touch with your servicer is important because they can explain repayment options such as income-driven repayment plans, deferment, or forbearance to help you get back on track. You should avoid default, which occurs when you are at least nine months past due; consequences include damage to your credit rating and future borrowing. Even if you are delinquent, you may still be able to avoid default, so contact your servicer immediately. Missing a payment makes your loan delinquent and late fees may be assessed, and delinquency is reported to the three major national credit bureaus, which can make it difficult to obtain credit cards, home or car loans, or other consumer credit, and may result in higher interest rates.

The evidence explains that loans must be repaid, and if you've missed a payment or are having trouble making payments, you should immediately contact the organization that handles billing and other services for your loan to avoid defaulting. For the William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan Program or the Federal Family Education Loan Program, contact your loan servicer; for the Federal Perkins Loan Program, contact the school where you received the loan. If you don't know who your loan servicer is, call the Federal Student Aid Information Center (FSAIC) at 1-800-433-3243. Regarding delinquency: the first day after you miss a student loan payment, your loan becomes past due, or delinquent, and it remains delinquent until you repay the past due amount or make other arrangements such as deferment, forbearance, or changing repayment plans. If you are delinquent for 90 days or more, your loan servicer will report the delinquency to the three major national credit bureaus. Regarding default: if your loan continues to be delinquent, it may go into default, and the point of default varies by loan type. For Direct Loans or FFEL Program loans, you're considered in default if you don't make scheduled payments for at least 270 days; for a Perkins Loan, the holder may declare the loan in default if you don't make your scheduled payment by the due date. If you defaulted on any federal student loans, contact the organization that notified you of the default as soon as possible to explain your situation and discuss options; making repayment arrangements soon enough may allow you to resolve the default quickly. The consequences of default can impact your ability to borrow and your finances, and include the entire unpaid balance of your loan and any interest owed becoming immediately due.

Repayment of a Direct Consolidation Loan generally begins within 60 days after the loan is disbursed, and your loan servicer will let you know when the first payment is due. If any of the loans you want to consolidate are still in the grace period, you have the option of indicating on your Direct Consolidation Loan application that you want the servicer processing your application to delay the consolidation of your loans until closer to the grace period end date. If you select this option, you won't have to begin making payments on your new Direct Consolidation Loan until closer to the end of the grace period on your current loans. Note that if you consolidate during your grace period without requesting a delay, you give up the remainder of your grace period and begin repayment after your Direct Consolidation Loan is processed.

After you have submitted your Direct Consolidation Loan application and promissory note, contact the servicer for your new Direct Consolidation Loan. The consolidation servicer you selected will be your point of contact for questions related to your consolidation application. If you submitted your application online, your consolidation servicer's contact information was provided at the end of the online process; if you submitted a paper application by U.S. mail, that contact information was available when you downloaded or printed the paper application.

For a defaulted federal student loan, the amount you pay depends on the rehabilitation agreement set by your loan holder. Under a loan rehabilitation agreement, your monthly payment is generally 15 percent of your annual discretionary income divided by 12, and depending on your income it could be as low as $5 per month. If you cannot afford that initial amount, you can ask your loan holder to calculate an alternative monthly payment based on your monthly income remaining after reasonable monthly expenses. You must choose one of the two payment amounts. Additionally, after default you are liable for collection costs, typically 17.92% of your outstanding balance (including principal, interest, and fees), and payments are first applied to those collection costs with the remainder applied to interest and principal.

Yes. Delinquency on a student loan can lead to a poor credit rating. If you are delinquent on your student loan payment for 90 days or more, your loan servicer will report the delinquency to the three major national credit bureaus. If you continue to be delinquent, your loan can risk going into default, and default is reported to credit bureaus, damaging your credit rating and affecting your ability to buy a car or house or to get a credit card. A poor credit rating can make it difficult to obtain credit cards, home or car loans, or other forms of consumer credit, and you may also be charged a higher interest rate than someone with a good credit rating.

If you're having trouble making your student loan payments, contact your loan servicer as soon as possible. Your servicer can explain your options, which may include changing to a repayment plan that lowers your monthly payment (in some cases based on your income), applying for an income-driven repayment plan, deferment, forbearance, or loan consolidation. Staying in touch with your servicer helps you stay on track or get back on track, and you should avoid default, which occurs when you are at least nine months past due and can damage your credit rating and future borrowing.

For a William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan, contact your loan servicer. If you don't know who your loan servicer is, call the Federal Student Aid Information Center (FSAIC) at 1-800-433-3243. You can also find information about all your federal student loans by logging in to My Federal Student Aid. Keep these important documents in an organized file: financial aid offers, loan counseling materials (entrance and exit counseling), your promissory note(s), the amount of all student loans you borrow, the account number for each loan, loan servicer contact information, loan disclosure(s), payment schedules, a record of your monthly payments, notes about questions you ask about your loan along with the answers and the name of the person you spoke to, and deferment or forbearance documents.

If you still can't pay everything you owe, contact your loan servicer immediately for help. Your servicer can offer temporary or long-term options such as changing repayment plans, deferment, forbearance, or loan consolidation. Options may also include applying for an income-driven repayment plan, which bases your monthly payment on your income and family size. Staying in touch with your servicer is important, and you should avoid default, which occurs when you are at least nine months past due.

For a William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan, you risk going into default if you don't make your scheduled student loan payments for at least 270 days. More generally, default occurs when you are at least nine months past due on your student loan. If you continue to be delinquent, your loan may go into default, and defaulting can have serious consequences, including damage to your credit rating and future borrowing.

If you miss a payment, your loan becomes delinquent (past due) starting the first day after the missed payment, and late fees may be assessed. Your account remains delinquent until you repay the past due amount or make other arrangements such as deferment, forbearance, or changing repayment plans. If you're delinquent 90 days or more, your servicer will report the delinquency to the three major national credit bureaus. If you're having trouble making payments, contact your loan servicer immediately—they can explain options like income-driven repayment plans, changing repayment plans, deferment, forbearance, or loan consolidation to help you get back on track. One thing to avoid is default, which occurs when you are at least nine months past due; consequences include damage to your credit rating and future borrowing. Even if you are delinquent, you may still be able to avoid default, so contact your servicer immediately.

If you believe your William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan was placed in default by mistake, you can take steps to correct the error. The guidance indicates that if you believe your loan has been placed in default by mistake, there are actions you can take to correct the error. For a defaulted Direct Loan, one option for getting out of default is loan rehabilitation, which begins by contacting your loan holder; if you're unsure who your loan holder is, you can log in and select View loan servicer details to get the contact information. Also, if you're concerned about the status of your federal student loan, contact your loan servicer to discuss how to get back on track with payments.

A poor credit rating can make it difficult to obtain credit cards, home or car loans, or other forms of consumer credit, and you may be charged a higher interest rate than someone with a good credit rating. You also may have trouble signing up for utilities, getting homeowner's insurance, getting a cell phone plan, or getting approval to rent an apartment, since credit checks usually are required for renters. In the student loan context, delinquency of 90 days or more is reported to the three major national credit bureaus, and continuing delinquency can lead to default, which is reported to credit bureaus and damages your credit rating, affecting your ability to buy a car or house or get a credit card; it may take years to reestablish a good credit record.

If you have defaulted on any of your federal student loans, contact the organization that notified you of the default as soon as possible so you can explain your situation fully and discuss your options; if you make repayment arrangements soon enough after the loan has gone into default, you may be able to resolve the default quickly. Default has serious consequences: the entire unpaid balance of the loan and any interest owed becomes immediately due (acceleration), and once accelerated you no longer have access to deferment or forbearance options or a choice of repayment plans. If you do not make repayment arrangements with your loan holder and comply with their terms, your loan may be placed with a collection agency, and you would be responsible for collection costs. Other consequences include damage to your credit rating and future borrowing ability, and possible garnishment of your wages and withholding of your tax refunds. You should not get discouraged, because there are multiple options to get out of default, including loan rehabilitation (which restores benefits like deferment, forbearance, choice of repayment plans, and loan forgiveness, makes you eligible for federal student aid, and removes the default record from your credit history, though late payments reported before default remain; rehabilitation is a one-time opportunity) and consolidating the defaulted loan into a Direct Consolidation Loan. During the COVID-19 national emergency, the U.S. Department of Education stopped collection activity on defaulted federally owned student loans and/or grant overpayments and temporarily set interest at 0% on defaulted federally owned student aid debt, from March 13, 2020 through the period described.

You may be eligible for Public Service Loan Forgiveness if you are employed by a U.S. federal, state, local, or tribal government or a not-for-profit organization. To qualify, you must work full-time for that qualifying employer, have Direct Loans (or consolidate other federal student loans into a Direct Loan), repay your loans under an income-driven repayment plan, and make 120 qualifying monthly payments. FFEL Program and Perkins Loan Program loans don't qualify unless consolidated into a Direct Consolidation Loan, and private lender loans do not qualify.

Working part-time generally does not satisfy the PSLF full-time employment requirement. For PSLF, you are generally considered to work full-time if you meet your employer's definition of full-time or work at least 30 hours per week, whichever is greater. However, if you are employed in more than one qualifying part-time job at the same time, you will be considered full-time if you work a combined average of at least 30 hours per week with your employers. PSLF also requires that you be employed by a qualifying government or not-for-profit employer and work full-time for that agency or organization.

Consolidation may help with difficulty paying, but whether it's right depends on your individual circumstances. Potential benefits include simplifying repayment into a single monthly bill if your federal loans are with different servicers, and lowering your monthly payment by extending the repayment period (up to 30 years). Consolidation can also increase your chances of qualifying for an affordable repayment plan and loan forgiveness options, and may give you access to additional repayment plans and forgiveness programs. However, it may not be the best option for you: consolidating can result in the loss of some benefits, and lowering your payment means you'll be in repayment longer and pay more interest. If you want to lower your monthly payment but are concerned about consolidation's impact, you could consider deferment or forbearance for short-term relief, or switching to an income-driven repayment plan for longer-term relief. There is no application fee to consolidate federal loans, and you don't need to pay anyone for help applying. Generally, you're eligible to consolidate after you graduate, leave school, or drop below half-time enrollment.

Consolidating a defaulted federal student loan into a Direct Consolidation Loan is one option for getting out of default. To do so, you must either agree to repay the new Direct Consolidation Loan under an income-driven repayment plan, or make three consecutive, voluntary, on-time, full monthly payments on the defaulted loan before consolidating it. If you make those three payments first, the required payment amount is determined by your loan holder but cannot be more than what is reasonable and affordable based on your total financial circumstances. Unless you make three voluntary, on-time, full monthly payments on the defaulted loan before consolidating, your choice of repayment plans for the new Direct Consolidation Loan will be limited to one of the income-driven repayment plans. After the defaulted loan has been consolidated, the Direct Consolidation Loan will be eligible for benefits such as deferment, forbearance, and loan forgiveness, and you'll be eligible to receive additional federal student aid. However, unlike loan rehabilitation, consolidation of a defaulted loan does not remove the record of the default from your credit history; the record of the default and late payments reported before default will remain in your credit history, and late payments remain on your credit report for seven years from when they were first reported. It's important to fully understand loan rehabilitation and loan consolidation before deciding.

Who you contact depends on where you are in the consolidation process. To ask questions about consolidating your loans before you apply for a Direct Consolidation Loan, contact the Student Loan Support Center at 1-800-557-7394. To request technical assistance while logged in and completing the online application, either complete and submit the feedback form or contact the Student Loan Support Center at 1-800-557-7394. To ask questions after you have submitted your application and promissory note, contact the servicer for your new Direct Consolidation Loan; if you applied online, your consolidation servicer's contact information was provided to you. The consolidation servicer will be your point of contact for questions related to your consolidation application.

For a Direct Consolidation Loan, the loans you consolidate must be in repayment or in the grace period. Generally, you cannot consolidate an existing consolidation loan unless you include an additional eligible loan in the consolidation. You are generally eligible to consolidate after you graduate, leave school, or drop below half-time enrollment. Since your loans are not in default, the defaulted-loan requirements do not apply.

Consolidating federal education loans can simplify your payments by combining multiple federal education loans into one loan, resulting in a single monthly payment instead of multiple payments. It can also give you access to additional loan repayment plans and forgiveness programs, and there is no application fee to consolidate into a Direct Consolidation Loan. If you consolidate loans other than Direct Loans, consolidation may give you access to additional income-driven repayment plan options and Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF), and you'll be able to switch any variable-rate loans to a fixed interest rate. However, consolidation also has downsides: it can result in the loss of some benefits, such as interest rate discounts, principal rebates, or some loan cancellation benefits; outstanding interest becomes part of the principal balance, so interest may accrue on a higher balance; and because the repayment period is usually longer, you will likely make more payments and pay more in interest than if you didn't consolidate.

Whether to consolidate a federal Perkins Loan depends on your circumstances, so a single recommendation isn't possible from the evidence. Consolidating a Perkins Loan into a Direct Consolidation Loan can make it eligible for Public Service Loan Forgiveness, but only qualifying payments made on the new Direct Consolidation Loan count toward the required 120 payments, and payments made before consolidation don't count. Also, if you want to keep Perkins Loan cancellation benefits, you should not include your Perkins Loans when you consolidate, since leaving them out preserves those benefits. Consolidation can simplify repayment into one monthly payment, but there may be tradeoffs, and once loans are combined into a Direct Consolidation Loan they cannot be removed. For short-term payment relief you might consider deferment or forbearance, or an income-driven repayment plan for longer-term relief. Perkins Loan repayment plan options differ from Direct Loan and FFEL Program loans, so check with your school for more information.

Default occurs when your loan continues to be delinquent and you fail to make scheduled payments for a required period. For loans under the William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan Program or the Federal Family Education Loan Program, you're considered in default if you don't make your scheduled student loan payments for at least 270 days. For a Federal Perkins Loan, the holder may declare the loan in default if you don't make your scheduled payment by the due date. Consequences of default include the entire unpaid balance of the loan and any interest becoming immediately due (acceleration); loss of eligibility for deferment or forbearance and for choosing a repayment plan; loss of eligibility for additional federal student aid; reporting to credit bureaus, which damages your credit rating and future borrowing ability; possible withholding of tax refunds and federal benefit payments (Treasury offset); and possible wage garnishment. Your loan may also be placed with a collection agency. If you default, contact the organization that notified you of the default as soon as possible to explain your situation and discuss your options; making repayment arrangements soon enough may let you resolve the default quickly.

Default occurs when you are at least nine months past due on your student loan. The consequences of default include damage to your credit rating and future borrowing ability, and may also include garnishment of your wages and withholding of your tax refunds. Defaulting can also impact your finances: the entire unpaid balance of your loan and any interest you owe becomes immediately due. A poor credit rating can make it difficult to obtain credit cards, home or car loans, or other consumer credit, and you may be charged a higher interest rate; you also may have trouble signing up for utilities, getting homeowner's insurance, getting a cell phone plan, or getting approval to rent an apartment. If you defaulted on any federal student loans, contact the organization that notified you of the default as soon as possible to explain your situation and discuss your options; if you make repayment arrangements soon enough, you may be able to resolve the default quickly. You have multiple options to get out of default, and if you're struggling to make payments, your loan servicer can explain options such as an income-driven repayment plan, forbearance, or deferment.

A federal student loan can go into default if you do not make your scheduled payment by the due date, and continuing delinquency can lead to default. If you default, contact the organization that notified you of the default as soon as possible to explain your situation and discuss your options; making repayment arrangements soon enough may let you resolve the default quickly. Consequences of default include: the entire unpaid balance and any interest owed becomes immediately due (acceleration); loss of eligibility for deferment or forbearance and for benefits such as choosing a repayment plan; loss of eligibility for additional federal student aid; the default is reported to credit bureaus, damaging your credit rating and future borrowing ability and possibly making it harder to get credit cards, car or home loans, utilities, insurance, a cell phone plan, or an apartment; possible inability to purchase or sell assets such as real estate; withholding of tax refunds and federal benefit payments (Treasury offset); and garnishment of wages. You have multiple options to get out of default, and during the COVID-19 national emergency the Department of Education stopped collection activity on defaulted federally owned student loans and temporarily set interest at 0% on defaulted federally owned student aid debt.

A defaulted federal student loan can be resolved by consolidating it into a Direct Consolidation Loan. To consolidate a defaulted loan, you must either agree to repay the new Direct Consolidation Loan under an income-driven repayment plan, or make three consecutive, voluntary, on-time, full monthly payments on the defaulted loan before consolidating. If you choose the three-payment option, the required payment amount is determined by your loan holder but cannot be more than what is reasonable and affordable based on your total financial circumstances. After a defaulted loan is consolidated, the Direct Consolidation Loan becomes eligible for benefits such as deferment, forbearance, and loan forgiveness, and you become eligible to receive additional federal student aid; however, unlike loan rehabilitation, consolidation of a defaulted loan does not remove the record of the default from your credit history. Generally, loans being consolidated must be in repayment or in the grace period.

Yes. Health Professions Student Loans are listed among the federal student loans that are eligible for consolidation. Consolidating can simplify your payments into a single monthly payment, but it may also cause you to lose some benefits, so you should weigh the pros and cons.

You can get free help managing your student loans by contacting your loan servicer, who helps you with your loans for FREE. You can also create an online account on your servicer's website to get detailed, up-to-date information, make payments, and manage your loans (for example, change repayment plans or apply for a deferment). If you need help identifying your servicer, call the Federal Student Aid Information Center (FSAIC) at 1-800-433-3243. Never pay an outside company for help with your federal student loans.

No, not necessarily all of them. Only loans you received for a program that you were unable to complete because of the school's closure are eligible for discharge. For example, if you initially enrolled in Program A but decided not to continue and transferred to Program B, and then could not complete Program B because the school closed, only loans for Program B could potentially be discharged; loans for Program A would not be eligible because the school's closure did not prevent you from completing that program. Also, generally your federal student loans can't be canceled or forgiven because you didn't complete your education unless you couldn't complete it because your school closed.

Beyond the basic requirement of full-time teaching in a public or nonprofit elementary or secondary school system, here is what else you need to know about Perkins Loan cancellation: You may qualify for cancellation of up to 100 percent of a Federal Perkins Loan if you taught in a school serving students from low-income families, were a special education teacher (including teachers of infants, toddlers, children, or youth with disabilities), or taught mathematics, science, foreign languages, bilingual education, or another field of expertise your state education agency determined to have a shortage of qualified teachers. Eligibility is based on the duties in an official position description, not the position title, and you must be directly employed by the school system; there is no provision for canceling Perkins Loans for teaching in postsecondary schools. A teacher includes someone such as a school librarian or guidance counselor who provides students with direct services related to classroom teaching; you do not need to be certified or licensed, but your employing school must consider you a full-time professional for salary, tenure, and retirement purposes. Supervisors, administrators, researchers, or curriculum specialists are not considered teachers unless they primarily provide direct and personal educational services to students. For each full academic year (or its equivalent) of full-time teaching service, a portion of your loan is canceled; there is no required number of hours per day, as the employing school decides full-time status, and an academic year or its equivalent is one complete school year or two complete, consecutive half-years from different school years. You also qualify for deferment while performing teaching service that qualifies for cancellation, and you should contact your college or its Perkins Loan servicer for information on applying for deferment.

If your TPD discharge was based on SSA documentation or a physician's certification and your three-year post-discharge period hasn't ended, you must resume repayment on your previously discharged loans or acknowledge that you are once again responsible for meeting the terms and conditions of your TEACH Grant service obligation. During the three-year post-discharge monitoring period, your obligation to repay your loans or complete your TEACH Grant service obligation will be reinstated if you don't meet certain requirements.

To apply for a federal student loan, you must first complete and submit the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) form. The FAFSA form lets you request federal grants, work-study, and loans all in one application. Based on your FAFSA results, your college or career school will send you a financial aid offer, which may include federal student loans, and your school will tell you how to accept all or part of the loan. Before receiving loan funds, you must complete entrance counseling to ensure you understand your obligation to repay the loan, and sign the required documents. Keep in mind that a loan is money you borrow and must pay back with interest, so understand who is making the loan and its terms and conditions. Federal student loans usually have more benefits than loans from banks or private sources. After graduating, federal student loan borrowers have a six-month grace period before payments begin, and you should complete a FAFSA form each year.

To qualify for federal student aid (grants, work-study, and loans), you must meet certain basic eligibility criteria: demonstrate financial need for most programs; be a U.S. citizen or an eligible noncitizen; have a valid Social Security number (with exceptions for students from the Republic of the Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, or the Republic of Palau); be registered with Selective Service if you're male (registration between ages 18 and 25); be enrolled or accepted for enrollment as a regular student in an eligible degree or certificate program; be enrolled at least half-time to be eligible for Direct Loan Program funds; maintain satisfactory academic progress in college or career school; sign the certification statement on the FAFSA stating that you are not in default on a federal student loan, do not owe money on a federal student grant, and will use federal student aid only for educational purposes; and show you're qualified to obtain a college or career school education by having a high school diploma or recognized equivalent such as a GED certificate, completing a high school education in an approved homeschool setting, or enrolling in an eligible career pathway program and meeting one of the "ability-to-benefit" alternatives. Additional eligibility requirements can apply in certain situations, including for non-U.S. citizens, students with criminal convictions, and students with intellectual disabilities, and some federal student aid programs have their own eligibility criteria in addition to the general requirements.

To qualify for federal student aid, you generally must be a U.S. citizen or an eligible noncitizen, along with meeting other basic criteria such as demonstrating financial need for most programs, having a valid Social Security number (with certain exceptions), being registered with Selective Service if required, and being enrolled or accepted in an eligible degree or certificate program. Many non-U.S. citizens do qualify: the most common category of eligible noncitizen is a permanent resident with a green card, and other categories exist, such as U.S. nationals (including natives of American Samoa or Swains Island). Certain eligible noncitizens may need to provide evidence from USCIS that they are in the United States for other than a temporary purpose with the intention of becoming a U.S. citizen or permanent resident. However, undocumented students, including DACA recipients, are not eligible for federal student aid. Because additional eligibility requirements can apply to non-U.S. citizens, you should check with your college's financial aid office for more information about your specific situation.

The evidence does not provide the specific requirements for a non-U.S. citizen with intellectual disabilities to study in the United States or to qualify for federal student aid. It only notes that additional eligibility requirements can apply in certain situations, including for non-U.S. citizens and students with intellectual disabilities, and that some federal student aid programs have their own eligibility criteria beyond the general requirements. General criteria mentioned include demonstrating financial need for most programs, being a U.S. citizen or eligible noncitizen, having a valid Social Security number (with certain exceptions), Selective Service registration if male aged 18–25, and being enrolled or accepted in an eligible degree or certificate program. For noncitizens, certain eligible noncitizens must provide USCIS evidence that they are in the United States for other than a temporary purpose with the intention of becoming a U.S. citizen or permanent resident, and undocumented students, including DACA recipients, are not eligible for federal student aid. The evidence does not address school-based support for intellectual disabilities or the specific steps for a noncitizen with intellectual disabilities to study in the U.S.

If you are not an eligible noncitizen, you cannot receive federal student aid, but there may be some scholarships and other aid you can get. Check with your country's embassy or a consulate in the U.S., or with the appropriate government office. Undocumented students, including DACA recipients, are not eligible for federal student aid, but may still be eligible for state or college aid, in addition to private scholarships; check with your college or career school's financial aid office for more information. You can also check with your high school counselor or financial aid office to see whether completing the FAFSA form is the way to apply for state and college student aid.

The evidence provided only describes types of federal student aid (grants such as Pell Grants, FSEOG, TEACH Grants, and Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grants; work-study; loans; and scholarships) and does not identify any federal aid program outside Federal Student Aid. It also does not provide application instructions beyond noting that grant program details include how to apply. Therefore, the evidence is insufficient to answer whether the federal government offers other types of aid or how to apply for them.

The evidence does not address military service or loans related to military service, so it cannot confirm whether Loan Simulator information would make assistance more accurate for someone in that situation. The evidence does indicate that Loan Simulator is a tool to help make decisions about student loans, such as finding a repayment plan or deciding whether to consolidate, and that providing complete and accurate information yields the most realistic results. However, it also states that results are for informational purposes only and cannot predict future payments with 100% accuracy, so it should not be considered financial advice.

The Loan Simulator includes an option to simulate borrowing more money, which lets you find out what happens when you borrow more to pay for educational expenses, return to school, or finish your studies later than expected. That option is listed as 'Coming Soon,' and you can also start from scratch to explore the impacts of borrowing more, learn about federal loan limits, and see how your choice of school affects how much you may need to borrow. For the most realistic results, provide complete and accurate information when using the Loan Simulator. Note that the evidence addresses borrowing more for educational expenses rather than an extraordinary situation generally.
Yes. The Loan Simulator page invites users to share the tool with friends and family.

The evidence does not identify a specific list of documents to keep in a well-organized file for education tax benefits or IRA withdrawals for college costs. It does mention that you should read IRS Publication 970, Tax Benefits for Education, to see which federal income tax benefits might apply to your situation. It also notes that if you receive a Form 1099-C in connection with a total and permanent disability discharge, you should keep the form for your records, though you do not need to include it when filing your federal tax return.
