For a parent borrowing for a son's college costs, the key differences are: federal loans are made by the government with terms and conditions set by law, and include benefits such as fixed interest rates and income-driven repayment plans not typically offered with private loans; private loans are made by private organizations such as banks, credit unions, and state-based or state-affiliated organizations, with terms set by the lender, and are generally more expensive than federal student loans. Federal parent loans are Direct PLUS Loans for parents, and parents are fully responsible for paying these loans even though they are taken out to benefit students. A parent of a dependent undergraduate student can receive a Direct PLUS Loan for the remainder of the child's college costs not covered by other financial aid, and should borrow only what is needed. To get a federal loan, you must first complete the FAFSA form. Federal loans are generally recommended first, as they usually have more benefits than loans from banks or other private sources.

Private student loans are nonfederal loans made by a lender such as a bank, credit union, state agency, or school, and their terms and conditions are set by the lender. They differ by lender and by type of loan, so it's important to understand the terms of your loan and keep in touch with your lender with any questions. Private student loans are generally more expensive than federal student loans, and federal student loans usually have more benefits, so if you need to borrow, consider federal loans first. As for your son applying for financial aid: if he applies for financial aid, he may be offered loans as part of the school's financial aid offer, and the school will likely include student loans in the financial aid package, so it's important to understand what types of loans are offered. To get a federal loan, he must first complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) form.

To get a federal student loan, your son must first complete and submit a Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) form. Based on the FAFSA results, his college or career school will send him a financial aid offer, which may include federal student loans, and the school will tell him how to accept all or part of the loan. Before receiving loan funds, he will be required to complete entrance counseling to ensure he understands his obligation to repay the loan, and sign the required documents. Separately, as a parent of a dependent undergraduate student, you may be able to receive a Direct PLUS Loan for the remainder of your child's college costs not covered by other financial aid; before applying for a PLUS loan, your child must have already filled out the FAFSA.

Yes. Whether the amount of a loan written off due to TPD can be treated as taxable income for federal tax purposes depends on when the discharge was received. If the TPD discharge occurred before January 1, 2018, the discharged loan amount may be considered income for federal tax purposes under IRS rules. If the TPD discharge occurred during the period from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2025, the discharged loan amount will not be considered income for federal tax purposes. The date the discharge is considered received for federal tax purposes differs depending on how you qualified: veterans who showed total and permanent disability based on a VA disability determination are considered to have received the discharge on the date the discharge was approved, while those who qualified based on SSA documentation or a physician's certification (subject to a three-year postdischarge monitoring period) are considered to have received the discharge at the end of that monitoring period. Discharged loan amounts may still be considered income for state tax purposes.

If you have two email addresses associated with your borrower defense application, ED sent a notification email to both addresses. This is one of the two circumstances that would result in your receipt of more than one notification email. To check the notification emails you received, contact the borrower defense hotline at 1-855-279-6207 from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET on Monday through Friday.

For purposes of borrower defense discharge only, the term Direct Loan in 34 CFR 685.206 is interpreted to include Direct Consolidation loans. This interpretation enables borrowers with loans eligible for Direct Loan consolidation, including Federal Family Education Loan (FFEL) Program loans or Federal Perkins Loans, to use the borrower discharge process by consolidating those loans into the Direct Loan Program.

If a borrower defense applicant is due to receive a Manriquez v. DeVos lawsuit notification but does not have a good email address, the U.S. Department of Education will mail the notification instead. The mailed notification will be sent in an envelope marked with Federal Student Aid's return address. Each borrower will receive either an emailed notification or a mailed notification.

Based on the evidence, a 100 percent discharge of Direct Loan, FFEL, or Perkins loans requires that you were unable to complete your program because your school closed, and that one of the following applies: you were enrolled when your school closed; you were on an approved leave of absence when your school closed; or your school closed within 120 days after you withdrew. Since you were not enrolled and not on an approved leave of absence when your school closed, the remaining possible basis is that your school closed within 120 days after you withdrew. You would not be eligible if, except in exceptional circumstances, you withdrew more than 120 days before the school closed, or if you are completing a comparable educational program at another school through a teach-out, by transferring credits, or by other comparable means, or if you completed all coursework for the program before the school closed. You must apply to get a discharge by contacting your loan servicer, and you should continue making payments while your application is processed.

Borrowers may qualify for borrower defense to repayment forgiveness of the federal student loans they took out to attend a school if that school misled them or engaged in other misconduct in violation of certain laws. Specifically, a borrower may assert borrower defense by showing that the school, through an act or omission, violated state law directly related to the federal student loan or to the educational services for which the loan was provided. Eligibility does not depend on whether the school closed or whether the borrower is otherwise eligible for loan forgiveness under other laws. Eligibility is limited to federal student loans taken out for payment to the school relating to the borrower defense application, and separate applications are required for each school attended. For Direct Loans, a borrower may be eligible for discharge of part or all of one or more Direct Loans if the school engaged in acts or omissions that would give rise to a cause of action against the school under applicable state law, and the cause of action must directly relate to the Direct Loan or to the school's provision of educational services for which the loan was provided. Additionally, borrowers who attended Corinthian Colleges (Everest, Heald, and WyoTech) with a first date of attendance between July 1, 2010, and Sept. 30, 2014, and who are seeking federal student loan forgiveness through borrower defense complete a Corinthian-specific application.

If a borrower defense application is denied, you will not receive a discharge of any of your federal student loans, and the forbearance or stopped collections period will end for all of your loans. You will be responsible for repaying these loans, including interest that accrued during the forbearance or stopped collections period. If the application is partially approved (partial discharge), you will be responsible for repaying any amounts not discharged through borrower defense, including any interest that accumulated, and the forbearance or stopped collections period for any of your other federal student loans will end; you will be responsible for repaying those other loans, including interest that accrued during the forbearance or stopped collections period. In addition, when you are taken out of forbearance or stopped collections, the interest that accumulated will be added to the amount you owed when you entered forbearance or stopped collections.

The evidence addresses the CCI association but not the requirements to be a highly qualified teacher. Regarding CCI: if your program earnings exceed the comparison earnings, even with an approved claim you will not receive a discharge unless your approved application is associated with Corinthian Colleges, Inc. (CCI). If your approved application is associated with CCI, you will receive at least a 10% discharge, and the larger the negative gap between your program earnings and comparison earnings, the greater the amount of loan discharge you receive. Borrowers who attended Corinthian Colleges Everest, Heald, and WyoTech with a first date of attendance between July 1, 2010, and Sept. 30, 2014, and are seeking federal student loan forgiveness through borrower defense complete a Corinthian-specific application. The evidence contains no information on the requirements to be a highly qualified teacher.

You may be able to pursue forgiveness through borrower defense to repayment, which applies to federal student loans you took out to attend a school that misled you or engaged in other misconduct in violation of certain state laws. You assert borrower defense by demonstrating that the school, through an act or omission, violated state law directly related to your federal student loan or to the educational services for which the loan was provided. The misconduct must directly relate to your loan or the educational services provided; claims not directly related, such as personal injury or harassment allegations, are not bases for a borrower defense application. Eligibility is limited to federal student loans taken out for payment to the school relating to your borrower defense application, and if you attended multiple schools you must submit separate applications for each school. If eligible, you may have all or part of your outstanding federal student loan debt forgiven and may be reimbursed for amounts already paid. The evidence describes the borrower defense application process but does not provide the specific steps or form for submitting a general application (beyond noting a Corinthian-specific application for certain Corinthian Colleges borrowers).

The evidence does not support 100 percent discharge for someone who was neither enrolled nor on an approved leave of absence when the school closed. The 100 percent discharge criteria require that you were unable to complete your program because your school closed and that you were enrolled when your school closed, were on an approved leave of absence when your school closed, or your school closed within 120 days after you withdrew. The evidence also notes that you are not eligible if you withdrew more than 120 days before the school closed, except in exceptional circumstances. The borrower defense evidence provided concerns ineligibility determinations and does not establish eligibility requirements for 100 percent discharge in your circumstances.

Yes, it is possible to potentially receive forgiveness under both the Teacher Loan Forgiveness Program and the Public Service Loan Forgiveness Program, but not for the same period of teaching service. For example, if you complete five consecutive years of qualifying teaching and receive forgiveness of your Direct Loans under the Teacher Loan Forgiveness Program, any payments you made on your Direct Loans during that five-year period cannot be counted toward the required 120 monthly payments for the Public Service Loan Forgiveness Program; to receive Public Service Loan Forgiveness, you would need to make 120 more qualifying monthly payments. Under the Teacher Loan Forgiveness Program, if you teach full-time for five complete and consecutive academic years in a low-income school or educational service agency and meet other qualifications, you may be eligible for forgiveness of up to $17,500 on your Direct Subsidized and Unsubsidized Loans and your Subsidized and Unsubsidized Federal Stafford Loans. You may receive up to $17,500 if you were a highly qualified full-time mathematics or science teacher who taught students at the secondary school level, or a highly qualified special education teacher at either the elementary or secondary level whose primary responsibility was to provide special education to children with disabilities and who taught children with disabilities corresponding to your area of special education training and demonstrated knowledge and teaching skills in the content areas of the curriculum you taught. If you didn't teach mathematics, science, or special education, you may receive up to $5,000 if you were a highly qualified full-time elementary or secondary education teacher. If you have eligible loans under both the Direct Loan Program and the FFEL Program, $17,500 or $5,000 is a combined maximum forgiveness amount for both programs. For the Public Service Loan Forgiveness Program, you may qualify if you are employed by a government or not-for-profit organization and must make 120 qualifying payments under an income-driven plan to qualify.

Yes. The evidence describes several savings options for school or college expenses: a Coverdell Education Savings Account, which allows up to $2,000 a year to be put aside for a student's education expenses (elementary, secondary, or college or career school); Qualified Tuition Programs, also known as 529 Plans; and prepaid tuition and education savings 529 plans, which are suggested as ways to start saving before college. The evidence also notes that tax benefits can be used to maximize your college savings.

If your parent or guardian died as a result of military service in Iraq or Afghanistan after the events of 9/11, you might be eligible for additional Federal Pell Grant funding or for an Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant. To be eligible, at the time of your parent's or guardian's death, you must have been less than 24 years old or enrolled at least part-time at a college or career school. Payments will be adjusted if you are enrolled less than full-time. If you meet these requirements and are eligible to receive a Pell Grant, you will receive an Expected Family Contribution (EFC) of zero, which maximizes your Pell Grant eligibility and can increase your eligibility for other federal student aid programs.

Students may qualify for additional federal student aid if their parent or guardian died as a result of military service in Iraq or Afghanistan after the events of 9/11. At the time of the parent's or guardian's death, the student must have been less than 24 years old or enrolled at least part-time at a college or career school. Payments are adjusted if the student is enrolled less than full-time. Eligible students who qualify for a Pell Grant receive an Expected Family Contribution (EFC) of zero, maximizing Pell Grant eligibility and potentially increasing eligibility for other federal student aid programs. Students who meet the requirements but are not eligible for a Pell Grant based on their EFC may receive an Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant, whose maximum amount equals the maximum Pell Grant award; their EFC is not affected.

Yes. The evidence says that if you are not an eligible noncitizen, there may still be some scholarships and other aid you can get, and it advises checking with your country's embassy or a consulate here in the U.S., or with the appropriate government office back in your country, to see what they offer. It also suggests asking the college or career school you plan to attend whether they offer any aid for students like you.

Yes. If you don't have a high school diploma or GED, you can show you're qualified for higher education by passing an approved ability-to-benefit test, which a college can administer to determine whether you can benefit from the education offered at that school. This applies if you were enrolled in college or career school prior to July 1, 2012, or if you are currently enrolled in an eligible career pathway program. Alternatively, you can qualify by completing six credit hours or equivalent course work toward a degree or certificate, though you may not receive aid while earning those six credit hours. For more information about these criteria, talk to the financial aid office at your school.

Yes. If your parent died as a result of military service in Iraq or Afghanistan after the events of 9/11, you may be eligible for additional federal aid. To qualify, at the time of your parent's death you must have been under 24 years old or enrolled at least part-time at a college or career school. This aid can include additional Federal Pell Grant funds—if you're eligible for a Pell Grant, you'd receive an Expected Family Contribution (EFC) of zero, which maximizes Pell Grant eligibility and can increase eligibility for other federal student aid programs—or an Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant. Payments are adjusted if you're enrolled less than full-time. Note that this specific aid applies to parents who died as a result of military service in Iraq or Afghanistan after 9/11; the evidence does not describe programs for other military service circumstances. More generally, there is no income cut-off to qualify for federal student aid, and factors such as family size and year in school are taken into account.

Yes, many non-U.S. citizens qualify for federal student aid, so you shouldn't assume you can't get aid just because you're not a citizen. The most common category of eligible noncitizen is a permanent resident (green card holder), but there are other categories as well, such as U.S. nationals (including natives of American Samoa or Swains Island), permanent residents with a Form I-551, I-151, or I-551C card, and others. You should check with your college's or career school's financial aid office for more information. Note that some noncitizens are not eligible for federal student aid—for example, those with only a Notice of Approval to Apply for Permanent Residence (I-171 or I-464), those on an F-1 or F-2 student visa, a J-1 or J-2 Exchange Visitor Visa, or a G series visa—but even then there may be scholarships and other aid available, such as through your country's embassy or consulate. Undocumented students, including DACA recipients, are not eligible for federal student aid but may be eligible for state or college aid and private scholarships.

Based on the evidence, the general eligibility requirements for federal student aid include having financial need, being a U.S. citizen or eligible noncitizen, and being enrolled in an eligible degree or certificate program at your college or career school. There are additional eligibility requirements you must meet to qualify, and there is no income cut-off to qualify for federal student aid—factors such as family size and year in school are taken into account. The evidence also notes that homeless students are among the groups whose eligibility situations are addressed. Regarding a parent killed in Iraq or Afghanistan, additional aid (such as additional Federal Pell Grant funding or an Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant) may be available only if the parent died as a result of military service in Iraq or Afghanistan after the events of 9/11; since your parents were not performing military service, that specific provision would not appear to apply to you. The evidence does not provide further details on the specific requirements for homeless students.

The evidence does not state that students experiencing homelessness must prove they are qualified for university studies. It says homeless students can receive money for college if they meet the eligibility requirements for federal student aid, and the basic eligibility criteria include being enrolled or accepted for enrollment as a regular student in an eligible degree or certificate program. No separate proof of qualification for university studies is described.

No. Signing the FAFSA certification statement requires you to state that you are not in default on a federal student loan, so signing it does not make you eligible if you are in default. To regain eligibility for federal student aid after default, you must get out of default, for example through rehabilitation (which restores eligibility for benefits and federal student aid) or by consolidating the defaulted loan into a Direct Consolidation Loan.

Yes. In most circumstances, there are things you can do to get back your eligibility for financial aid, even if you've been told you can no longer get federal student aid. You might lose eligibility for various reasons, such as no longer meeting a basic eligibility criterion or changing majors so you're no longer enrolled in a program that qualifies you for a specific type of funding. It's recommended that you talk to your financial aid office about your circumstances and options for regaining eligibility.

The information available concerns students whose parent or guardian died as a result of military service in Iraq or Afghanistan after the events of 9/11. If that applies, you may be eligible for additional aid, including an Iraq and Afghanistan Service Grant or additional Federal Pell Grant funds. To be eligible, at the time of your parent's or guardian's death you must have been less than 24 years old or enrolled at least part-time at a college or career school. Payments will be adjusted if you are enrolled less than full-time. If you meet these requirements and are eligible for a Pell Grant, you will receive an Expected Family Contribution (EFC) of zero, which maximizes your Pell Grant eligibility and can increase your eligibility for other federal student aid programs.

If your parents are incarcerated, you may be able to submit your FAFSA form without parent information even though you are considered a dependent student. When the FAFSA form asks for information about your parents, select the "I am unable to provide information about my parent" option. Note that if you submit without parent information, you will not receive an EFC, and some state- or school-based aid programs look at the EFC, so this may affect certain aid.

If you cannot provide your parents' information, you can select the "I am unable to provide information about my parent" option when the FAFSA form asks for parent information. If you have special circumstances (such as your parents being incarcerated, leaving home due to an abusive family environment, not knowing where your parents are and being unable to contact them without having been adopted, or being older than 21 but not yet 24, unaccompanied, and homeless or self-supporting and at risk of homelessness), you can indicate that you have special circumstances and submit your application without parent data, though it will not be fully processed and you will not receive an Expected Family Contribution. If your parents simply refuse to provide their information, you cannot be considered independent for that reason alone, but you may submit your FAFSA form without their information; however, you won't be able to get any federal student aid other than an unsubsidized loan, and even that is up to the financial aid office at your school. You must immediately contact your school's financial aid office to discuss the possibility of getting an unsubsidized loan, and they may ask for a written statement from your parents indicating that they refuse to provide their information.

You may be able to submit your FAFSA form without parent information despite being considered a dependent student in special circumstances such as: your parents are incarcerated; you have left home due to an abusive family environment; or you do not know where your parents are and are unable to contact them and you have not been adopted. Additionally, if your parents don't support you and refuse to provide their information on the application, you may submit your FAFSA form without their information, though you won't be able to get any federal student aid other than an unsubsidized loan (and even that might not happen, as the decision is up to the financial aid office at your school). In that case you won't get an EFC, and you must immediately contact your school's financial aid office to discuss the possibility of getting an unsubsidized loan.

You can submit a request to your student loan servicer, often using a form; for some types of forbearance you must also provide documentation showing you meet the eligibility requirements. A general forbearance is discretionary—your servicer decides whether to grant it—and you can request one if you are temporarily unable to make your scheduled monthly loan payments for reasons such as financial difficulties, medical expenses, a change in employment, or other reasons acceptable to your servicer. Note that the evidence does not specifically address applying when you are not currently in financial difficulty but anticipate possible future difficulties.

To apply for forbearance, you submit a request to your student loan servicer, often using a form. For some types of forbearance, you must also provide documentation showing you meet the eligibility requirements. A general forbearance is discretionary—your loan servicer decides whether to grant it—and you can request one if you are temporarily unable to make your scheduled monthly loan payments for reasons such as financial difficulties, medical expenses, a change in employment, or other reasons acceptable to your loan servicer. Note that the evidence describes eligibility based on being temporarily unable to make payments for these reasons; it does not specifically address applying when you are not currently experiencing financial difficulties or extra medical expenses.

An income-driven repayment plan is more effective at obtaining relief because it bases your monthly payments on your income and family size, which can make your student loan debt more manageable by reducing your monthly payment amount. It is presented as a better option than deferment when you are having trouble repaying due to circumstances that may continue for an extended period or when you are unsure when you will be able to afford monthly payments again. Deferment lets you temporarily stop making payments, but you probably will not make progress toward forgiveness or paying back your loan, whereas under income-driven plans any remaining balance is forgiven if your loans are not fully repaid at the end of the repayment period. Note that lower payments or an extended repayment period will likely mean paying more in interest over time, sometimes significantly more.

If you don't pay the interest on your loan and allow it to capitalize, the unpaid interest is added to your loan principal balance at the end of the forbearance or deferment period. As a result, the total amount you repay over the life of your loan may be higher. Because interest accrues on your principal balance, capitalization will cause more interest to accrue over time than if you had paid the interest, and it will also increase your monthly payment under most repayment plans. For example, with a $30,000 balance at 6% interest in forbearance for a year, $1,800 in interest accrues; if unpaid, it capitalizes, and under the Standard Repayment Plan this would increase your monthly payment by $20 per month and increase the total amount you pay by about $600. Note that unpaid interest is capitalized only on Direct Loans and FFEL Program loans, and is never capitalized on Federal Perkins Loans.

It only explains that a credit balance is the money left over after financial aid is applied to tuition, fees, and other school charges, and that a school may keep the credit balance to pay for future institutional charges if the student authorizes it.

When deciding whether to accept a private student loan, consider that federal student loans generally offer advantages over private loans, so you should start with federal loans first. If you must accept loans, accept the ones with the most favorable terms and conditions, which usually means the federal student loans offered to you. If you are considering a private student loan, learn about the differences between federal and other loans, and make sure you understand what you're accepting and the repayment terms. If your aid offer includes loans, compare the amount of debt you would be taking on; if you'd need to take out a larger amount in private loans at one school than another, pay special attention to the terms and conditions of the private loans so you understand your obligations. Borrow only what you need, keep track of how much you're borrowing, and think about how the loan amount will affect your future finances and how much you can afford to repay. Also consider free money first (scholarships, grants), earned money second (work-study), and borrowed money last.

Your college or career school, not the U.S. Department of Education, will distribute your federal student aid. Generally, your school will give you your grant or loan money in at least two payments called disbursements, and in most cases at least once per term (semester, trimester, or quarter). Schools that don't use traditional terms usually must give you your grant or loan money at least twice, such as at the beginning and midpoint of your academic year or program. If you're a first-year undergraduate and first-time borrower, you may have to wait 30 days after the first day of your enrollment period before your school is allowed to give you your loan money. First-time borrowers of a Direct Subsidized or Unsubsidized Loan must complete entrance counseling before the school can give the loan money, and graduate or professional students taking out a Direct PLUS Loan for the first time must complete entrance counseling before the first loan disbursement. If you have a work-study job, you'll be paid at least once a month.

A credit balance is the money left over after your financial aid is applied to your tuition, fees, and other school charges. If you have a credit balance, your school must pay that amount to you directly within 14 days, unless you authorize the school to keep the money to pay for future institutional charges.

Cost of attendance (COA) is the amount it will cost you to go to school; most two-year and four-year colleges calculate it to show your total cost for the school year (for example, fall plus spring semester), and schools with programs lasting a different period may give a COA covering that other time period. If you're attending at least half-time, your COA is the estimate of tuition and fees; the cost of room and board or living expenses for students who do not contract with the school for room and board; and the cost of books, supplies, transportation, loan fees, and miscellaneous expenses. The financial aid office determines your COA and uses it in calculating aid: it subtracts your Expected Family Contribution from your COA to determine your financial need and how much need-based aid you can get, and for non-need-based aid it subtracts any financial aid already awarded from your COA.

The FAFSA form is the key step in applying for federal grants, work-study, and loans for college. The aid application process has six steps: (1) Get prepared by gathering the documents you'll need; (2) Complete the FAFSA form, applying early to maximize your aid; (3) Review your Student Aid Report and make corrections if necessary; (4) Respond to your aid offer by accepting the aid you want; (5) Receive aid from your school; and (6) Renew your FAFSA form by reapplying each year. To fill out the form, select the Fill Out the FAFSA button on the home page and follow the directions on the screen; the forms are also available on the myStudentAid mobile app.

Besides federal student aid, financial aid can come from state, school, and private sources. You can look for scholarships by contacting the financial aid office at the school you plan to attend, checking a public library or online, asking a high school or TRIO counselor, using the U.S. Department of Labor's free scholarship search tool, contacting your state grant agency, checking your library's reference section, and reaching out to foundations, religious or community organizations, local businesses, or civic groups. Be careful to make sure scholarship information and offers are legitimate, and remember you don't have to pay to find scholarships or other financial aid.

If you can't make your monthly payment, contact your loan servicer immediately; your servicer can help you understand your options. Possible options include switching to a different repayment plan to lower your monthly payment, requesting deferment or forbearance to temporarily stop or lower payments, or loan consolidation. Deferment lets you temporarily stop making payments, though you generally won't make progress toward forgiveness or paying back the loan; income-driven repayment plans, which base payments on income and family size, may be a better alternative if your difficulty will continue for an extended period. Note that missing payments or not paying the full amount on time can make your loan delinquent and may result in late fees.

The evidence does not describe a specific application procedure for claiming education-related tax deductions or credits. It explains that the IRS provides tax benefits for education and directs readers to IRS Publication 970, Tax Benefits for Education, to see which federal income tax benefits might apply to their situation. It also notes that even if you normally wouldn't file a tax return because of your income level, you should do so to avoid missing out on tax credits. For the student loan interest deduction, student loan interest payments are reported to the IRS and to you on IRS Form 1098-E, and you should check with the IRS or a tax advisor to see if you qualify.

Qualified Tuition Programs (QTPs), also known as 529 Plans, are programs established by a state or school that let you either prepay or save up to pay education-related expenses. Once you're in college or career school and withdraw money from your account to pay education expenses, the money you withdraw will not be taxed. To find out whether the college you plan to attend participates in a QTP, ask the financial aid or admissions staff.

If you normally wouldn't file a tax return because of your income level, you should still file one. If you don't, you'll miss out on tax credits that would put money in your pocket. The IRS provides tax benefits for education that can help you get back some of the money you spend on tuition or loan interest or maximize your college savings. These include tax credits for higher education expenses—the American Opportunity Credit (up to $2,500 per student per year for the first four years of school) and the Lifetime Learning Credit (up to $2,000 per student per year for tuition, fees, and required books, supplies, and equipment)—as well as the student loan interest deduction of up to $2,500 a year.

You can also contact Nelnet, the TPD discharge servicer, by email at disabilityinformation@nelnet.net or by phone at 1-888-303-7818 (Monday–Friday 7 a.m.–2 a.m. ET, Saturday 8 a.m.–7 p.m. ET), and visit the TPD discharge website for additional ways to contact Nelnet and more information about applying for a TPD discharge.

If you received a TPD discharge based on SSA documentation or a physician's certification and your three-year postdischarge period hasn't ended, you must resume repayment on your previously discharged loans or acknowledge that you are once again responsible for meeting the terms and conditions of your TEACH Grant service obligation.

To get information about changing your federal student loan repayment plan, contact your loan servicer. You can also get information about all of the federal student loans you have received and find the loan servicer for your loans by logging in to "My Federal Student Aid." Before contacting your loan servicer, you can use the Loan Simulator to get an early look at which plans you may be eligible for and see estimates of what you would pay monthly and overall.

If your TPD discharge application is approved based on VA documentation, Nelnet will notify you that your loans and/or TEACH Grant service obligation have been discharged and will instruct your loan holders to return any loan payments received on or after the effective date of the VA's disability determination to the person who made the payments. As a veteran whose TPD discharge application is approved based on VA documentation, you are not subject to a postdischarge monitoring period. For federal tax purposes, if you're a veteran who showed total and permanent disability based on a VA disability determination, you're considered to have received the discharge on a date that differs depending on how you qualified (the evidence text is cut off on this point). Also note that a loan discharged before Jan. 1, 2018 may be considered income for federal tax purposes, while a TPD discharge received between Jan. 1, 2018 and Dec. 31, 2025 won't be considered income for federal tax purposes.

To qualify for Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF), you must: be employed by a U.S. federal, state, local, or tribal government or not-for-profit organization; work full-time for that agency or organization; have Direct Loans or consolidate other federal student loans into a Direct Loan; repay your loans under an income-driven repayment plan; and make 120 qualifying payments. The PSLF Program forgives the remaining balance on your Direct Loans after you have made 120 qualifying monthly payments under a qualifying repayment plan while working full-time for a qualifying employer. Note that FFEL Program loans and Federal Perkins Loans do not qualify for PSLF, but they may become eligible if you consolidate them into a Direct Consolidation Loan; private lender student loans do not qualify. If you consolidate, only qualifying payments made on the new Direct Consolidation Loan count toward the 120 payments, and payments made before consolidation do not count. You should submit a Public Service Loan Forgiveness Employment Certification Form annually.

A qualifying monthly payment is one made after Oct. 1, 2007, under a qualifying repayment plan, for the full amount due as shown on your bill.
